# Changelog


## [Unreleased] (alpha)
<!-- #474, #476, #748 -->

### Erasure keeps the worker's name on the records they made, and says plainly what stays (#703; D-016, D-110 to D-113, D-116; migration 272)

- **An erased worker's NAME and account number stay on the safeguarding records they made**:
  - the pastoral visits they made (D-016);
  - the DBS checks they recorded;
  - the care cases they opened (D-110);
  - the children they checked in or out (D-111).

  Before, the erasure removed the number and kept no name, so a safeguarding record lost who had acted.
  Migration 272 adds `visitedByName`, `recordedByName`, `openedByName`, `checkedInByName` and `checkedOutByName`,
  written by each record's own page when the record is made. Names are copied onto older records from the
  account they point at, never from an account already emptied. The pastoral page shows the kept name once the
  worker's account has been emptied. A worker's name is kept even on a visit to their own case (D-112).
- **What members read about erasure is now true, and says the number can be matched back (D-113).** My data,
  Request erasure, Delete my account, the privacy notice and its retention section, the admin help and
  `docs/gdpr-erasure-policy.md` were read in full and corrected. Two statements are now given everywhere:
  - the records that keep a person's name or number ON PURPOSE (expense claims, own DBS checks, tax
    declarations, giving statements, kept gifts and envelopes, an approval step given by name, and the worker
    records above);
  - the records kept for security and as a history (the activity log, the change history, which is kept for
    ever (D-116), and rate-limit records). These can mention the person.

  Neither list is claimed to be complete. No page says an erased person "cannot be traced" any more.
- **A giver is told what will really happen to each of their gifts.** My data and Request erasure now work it
  out with the erasure's own rules (`GdprEraser::givingOutlook()`), per organisation and by name:
  - gifts and envelopes that keep the name, and until when;
  - those that lose it;
  - those already past their keep-until date, which lose it as the erasure runs;
  - those under the organisation's hold, the installation's hold, or both.

  Before, every gift was counted as kept.
- Organisation names in these sentences are shown as text, never markup.
- Open: #926–#931, #933, #934, #938–#941. #940 (the activity log's "never delete" wording) follows next.

### The activity log can be kept for ever, by choice (#932, D-117, D-118, D-119)

- **"Never delete" is now a choice for the activity log** (`audit.retentionDays`, stored as 0), on Admin →
  Maintenance → Retention. Before this, a stored 0 silently fell back to a year; that was never an owner's
  decision.
- **The installation's figure caps every organisation's** (#668, D-013). An organisation may choose "never"
  only where the installation has. "Never" is not clamped to the ten-year maximum.
- **An organisation's own administrator sets its figure** (D-118); the installation's figure is a global
  administrator's.
- **Lowering the installation's figure below one an organisation has chosen is refused, naming the
  organisations** (D-119). Nothing of theirs is deleted until they lower their own.
- The page says what "never" costs: the log grows without limit, and some records describe a person (by
  account number, and sometimes by name or e-mail address) for ever, even after that person asks to be
  erased (#933).
- The general settings editor now refuses `audit.retentionDays`. The nightly clear-out deletes nothing under
  "never". The error log is unchanged: its stored 0 still means a year.
- A post to the page carrying an action it does not recognise now runs nothing; before, any post ran the clear-out.
- Open: #940 (the wording on the privacy and help pages, after #703), #933.

### No time zone is built in any more (#782, migration 273)

- **The livestream schedule, venues, the venue availability check and the Sabbath quiet window now use
  the organisation's own time zone** (Admin → Organisations). Each used to answer "Europe/London"
  whenever nobody had chosen a zone, so an organisation anywhere else had its livestream countdown,
  its hall bookings and its quiet hours worked out on London's clock.
- The livestream and venue forms start on the organisation's zone. They now **refuse** a zone the
  portal does not know, where they used to store it or quietly replace it with London. That includes
  names PHP accepts and that were stored before: the `Etc/*` names, legacy aliases such as `GB` and
  `US/Eastern`, and other capitalisation (`europe/london`), the same rule the event and organisation
  forms already use. A venue already holding such a name still saves when its zone is left unchanged.
- The Sabbath page has a new first choice, **"Each organisation's own time zone"**, which new
  installations start on. An upgraded installation keeps the zone it already holds. With that choice,
  each held text is judged on the quiet hours of the organisation it belongs to.
- `/api/venues/check` without `tz` now reads times on the organisation's clock. It used to read them
  as London's, and the API description said so.
- `tblLivestreamSchedule.timezone` and `tblVenues.timezone` no longer default to London. No stored
  value is changed: both columns were always written by their own pages, so a stored London may be a
  choice.
- A new hard gate, `check_no_built_in_time_zone.py`, fails when a zone name is written into the code.
- Open: #935, #936, #937.

### Attendance: who sees the totals, who sees a session's figures, and who may delete a session (#529, #917, #921, D-106, D-109, D-114, D-115, migration 271)

- **The attendance totals are seen by administrators and by a role the organisation chooses (D-106).**
  The reports page, the attendance spreadsheet (`/attendance/export`) and the "Total Headcount This Month"
  card on `/attendance` now need the new permission **"See the attendance totals"**
  (`attendance.reports`), which an organisation points at a role on Admin, Roles. It ships pointing at a
  new standard role, **Attendance Coordinator**, held by nobody, so out of the box only administrators see
  the totals. A member, or an account from another organisation, gets the same "page not found" as an
  address that does not exist (a refused member used to get 403).
- **The three-way setting `attend.reports.visibleTo` is deleted** (migration 271) and gone from
  `/admin/settings/attendance`. An organisation that had chosen something wider, such as "any member",
  loses that choice (D-106 rules out "any member"). No customer installation exists yet.
- **The attendance spreadsheet follows the same rule.** It used to be for administrators only. Its
  `notes` column is free text, and the Roles page now says so. The ANONYMOUS check-in spreadsheet is
  unchanged: administrators only.
- **Members no longer see any session's headcount (D-109, #917).** On `/attendance` the Headcount column
  and each row's Edit button are drawn only for administrators and permission holders. The form for an
  existing session (`/attendance/record?edit=N`) answers "page not found" to anybody else, and its update
  is answered exactly as for a session that does not exist, writing nothing. Any member still records a
  NEW session and sees the counts they type.
- **Who may delete a session (D-114, D-115).** Administrators, permission holders, and the member who
  recorded that session, on the list (the control is drawn only for them), in the delete handler and in
  `api/attendance/delete`. An API key with `attendance:write` may still delete any session; one without
  it cannot. Anybody else, and a session already deleted, gets "Attendance session not found." and
  nothing is written. (A session that did not exist used to be answered "Attendance record deleted.")
- **`api/attendance/list`** no longer gives a signed-in caller who is not an administrator or permission
  holder deleted sessions, session notes or `updatedByID`.
- **#921 fixed:** `/attendance` prints the message the attendance handlers leave, so "Attendance recorded
  successfully" and "deleted" appear where the person lands.
- The download refuses a non-string form token cleanly instead of answering 500.
- Open: #925, #930.

### Sign-in and password reset: ten fixes (#598, D-104, D-105, D-108, migration 270)

- **A password reset, a password change while signed in, and an administrator setting the password now sign
  the person out of every other browser** (D-104, D-108). The browser making the change stays signed in; an
  administrator's own session is untouched. The account holds a sign-in version (`tblUsers.signInVersion`,
  migration 270) that each of those raises by a random amount; every session carries the number it signed in
  under, read in the SAME statement as the password, and a session whose number differs from the account's —
  after a password change, or after a whole-database restore — is ended on its next request, recorded as
  `SessionEndedSignInNotCurrent`. No extra query per request. Remembered devices are still revoked by the reset
  and change pages, and a sign-in waiting for its two-factor code when a reset happens is no longer given a
  "trust this device" cookie.
- **The health page's mail line counts only the viewer's own organisation** for an
  organisation's administrator; a global administrator, and the monitor's address, see the
  installation's count (D-105).
- **One person gets at most three password-reset e-mails an hour**, whoever asks; the visitor's
  answer is unchanged.
- **Requests for one person at the same moment leave exactly one working reset link**: the
  per-person count, cancelling the old links and storing the new one are one transaction after
  locking the person's account row.
- **The anonymous prayer form and public forms no longer throw a submission away** because
  somebody at the same address mistyped a password. The prayer form has its own limit (five in
  15 minutes per address), says plainly that a refused request was NOT sent, and keeps the typing.
- **Changing your password and switching two-factor sign-in off share a limit of five wrong
  current passwords in 15 minutes** for the account; before, there was no limit.
- **The general rate limiter counts in UTC.** The sign-in counts still use the database
  server's clock: #920.
- **"Can the portal send mail?" no longer says yes** for a Google key file name with a folder in
  it, a key file that is not a key, or a Microsoft "from" address that is not an e-mail address;
  the Google sender and the Integrations page ask the same one judge.
- **The asset kiosk refuses a PIN try whenever a limit is reached**, including the last second.
- **The failed sign-in counts got their indexes** (50,000 rows: full scan → range of 2).
- **Tests:** `tools/sign-in-limits-selftest.php`, `tools/two-step-selftest.php` and `tools/admin-password-selftest.php` over real HTTP (each total pinned in its file), including a deterministic race between a sign-in and a password change, a database restore, and forced failures at each page's commit. Four check rounds by fresh Claude agents (protected arm: sign-in, stored data); round 1 measured a sign-in with the OLD password surviving a change (closed by reading the version with the password), round 2 a higher number surviving a restore (closed by ending any difference and a random step), round 4 was clean. The migration harness passed on MySQL 8.4.11 and MariaDB 11.4.13. Raised from it: #920, #922, #924. Codex has not reviewed it.

### Expense claims: the Approver role sees only its own departments, and no claim number can be confirmed by guessing (#648, #915, D-103, D-040, migration 269)

- **Expenses: nobody can find out which claim numbers are real (#648 round 1, #915, #541 item 5).**
  Every expense address now answers somebody else's claim that a person may not touch exactly as
  a claim that does not exist: the edit form (was 403, now 404), the edit form's save (was "You can
  only change your own expense claim", now "That claim could not be found."), the delete API (was
  403 "Access denied", now 404 "Expense claim not found"), and the decision handler (was a bare
  "Forbidden" for another department's pending claim, now the "Claim not found or not in Pending
  status." a made-up number gets). The Expense Approver role is no longer a way past the decision
  handler's first check, so a role-holder with no department is refused before any claim is looked
  up; that refusal now reads "Access denied — only an administrator, or a lead or approver of a
  department, can decide expense claims." (it used to say "Approver or Admin role required", which a
  role-holder would have been told while holding the role).
- **Roles:** the Expense Approver role's description now says what it gives (migration 269 rewrites
  it only where it is still the old sentence "Approves or rejects expense claims").
- **Expenses: the organisation-wide Approver role no longer sees every claim (#648, D-103).**
  The claim page opened ANY claim of the organisation to a holder of the role (line items,
  suppliers, receipts), and the Export spreadsheet gave them every claim, while the approvals
  list and the decision page kept them to the departments they approve for. Now a role holder
  opens and downloads only the claims of departments they are a lead, approver or required
  approver of. Administrators and treasurers still see every claim; a claimant always sees
  their own. A claim somebody may not open is now answered exactly as a claim that does not
  exist (404, the same page) — it used to be a 403, which told any signed-in member that the
  number was a real claim.
- **A treasurer may download the claims spreadsheet (D-040, #541 item 2).** The Export button on
  `/expenses/approve` is now offered to treasurers, and their file holds every claim.

- The approvals list (`/expenses/approve`) is one query whose department condition comes from
  `ExpenseRules::reachToDecide()`; who is listed what is unchanged.
- "Go to Approvals" on a claim page, and the claimant's "you cannot decide your own claim"
  note, are now shown only to somebody who may actually decide the claim (an administrator, or
  a lead / approver / required approver of its department) — no longer to a holder of the
  Approver role for a department they cannot decide.
- Roles page: the `expenses.approve` capability is now labelled "Expense approver: download the
  claims spreadsheet", and its description says what it really opens. Its old description
  ("approving or rejecting claims across the whole organisation, opening any claim") was never
  true of deciding and stopped being true of reading.
- **Tests:** section L3 of `tools/access-pages-selftest.php` over real HTTP (headers and the server's query log compared, not only bodies) and section 5 of `tools/expense-rules-selftest.php` (the SQL form run against real rows and matched with the PHP form); each total pinned in its file. Two check rounds by fresh Claude agents (protected arm: money, personal details); round 2's only finding was an untrue comment, corrected. The migration harness passed on MySQL 8.4.11 and MariaDB 11.4.13. Raised from it: #916. Codex has not reviewed it.

### The public door, part four: test copies, and a set-up check that the public address reaches the door (#493 P4d)

- **Added: who a test copy's public door answers is a tiered setting** (D-087). On a test copy only (alpha, beta
  or dev), Admin → Public website shows a card: the installation's global administrator chooses whether
  organisations may open their door there to anybody, and an organisation's global administrator chooses within
  that. "Signed-in testers only" is the default and the stricter answer; "open to anybody" posted while the
  installation forbids it is refused with the reason; every save and every refusal is recorded; both settings are
  refused on the live portal and by the general settings editor. Every answer from a test copy's door tells search
  engines not to list it, whichever is chosen. `PublicWebsiteSetup::testCopyDoorRule()` is the one answer.
- **Added: "Check my set-up" confirms an approved public address really reaches your door.** It fetches a one-off
  proof from the address (through the safe fetcher; https only; no redirects followed) and says whether it came
  back from a door holding your door's current name, from a door that is not yours, or not at all (with the last
  status), or why it was not checked. It names no cause it cannot know.
- **Changed: every sentence about who the door answers comes from one place** (`doorReachWords()`), spelled out
  whole for each state — the door on, off, spoiled or unreadable; a public address in effect or not; a `/w/`
  address or not; Calendar and the Noticeboard on or off; live, gate off, testers only, or open to anybody. On a
  testers-only copy it says the public sees nothing, a tester opens the door directly at its `/w/` addresses, a
  pasted script and a website's own server get nothing, and a public address answers nobody; whether a FRAME shows
  anything is left to the framing card.
- **Tests:** section U of `tools/public-door-selftest.php` — a truth table over every combination of the facts,
  every page state over real HTTP, every change of choice posted and its message and colour compared (its total
  pinned in the file). Five check rounds by fresh Claude agents (protected arm): the code and the tiered rule were
  sound from round 1; the sentences were simplified into one place after failing two rounds running; round 5's
  findings were all in test labels and comments, fixed, and review closed there (D-064). Codex has not reviewed it.

### The backup self-test no longer fails on a slow run (#912)

- **Backup self-test, proof 27, no longer fails on the timing of the run (#912).** Its
  final "every value of every table is exactly as it was" comparison failed in three
  consecutive whole-suite runs and passed when run alone. The cause was the TEST, not
  the restore: section C deletes made-up account 970941 and later put it back by id and
  e-mail address only, so `tblUsers.createdAt` (`DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`) took a new
  value whenever the run crossed a second between the first insert and the re-insert —
  which a slow, loaded run always does. The account is now kept whole and put back
  column by column. The restore and the put-back were exact throughout. The proof now also waits for the database's clock to move on a second after its "before" picture, so a
  restore that lets a self-stamped column be stamped again fails every run, and a failure names the column and the
  row (by key, never a value). Two check rounds (protected arm: backups), round 2 clean. Raised from it: #914.
  Codex has not reviewed it.

### A "come back to" address is always judged, and the newsletter click counter is no longer an open redirect (#620, migration 268)

- **Three older pages no longer send people to addresses they were handed
  (#620).** The payments checkout and the asset assignment page each had a
  "come back to" judge of their own, and both let something through: the
  checkout accepted "/<tab>/outside.example", which a browser reads as another
  site, and any other organisation's address; the asset page accepted a ".."
  part that left the organisation. Both now ask `Auth::safeRedirectUrl()`, the
  judge every sign-in page uses, which now also refuses a "." or ".." part in
  every set-up (it used to only where organisations are told apart by the
  first part of the address). A refused address on the asset page returns to
  that asset's page, where the result message is shown. The newsletter's click
  counter forwarded to ANY web address in its link — an open redirect wearing
  the portal's address. Its links now carry a random token for an address
  recorded with that newsletter when it is sent (migration 268,
  `tblNewsletterLink`), and anything else gets "this link cannot be used / is
  no longer valid" (404). **Links in newsletters sent before this change stop
  working** — chosen knowingly; no installation exists yet and click counting
  ships switched off. A counted link whose address had two query parts used to
  reach the wrong page (it carried `&amp;`); fixed. A new hard gate,
  `check_redirect_targets_judged.py`, reports a request value written
  straight into a `Location` header outside the one judge;
  it does not follow values (see DEV_NOTES).
- **Tests:** new `tools/come-back-addresses-selftest.php` over real HTTP (its total pinned in the file), and the
  check's own self-test; both wired into the workflows. Three check rounds by fresh Claude agents (protected arm:
  security); every finding after round 1 was in the static check, so review closed at the three-round cap (D-064),
  with what round 3 found on #913. The migration harness passed on MySQL 8.4.11 and MariaDB 11.4.13. Raised from
  it: #909, #910, #911, #913. Codex has not reviewed it.

### Outbound webhooks can no longer be pointed inside the host's network (#615, D-102)

- **Fixed (security):** saving a webhook now refuses an address on this machine, on a private or internal
  network, at the cloud metadata address, a name that resolves to any of those, or an unusual spelling of a
  number, with one plain message. Every delivery goes through the new `SafeFetch::post()`, which checks the
  address again at the moment of sending, pins the connection to the checked address (so a re-pointed name is
  refused), ignores proxies, follows no redirect and caps the time and the reply. The target address is never
  written to a log.
- **Changed: the receiver's reply is no longer stored.** A failed delivery records one word saying why, and the
  deliveries list shows it in plain words ("refused" for where an address leads, "not-allowed" for how it is
  written). Older rows keep their reply until the nightly payload clear-out (#713) empties it.
- **Changed, and existing webhooks may stop:** only ports 443 and 80 are allowed unless the installation's global
  administrator allows other ports on public addresses, on the Webhooks page (D-102; the general settings editor
  refuses that setting). A webhook already saved on another port is refused at every delivery until then, and
  dead-letters. A user name and password inside the address, formerly sent as a basic sign-in, are refused. The
  request timeout is now kept between 1 and 30 seconds. Pausing a webhook is never refused.
- **Tests:** new `tools/webhook-delivery-selftest.php` (its total pinned in the file), real MySQL, a local
  receiver and the Webhooks page over real HTTP; parts A and B went red on the code before the fix. Wired into
  `portal-selftests.yml`. Two check rounds by fresh Claude agents (protected arm: security, stored data); round 2
  was clean. Raised from it: #908. Codex has not reviewed it.

### Passkeys work on a fresh installation (#903)
- The name a passkey is tied to (WebAuthn's "relying party ID") was read with
  `??` from a setting the install script seeds as an EMPTY string, so every
  installation where nobody had typed a value sent `rpId: ""`. Measured in a
  real browser (Edge 157 with a virtual authenticator): an empty rpId is
  refused for adding a passkey and for signing in with one. So passkeys could
  not work at all until an administrator set the value by hand.
- `Portal\Core\PasskeyAddress` is now the ONE place that decides the rpId and
  the origin a browser must report. The rpId is the installation-wide
  `auth.webauthn.rpID` setting when it holds a usable name, else the host name
  of the portal's own address (`PortalAddress::base()`, with no port); the
  origin is `PortalAddress::base()`. With no address at all, both passkey pages
  refuse with a sentence saying why, rather than send an empty rpId.
- The general Settings page refuses an unusable passkey address (a scheme, a
  port, a path, a user name, an IP address) with the reason, tidies capitals
  and a closing dot, and refuses adding it as one organisation's own row.
- The "Address of this portal" card says that passkeys are tied to that name.
- Behind a proxy with the portal's address set, the passkey origin is now the
  address the visitor's browser shows, not the inside name and http.
- **Tests:** `tools/two-step-selftest.php` (passkey sign-in on the stock state, the name chosen in every case,
  the Settings page's refusals and the card's sentence in all its states) and the new
  `tools/passkey-address-browser-selftest.mjs` (a real headless browser with a virtual authenticator, measuring
  what browsers accept as a passkey name); each total is pinned in its file. The browser test runs in its own
  job in `pr-security.yml`. The builder ran seven check rounds of its own; a separately briefed independent
  check (protected arm: sign-in) was clean. Raised from it: #905, #906, #907. Codex has not reviewed it.


### The public door, part three: a page an organisation's website can frame (#493 P4c)

- **Added: a page for a frame** (D-056, D-082, D-094), for a website that cannot take a script. It is
  `/w/{name}/page.html` on the portal's own address, or `/page.html` on the organisation's approved public
  address, and takes `?show=events` (the default), `posters` or `both`, and `limit` (1 to 50, default 10 of
  each). It is drawn on the server with no JavaScript, every value escaped, pictures and links only to `https:`
  addresses, and each event's time on its own clock as stored. Only the websites the organisation lists may
  frame it, and none while the installation forbids framing: its framing rule comes from
  `PublicWebsiteSetup::frameAncestorsFor()` alone. It answers through the door's one gate, so every refusal is
  the door's identical "not found". Admin → Public website prints the frame to paste and says where it will and
  will not work — only on the listed websites, in every current browser; a very old browser such as Internet
  Explorer 11 does not understand that rule and would let any website frame it; and nothing while its app is
  switched off. The in-app help says the same.
- **Tests:** sections V and T of `tools/public-door-selftest.php` over real HTTP on BOTH forms of address, and
  section F of `tools/public-door-script-selftest.mjs`, where a real browser frames the page from a listed and
  an unlisted website (each total pinned in its file). The browser test now runs in its own job in
  `pr-security.yml`, because it needs PHP. Three check rounds by fresh Claude agents (protected arm: outside
  websites); every finding was a test that asked on only one form of address, and round 3's was confirmed
  fixed by planting the same fault. Codex has not reviewed it.

### No new way of signing in can skip what #900 fixed; the passkey sign-in tested for real (#902)

- **A new hard gate, `tools/audit-checks/check_sign_in_begins_session.py`,** reads every PHP file under `web/`
  with PHP's own tokeniser and fails when a write of `$_SESSION['user_id']` or `$_SESSION['2fa_user_id']` has
  no call to `Auth::beginSessionFor()` before it in the same function, and fails both ways on the list of ten
  grants and six call sites. It checks that the call is there and comes first, not that it runs; the HTTP
  tests drive that. It runs in `pr-security.yml` with its own self-test.
- **The passkey sign-in is now tested for real.** `tools/two-step-selftest.php` makes a real P-256 key,
  registers it as the portal stores a passkey and signs the portal's own challenge; a tampered signature is
  refused. Before, putting the passkey path back to a bare `session_regenerate_id()` left the test green.
  **A kiosk browser** is tested too: a real sign-in on a browser holding the asset kiosk's hand-over starts
  clean.
- **Fixed: the invitation page's message after a failed sign-in.** When signing the new person in failed
  after their account had been made — reachable on a database failure, because outside multi-site session
  mode `Auth::initSessionSite()` runs queries that throw under the portal's strict database reporting — the
  page said "That username or email is already in use." for an invitation that was now spent, with the person
  half signed in. It now takes the half-made sign-in back, records `INVITE_SIGNIN_FAIL`, and says the account
  was created and to sign in.
- **Tests:** part K of `tools/two-step-selftest.php` and the check's own self-test (both totals pinned in
  their files). Three check rounds by fresh Claude agents (protected arm: sign-in); every finding in rounds 2
  and 3 was in the static check, so review closed at the three-round cap (D-064), with the four small holes
  round 3 found recorded on #904. Raised from it: #903, #904. Codex has not reviewed it.

### The public door, part two: the script a website pastes in, and the old countdown widget removed (#493 P4b, migration 264)

- **Added: a one-line script an organisation pastes into its own website** (D-056). Once its door is on,
  Admin → Public website shows three: its events, its noticeboard posters, or a countdown to its next event
  (the countdown is the script's "next" mode, D-084). The script is served only through the door's one gate,
  at `/w/{name}/door.js` or `/door.js` on an approved public address, from a file kept outside the web root,
  and needs Calendar or the Noticeboard switched on; every refusal is the door's identical "not found". It
  reads the feed beside it without cookies and with no referrer, and draws only plain text (and `https:`
  pictures and links) inside a shadow root of its own: nothing it is given is ever turned into page markup,
  its styles and the website's cannot reach each other, it adds no global variable, and it works under a
  strict content security policy. Each event's time is shown on that event's own clock — including on the
  morning the clocks go forward, when the feed now also carries each time exactly as stored
  (`startsOnClock`, `endsOnClock`) beside its true moment. When the door is off it draws nothing.
- **Removed: the old countdown widget.** `web/public_html/widget/` (`countdown.js`), its two public addresses
  `widget/countdown.json` and `widget/countdown` (migration 264 and the install script), their handlers, and
  the old embeddable `/widget` page with its loader. That page had no sign-in check of its own and was
  unreachable only because its route had been removed (migration 189); deleting the folder alone would have
  left the missing route as its only guard, so the page went in the same change. `/widget` and every old
  widget address now answer the portal's own "not found". robots.txt now asks crawlers to keep off `/w/`.
- **Changed:** every sentence saying what "Show on the public website" governs now names the public door in
  place of the countdown widget — the event form, the calendar and imports help, the outside-calendar pages
  and `api-spec.json`. The card's advice about a website's content policy now says pictures come from the
  portal and from any outside picture a poster uses.
- **Tests:** `tools/public-door-selftest.php`, `tools/public-door-script-selftest.mjs` (a real headless
  browser against a strict policy, with hostile text in every field it draws) and
  `tools/htaccess-apache-selftest.php` (each total pinned in its file), with planted faults for every gate,
  every drawn field and every countdown box. Two check rounds by fresh Claude agents (protected arm: outside
  websites, stored data); round 2 was clean. Raised from it: #898, #899. Codex has not reviewed it.

### A sign-in keeps nothing of the previous person's session (#900)

- **Fixed (security): signing in on a shared browser no longer hands the previous person's waiting session
  data to the next person.** Every sign-in replaced the session's identifier but kept everything in it, and
  the Microsoft and Google sign-in addresses, the passkey sign-in and an invitation link do not refuse a
  browser somebody is already signed in on. So a waiting message, kept form typing or a come-back address
  passed to whoever signed in next. Measured on the code before the fix: after a Microsoft or Google
  sign-in, the second person was shown the first person's waiting message AND was sent to the page the first
  person had been waiting to come back to. `Auth::beginSessionFor()` is now the one place each of the six
  ways of signing in decides what survives: a DIFFERENT person (including the first sign-in on a browser)
  starts with only the browser's chosen language; the SAME person signing in again (finishing a two-step
  code, or proving themselves again to add a password, #731) keeps everything. The session identifier is
  replaced either way, now including at the two-step code step.
- **Tests:** part K of `tools/two-step-selftest.php` (its total pinned in the file), driving the password,
  Microsoft, Google, invitation and two-step paths over HTTP — Microsoft and Google with the provider stubbed
  in the test's own copy; ten of its behaviour checks went red on the old code. The passkey path calls the same
  method and is not driven by any test (#902). Independent check (protected arm: sign-in) clean at round 1.
  Codex has not reviewed it.

### Expense claims: a refused claim comes back filled in, and a failed save leaves no PDF behind (#869, #870, #871)

- **A claim that is not saved no longer leaves its PDF behind (#869).** The claim's PDF holds the claimant's
  name, department and every figure, and is written while the claim is still being saved. When the save then
  failed and was undone, #649 removed the receipts but left the PDF, with nothing in the database pointing at
  it, so no erasure could ever find it. It now follows the receipts' rule exactly: before the save is
  committed it is removed (and if it cannot be, its path is recorded as `CLAIM_PDF_LEFT_BEHIND`); once the
  commit has been sent it is never deleted, and its path is recorded as `CLAIM_PDF_KEPT_AFTER_FAILED_COMMIT`.
  `ExpensePdf::pathFor()` is now the one place a claim's PDF path is built.
- **A refused claim comes back filled in (#870).** Every refusal after the form's security token has been
  accepted — a missing title, a total of zero, a department that is not one, the receipts folder failing, a
  save that failed and was undone, a failed captcha — keeps the title, department and item lines, and the
  form fills itself in from them once. Receipts are never kept (a page cannot choose files for somebody), and
  the form says so. What was typed is given back only to the same person in the same organisation. Nothing is
  kept after a refused token (the post may have come from another website), after a submission too large for
  the server (nothing arrived), or after a save that could not be confirmed (it may be saved, and refilling
  would invite a second claim for the same money).
- **A submission larger than the server accepts is told so (#870).** PHP empties the whole post, token
  included, when it is over the server's `post_max_size`, so the claimant used to be told "Invalid CSRF
  token." It now says the claim was not saved because everything sent came to more than the server accepts,
  with both sizes. The server's limit is always rounded DOWN, so the advice never names a size the server
  would refuse; the size sent always reads larger than the limit.
- **The file chooser offers every kind of receipt the portal accepts (#871).** Its list was a hand-written
  `image/*,application/pdf`, which hid the Word, Excel and CSV files the rule and the help page accept. It is
  now built from `ExpenseRules::RECEIPT_TYPES`, so the two cannot disagree, and it no longer offers picture
  kinds the rule refuses. Not tested on a real phone: whether a phone still offers its camera with the new
  list is not established.
- **Tests:** `tools/expense-receipts-selftest.php`, 201 checks over real HTTP (its total pinned in the
  file), with 18 planted faults each caught, including a stand-in for the PDF library so the real
  `ExpensePdf::generate()` runs on a test machine. Three check rounds by fresh Claude agents (protected arm:
  money and personal details); round 3 was clean after sweeping about a million size pairs through the real
  message. Raised from it: #900 (a Microsoft or Google sign-in keeps the previous person's session data).
  Codex has not reviewed it.

### On MySQL 9.7 a password sign-in works again, and a sign-in the database cannot serve says so (#887)

- **Fixed: on MySQL 9.7 nobody could sign in with a password.** MySQL 9.7 has no `SHA1()`, `SHA()` or
  `MD5()` functions (measured on 9.7.4: ERROR 1305, "function does not exist"). The lock that makes sign-in
  tries from one address take turns was named with `SHA1()`, so the lock request failed, and the portal
  treated that as "another try is still being checked": every password sign-in was refused with "Too many
  failed attempts. Please try again in 1 minute(s)." and no password was checked. Single sign-on was not
  affected. The same function named four more locks, so on MySQL 9.7 the scheduled mail-queue job (and
  erasing an address from the queue), the held-texts job, the activity-log clean-up and an event's "send to
  everyone" press failed too. All five now use `LEFT(SHA2(…, 256), 40)`, the same length as before, measured
  working on MySQL 8.0.36, 8.4.11 and 9.7.4 and MariaDB 11.4.13 and 12.3.3. Nothing else in the portal calls
  those functions.
- **Fixed: a sign-in lock the database will not answer is now said truthfully.** Any failure to take the
  sign-in lock — a missing function, a refused statement, the lock request answering "no answer" — was
  reported as "another try is still being checked": the member read "Too many failed attempts", the
  activity log said the same untrue thing, and nothing reached the error log. The try is still refused
  (tries from one address must keep taking turns), but the member now reads "Signing in with a password is
  temporarily unavailable…", the activity log records `LoginUnavailable`, and a Critical error record is
  written (`Auth` / `SIGN_IN_LOCK`, naming the fault's kind and code), which the default alert settings
  e-mail. The record's title and detail, the alert e-mail and the outside error monitor never carry the
  visitor's address; the record's own `visitorIP` column holds it, as every error record's does. A lock
  genuinely held by another try still says "Too many failed attempts", as before. The new message is in
  English only for now; Welsh falls back to it.
- **Upgrade note:** during the deploy, old and new lock names do not exclude each other, once. A request
  still running the old code and one running the new code take DIFFERENT locks, so for the few seconds both
  are running one mail-queue run could overlap another, the held-texts job's hourly and daily limits could be
  overshot once, an activity-log clean-up could run twice, an event broadcast pressed twice at that moment
  could both get in, and two sign-in tries from one address could be checked side by side. Each settles at
  the next run. On MySQL 9.7 the old code could take none of these locks, so there it is purely an
  improvement.
- **Still open on MySQL 9.7 (#892):** a held text message whose use-by date does not exist (such as 31
  February) can be kept for up to 48 hours instead of refused, because 9.7 reads a bound impossible date as a
  real one. Not fixed here.
- **Tests:** sections 0 and 0b of `tools/sign-in-limits-selftest.php` (its total pinned in the file) take the
  real lock on the server in front of them, and drive a planted database fault and a genuinely held lock;
  `calendar-selftests.yml` now runs that test on all five of its engines, MySQL 9.7 included (not a live gate
  until GitHub has registered the workflow, #754). New hard gate `check_no_removed_sql_functions.py`. Two
  check rounds by fresh Claude agents (protected arm: sign-in); round 2's only finding, a comment and a check
  label saying the error record "never" holds the visitor's address, was corrected without a behaviour change.
  Codex has not reviewed it.

### The public door, part one: an organisation's own website can read its public events and posters (#493, package P4a, migration 263)

- **Added: the public door (D-056, D-097).** An organisation's own website can now read, as data (JSON, a
  plain text format programs read), the events and noticeboard posters somebody has put on the public
  website: `events.json` and `posters.json`, each described by a schema file
  (`web/_core/data/public-door-events.schema.json` and `…-posters.schema.json`). A poster's uploaded
  picture or video is given at the door's own media address, which answers only while a poster on the
  public website uses it. Nothing else goes through the door: only items somebody ticked, only while their
  dates allow, never anything members-only, deleted or a draft, and never an event that has finished on
  its own clock. An all-day event stays on the feed for the whole of its last day; any other event with no
  end time leaves it the moment it starts.
- **Where it answers.** At `/w/{name}/…` on the portal's own address, where the name is 24 random
  characters the portal makes for each organisation; or at `/…` on the organisation's own public address
  (D-095), once the installation has approved that address (below). A public address answers door requests
  only (D-098): the portal's sign-in, pages, error page and API description are not reachable there (files
  the web server sends straight from disk, such as stylesheets and the service worker, still are).
- **Every organisation's door starts switched off (D-097).** A new card at the top of Admin → Public website
  turns it on, replaces its name and switches it off; each is recorded, and replacing or switching off asks
  for an "I understand" tick. Replacing the name stops every copy that uses the portal's own address with the
  old name. **It does not stop copies that use the organisation's public address**, which carries no name,
  and switching the door off and on again does not either: the public address answers again the moment the
  door is back on. To stop a public address that has gone somewhere it should not, change or remove it. The
  card and the help page say so.
- **A public address takes effect only once the installation approves it (D-101).** An organisation's public
  address does nothing until the installation's global administrator approves it on Admin → Public website,
  which lists every organisation's address with **Approve** and **Withdraw approval**. Withdrawing takes effect
  on the next request; saving or changing an address asks again; and no address can be saved or approved while
  the portal's own address is not set. Before this, an organisation's administrator could save an address
  members really sign in at that the portal had no record of (an alias, a `www.` form), and every page there,
  sign-in included, became the door's "not found". The organisation's card says **Waiting**, **Approved**,
  **Approved, not in use** (members sign in at it, so the door does not answer there) or **Approved, not
  checked**.
- **What a visitor's browser and an outside website see.** Every refusal — an unknown name, a door switched
  off, a switched-off organisation, a page asked for on a public address — is one identical "not found"
  answer, so nothing can be learnt by comparing them. No cookie is ever set and no session made. While the
  portal is closed for an upgrade the door answers "closed for maintenance"; if the portal cannot read its
  list of public addresses, every way in answers a plain "Please try again" naming nobody. Data answers can
  be read by any website's script and can never be shown in a frame.
- **On a test copy** (the alpha, beta or dev channel) the door answers signed-in testers only in this
  version (D-087). The general settings editor now refuses both of D-087's settings; the card that changes
  them is package P4d.
- **Fixed: `.htaccess` refused a PHP file run directly only when the address ENDED in `.php`.** On Apache
  2.4, `/robots.php/x` ran `robots.php` with "/x" as extra path information, and with PHP's error display on
  printed a fatal error naming the server's file path. It now refuses `.php` and the other endings a host may
  run as PHP (`.php5` and the like, `.phtml`, `.phar`), followed by `/` or the end, in any capitals; only the
  three entry points are allowed, exactly.
- Migration 263 adds `tblPublicDoorNames`, the installation-wide setting `public.door.testCopies.permitted`
  (seeded `testers`), and `tblPublicHosts.approvedAtUtc` and `.approvedByID`. Every existing public address
  starts not approved. Not in this package: the script an organisation pastes into its website (P4b, which
  also removes the countdown widget), the frameable page (P4c), and D-087's card (P4d).
- **Tests:** new `tools/public-door-selftest.php` (170 checks over real HTTP, the count pinned in the file),
  which also runs every PHP file in the web root directly, as a server ignoring `.htaccess` would; and new
  `tools/htaccess-apache-selftest.php` (53 checks, pinned), which serves the real `.htaccess` from a real
  Apache in Docker and refuses to run without Docker. New hard gates: `check_public_door_schema.py`,
  `check_public_door_reads.py`, `check_webroot_door_handoff.py` and `check_htaccess_php_denied.py`. Nine
  check rounds by fresh Claude agents (protected arm, D-051); round 6 reopened the package with D-101. Round 9
  found the portal correct and its two findings in a test (D18 passed with the waiting row planted as "set and
  ready") and an untrue `.htaccess` comment; both were fixed, the test fix was confirmed by planting the same
  fault, and review closed there under D-064. Raised from it: #894, #895, #896, #897. Codex has not
  reviewed it.

### An event's web address is made in one place (#883)

- **The events API no longer answers 500 for a name already used.** `POST /api/events/create`
  (and `/api/v1/events`) made an event's web address from its name alone, and the database allows
  one address per organisation — a deleted event's included — so the second event of any name was
  refused as a bare HTTP 500 with nothing created. Measured against the code before this change:
  the second, third and fourth creates of one name answered 500. The address is now the name and
  the start date (`sunday-service-2026-06-07`), with `-2`, `-3` … when that is taken, asked of the
  database at the moment of saving. If another writer takes the address between the question and
  the save three times running, the API answers **409** (new, documented) and creates nothing.
- **The Manage Events form** asks the same helper. Its second event of a name on one day is now
  `-2` (it was `-1`), its uniqueness loop is bounded, and an address taken between asking and saving
  is asked again instead of showing an error page (measured before: 500, nothing saved).
- **The dates of a repeating event made by the form** each get their own date in their address
  (`…-2031-08-10`), asked of the database — except the FIRST date when the form moves it onto
  the pattern (a Tuesday typed, Thursdays ticked): its address keeps the TYPED date, because the
  address is made when the event is first saved and the move comes after. An address is a label,
  never a date to parse; api-spec.json says so, and names the `imp-` + 16 hex characters shape
  of events copied in from outside calendars. Before, every date was the FIRST date's address plus
  `-2`, `-3` … and was never asked of the database, so a held address made that date fail to save
  silently (measured: a three-date series saved two and said "1 more date(s) were added").
- **The series pattern page** asks the same helper. A date it adds is now `name-date` rather than
  the template's whole address plus the new date (`…-2031-10-05-2031-10-19`), and an address taken
  in between is asked again instead of rolling the whole change back.
- **The public suggestion form** used four random characters (never asked of the database, about a
  7% chance of a clash among 100 suggestions of one name — worked out, not measured); it now gets
  `name-date` and `-2` like the rest.
- No installation exists yet, so no link anybody has kept changes. Existing rows keep their
  addresses; only new events get the new shape.
- **Tests:** new `tools/event-address-selftest.php`, 32 checks on MySQL 8.0.36, MariaDB 11.4.13 and 12.3.3, with three real two-writer races; red 17 of 23 on the old code. One check round by a fresh Claude agent; its only finding was an untrue sentence in the API description, corrected. Raised: #885, #887, #888.

### A calendar file with the same event on several dates imports every row; a row already in the calendar is skipped (#877, D-100)

- **A calendar file holding the same event on several dates now imports every
  row (#877).** An imported event's web address was made from its name alone,
  and the database allows one address per organisation, so a file of weekly
  services imported only the first and listed the rest as refused (before #790
  it stopped with an error page). The address is now the name plus the date, as
  the Manage Events form makes it, with `-2`, `-3` … where two events share a
  name and a day or a deleted event still holds the address. An address taken
  by another writer between the import asking and saving is asked for again, up
  to three times.
- **A row already in the calendar is left out unless the manager ticks to
  import it (D-100).** The name-only address had, by accident, refused a second
  import of the same file; #877 removed that, so a re-upload would have doubled
  every event. Now a row with the same name (letter for letter) and the same
  start as an event already in the organisation's calendar is marked in the
  preview, left out on Confirm, and listed as "Already in the calendar"; one
  tick, "Import these anyway", imports such rows too. Asked again at Confirm.
  The activity record counts these rows on their own.
- A row the file itself repeats (same name, capitals included, same start) is marked in the preview and left out in the same way, with one wording that points at the row it repeats.
- **Tests:** `tools/calendar-import-selftest.php`, 132 checks on MySQL 8.0.36 and MariaDB 11.4, including a real two-writer race against the page. Six check rounds by fresh Claude agents (protected arm); the repeat message was simplified after needing rewording three rounds running. Raised: #883.

### Calendar file import: one refused row no longer stops the import (#790, D-099)

- **Calendar file import: one refused row no longer stops the import (#790,
  D-099).** Each row is now saved on its own. A row the database refuses is
  listed as "Skipped" with the database's reason, and the rest of the file
  carries on.
  - **Before:** under the portal's strict database reporting, one refused row
    gave an error page. The rows before it were already saved, the rows after
    it were never tried, there was no list of which rows landed, and no
    activity record was written.
  - **This was reachable by an ordinary file:** two rows with the same event
    name (#877). A row with the same name as another event now gets a plain
    sentence saying so.
  - **Activity record:** it gives the counts ("N events created, M rows not
    imported").
  - **Admin, Errors:** each import writes at most one record per kind.
    - A refusal about the ROW (a duplicate name, a value too long, a broken
      rule) is a "Notification", which the alert e-mail leaves out by default.
    - A refusal about the DATABASE (a full table or disk, a read-only database,
      a lock timeout) is an "Error", the level an installation can ask to be
      e-mailed about. The organisation administrator reading the results cannot
      fix those; the installation's administrator can.
  - **Lost connection:** a connection lost part-way stops the import at that
    row. The page says that row's outcome is not known, rather than claiming it
    was or was not saved.
    - The page also says the activity record may be MISSING in that case: it is
      written over the same connection that went. When it does get written, it
      adds "1 row whose outcome is not known".
- **Tests:** new `tools/calendar-import-selftest.php`, 57 checks over real HTTP on MySQL 8.0.36 and MariaDB 11.4, with planted faults for each rule. Four check rounds by fresh Claude agents (protected arm); round 3's only finding was an untrue comment, corrected. Raised from it: #877, #878, #881.

### Notification choices are no longer lost between two pages (#667)

- The Notification preferences page used to rebuild a member's whole set of
  notification choices from its own list and write it over the top, so any
  choice it did not list was thrown away the next time the member pressed Save
  — including the one the small card on the Account page owned. Both pages now
  change only the switches they actually show and keep every other choice
  exactly as it was.
- Two saves at the same moment can no longer lose each other's change: the
  save now holds the member's row while it reads and writes.
- A page left open from before an update, or a request that does not say which
  switches it showed, now changes nothing and tells the member so, instead of
  switching everything it did not see off.
- Saving the Notification preferences page while the organisation has the
  Sabbath quiet-hours feature switched off no longer resets the member's own
  Sabbath choice to "inherit".
- The Account page's notification card now shows "saved" (or why not) after
  Save. Its message used to be put somewhere that page never reads.
- Retired: the `emailDigest` and `expenseUpdates` keys the Account card used to
  write. Nothing has ever read either (#662), and `expenseUpdates` was a second
  name for `expenseStatusUpdates`. Values members already have are left in
  place and still read by nothing.
- **Tests:** new `tools/notify-prefs-selftest.php`, 44 checks over real HTTP, including a race between two real saves and a measurement that the save's own transaction holds the row; eleven planted faults, each caught. Four check rounds by fresh Claude agents (protected arm); round 3 found the behaviour clean. Raised from it: #874, #875.

### Admin → Public website, and only a global administrator hands the job out (#493, package P3, migration 262)

- **Admin → Public website** (`/admin/public-website`, #493 package P3; D-085,
  D-093, D-094, D-095). An organisation records its **main website**, an
  **optional public address** for the portal's own public pages (such as
  `events.ourchurch.org`; no two organisations may share one — a database
  unique key enforces it; it cannot be an address members sign in at), and
  **which outside websites may show its public pages in a frame** (https only,
  scheme + host + optional port, no wildcards, paths, keywords or numbers in
  place of a name, at most 20; one bad line refuses the whole list, naming the
  line). The installation's global administrator can **forbid framing for
  every organisation** with one switch (on by default; the stricter wins).
  Every value is checked, refused with its reason, and recorded; every value
  is checked again whenever it is read. **Nothing from the portal appears on
  any outside website yet** — the public door that uses these settings is
  package P4, and the page says so.
- **"Check my set-up"** (POST, form token, at most six runs in ten minutes per
  person; its result is shown once and kept nowhere else). It says what is
  certainly known and names no cause it cannot be sure of. For the main
  website: "it answered" for a complete HTTP 200; "it could not be checked on
  this server" when PHP's curl extension is not installed or is switched off;
  "it uses port N, which is not the standard https port, so this check cannot
  reach it" for a website stored at another port (it is not fetched); and
  otherwise one sentence — "This check did not get a normal page from your
  main website. That can happen, for example, when a website is down, its name
  does not exist or points at a private or internal address, it sends visitors
  on to another address this check will not follow, it has a
  security-certificate problem, it turns away automated visitors, or this
  server is not allowed to make outside connections. Open it in your own
  browser to see what your visitors get." — plus, where one was received, "The
  last answer this check received was HTTP N." 403 and 429 are shown "For
  information" (the website answered and turned the check away); everything
  else, including no answer at all, is "Needs attention". It also reports the public
  address (unique, not a sign-in address, whether its name exists — and that
  whether it reaches THIS portal cannot be known until the public door
  exists), each framing website, how many events and posters are marked to
  appear on the public website today, whether the portal's own address is set,
  and a door row that always says it cannot be tested yet.
- **A new permission, "Set up the public website"** (`website.setup`), shipped
  pointing at a new standard role **Website Set-up** that nobody holds
  (migration 262). Out of the box only a **global** administrator (of the
  installation or of the organisation) opens the page; an ordinary
  administrator does not.
- **Only a global administrator may hand that job out** (D-093): changing which
  roles open "Set up the public website" on the Roles page, forgetting that
  choice, deleting a role that opens it, and giving or taking away a role that
  opens it on the Users page are refused for an ordinary administrator, with
  the reason, and recorded. The Users page draws those role boxes locked for
  them.
- The general settings editor refuses `public.website.address`,
  `public.frame.origins` and `public.frame.permitted`, names Admin, Public
  website as the place they are changed, and — where the viewer cannot change
  one there — says who can (the installation's global administrator for the
  framing switch; a global administrator or somebody given "Set up the public
  website" for the other two).
- **Tests:** section W of `tools/public-website-tick-selftest.php` (W1-W23) with plants P66-P108: 240 checks. Ten check rounds by fresh Claude agents (protected arm); the set-up check's verdict was simplified after failing two rounds running, and round 10 was clean. Raised from it: #866, #873.

### A receipt that is not attached is said out loud, and no saved claim loses its receipt (#649)

- **Fixed:** submitting an expense claim used to skip, without a word, any receipt that was too big, of a
  kind not on the list, refused by the server, or could not be stored — then save the claim as though every
  receipt had gone, and show no message at all. The claim is still saved, and the claimant is now told which
  files were not attached, why, and what to change; files beyond the server's per-submission limit
  (`max_file_uploads`) are reported too (unnamed — PHP never passes their names on). The claim is refused
  outright only when the receipts folder cannot be made. A successful submission says "Your claim #N has
  been submitted."
- **Fixed:** a claim that fails before it is saved takes its receipt files with it, even on a lost database
  connection. **Once the save has been sent, no receipt file is ever deleted**: if no confirmation comes
  back, the files are kept and logged for the administrator, and the claimant is told either that the claim
  WAS saved (approvers not e-mailed; do not submit again) or that it is not known and to check their claims
  list first. The cost, chosen deliberately: a commit that truly failed leaves its files on disk, logged by
  path — an orphan can be removed, a saved claim's lost evidence cannot be recovered.
- **Changed:** HEIC/HEIF photos (an iPhone's default) are accepted as receipts (D-096); an empty file is not.
  Claimants' file names never reach a log or the database (#714).
- **Tests:** new `tools/expense-receipts-selftest.php`, 148 checks over real HTTP, real files and a real
  database, including a proxy that drops the reply to a COMMIT; 31 planted faults, 28 caught and three
  stated as beyond reach. Five check rounds by fresh Claude agents; the after-commit design was simplified
  after failing two rounds running. Raised from it: #867-#872.

### One page, one canonical address; an error page carries none (#823)

- **Fixed:** Settings answers both `/settings` and `/admin/settings`, and the Dashboard both `/` and
  `/dashboard`; each told search engines and preview cards that its "one true address" was whichever
  it was reached by. Each now names the address the portal itself links to — `/settings` and `/`. Both
  addresses keep working.
- **Fixed:** an error page (any answer of 400 or above whose code is set before the page is drawn, as
  every error page here does) now carries no canonical address and no preview card; `/index.php` and
  every unknown address used to call their "page not found" page by the address they failed at. The one
  exception, said plainly: a page that crashes after drawing its header can, on a host that buffers
  output, answer 500 still carrying them — no worse than before.
- **Tests:** part I of `tools/page-head-selftest.php` (eleven checks, three planted faults each caught):
  49 checks. One check round by a fresh Claude agent; its one finding was an untrue comment, corrected.

### Three full-screen pages stop asking for an icon that does not exist; the API description file carries no brand (#821)

- **Fixed:** the projector display (`/worship/display`), the page reached by scanning an asset tag and
  the speaker's confidence monitor (`/service-plans/confidence`) draw their own page head with no icon
  link, so the browser asked for `/favicon.ico`, which nothing answers, and reported a "not found" error
  (measured in headless Edge, once per run). Each now says plainly that it has no icon, as the kiosk
  screen does, and carries a one-line description.
- **Fixed:** `web/_core/api-spec.json` named the product and the publishing company. Neither was ever
  served — `/openapi.json` already fills in the installation's own product name and publisher (#307) —
  so **what a visitor sees does not change**; the file now carries a plain placeholder.
- **Changed:** `tools/layout-audit.mjs` names the address of each console error, the script and line of
  each JavaScript exception, and the addresses of requests that failed.
- **Tests:** `tools/page-head-selftest.php`, 38 checks. The icon checks read the page head the way a
  browser does (comments removed, the `<head>` only) and three planted faults — the icon line deleted,
  commented out, and moved into the body — each turn them red. Two check rounds by fresh Claude agents.
  Raised from it: #863, #864.

### A foyer screen can play the noticeboard's posters, opened by a secret link (#493, package P2b, migration 261)

- **Added:** `/noticeboard/foyer?token=…` plays an organisation's posters full-screen in a loop with nobody
  signed in, for a screen in the building. An administrator makes the link on **Noticeboard, Foyer
  screen** (`/noticeboard/foyer/setup`), which shows it and draws its QR code into the page; making a new
  link stops the old one at once. The link names one organisation, so one organisation's screen can never
  show another's posters.
- **What it shows (D-086):** posters on the public website only, unless the installation's global
  administrator permits a choice and the organisation's global administrator then chooses every poster.
  The stricter wins, and anything that cannot be read counts as public posters only. Both settings are
  changed only on that page; the general settings editor refuses them.
- **The screen** sends no referrer (its address is the secret), asks not to be indexed or stored, and
  runs only its own script. A missing, wrong or replaced link answers a bare 404.
- **Switching the Noticeboard off** for an organisation stops its screen, and only its screen. If the
  portal is closed for an upgrade when the screen checks for changes, it keeps playing and tries again.
- **Tests:** section S of `tools/public-website-tick-selftest.php` (fourteen checks) with eighteen plants
  (P48-P65), seventeen going red when their guard is taken out and one measured to stay green. The screen's
  script is read as text; no browser runs it.

### Noticeboard posters can go on the public website, one at a time (#493, package P2a, migration 260)

- **Added:** each poster has "Show on the public website" and an optional first and last day (D-057,
  D-078), set on a new page, **Noticeboard, Public website** (`/noticeboard/website`), by whoever holds
  "Choose what appears on the public website" (D-077). Every poster starts off the website, including
  every existing one after the upgrade and every new one. A change by somebody who may not make it is
  refused with the reason and recorded, by the same judgement events use.
- **Why a page of its own:** the board's editor is a generated bundle that cannot gain a control here.
  Its save never puts a poster on the public website; deleting a poster takes it off, so one brought
  back (for example by an editor tab opened before the deletion) is off until somebody ticks it again.
- **Not yet:** nothing shows the ticked posters to the public — the public door is #493 package P4. One
  rule, `PublicWebsite::posterWhere()`, decides which posters it will show.
- **Tests:** section Q of `tools/public-website-tick-selftest.php` — the rule (both days counting), the page,
  a Website Editor who is not an administrator, a member refused, another organisation's poster refused, a
  bad date range, an editor save keeping the switch, and a deleted poster brought back staying off — with
  four plants (P43-P46), each going red when its guard is taken out.

### A new event starts members-only (D-079, #493, migration 259)

- **Changed:** an event's "Public" box decides whether somebody who is not signed in sees it on the
  portal's own pages, and is one of the three things the public website needs. It started ticked, so
  every event was public unless somebody remembered to untick it. A new event now starts members-only
  until somebody ticks it: the Manage Events form starts it unticked, the events API treats a missing
  `isPublic` as false, the CSV import treats an empty `isPublic` cell as members-only, and the database
  column starts at 0 (migration 259). **Events that already exist keep what they have** — the migration
  changes nothing stored. Approving an event a member of the public suggested no longer makes it public
  (D-092; Approve used to make it public at the same moment, with no "Public" choice shown): it stays
  members-only unless "Public" is ticked on the event, and the moderation page says so. A date a pattern change adds to a series copies the setting
  of the existing date it is made from.

### Any organisation colour stays readable, in light and dark mode (#852 item 3, D-091)

- **Changed:** in dark mode the hover, pressed and faint-panel shades of an organisation's own colour
  were always the standard indigo; they now follow the chosen colour, as in light mode.
- **Fixed — words that could not be read:** the words on a primary button were always white (Bootstrap's
  own), so on a pale chosen colour they could not be read; in dark mode the words on the colour were a
  fixed near-black, below the 4.5:1 normal text needs even on the default colour, and unreadable on a
  dark one; and where the colour itself is used for words (menu links, "current" markers, outlined
  buttons) a pale colour on white, or a dark one on dark mode's background, could not be read. The
  portal now works these out from the chosen colour (`Portal\Core\BrandColour`): white or dark words
  on it, hover and pressed shades that only ever read better, and a darker or lighter shade where the
  colour is used for words, only as far as needed — light mode's links included; a button-style or menu
  link's hover only ever reads better, and an ordinary link keeps its colour on hover. A selected outlined button and a "primary" badge now sit on the
  organisation's colour rather than Bootstrap's own blue, and the remove "x" on the report builder's
  column chips is white only where the words are. The colour itself is unchanged wherever it is a
  background. The signed-out event page (`/calendar/public-landing`) uses the same values, and its
  countdown boxes now tint away from the words rather than towards them. On the
  default indigo, light mode's coloured words are now very slightly darker (`#5965c8`), because the
  original falls just short of 4.5:1 on the hover background.
- **Not covered, said plainly:** borders and other non-text uses of the colour (a ticked box, a progress
  bar) keep the chosen colour; the coloured times on calendar events (an event category's own colour, on
  a tint of it) are not adjusted; and a page that draws the colour on a background of its own is not
  checked.
- **Tests:** `tools/brand-colour-selftest.php` checks 353 colours in both themes; `tools/brand-colour-
  selftest.mjs` builds a page from the real stylesheet in a browser, measures every pair a person reads
  (buttons, outlined and selected buttons, a badge, links and their hover, the colour as words) for eight
  colours in both themes, and six plants each make it fail.

### An event's search-engine markup needs the public-website tick too (#850, D-089)

- **Changed:** an event's own page on the portal carries hidden markup that lets Google and others list
  the event in their own results. For the portal's own events it followed the "Public" box alone. It now
  goes out only for an event that is on the organisation's public website — asked of the same rule the
  countdown and the sitemap use — so an own event also needs "Show on the public website" ticked and
  today inside its website dates. The page itself deliberately still follows "Public" (D-089): anybody
  who may open it still can. A copied-in event also still needs full detail for the person viewing, which
  for a search engine (it visits signed out) means full detail for a signed-out visitor, because the markup
  carries the description and the place.
- **Tests:** `tools/public-website-tick-selftest.php` reads the event's page signed out with the box off,
  on, and on with today outside its dates, and a plant puts the old "Public alone" test back. Its
  section D now also checks the page judges the website dates on the organisation's calendar, not UTC's.
  `tools/time-zones-selftest.php` reads a start time out of that markup, so it now ticks its events.

### Events go on the public website only when somebody ticks them (#493, package P1)

- **Changed — a live exposure closed (D-057, D-078).** The event countdown that other websites can
  show (`/widget/countdown.json`) and the portal's sitemap (`/sitemap.xml`) are open to anybody, with no
  sign-in. They used to show every published event marked "Public", and that box starts ticked. They now
  show an organisation's own event only while somebody has ticked the new **Show on the public website**
  on the Manage Events form, the event is also marked Public, and today is inside the optional "from" and
  "until" dates (both days included; an empty date means no limit; judged on the organisation's
  calendar). Migration 258 adds the switch at OFF on every existing event, so after the upgrade nothing
  of an organisation's own is on its public website until somebody ticks it.
- **Added — who may tick it (D-077).** A new permission, "Choose what appears on the public website"
  (`website.publish`), which each organisation can give to any role on its Roles page. Out of the box only
  the organisation's administrators hold it; a new standard role, Website Editor, exists to give it to,
  though today only administrators can open the pages that change an event, so giving it to anybody else
  changes nothing yet (it is for the noticeboard package that follows). A
  change by somebody who may not make it is refused with the reason and recorded, never quietly dropped.
  The events API accepts `showOnWebsite`, `websiteFrom` and `websiteUntil`; an API key may send the stored
  values back but cannot change them (403), because a key is not a person. The public "submit an event"
  form cannot set them at all.
- **Added — events copied in from an outside calendar (D-080, D-081).** How they reach the public website
  is a rule: "one box per subscribed calendar" (the earlier behaviour) or "one tick per event", where only
  a choice made about that event counts. The installation's global administrator chooses; an
  organisation's global administrator may choose the same or the stricter rule, never the looser, on a
  new card on Admin, Outside calendars. It ships as the stricter rule, and a rule that cannot be read
  counts as the stricter. Under the stricter rule neither a calendar's nor a rule's "Also show on the
  public website" box can put an event there or let a choice skip its approval. Under either rule,
  nothing answers a new choice's website question for you: it asks "Show these dates on the public
  website?" as Yes or No with neither chosen, keeps it unanswered when the form comes back after any
  other refusal, and refuses to save an Everyone choice that does not answer it. A form opened as a new
  choice never saves over a choice saved since, from anywhere; it says so and shows that choice.
  Saving the rule re-works every outside calendar it governs at once. Loosening it asks again about a rule with its website box
  ticked that was approved while the stricter rule applied, and until somebody approves, such a date shows
  to its calendar's own audience; tightening keeps every approval already given (and a newer
  approval outranks an older decline). The rule is set only on that card: the general settings editor
  refuses it, because saving it there would re-work nothing. The upgrade itself re-works nothing: a
  copied-in date that a choice put on the website without an approval, before this change, can stay there
  until its calendar is next re-worked in full. A refresh that finds the calendar's file unchanged skips
  that for up to 20 hours after the last full one (and nothing refreshes while the scheduled feed job is
  not running); saving the rule re-works every calendar at once.
- **Not yet, each with an issue:** a repeating series made with the box ticked gives every date the same two dates (#847). The series
  bulk-edit page has no control for it (#844), and the events API's list and detail do not report it
  (#843). The noticeboard, the portal's own signed-out calendar and the public website "door" are later
  packages of #493.
- **Tests:** new `tools/public-website-tick-selftest.php` drives the Manage Events form, the events API
  (a key and a session), the public submission form, the countdown, the sitemap and the copied-in rule's
  card over real HTTP, reads every result back from the database, and plants each guard out of a copy of
  the portal to prove it can fail. Its section D moves the organisation to a time zone whose date is not
  UTC's, so a reader judging the dates on the wrong calendar is caught; before that, the organisation
  and the test machine were both on UTC and nothing could tell the two apart. `feed-resolver-selftest.php`'s
  website check now names the copied-in rule it is asking under.

### Three older layout faults: a doubled "…", text under an alert's close button, a badge at tablet width (#852)

- **Fixed (#852 item 1):** six page lists printed two "…" side by side when a long list was opened at
  or near either end (« 1 2 3 … … 6 7 8 »), because each placed an ellipsis at a fixed position: /attendance and
  /admin/users, which the issue named, and four more found by the check — announcements, the calendar's
  list view, Admin, Activity and Admin, Errors. Each now prints one "…" for each run of hidden pages, and
  a new hard gate, `tools/audit-checks/check_pagination_one_ellipsis.py`, refuses the fixed-position shape.
- **Fixed (#852 item 2):** a dismissible alert's words could run underneath its close button: the
  portal's own alert padding replaced Bootstrap's, including the room it keeps for the X. The room is
  kept on whichever side the X is, so a right-to-left page is covered too.
- **Fixed (#852 item 4):** on /attendance, a long service-type name in a badge ran over the next columns
  from 768px up. A badge in a list row now wraps at its spaces at every width (it never splits a word),
  except a badge in a row's right-hand part beside its title (such as "2/3 reminders sent"), which stays
  on one line as before.
- **Not done:** item 3 (in dark mode an organisation's colour does not tint the hover, active and subtle
  shades) is a design choice for the owner, since following the comment would visibly change dark mode
  for every organisation.
- **Tests:** `tools/top-bar-selftest.mjs` checks one "…" per gap and no unmarked gap (page 1, and a page
  in the MIDDLE of each list, where the second "…" can go missing), the alert's words clear of its close
  button, the badge inside its column at 768 and 1024, and a badge beside a long title on one line; each
  fault planted back turns it red.

### The top bar's keyboard focus ring can be seen, and four pages fit a phone (#832, #833)

- **Fixed (#832):** a keyboard user tabbing along the top bar could not see where they were: Bootstrap's own
  focus ring is a 25%-opacity blue, about 1.4:1 against the bar (WCAG 2.4.7 and 1.4.11 ask for a visible
  ring of at least 3:1). The bar now draws a 3px ring in the colour of its own words, which every theme
  already guarantees against the bar and which no organisation colour or the colour-blind palette changes:
  at the lowest the test measures, 14.09:1 light and 12.11:1 dark. Only for keyboard focus; a mouse click
  shows nothing new.
- **Fixed (#833):** /settings, /attendance, /photos and /admin/users were wider than a 320-390px phone and
  scrolled sideways. Page titles and their buttons now wrap; on a phone, a cell spanning a list row breaks a
  word only when it would otherwise run out of the row (a long e-mail address, a comma list with no spaces,
  a long service name in a badge); the page lists on /attendance and /admin/users wrap; and an alert quoting
  a long setting name breaks it rather than widening the page. A word that fits is never broken: an earlier
  version used `overflow-wrap: anywhere`, which split a button's one-word label ("Ignore" on
  /giving/reconcile/view) and is replaced by `break-word`.
- **Tests:** `tools/top-bar-selftest.mjs` tabs along the bar in both themes, with and without the
  colour-blind palette, and fails below 3:1; it loads the four pages at 320 and 390 with real-looking rows,
  including enough sessions and people that /attendance and /admin/users (page 4) draw a long page list;
  and it lays out copied rows to prove a money figure, a word, a one-word badge and a button's label are
  not split, and that the alert fits. Six gaps in that test are #851.

### The general settings page cannot delete a protected setting; two tests no longer clash (#836, #842)

- **Fixed (#836):** the general settings editor (`/settings`) now refuses to
  DELETE how long transcripts are kept (`transcription.retentionDays`), as it
  already refused to change or add it. Before, a global administrator could
  delete the installation's row or an organisation's from `/settings`; the
  clear-out then fell back to its built-in period with nothing on the
