  transcription pages to say so, and nothing recorded who removed it. The
  giving-records refusal on delete now asks
  `GivingRetention::lockedInGeneralEditor()` instead of keeping its own copy of
  the prefix test (same answer: every `giving.retention.` row, for everybody).
  New test `tools/settings-locks-selftest.php` presses Delete, Save (change)
  and Add over real HTTP for every key any lock method locks (25 on a fresh
  install, counted by the run itself), at both levels, as a global
  administrator. Before it, nothing in `tools/` posted
  `transcription.retentionDays` to the editor at all, so the change and add
  refusals of #722 were guarded by nothing (found by round 1 of the check).
- **Fixed (#842, tests only):** `tools/expense-edit-selftest.php` no longer
  empties `tblSites`, `tblUsers` and four expense tables (`DELETE … WHERE 1=1`);
  it removes only its own numbered rows, before and after, and a new section E
  checks it left nothing of its own and touched nothing else.
  `tools/page-scripts-selftest.php` puts its made-up rows into the organisation
  the portal really serves (`Site::preDetect()`), not `MIN(siteID)`, and
  refuses when that organisation is missing. The pair now passes in both orders
  on one database.

### A member can now find their own expense claims (#834)

- **A member can now find their own expense claims (#834).** The Expenses page (`/expenses/submit`, reached from the
  Apps menu and the dashboard's "My Pending Claims" card) now lists the signed-in person's own claims in the
  organisation they are in, above the form for a new one: newest submitted first, ten to a page, with number and
  title, department, date submitted, total and status, each linking to the claim's own page. Until now the page was a
  form only and nothing listed a member's claims anywhere, so changing or withdrawing a pending claim — offered only on
  the claim's own page — could not be reached by an ordinary member. The page is now called "Expense Claims"; the
  claim page's back button reads "Back to your claims". The in-app help's "Viewing Your Claims" and "Withdrawing a
  Claim" steps now describe the list that exists, and the dashboard card's comment no longer claims something untrue.
- **Two help sentences that were untrue are corrected**: the withdraw note said a claim could be neither changed nor withdrawn once an approver had decided — a claim one of several approvers has approved stays Pending and can still be withdrawn, though no longer changed; and the dashboard card is shown only when you have a claim waiting.

### An optional ceiling on how long event registrations are kept (#816, migration 257; D-074)

- **An optional ceiling on how long event registrations are kept (#816, migration 257; D-074).** A global administrator can set, on the new page Admin, Registration retention (`/admin/settings/registrations`), the longest period any organisation or any single event may keep a registration's details (a child's name, date of birth, allergies and medical notes, a parent's contact details). **It ships switched off and nothing changes until somebody sets one**, because a registration period can be a legal requirement. A period above the ceiling is refused with the reason; a ceiling below a period an organisation, an event, or the installation itself already holds is refused and they are named — whether the ceiling is being raised or lowered, as the giving-records ceiling does. Removing the ceiling is always allowed. The same page lets an organisation choose its own period for the first time (the general settings editor could never add one) and lets a global administrator change the installation's own period.
- The general settings editor (`/settings`) now refuses `events.registrationRetentionDays` and the new `events.registrationRetentionMaxDays`, to change, add or delete, for everybody; they are written on the new page.
- The nightly registrations clear-out reads each organisation's period through `Portal\Core\RegistrationRetention::daysForSite()`. The reading is unchanged (no row = 90 days, a negative number = 90 days, otherwise PHP's `(int)` of the text — so an EMPTY stored value still means "keep indefinitely"). It deliberately does NOT apply the ceiling: a period above it can only come from SQL or a restore, and then the details are kept longer rather than deleted early (D-032's reasoning, which D-074 follows).
- **The registrations clear-out switch is honoured on the pages too:** while `events.registrationRetentionRun` is off, the new page and the Retention page say nothing is deleted, rather than quoting a period.

### Tests that could pass without reading the page, and two translation cases nothing tested (#829, #831)
- **A pattern search that could not run is no longer read as "not there" (#829).**
  Four self-tests (`access-pages`, `gdpr-coverage`, `go-live-button`, `time-zones`)
  read every `preg_match()` / `preg_match_all()` answer with `=== 1`, `!== 1`,
  `> 0` or by its filled-in matches, so `false` (the search could not run: PCRE's
  JIT stack or backtracking limit) gave the same answer as "found nothing", and a
  check asking for ABSENCE passed on a page it never read. Each test now routes
  its searches through `<prefix>_find()` / `_findAll()`, which answer exactly what
  PHP answers when the search runs and, when it cannot, record a red check naming
  the pattern, the size of the text and PHP's reason, then stop. `preg_replace()`
  and `preg_split()` in the same four files go through `_replace()` / `_split()`
  for the same reason: their failure was being cast to empty text or an empty
  list, and empty text "contains nothing". Measured: with the regex engine
  starved (`-d pcre.jit=0 -d pcre.backtrack_limit=1500`) the OLD go-live test
  reported 51 passes including six "the console does NOT draw the button"
  checks it had never been able to answer; the new one stops at the first search
  with a red line naming `#<form\b([^>]*)>(.*?)</form>#s` over 50,515 bytes.
- **Translation stored as `'true'`, and a withdrawal made while translation is
  off, are tested now (#831).** Section E2 of `tools/content-translation-selftest.php`
  (13 checks) stores `translation.enabled = 'true'` — which the router counts as on
  and the engine as off — and requires that no Translate control is drawn, the
  member's page says translation is off, a press is refused by the HANDLER (403,
  "Translation is switched off for this organisation.") with `meta.csrfToken`
  handed back, and nothing is sent, counted or cached; then that the handed-back
  token works once the switch says `'1'` and that press IS sent and counted (so
  the "nothing sent" checks can fail). It also posts a member's withdrawal while
  the app is off and reads the stored choice back as withdrawn. Five plants, each
  caught by the checks meant to catch it.

### The top bar no longer makes every page scroll sideways (#822)

- **The apps are one "Apps" menu on the top bar instead of one entry each.** Signed in as a
  root administrator with every app switched on, the bar held 41 entries (an ordinary member
  35) and was 5,091px wide on a 1024px screen (4,484px for the member), so every page scrolled
  sideways on an ordinary desktop. Measured in Edge, 7 November 2026. Every entry is still
  there, by the same tests as before; they are now sorted by name and laid out as a grid of
  columns that fits the screen and scrolls inside itself when taller than the window. The entry
  for the page you are on is marked as current for screen readers.
- **A long organisation name is cut short with "…" instead of widening the bar.** A
  75-character name made a 320px phone 826px wide on its own. The full name is still read by
  screen readers and shown when you point at it. The signed-in person's name is cut the same
  way and, between 992 and 1199px, left to the avatar (whose picture carries the name).
- **The cookie banner and the "Install app" prompt no longer sit on top of each other.** Both
  were pinned to the bottom of the screen; the script that was meant to lift one above the
  other never worked, because Bootstrap's `bottom-0` is `!important`. They now share one
  stacking column. They are also now hidden when printing (the print stylesheet names
  `.portal-cookie-banner`, a class the banner does not carry — it has that only as an id).
- **The bar's menus are no longer drawn underneath the page.** The bar's blurred background made
  it a layer of its own at the bottom of the stack, so positioned page elements (the calendar's
  Day/Week/Month buttons, dashboard cards) were drawn on top of an open menu.
- In the phone menu, the language menu, display buttons and avatar now wrap onto a second line
  instead of running 12px off a 320px screen.
- **The bar's menus no longer open on keyboard focus or under a passing pointer while scripts run**
  (round 1 of the independent check). A section of portal.css meant only for browsers without
  JavaScript applied always, so focusing a menu button showed the menu while the button said
  `aria-expanded="false"`, and Escape left it on screen (WCAG 1.4.13 and 4.1.2). That rule now
  applies only where the menu buttons cannot open their menus: portal.js sets `data-portal-menus`
  on `<html>` once Bootstrap's dropdown code exists. This changes the Admin and account menus
  too: where Bootstrap works they open on a click or a key press, not on hover. **If Bootstrap's
  script fails to load** (both the CDN copy and the local one), the mark is never set and every
  menu still opens on hover and keyboard focus — round 2 measured that an earlier version, which
  set the mark from header.php's head script, left every menu on the bar dead in that case.
- **Without JavaScript, every app can be reached with a mouse again.** On a wide screen the Apps
  menu hangs from the whole bar, so a 13-14px gap lay under its button and the menu closed while
  the pointer crossed it. An invisible extension of the button now bridges the gap (no-JS only).
- **With several organisations, the brand shows the logo only on a wide screen**, because the
  organisation switcher beside it names the organisation; the brand's copy used to be squeezed to
  a 0-4px sliver between 992 and 1439px. On a phone the brand keeps the name.
- Help: getting-started now says the bar has Dashboard, an Apps menu and (for administrators) an
  Admin menu containing Settings, and that your name shows beside your avatar only from about
  1,200 pixels; admin.php says Settings is in the Admin menu.
- Help: the Expenses and Approvals guides now say to open the Apps menu and choose Expense Claims.
- New self-test `tools/top-bar-selftest.php` (with `tools/top-bar-selftest.mjs`): builds a
  crowded bar on purpose — every app on, a long organisation name — signs in a root
  administrator and an ordinary member, and checks in a real browser at 320, 390, 768, 1024 and
  1440 that the bar fits closed and with its Apps menu open, that every bar entry is one line,
  that nothing on the page is drawn over the open menu, and that the two notices do not overlap.
  It also drives the keyboard (focus alone shows nothing; Enter opens with
  `aria-expanded="true"`; Escape closes, says `false`, keeps focus), checks a resting pointer opens
  nothing while scripts run, and with scripts OFF moves the mouse from the Apps button to its first
  entry in 2px steps, and with Bootstrap's bundle BLOCKED checks the page does not claim its
  menus work and that focus opens every menu. Focus and resting-pointer checks cover every menu
  button on the bar. It runs twice — one organisation, then several (switcher on the bar) — at six
  widths (320, 390, 768, 1024, 1200, 1440), and checks the organisation's name is readable or left
  to the switcher, never a sliver. It empties the stored secrets for the run, writes them back and
  CHECKS they are back; it leaves its accounts and, where it had to make one, a second organisation
  (`top-bar-second`). Six planted faults turned the first version red, and five more the second (each planted in a scratch copy, the working tree never touched). It is in
  `tools/run-all-selftests.sh` (`top-bar`) and in `portal-selftests.yml`'s database job, which —
  like that whole workflow — GitHub has never run (#754); it uses the runner image's
  `/usr/bin/google-chrome` and node 22 set up just before it. Without a browser it refuses (red).

### Content translation follows its own app switch (#792, D-075)

- **The Translation app's switch in Admin → Apps now closes the translation
  endpoint at the door, like every other app.** `api/translation/…` was tied to
  no app in `AppRegistry::API_FOLDER_APPS`, so a press with translation switched
  off got past the router, had its form token replaced, and was only then
  refused by the handler. It is now refused before the handler loads, with the
  sentence every switched-off app gives: "The Translation app is switched off
  for this organisation." The switch itself is not new — `translation.enabled`,
  seeded off — and nothing that was off has come on.
- **The Translate control, the handler and the member's Translation page ask one
  method, `ContentTranslation::isSwitchedOn()`,** instead of each reading the
  setting for itself. It counts the feature as on only where both the router
  and the translation engine would.
- **A member's own Translation page now says when the organisation has switched
  translation off**, instead of promising a Translate button that cannot
  appear. The page stays open so a member can always withdraw their permission,
  and their choice is kept.
- **The Translation admin page explains that its "Enable translation" tick-box
  is the same switch as Admin → Apps**, and that switching it off closes that
  page too.
- **The Translation app's description on Admin → Apps no longer says it
  translates prayer requests.** It never has (D-049).
- **Test fix: `tools/db-strict-mode-selftest.php` could no longer read the admin
  dashboard's strictness alert.** The dashboard was right; the test's regular
  expression ran out of PCRE stack ("JIT stack limit exhausted") once the page
  grew, and the failure was read as "no alert" — which also meant part P's
  "shows no alert" check would have passed on any alert NOT containing the
  words "NOT strict" (it also looks for those words, so a real strict-mode
  alert would still have failed it). The
  extractor no longer backtracks, and a failed search now fails both checks.

### A translation of edited words is no longer shown as current (#799, migration 256)

- **An edited announcement, project description or project update no longer
  keeps showing the translation of its OLD words (#799, migration 256).** The
  translation cache was found by which piece it was and which language, and
  nothing else, and nothing ever cleared it, so once a piece had been
  translated into a language every later reader of that language saw the
  translation of what it used to say — after a corrected date, a moved event
  or a cancellation. Each cached translation now carries a fingerprint
  (SHA-256) of the exact words it was made from and is shown only while those
  are the words in the original now. An edited piece is translated again on
  the next press, checked against both monthly limits and counted like any
  other request, and the new translation replaces the old one. When a limit is
  reached, an edited piece is refused rather than answered with the old words.
- **Translations cached before this release are translated once more.** They
  have no fingerprint, so nobody can tell which words they were made from;
  each is translated again (and paid for and counted) the first time anybody
  asks for it in that language. Filling the fingerprint in from the current
  words would have marked every old translation as matching, edited or not.
- **The cache recorded every translation's provider as `0`.** The statement
  that stores a translation bound the provider's name as a number, which it
  had done since the table was first built (`8625b9e`). Nothing reads that
  column, so nothing showed it. It now records the name.

### A discipleship pathway no longer counts another organisation's events (#812, #819)

- **Fixed (#812):** the Discipleship sweep's third rule ("RSVP'd going to this event") now requires the event to belong to the pathway's own organisation, as the other two rules always did. Before, a step naming another organisation's event could be completed by an RSVP to it, writing a permanent progress row. No page could write the rows needed to reach it (the step form refuses another organisation's event, and the RSVP page stores an RSVP under the event's own organisation), so it took a hand-written or restored row.
- **Fixed (#819):** the scheduled sweep (`/cron/discipleship-sweep`) now asks each organisation whether Discipleship is switched on for it, and skips one that has it off. It used to ask only the organisation the scheduler's request landed on and apply that answer to every organisation, so it either swept organisations that had switched it off or swept nobody. It also skips an organisation that is itself switched off (`tblSites.isActive = 0`), as the giving-statements job does. Its summary line gains a `sitesSwitchedOff` count. When every active organisation with an active pathway has Discipleship off it says exactly that ("Discipleship is switched off for every active organisation that has an active pathway, so nothing was swept", replacing "Discipleship disabled") and records the run as refused; with no active pathway anywhere it finishes normally with a count of 0, recorded ok.

### Outside services: what a member's browser may tell another company (#778; D-058, D-072, D-073)

- **Gravatar pictures, a sign-in provider's photo and maps of a member's home are now off by
  default, and each can be allowed in three tiers.** The installation decides what is allowed at
  all and the default; each organisation may allow less, never more; each member may switch a
  service off, or on where it is allowed. A member who belongs to several organisations is held to
  the strictest of ALL of them, whichever organisation's pages they are reading (D-058 point 4).
- New pages: **Admin, Outside services** (`/admin/settings/outside-services`; the installation's
  card for a global administrator only) and **My account, Outside services**
  (`/account/outside-services`).
- **Maps of a member's home** on a directory profile are drawn only when the member shown has
  switched maps on AND the person looking has not switched them off (D-072). **A map can never be
  made on by default:** for maps an administrator may choose only "not allowed" or "off until a
  member switches it on"; both writers refuse "on" and the reader treats a stored "on" as "off". Otherwise the location
  is shown as text, coarsened as before for anybody but the member and administrators, and the
  Leaflet library is no longer loaded on that page.
- **What members will notice:** a plain silhouette where a Gravatar or Google picture used to be
  asked for (D-073; a photo upload is #798). Before this, every page that draws the top bar sent
  `img-src 'self' data:`, so the browser REFUSED the Gravatar picture and drew it broken; only on
  `/noticeboard`, whose rule is `img-src https:`, did the request really go out. An administrator
  may make the two picture services on by default; maps never.
- Migration **255** (`255_outside_services.sql`): three `privacy.outside.*` settings seeded `off`,
  the table `tblUserOutsideServicePref`, four addresses. The general settings editor refuses these
  keys on change, add and delete.
- Personal data: `tblUserOutsideServicePref` is in the catalogue (`erase`), deleted by an erasure,
  and included in the member's own data download.
- Help: the FAQ and Getting started no longer say the avatar is the Microsoft 365 picture, and say
  truthfully that a picture may start on or off depending on what the portal's and the member's
  organisations choose.

### Pages that looked unfinished: the API documentation, the admin help on a phone, the kiosk (#569)

- **`/api-docs` no longer reports a console error, and has a heading and a description (#569).**
  The "JavaScript error at 320px" was not Swagger UI and not the content-security
  policy: the page drew its own `<head>` with no icon link, so every browser asked
  for `/favicon.ico`, which nothing answers, and logged the 404. It now requires
  `head-meta.php` like every other own-head page, so it gets the icon, a description,
  a canonical address and a preview card; it gains a visible `<h1>`; and its title is
  built from the organisation's name instead of the product name typed into the page.
- **`/help/admin` no longer scrolls sideways on a phone (#569).** Two lists of setting
  keys stack the key above its description or value below 576px, and the long
  password-setting keys break only at a dot.
- **The kiosk screens have a description and an explicitly empty icon (#569)**, so a
  kiosk tablet no longer requests `/favicon.ico` on every load.
- **`/api-docs` has ONE canonical address however it is reached** — `/api-docs`, `/api-docs/` or `/api-docs/index.php` (#569 round 1: the last gave itself a `.php` address). A page reachable at more than one address now names its own canonical path (`$pageCanonicalPath`).

### A scheduled job called every few minutes now counts as stopped within the hour (#793, D-076)

- **A scheduled job called every few minutes now counts as stopped within the hour, not after a day and a half (#793, D-076).**
  The "Check this portal" page gave eleven of the fifteen scheduled jobs 36 hours before calling them overdue, on the
  premise that they were nightly. Six of them say in their own page headers that they are called every 5 to 60
  minutes, so the retry for this portal's own outgoing webhooks could stop for a day and a half while the page said every job had run in
  time. Each of those six now has an allowance of **three times the longest gap its own page states, and never under
  30 minutes**: the "We're live" push 30 minutes, the webhook retry and task and personal reminders 45
  minutes, and asset reminders, venue reminders and approval chasing 3 hours. The health check, whose page header
  states no timing, is judged hourly from the line the staff health page tells customers to schedule (`0 * * * *`),
  so it also gets 3 hours. The discipleship sweep, also silent, is optional and works by the day, so it keeps 36
  hours with the retention sweep and both backup jobs. The mail queue (15 minutes), event reminders (2 hours), feed
  imports (6 hours) and giving statements (8 days) are unchanged (D-070).
  - **The setup guide now says how often to call every job and when each counts as stopped** — `INSTALL.md` step 6
    has a table of all fifteen. Before this, nothing a customer reads gave a timing for most of them, so a customer
    who chose an hourly schedule for a 5-minute job would have been told every day that it had stopped.
  - **The Venues settings page said "on a daily schedule"** for the venue reminders job, whose own page has always
    said every 30-60 minutes (both written in `37bf418`). It now says every 30 to 60 minutes; under the new 3-hour
    allowance, "daily" would have produced a false "stopped" report every day.
  - The page's all-clear lists each allowance, NAMING the job when only one job has it — "6 hours (feed imports)",
    "2 hours (event reminders)" — and otherwise how many jobs share it ("45 minutes (2 jobs)"). Feed imports are
    called every 15 minutes and keep D-070's 6 hours, so naming them lets an administrator see that a job called
    often can still be hours late without being reported; the old general warning to that effect was dropped.
  - **A job serving one app is no longer reported or counted while that app is off for every active organisation
    AND none of its work is waiting (#793 rounds 1 and 2).** Round 2 found the first version hid a dead job:
    `cron/giving-statements` never checks `giving.enabled` and sends every statement a treasurer queued, so with
    Giving switched off after a run was queued the page said "there is nothing for it to do" about a job with
    statements nine days in the queue. Giving now counts as needed while any statement is waiting by the job's own
    selection (`queuedAt IS NOT NULL AND emailedAt IS NULL AND errorMsg IS NULL`, held equal to the job's page by
    check Q8). Inactive organisations do not count, and a read that fails counts as needed, never as "nothing to
    do" (checks Q9-Q11). The allowance list leaves out a job it says is not counted.
  - (Round 1's wording, superseded by the line above:) **A job whose app is switched off for every organisation is no longer reported or counted (#793 round 1).**
    `PortalCheck::JOB_NEEDS_FEATURE` lists the two jobs that serve one app each — giving statements (Giving) and
    the reading-plan sweep (Discipleship Pathways). While that app is off for every active organisation, an empty
    token is not a problem and the job is left out of every finding and of the all-clear's count, which names it
    as set aside; while the app is on for ANY organisation (its own row included), an empty token is the problem it
    always was. Before this, a fresh installation — where Giving ships switched off — was told "Some scheduled jobs
    can never run" about a job with nothing to do, and the setup guide's advice to leave those two out produced the
    same false problem.
  - **The webhook-retry job was described as retrying "payment messages from Stripe or GoCardless".** It retries the
    webhooks THIS portal sends (`WebhookDispatcher::retryDue()` over `tblWebhookDeliveries`), as FEATURES.md's #324
    entry has always said. The description on the Check this portal page is corrected; any document repeating the
    payment wording (#793's own issue text, the #775 bullet in the instruction files) is wrong the same way.
  - The all-clear's "the 1 part-way through, which have not recorded a finish" now agrees with its number.
  - Tests (rounds 1 and 2): every job's cadence is typed once and held to the setup guide's "Call it" column
    (E9), to each job's own page header (E11), and to every other schedule printed for a customer that a stated
    search finds — fourteen places across the Venues settings page, the health, backup and backup-check pages,
    the calendar reminders page, two help pages and README (E12, E12c); each typed wording is held to its typed
    gap (E9b), and every allowance is held to its gap — at least three times for D-076's seven, longer than one
    gap for D-070's (E10). Section Q of `tools/portal-check-selftest.php` drives the switched-off and switched-on
    states for both apps, including Giving on for one organisation by its own row.
  - Tests: every job's figure is now typed out by hand in `tools/scheduled-jobs-selftest.php` and compared (it used
    to assert only that the figures differed); a job called every few minutes reads overdue at two hours while a
    nightly one does not, on the class and on the page (`tools/portal-check-selftest.php` section P); each new
    figure is tested a minute either side of its boundary; the setup guide's table is held to the same figures; and
    the all-clear's sentence is compared with a sentence written out by hand rather than with the method that builds
    it, which closes the first item of #795.

---
  - **A statement queued for an organisation that has since been switched off is not counted as waiting work**, because the
    job never sends it (it refuses an inactive organisation); counting it made the page report a problem that could never clear.

### The nightly clear-out no longer deletes event registrations before their time is up (#810)

- **The nightly clear-out no longer deletes event registrations before their time is up (#810).**
  A registration's personal details (names and contact details) are deleted a set
  number of days after its event ends. The end time is a reading of the EVENT's own clock, but it
  was compared with the database server's clock (`NOW()`). For an event on a clock BEHIND the
  server's, registrations went early by the difference: twelve hours for an `Etc/GMT+12` event on a
  database in UTC, four or five for New York, eleven to thirteen for a London event on a database
  set to New Zealand time, up to twenty-six at the extremes. (Events AHEAD of the server were
  deleted late, which was harmless. The issue's text had the direction the other way round; the
  self-test runs the old expression on real rows and shows which way it really went.)
  Now:
  - the period is measured on each event's own clock;
  - the deadline is the LATER of "n days on the event's clock" and "n × 24 real hours", so a night
    the clocks go forward (or a date-line jump) can never make it earlier. The price is lateness: a
    registration can wait past that by the gap between its zone's offset when the event ended and the
    zone's lowest offset over the organisation's look-back — an hour for ordinary summer time, about
    two hours measured for Antarctica/Troll and America/Nuuk. The look-back is the organisation's
    LONGEST period, so one event kept for ten years widens it for all that organisation's events;
  - a row whose zone was written in the instant between the two statements waits until the period
    is up on every clock on Earth;
  - zones are compared byte for byte, so a hand-written misspelling such as `Europe/Zürich` cannot
    put real `Europe/Zurich` events on the wrong clock (this also applies to every page #804 fixed);
  - a zone text with no list of clock changes (`EST`, `+05:00`, only possible in old or hand-written
    rows) is judged on the earliest clock on Earth, which makes it late, never early.
  If the database cannot be read part-way, the clear-out stops with an error and deletes nothing
  (strict error reporting); it does not guess. The number of days itself is unchanged.

### Events count as upcoming, today or begun on their own clock (#804, #805, #806)

- **Events now count as "upcoming", "today" or "begun" on their OWN clock, not the database server's (#804).** Nine statements compared an event's start (a reading of the event's clock) with the database's `NOW()`, `CURDATE()` or `UTC_TIMESTAMP()`. Fixed: the calendar list's "upcoming", the public countdown feed (which, with an Auckland organisation on a database in UTC, went on publishing an event that had begun up to thirteen hours earlier as "next"), the "all upcoming" calendar subscription, the dashboard's "Events This Week", the Host Console's "starting today", the admin reminder preview's "next 48 hours", the newsletter's "Upcoming events" block, and the discipleship sweep's "has the event started" (which could mark a pathway step complete up to five hours before a New York event began, permanently). (The embeddable events widget page was changed too, but it has no address today.) Four were left on purpose, each with its reason written beside it: the sitemap, the attendance-recording picker (±30 days), the asset page's event picker and "My volunteering" (both "since a day ago").
- **The month and year grids now show a multi-day event on its last day (#806).** An event from 1 June 10:00 to 3 June 09:00 was missing from the 3rd, because the grids walked from the start TIME and stopped once past the end time. Long events also no longer cost one step per day of their whole length in the year view.
- **The attendance register no longer offers a day the event was not on (#806).** In a zone whose clocks go forward at 23:00 (America/Nuuk, America/Scoresbysund), an event at 23:30 that night was listed on the following day.
- **An event ending at exactly midnight is now on one day in the month and year grids and the attendance register (#806)**, not two — stated because it is a deliberate change: the old attendance register gave a 23:00-to-midnight event two columns.

### Translation now counts the NUMBER of requests as well as money (#762, D-059, migration 254)

- **A second monthly limit, `translation.monthCallCap`**, default 1,000 requests per
  organisation per month, hard maximum 100,000, 0 meaning no limit. It works whatever a
  provider reports, which matters because LibreTranslate reports a cost of 0 for every
  call, so on that route the money limit could never stop anything.
- **Which limit bites first depends on the company** (measured with the code's own price
  formulas, ~1,000-character announcement): on Google and DeepL (~1p a request) the
  NUMBER limit is reached first, at about £10, well before the £50 money default (which
  alone would allow ~5,000); on Anthropic (~13p) and OpenAI (~20p) the MONEY limit is
  reached first (~385 and ~250 requests). 1,000 is chosen as roughly ten times ordinary
  use and a stop on runaway use; no customer installation exists, so nobody loses
  anything they had.
- **Both limits are now counted in a new table, `tblTranslationUsage`** (one row per
  organisation per calendar month in UTC), written at the moment a request is made — not
  read back out of the translation cache. The cache holds one row per piece and language,
  so it counts pieces, never requests.
- **The request is counted just BEFORE it is sent, by one conditional UPDATE**, so two
  presses at the same moment cannot both slip under the limit, and a request that was sent
  and failed still counts, because the portal cannot tell whether it reached the company
  (an address that cannot be connected to looks the same as a timeout after the company
  accepted it), and it may have been charged for.
- **A request that could never be sent is not counted:** with no API key, or a provider
  name the portal does not know, nothing is sent, nothing is counted, and the member is
  told translation "has not been fully set up". `Translation::providerReady()` decides
  this before anything is counted. The admin page warns when translation is switched on
  and it is not fully set up (no key, no address, or a company name it does not
  recognise).
- **A spend lost because the month's row vanished between reservation and recording is
  now logged** in fixed words naming only the organisation number.
- **A reported cost reaches the record through `Translation::settle()`**, which also
  returns the translated words, so the translation path cannot skip it.
- **If this month's use cannot be read, nothing is sent.** The old money reader answered
  0 ("nothing spent") when its statement could not be prepared.
- **The admin Translation page says WHICH limit is stopping translation** (money, number,
  both, or "could not be read"), and that raising the other one will not help. It shows
  the month's requests beside the month's spend, and says that LibreTranslate adds nothing
  to the money figure (never that the money limit cannot stop translation: money spent
  earlier in the month on a paid company stays in the organisation's record). The page and
  `translate()` share one comparison each (`moneyReached()`, `callsReached()`).
- **The "Cached translations" card showed 0 on every installation** (it printed a key the
  query never produced) and counted the whole installation; it now counts this
  organisation's cached translations (#800 item 2).
- **Personal-data catalogue:** entries added for `tblTranslationUsage` and
  `tblScheduledJobRun` (neither holds personal data), and the `tblContentTranslation`
  entry rewritten — it still said the feature was unreachable and the table empty (#800
  item 1).
- A member sees the same words for either limit ("This organisation has reached its
  translation limit for this month. Ask an administrator."), on purpose.
- The save handler refuses an empty, negative, fractional, non-numeric, array or
  over-maximum count with the reason, records it as `TranslationCallCapRefused`, and saves
  nothing — never clamps.
- Migration 254 creates the table, seeds the setting, and backfills each organisation's
  past months from the cache (a lower bound for requests; exactly the old money sum),
  taking the larger figure on a second run.
- Tests: section F rewritten onto the usage record (with F01d, money uses no slot, and
  F01e, spend exactly at the limit refuses), new F2, F3 and J2 in
  `tools/content-translation-selftest.php`; J10b added so J11 can tell a refusal from a
  clamp. F2-10 makes the reservation's write fail with a trigger while the read succeeds;
  F3-04 drives `Translation::settle()` through a probe page in the scratch copy with a
  reported cost of 37p; the whole engine file is pinned by a new hard gate (below). F3-07 is a 23-case table for `providerReady()`, both directions; F2-04e
  requires the "not fully set up" warning to be ABSENT on a complete set-up. 143 checks.
- **The translation engine's code is pinned whole by a new hard gate,
  `tools/audit-checks/check_translation_engine_pinned.py`**, because no test can reach a
  paid provider: every behavioural check of the limits runs on LibreTranslate, which
  reports a cost of 0. Seven review rounds each switched the limits off for PAID providers
  with one line that every behavioural test passed, each just outside whatever had been
  pinned; the gate now pins all of `Translation.php` as one PHP token per line (comments
  and spacing free), and every built-in function and constant in the engine is written
  with a leading `\` so no other file in the namespace can silently replace one — the gate
  refuses one that is not. Review: eight rounds by fresh Claude agents, the eighth clean;
  Codex has not reviewed it.

### Event times are right on the morning the clocks go forward, on every page (#777 part two)

Twenty-four pages showed an event's time by turning the stored time into a
moment in the server's default time zone. On the morning the clocks go
forward, an event at 01:30 was shown at **02:30**; and in a zone whose clocks
go forward at 23:00 (Greenland), an event at 23:30 that night was shown on the
**next day**, in the wrong square of the month grid. Every one now shows the
time as stored, on the event's own clock: the event page, the month, year,
day and list views, the photo view, the public event page, My events, My
volunteering, event moderation and reminders, the host console, the
denominational report, asset bookings, attendance, the RSVP and invitation
pages, the event hub, anonymous check-in, the calendar widget, venue bookings,
the countdown feed, the newsletter's "Upcoming events" block, and the start
time sent to Zoom (with a meeting across the skipped hour given its real
length).

**"Has this event begun?" and the public countdown now use the event's own
time zone**, not the organisation's — so an event kept on another clock is no
longer greyed out as past, or counted down to, hours early or late. The list
view's "Today" badge follows the event's clock too, so a viewer in London can
see "Today" on an Auckland event that is tomorrow by their own calendar; that
is deliberate, because the event's day is the one that matters to people
attending it.

**Room bookings decide "still to come" on the organisation's clock (#783).**
My Bookings and a resource's page used to compare with the database server's
clock, so an organisation in a different zone from its database had finished
bookings kept, or bookings still to come hidden, by hours.

Still open, each with an issue: thirteen other places decide which events are
upcoming with the database server's clock (#804); three of these fixes are not
yet guarded by a test (#805); and two day lists put an event on the wrong day
or leave out its last day (#806).

### Importing events: a cell with no full date is refused, not given today's date (#797)

When events were imported from a spreadsheet, a date cell that did not say
which day it meant was filled in from **the moment the import ran**, and the
row was reported as imported. So a cell holding just `2026` became an event
**today at 20:26**; `10:00` became today at ten; `Monday` became the next
Monday; and `1 June 10:00`, with no year, went into whichever year somebody
happened to press Import — so next January's services, imported in December,
were stored eleven months in the past.

Such a cell is now refused, and the administrator is told it could not be read
as a complete date and shown an example. The test is one rule rather than a
list of spellings — the cell is read against two different moments, and if the
answers differ, the date came from the import and not from the cell.

**Changes in behaviour to know about:**

- A date with a day and month but no year (`1 June 10:00`) used to import into
  the current year and is now refused. Add the year and it imports.
- A dotted date with a **two-digit year** (`01.06.26`) is now refused. It was
  never imported correctly: PHP reads it as the time 01:06:26, so it was stored
  on the day of the import. Write the year with four digits (`01.06.2026`).
- An Excel date number with a decimal part (`46174.5`) is now refused; it was
  stored in the year 4617.

Dates written with a four-digit year, in any format that imported correctly
before, are unaffected — checked by running the old and new readers over a
large generated set of cells, where nothing that used to store correctly was
refused and nothing was stored differently. (The set was not committed, so no
count is given; the committed cases are in the clock-change self-test.) One
narrow exception: a year written BEFORE the day and month (`2026 1 June noon`)
imported correctly only because the import ran in 2026 — PHP reads that `2026`
as the time 20:26 — and is now refused.

**If you imported test data containing any of the cells above before this
change**, check those events: a bare year, a bare time or a two-digit-year
date may be dated on the day of the import, a date with no year in the year of
the import (possibly months in the past), and an Excel number with a decimal
part in the year 4617.

### The portal now notices when a scheduled task has stopped (#775)

This portal relies on tasks that run on a timer: sending reminders, clearing
out personal information once the time you said you would keep it has passed,
taking backups, sending messages that could not go out at once. Whoever set
the portal up arranged for these to be called.

**Until now, only one of the fifteen left any trace that it had run.** So if
the arrangement was switched off, moved, or given the wrong address, the tasks
simply stopped — with no error, no message and nothing on any page to show it.
The first sign was usually somebody asking why they had stopped getting
reminders.

That matters most for the task that clears out old personal information. If it
had quietly stopped six months ago, the portal was keeping records it had told
people it would delete, and the only way to find out was to look in the
database by hand.

**Every one of the fifteen now records when it last ran and whether it
finished**, and the "Check this portal" page reads it. It tells you:

- a task that has not run for longer than it should have, which is a problem;
- a task that started and did not finish, which is a different problem and
  usually means it ran out of time or hit an error;
- a task that ran and reported that it could not do its work;
- a task that was part-way through when the page was drawn — usually it is
  running at that moment, and if it is still listed later it becomes a problem;
- a task that was called and deliberately did nothing. That is not a fault, and
  there are three ordinary reasons: a setting switches it off, another run of it
  was already in progress, or its work was not due yet. **A nightly backup on a
  weekly schedule reports this on six nights out of seven, which is correct** —
  so the page says what it knows and lists the three reasons rather than
  guessing which;
- and, straight after an update, that **nothing is known yet** about a task.

**How late is too late differs by task**, because they do not run on the same
timetable. One figure for all fifteen would either let the mail task sit dead
for a week, or complain about the nightly backup every single day.

**How late counts as stopped is set for each task from how often it is meant
to run** (tightened by #793, see the entry above). It is meant to tell you a
task has *stopped*, not that one run was a little late, so each allowance is
several of that task's own gaps — a stricter figure would complain every time a
host paused its scheduler for a few minutes.

**Straight after this update almost every task will say "nothing is known yet",
and that is expected.** Each one starts being watched the first time it runs,
with nothing for anybody to do. It deliberately does not warn, because that
would show every portal a page of warnings about tasks that are working
perfectly well. It also does not pretend everything is fine — "nothing is known
yet" says exactly what it means.

**One task is an exception, and only when there is something real to say.** The
mail task has kept its own record of when it last ran since long before this
change, and that record survives the update. So if it has run before and has now
stopped, the page says so straight away rather than waiting — the information is
already there, and hiding it would be the opposite of the point. On a portal
where it has never run there is nothing to read, and the page says "nothing is
known yet" like the rest.

A task that was never set up at all is still reported as a problem, as before,
because that can be seen directly.

### A meeting at half past one showed as half past two, one morning a year (#777)

A time written on a clock — "the group meets at 19:30" — is not a point in
history until something gives it a date **and** a place. Four pages gave it
neither and asked PHP to work it out anyway, which quietly means "today, in
whatever time zone this server happens to use".

On the morning the clocks go forward, half past one does not exist. So a group
whose meeting time is stored as `01:30` was displayed as **2:30 AM on 29 March
2026** — and two different stored times, `01:00` and `01:30`, came out as the
same words. Measured on three dates before anything was changed. The stored
data was right in those four places; only the display was wrong, for one day a
year.

**And in a fifth place the stored data was wrong too.** Booking a resource
built the same kind of value and then put it through the same conversion, so on
that morning a room asked for from 01:00 to 01:30 was **saved as 02:00 to
02:30**, an hour asked for from 00:30 was saved as two, and a booking from 01:30
was refused with "End time must be after start time" — which was not true. Two places in the data-entry interface for attendance also
rejected every session time between 01:00 and 01:59 that morning as invalid.
All three are fixed, and all three were found by the independent review rather
than by the first sweep.

**And a fourth place, which my own fix brought into view.** Once the booking
form stopped moving the hour on the way in, the three pages that SHOW a booking
— "My bookings", the approvals list and the resource's own page — were reading
it back the old way, so a booking made for half past one was displayed as half
past two. Before the form was fixed the two mistakes cancelled out and nothing
looked odd. Fixed, and now guarded: the two columns say in the database itself
that they hold a time on a clock rather than a moment in history, and the
automatic check reads that.

Reading those declarations found **four more columns that have said the same
thing since long before this work** — an event's start and end, and the two
copies kept in an event snapshot — and **25 files that still treat them as
moments, with at least two more doing it in a form the automatic check cannot
see.** Those are listed rather than fixed: an event's time zone need not be the
organisation's, so each needs a person to look at it, and that is the next part
of this work. Nothing new may join the list.

**A time written with a decimal fraction was being stored with the fraction
thrown away.** `2026-06-01T10.5` means half past ten in the international
standard, and for a few hours it was accepted and stored as ten o'clock — up to
59 minutes lost, with no error. It had been refused before, and is refused
again. Fractional *seconds* are still accepted and dropped, because they cannot
be stored and every JavaScript client sends them.

**Updating an event through the API now refuses an end before its start.** It
never checked, although the published description said it did and creating an
event has always checked. The check also found that two of our own tests had
been quietly storing events that end before they begin.

**And a repeating event is no longer stored on the wrong date.** In two time
zones in the world the clocks go forward at eleven at night, so a time typed
between 23:00 and midnight landed on the following day — and for a repeating
event that meant the whole series was stored on a day nobody chose, permanently,
with the administrator told the first date had moved as though it were
deliberate. A monthly series lost one of its months outright. The event form and
the part that works out the repeat dates were both doing it, and **fixing only
the form made the monthly case worse**, which is why this is being described
again: an earlier note in this file said the form was the whole of it. Both are
fixed now, and every date after the first keeps the time that was typed.

**And this affected far more than two time zones, which an earlier note in this
file got wrong.** Swept across all 419 time zones: **130 are affected**. Two of
them — both in Greenland — had the wrong *date*, which is the case described
above. In the other 128, including the United Kingdom and the United States,
the date was right and **every occurrence after the first carried the wrong
hour, permanently**. So a customer in London or Chicago reading the earlier
sentence would have concluded this did not reach them, and it did. A date with
no time is affected in no zone at all.

**The events API can read this portal's own calendar format again.** Tightening
the check a few hours earlier had started refusing `20260601T100000Z` — the form
this portal itself writes into every `.ics` calendar file — so a script that read
our own feed and pushed the events back worked one day and was refused the next.
That form, and two other standard ways of writing the same moment, are accepted
again. Genuinely ambiguous text is still refused, and the published description
now lists exactly which shapes work.

**And the spreadsheet import no longer refuses an event because one of its two
times is written differently from the other.** An event from `2026-03-29 01:30`
to `29 March 2026 2:15am` was refused as "end before start", which was not true;
the reverse pair was accepted and stored with its end before its start. The
check now compares the two values it will actually store, so it cannot disagree
with what goes into the database whichever way the dates are typed.

**The events API stored a date six months wrong for one plausible way of
writing it.** A value that names its own time zone — `01/06/2026 10:00 +0100` —
was converted without any check on its shape, and PHP reads a slash date
month-first, so a client sending 1 June 2026 got an event on **6 January
2026**, with no error. A bare time-zone marker on its own created an event at
the current moment, and an impossible date such as 31 February was rolled
silently forward. All three are refused now, and the published API description
says so instead of listing them as refused while they were accepted.

**The spreadsheet import also refused a perfectly ordinary event** spanning the
morning the clocks go forward — a 45-minute event from 01:30 to 02:15 — telling
the administrator the end was before the start, which was not true. It compared
the two times as moments in history while storing them as readings on a clock.

**The spreadsheet import briefly stopped accepting ordinary date formats, and
that is fixed too.** A fix made a few hours earlier mangled any cell containing
a capital `T` — so `Tue, 3 Mar 2026 19:00` was refused outright and
`2026-03-29 01:30 UTC` was read as half past ten, eight hours out. Excel's own
long date format begins with a weekday name, so the commonest spreadsheet
format stopped importing. A row whose end time could not be read also imported
successfully with **no end time at all**; it now refuses the row and says so,
because a refused row can be corrected and a silently emptied column cannot.

**Three shapes that had started being refused are accepted again.** A time zone
written in lower case (`...10:00:00z`, which the standard allows), fractional
seconds (which every JavaScript client sends), and a date with no time (which
an all-day event needs). None of those needs the conversion that caused the
original fault. **This covers the public submission form as well as the
API**, because they share one rule — so a date with no time submitted through
the form now stores midnight on that day rather than being refused. Genuinely
loose text — `June 1 2026 10:00`, a day-first date — is still refused there,
and **the published API description now says exactly which shapes are
accepted** instead of promising that anything readable is.

**The spreadsheet import is deliberately more forgiving, and an earlier version
of this note wrongly said it was not.** It said the rule was shared by all four
places and that loose text was refused everywhere. It is not: a spreadsheet
holds whatever somebody typed, so the import still accepts `June 1 2026 10:00`,
`Tue, 3 Mar 2026 19:00` and `2026-06-01 7pm`, and it reads `01/06/2026`
month-first as 6 January. Refusing those would turn imports that work today
into failures. What the import now refuses is a date that cannot exist — a cell
reading `2026-02-31`, in any spelling, and that includes a day or a month of
zero and a date with no year at all — which it used to accept and store days or
months later without telling anybody. `0000-00-00`, which is what a spreadsheet
exported from an old database contains, used to stop the whole import part-way
through with some rows already added; it is now refused on the preview screen
before anything is written.

**One thing the import will no longer accept, said plainly because somebody
could notice it.** A cell writing the time with a decimal point — `10.5` meaning
half past ten — used to be stored as **five past ten**, which is neither
reading. It is refused now, in every way of writing the date.

⚠️ **AND AN EARLIER VERSION OF THIS NOTE SAID "nothing else was narrowed",
which was wrong.** The first attempt at that refusal also turned away **189**
ways of writing a perfectly good time — anything with fractions of a second
followed by a time zone, such as `2026-06-01 10:00:00.000 UTC`, which is what a
spreadsheet exported from a database or a log contains. Those import again.
What is refused is only a time whose decimal point is on the hour or the
minute, where the time it means is not the time it would be read as.

Nothing else was narrowed, and this time the list is checked on every run:
`10:00 PM`, `7pm`, `March 3 2026`, `Tue, 3 Mar 2026 19:00`, an unpadded
`2026-6-1`, a dotted `01.06.2026`, an e-mail-style date with a time zone, a
day-first `01/06/2026`, and fractions of a second in several shapes. **The
numbers are checked by the test itself and are deliberately not quoted here** —
they have been wrong in this file twice, and a count in prose goes stale the
next time somebody adds a case.

⚠️ **AND THE FIRST ATTEMPT AT THAT REFUSAL ALSO TURNED AWAY THE ORDINARY WAY A
BRITISH SPREADSHEET WRITES A TIME.** A cell reading `19.30` meaning half past
seven was refused, in every way of writing the date — including
`Tue, 3 Mar 2026 19.30`, which is Excel's own long date format. They import
again. What is refused is only a **single** digit after the point, such as
`10.5`, where the file genuinely does not say whether five past ten or half past
ten was meant. **Two digits are stored as written** — `19.30` is kept as half
past seven, which is what somebody typing it into a spreadsheet means.

(Two corrections to earlier versions of this note. It said "six shapes" and "40
formats" where the numbers were eight and 47. And it said two digits are
"unambiguous", which is not quite the reason: strictly, `19.30` read as a
decimal hour would be 19:18, so the two readings differ there too. They are
stored because the portal follows what a spreadsheet writer means, and nobody
typing `19.30` means 19:18. A **single** digit is refused because there the
intention genuinely is unclear — `10.5` reads as naturally as five past ten as
it does as half past.)

⚠️ **AND IT WAS STILL REFUSING FRACTIONS OF A SECOND WHEN NOTHING FOLLOWED
THEM.** The correction above restored `2026-06-01 10:00:00.000 UTC`, where a time
zone comes after the fraction — but `2026-06-01 10:00:05.5`, the same kind of
cell with nothing after it, was still turned away, with a message about an
ambiguity that cannot arise there. **Fractions of a second are never unclear**,
because a stored date and time has no fractional part at all, so both ways of
reading such a cell save the identical value. Those import again, in every way
of writing the date. Only a single digit after a decimal point on the **hour or
the minute** is refused.

**And a refused cell now says which it is.** It used to say "startDateTime not
parseable" for every refusal, which was untrue of all of them: a date that does
not exist and a decimal time are both perfectly readable — the portal has
decided not to accept them. The message now distinguishes "is a date that does
not exist", a time written with a single digit after a decimal point, and "cannot be
read", so somebody can fix the row.

**And an import can no longer stop part-way through.** A cell whose year came
out negative, or longer than four digits, used to get as far as being written to
the database, which refused it outright. The import then **stopped where it was,
with the earlier rows already added and no list of which ones**, after a preview
that had said every row was fine. Those cells are refused up front now.
Reaching one took something like a date arithmetic expression or a raw
timestamp, not a mistyped date.

**And a year before 1000 is now refused as well, which is a change of our own
rather than the database's.** We checked, and the database accepts a year like
0500 perfectly happily — so a cell reading `202-06-01` (a slip for 2026) used to
be stored as the year 202, and the row reported "Imported as event #N". It is
refused now with "has a year before 1000, which this portal does not accept —
check for a typing mistake". An earlier version of this note said the database
refused those too, and that was not true: it was never tested until somebody
asked.

**And it no longer blames a decimal point for a cell that simply cannot be
read.** A cell reading `1.6. 10:00` — a dotted date, which this portal cannot
read — was told it "writes the hour with a single digit after a decimal point",
about a cell with no hour in it. Whether a cell can be read at all is now
settled first, so a refusal only ever describes something the cell really does.

**And the preview screen for changing a repeating series showed an hour late**
on the clock-change morning — on the one screen whose purpose is comparing a
date's current time with its new one.

**And the same mistake was in the events API, where passing the *correct* time
zone did not help.** Creating or updating an event through the API turned the
time given into a moment in history before storing it. That looks right —
it used the event's own time zone — but on the morning the clocks go forward
the hour named does not exist at all, so it still moved: a 01:30 event became
02:30, stored for ever, with no error. An offset given in the value itself
(`+02:00`, or a trailing `Z`) really does name a moment and is still converted
exactly as before, so an integration in another country is unaffected.

The same mistake was also in the **spreadsheet import**, where its own comment
described the conversion as the design.

**And the location on a submitted event was being thrown away.** Every event
submitted through the public form that named a venue stored the venue as `0`,
because of a one-character mistake in the list of parameter types — fixed, and
it predates this work.

**The public submission form now says why it refused.** It could refuse for
eight different reasons and showed none of them: a visitor was simply returned
to an empty form with no message and everything they had typed gone. All eight
now explain themselves.

**And a fifth place was still storing the wrong hour — a form open to the
public.** Submitting an event for 01:30 on the morning the clocks go forward
saved it as **02:30, permanently**, because the submission handler turned the
time into a moment and back before storing it. This is worse than the display
faults above: nothing cancels it out, so the diary simply holds the wrong time
and every page shows it faithfully. Four reviews of this work missed it, and it
was found by reading the form rather than by any automatic check — so a check
for that whole shape (storing a time, rather than showing one) is now raised as
its own piece of work. The submission form also now refuses an impossible date
such as 31 February, which it used to accept and silently move to 3 March.

**The first count given for that was 28, and it was the count of nothing.** The
fourth review of this work re-derived it: two of the 28 were already correct
(they hand over a time zone in the same breath, which the check had not been
taught to recognise — so it was reporting correct code as a fault), and one does
not read the column at all. Two files that really do it were missing, because
they copy the value into a variable first, which the check says plainly it
cannot follow. Both are now named in the list's own notes. The length of that
list is not the size of the work, and it says so.

One more was raised rather than fixed (#783): two queries decide which bookings
are still to come by comparing them with the database server's own clock, which
has nothing to do with the organisation's. That changes which bookings somebody
sees, so it is a change in behaviour rather than a correction.

Three Small Groups pages and the Attendance list are fixed. They now put a clock
reading into words from its digits, through one place —
`I18n::formatClockTime()` — which never builds a moment at all, so there is no
clock change for it to fall into. **The Rota pages already did it correctly**, by
slicing the text, and that is the model the fix copied.

**Nothing else changes.** Proved by comparing the new wording with the old on
all 1,440 minutes of a day with no clock change: identical. The only days that
look different are the two the old code got wrong.

Guards: `tools/audit-checks/check_clock_time_not_a_moment.py`, a hard gate that
takes the list of clock columns out of the database's own description so a new
one is covered without anybody remembering, and section G of
`tools/clock-change-selftest.php`.

**And one honest limit, found by breaking it on purpose.** The behavioural test
*cannot* catch this fault: with the old code put back it still passed, because it
runs on an ordinary day and the two agree on every ordinary day. That is why the
formatter's own body is pinned instead — and why this entry says so rather than
claiming more than was proved.

### A member's chosen language is actually used now (#763, migration 251)

A member could choose their interface language, the choice was stored, and
**nothing applied it.** Every page came out in whatever language the browser
asked for, or the installation's default.

Nothing was broken. The question was simply asked too early. The portal works
out "what language does this person want?" during start-up — and the member's
session, which is where two of the four answers live, does not begin until
after start-up has finished. So those two answers were skipped on every single
request, for eight months.

**The way to choose a language had the same fault, and it was worse.** Adding
`?lang=cy` to an address is the only route there has ever been, and it also ran
during start-up, so it stored nothing: the choice applied to the one page that
carried it and was gone by the next. It is the only thing that has ever written
the saved language, which is why **every account still held the word "en" that
the database puts there when an account is made** — not because anybody chose
English.

So the saved language column now starts empty, and migration 251 empties the
ones still holding that untouched default. An account with nothing stored keeps
following the browser's own request, exactly as every page does today. Somebody
who picks a language from now on gets it, on every device, until they change
it. The owner chose this over letting the stored value win, which would have
pinned every signed-in member to English with nothing on any page explaining
why (D-060).

**So the globe menu in the top bar starts working.** It has been on every
page since March 2026, signed in and signed out, and it has never done
anything: one click now sets a member's language for good, on every device they
sign in on. A language control has also been added to the account page, beside
their name and telephone number, with a "Follow my browser" option so a choice
can be undone (D-062).

The two do **not** always offer the same languages, and the account page says
so. The top-bar menu hides any language translated less thoroughly than
`portal.i18n.minimum_coverage_for_switcher` allows, which an administrator can
set; the account page does not, because that is where a member needs to see and
change what the portal actually holds about them. The account page also always
offers the language a member has already stored, **even one with no translation
file at all** — leaving it out meant it matched no option, so every browser
pre-selected "Follow my browser" and pressing Save to correct a telephone
number silently deleted their language.

**THREE things change on the day this ships, and one of them costs money.** An
earlier draft of this entry said nothing anybody sees changes, which was wrong
three times over. The globe menu starts working, as above. And the **Translate**
button reads the same stored language to decide what to translate *into*,
falling back to the browser's language when nothing is stored — so for a member
whose browser asks for something other than English it will now really
translate, and really charge the organisation, where before it asked for
English, saw English and charged nothing. The owner accepted that deliberately
(D-063): it is what the feature is for. The exposure is bounded — translation
ships switched off and each member must also switch it on for themselves — and
the monthly money limit and translation count still apply.

**And the Members report changes answer.** It offers the stored language as a
column you can show and filter on, and report definitions are saved. Every row
held "en" before; an un-chosen row is now empty. So a saved report showing
Locale prints blanks, and one filtering `Locale = en` — which used to match
every member — now matches nobody, with nothing warning whoever saved it.
Tracked separately rather than guessed at.

Guards: `tools/i18n-member-language-selftest.php` (43 checks, with a real
MySQL, including the fault put back) and the hard gate
`tools/audit-checks/check_member_language_applied.py`. That gate pins **three
whole regions of code** — the part of `index.php` that starts the session and
handles `?lang=`, the account page's control, and its handler — along with how
deeply each sits, so any change to any statement in them fails and `--repin`
makes a deliberate change a visible act.

**And then most of that guard was deleted**, which is the part worth recording.
Eight independent review rounds went into it and found 52 problems — every one
after the first round in the guard rather than in the fix, which every round
confirmed was correct. By the eighth it still refused ordinary work: a passing
comment that merely mentioned the guarded code made it complain, and so did
adding a helper above it. A check that refuses good work is one people switch
off, and then it guards nothing.

So on the owner's decision (D-065) it was cut back to what it can do honestly —
that the calls exist, in the right order, and that start-up makes neither — and
the job it was really doing moved to a test that **measures** rather than infers:
`tools/i18n-member-language-http-selftest.php` signs a member in, loads the real
account page, chooses a language, saves, and reads the column back. Twenty-four
checks over real HTTP, including two that nothing else drove and one that plants
the fault and proves the test goes red.

**Where the property is "this code runs", drive it; where it is "this code looks
like this", pin it.** That judgement, and the eight rounds that produced it, are
recorded in D-065 and in the check's own header.

Neither guard can tell whether a page *renders* in the chosen language — that
needs a seeded installation over HTTP — and both say so.

### A page that tells an administrator what is wrong with their own portal (#477, migration 249)

Almost every fault the September 2026 audit found was invisible from inside the
product. The notification preferences page could not be opened for months. Six
help guides existed that nobody could find. Six menu links led to "page not
found". Every fresh install carried 479 duplicate settings rows and reported
itself as version 0.1.0.

**Not one of those produced an error, a warning, or a log entry.** They were
found by somebody reading the code against what it claims to do.

**Admin → Check this portal** now runs the equivalent checks against this
installation's own database and says, in ordinary words, what it found: an
address with no page behind it, an app switched on that cannot be opened, a
help guide the Help Centre does not link to, a data endpoint switched on with
nothing behind it, and whether the version the portal reports is the version of
its files.

It is **read-only**. It reports and never fixes, because fixing from a page like
this invites a different class of accident.

**Three things it deliberately does not claim.** It says plainly that a clean
result does not mean the portal is correct — only that none of the things it
knows how to look for is wrong today. It says it cannot tell whether a page
*works*, only whether the file it points at exists. And it says it cannot speak
for the scheduled jobs: only the mail job records that it ran, so reminders or
the clearing-out of old personal data could have been silent for months and
nothing here would know (#775).

**Who may open it is a choice, not something written into the page.** It ships
to the `staff` role and an organisation can point it at any role it likes, like
every other capability (D-017). It is deliberately not the narrowest possible
gate: what it shows is exactly what a tester is most likely to hit and least
able to describe, so hiding it would re-create the problem it exists to end.

**One finding while building it is worth repeating.** The first version of the
settings check asked "are any settings stored twice?" — and the database refused
the self-test's attempt to plant one. A rule added in March makes a second copy
impossible, so that question could never answer yes. The live question is
whether that rule is still there, which a database restored from a very old
backup would not have. The check asks that instead.

### One place writes the form token, and it writes every carrier (#768, D-050)

The portal replaces the anti-forgery token every time it accepts one, and there
is only one token per signed-in session. So the moment any background request
is accepted, every copy of that token the open page is holding goes out of date
together — and a page holds it in three places: a tag in the page's head, the
hidden field inside every ordinary form, and an attribute on each Translate
control.

**Five different pieces of JavaScript each wrote the replacement back, and no
two agreed about how many of those three places exist.** The shared one, in
`portal.js`, was the least complete: it wrote the tag in the head and nothing
else, and it reported "no token stored" whenever a page had no such tag, even
when it had just been handed one.

**What that did to somebody, measured rather than reasoned.** On the Host
Console an administrator can publish a message to the live chat, and the same
page carries the "Send 'We're live'" button. Publishing a chat message is
accepted in the background, which replaces the token — so pressing the button
afterwards was refused, and the press was simply lost. The existing test for
that button never saw it, because it presses the button without publishing a
message first.

**How the incomplete version spread, which is the part worth keeping.** Each
new page copied the nearest existing version rather than a shared one, and said
so in its own comment: the report builder's copy says "(event-hub-upload.js
precedent)", and the API documentation page says it follows "the event hub
upload widget". So the gap travelled and the complete version never did. The
shared helper had existed the whole time and its own comment told people to use
it instead of writing their own — it was simply the worst of the five. **A
shared helper is only a single source of truth while it is the best copy; the
moment it is the worst, its own documentation becomes an instruction nobody can
follow.**

`Portal.writeCsrf()` is now the one place all three are written. The four other
copies call it. The API documentation page is a stated exception, because it is
served directly by the web server, draws its own page head and loads none of
the portal's JavaScript; its single carrier is re-tested on every run rather
than taken on trust, so the day that page grows a form the check fails instead
of passing quietly.

**Three more faults of the same family were found while fixing this, and each
is its own issue.** Adding a passkey from the account page cannot work at all,
because the second of its two requests reuses the token the first one spent
(#770). Turning on push notifications spends the page's token and keeps the
replacement in a private variable, so pressing Save on the notification
preferences afterwards loses the member's changes (#774). And the worship
console refreshes its token only after a request has already been refused
(#771). None is caused by this change; all three were found by looking for the
shape rather than the instance.

**Guarded two ways.** A hard gate checks that one helper writes every carrier
and that nobody else writes one, and a new test drives a real browser to prove
what the files actually do to a page — because this fault was invisible to
every existing test: the page's own source was correct, and only what
JavaScript did to it afterwards was wrong.

### Content translation has a way in, and the handler was rewritten rather than re-routed (#485, #761, migration 248)

Automatic translation of what the organisation has published was built and
connected to nothing. The engine, the admin page with five providers' keys and a
monthly spend cap, and the member's opt-in all existed; **no address a user could
reach called any of them.** The owner decided on 4 November 2026 to finish it
(decision D-049).

**It is a rewrite, not a re-route, and that is the part worth reading.** The old
handler at `_apps/api/translate.php` could not be reached — `ApiRouter` wants
three segments and that address had two — so nothing was ever exposed. But
finishing this was precisely the act of making it reachable, and three faults
would have gone live together (#761):

1. **It took the words to be translated from `$_POST['text']`.** So the
   allow-list of tables constrained the *label* and not the text: a member could
   have spent the customer's money translating anything at all, and the answer
   was then cached against a real row's number — so the next reader of
   announcement 42 would have been shown text that was never in announcement 42.
2. **`lookupCached()` asks nothing about who is reading**, and the handler called
   it with whatever row number was posted. Anybody signed in anywhere could have
   read back the translated words of any row of any organisation.
3. **Nothing checked the caller could see the row at all.**

**Making an unreachable handler reachable is the act that makes its faults live.**
That is now recorded against AI Assist (#277, #658), which is the same shape and
still unreachable.

**What a member gets.** A **Translate** button on an announcement, a project's
description, and an update posted against a project. The original stays on the
page, unchanged, and the translation appears below it as plain text — set with
`textContent`, never as markup, because the words come from an outside company.

**A prayer request is deliberately not translatable, and that is a narrowing of
the five tables the old handler listed.** D-049's own requirement is that the
control "must not appear where it would send a third party's words". A prayer
request is the one table this portal already treats as *a person's own words
about themselves* (D-016, #715, migration 240), and such a request is routinely
about somebody who is not the submitter — "please pray for my mother's
operation". The mother can never agree, and **the reader's opt-in cannot stand in
for the writer's**: a congregation-visible request is read by every member, so one
member pressing a button would send another's words away. `tblNewsletter` is out
for a duller reason — no page shows it, and a surface nothing reads is a Save
button that does nothing (#671).

**Money and consent, which D-049 made requirements rather than caveats.** The
monthly limit is enforced in `Translation::translate()` where the money is spent,
not only where the figure is saved, and `Translation::capPence()` holds an
organisation to what the installation allows (D-013) — with 0 read as "no limit"
and therefore as the *largest* value, which is #668's trap. A member must switch
translation on for their own account; an API key is refused outright, because a
key belongs to a system and cannot hold a person's permission. The admin page's
boxes now read the installation's own rows rather than the merged settings, which
was #674's fault on that page, and a figure above the hard maximum is refused
with the reason rather than quietly reduced.

**Two measured limits, each with an issue.** On the **LibreTranslate** route
`costPence` is always 0 by design, so nothing is ever added to the month's spend
and the limit cannot bite there (#762). And a member's **saved interface
language** is applied nowhere in the portal: `I18n::init()` runs at
`bootstrap.php:891`, where no session is active, while the session starts at
`index.php:67` — so `resolveLocale()` can never reach its first two sources and
bootstrap's own `tblUsers.locale` block cannot run (#763). The Translate button
therefore reads that column itself rather than trusting `I18n::locale()`.

**Three traps found while building it, all by running the thing.** An HTML
comment in `footer.php` naming the control's own attribute put that name in
**every page the portal served** — which both shipped a developer's note to every
visitor and made four checks wrong, because searching a page for the attribute
then found the comment on pages with no control; that is #647's shape in a new
place. The gate's "no language was asked for" test normalised the value first,
