and `normaliseLocale('')` answers `'en'`, so it was a clause that could never
fire. And `Translation::detect()` is a cheap guess that read "money for a new
boiler" as **Welsh**, because `' a '` is one of its Welsh markers.

**THE FIRST INDEPENDENT CHECK FOUND FIVE REAL PROBLEMS, and the worst was on a
page that takes money.** `Auth::csrfToken()` is **one token per session** and
`Auth::verifyCsrf()` replaces it on every acceptance — so every control on a
page and every ordinary form on it are stamped with the same token, and the
first accepted press kills all of them. The script kept the replacement in the
pressed element alone. Measured on `/projects/view`: press Translate, then
pledge, and the pledge is refused with a bare "Bad request" and what the member
typed is gone; a second Translate control on the same page was refused for ever,
because **a refused form token carries no
replacement** — `ApiAuth::requireWrite()` answers it before recording the
rotation. (It is not the only one: five refusals carry none, measured, and
saying it was "the one" was corrected in round 3.) That is #634's fault re-created on a payment page. The token is now
shared with the whole page — every control and every `csrf_token` field — and a
refused token asks for a reload instead of showing a member the words "CSRF
check failed".

**Four more, each corrected rather than argued with.** "Nothing has been charged
for this" was said in three places about the customer's money and **cannot be
known** — a provider call that answers 200 with an unexpected shape, or times out
after the provider accepted it, has still been billed; the wording now says what
is certain, which is that nothing was added to the recorded spend. An **empty,
negative or non-numeric monthly limit silently became "no limit"**, the most
expensive outcome there is, because `(float) ''` and `(float) 'abc'` are both 0
and 0 means no limit — an administrator clearing the box and pressing Save turned
the cap off, and the comment above it claimed zero was "tested for separately"
when it was not; an unreadable figure is now refused. **Two conditions were
pinned by nothing**: the organisation test and `isPublic` on the two project
statements could both be deleted with all 66 checks and every gate green, because
the made-up world had organisation B's announcement but no project, no update and
no unpublished project — a condition no fixture can trip is not a condition.
And the hard gate's own "direct guard" looked only at `$body['…']`, so **one
planted line reading a request HEADER put #761's fault 2 back, live and complete,
with 61 audit checks and 66 self-test checks green**.

**Two of my own fixes were then wrong for the same reason, twice in one
afternoon:** a check looking for `$_SERVER['HTTP_` could never match, because
masking a file's string literals hides the key half of that name; and a check for
`shareToken(` was satisfied by `function shareToken(`, so deleting the only call
left it green. **A definition is not a use, and a name that is half code and half
string is not a name.** Both closed, and six plants now go red.

**The script was read by nothing at all** — deleting the token sharing and
changing `textContent` to `innerHTML` left every check green, and the second of
those is what stops an outside translation company putting markup into this
portal's pages. Check F of the gate now reads both rules. No test here drives a
browser, and the self-test's header says so rather than implying otherwise.

**A SECOND ROUND FOUND FIVE MORE, AND THREE WERE THE SAME FAULT ONE STEP ON.**
The token fix had missed the page's **third** carrier: `header.php` puts
`<meta name="csrf-token">` on every page and five scripts read the token from
there rather than from a form — `portal.js` and `portal-tour.js` load on every
page — so on the very page where the pledge fault was measured, a press then made
a guided-tour post answer 403 "Invalid CSRF token". The portal already had the
right pattern in `event-hub-upload.js`'s `syncCsrf()`, which writes the meta tag
AND every field; this was a third copy of that rule with a half missing. It now
writes all three.

**Three more conditions were still pinned by nothing**, and four documents said
otherwise: the project-UPDATE's own `isPublic`, and the announcement statement's
`isDeleted` and `publishAt` clauses — each deletable with every check green,
because every fixture had a public parent, `isDeleted = 0` and `publishAt` NULL.
Five conditions, not two. Three more rows and three more checks, each measured to
go red with its own clause removed. **The fix round's note had claimed the class
was closed, which is the shape the round before it was about.**

**The money fix was pinned by nothing at all** — deleting the whole refusal block
left all 73 checks and all 61 gates green, because nothing in `tools/` had ever
posted to `/admin/translation/save`. Section J now posts eleven figures (`""`,
`-5`, `abc`, `0`, ` 50 `, `50.00`, `1000`, `2000` and three good ones), reads the
stored value back each time with a good value before each bad one so "unchanged"
cannot be mistaken for "stored", and counts the refusals in the activity log.

**And check F passed on code where the whole token fix was gone, two ways**: a
call inside `if (false)` satisfied a check that pinned "a call that is not the
definition" — #709's lesson, *when you pin a call, pin the gate that decides
whether its block runs* — and making the write loop `index < 0` satisfied a check
that only asked whether the selector strings were present. `shareToken()` is
pinned WHOLE now, body and call line, as `check_table_name_comparisons.py` pins
its helpers; any edit to it fails on purpose and has to be read.

**One new message was untrue the moment it was written:** "please reload" was
shown for every 403 carrying no replacement, and `ApiRouter` answers 403 "This
API endpoint is disabled" before any rotation — so with the endpoint switched off
a member was told to reload, for ever, while the portal's own accurate words were
discarded. The reload wording is now used only where the portal said nothing
useful or said exactly the form-token refusal. The abort advice had the same
shape: "press Translate again" was a dead end in exactly the case it named, since
a first attempt that got through had spent the token.

Also corrected: `readerOptedIn()`'s claim that the preference has "ONE reader"
(the account page reads the column too); api-spec's claim that the replacement
token arrives "on the refusals as well as on success" (FIVE carry none, measured:
not signed in, a wrong method, an API key, a refused form token, and the endpoint
switched off — a first attempt at that correction said "two" and drew the wrong
conclusion from the wrong count, which would have had a client discard a token
that was still good); and a
seven-digit limit on the figure pattern that refused `99999999` for not being a
figure when what is wrong with it is that it is too large.

**A FOURTH ROUND FOUND TWO MORE, AND THE REAL LESSON IS THE PATTERN, NOT THE
FAULTS.** `shareToken = function () { return true; };` — a reassignment after
the declaration, one line — killed the whole token fix with the gate green,
because round 3 had closed the *second-declaration* spelling and a reassignment
is the same thing written differently. And `&&` changed to `||` in the reload
guard, ONE CHARACTER, restored the fault round 2 had found, because that
narrowing was pinned as two string literals rather than as a condition. Three
weaker one-edit bypasses besides.

**Four rounds, four times closing the spellings I had been handed and calling it
the class.** So the pins were thrown away and replaced with one: the script's
whole code — comments stripped, whitespace normalised — must equal
`tools/audit-checks/portal-translate.pinned.js`, so any change to a statement
fails the gate and has to be read by a person. `--repin` regenerates it as a
separate, visible act. That is proportionate here and nowhere else in this
repository for one reason: **nothing exercises that script's own behaviour**,
so there is no behavioural guard behind the pin. (It runs in production, of
course — `footer.php` serves it to every page.)

> **Corrected 5 November 2026 (#768).** This paragraph said "no test in this
> repository drives a browser". That was already untrue when written:
> `tools/layout-audit.mjs` has driven Edge over the DevTools protocol since
> `0186531` (30 October 2026), for #569. Establish it with
> `grep -rln "remote-debugging-port" tools/`. The reason for the whole-file pin
> is unchanged and still sound — nothing runs *that* script — but the sentence
> given for it was wrong, and a reader who believed there was no browser
> machinery would write a third copy of the DevTools client, which is #768's
> own fault shape.

**A FIFTH ROUND FOUND THE PIN'S OWN HOLE, AND IT IS WHITESPACE.** The first
version collapsed all whitespace, and **in JavaScript a newline is a
semicolon** — automatic semicolon insertion ends a statement after `return`,
`throw`, `break`, `continue` and `++`/`--`. So one added newline changed what
the script does with the gate green: `return` on its own line made
`outputBlock()` answer `undefined`, which meant **a translation that had arrived
and been paid for was thrown away while the member was told nothing came
back** — measured by running the file in node, and it still parses, so it is the
silent kind. The same lever reached `shareToken()`'s own `return true;` and the
button labels. The pin keeps line breaks now; re-indenting, blank lines and
comment text remain free, which was checked both ways. Three sentences promising
that "any change" failed were untrue in the reassuring direction, and the pin
had been adopted precisely so that no further reading would be needed. One
residue stated rather than hidden: a double space inside a string literal is
still invisible. Every bypass from all four rounds now goes
red, and so does a harmless variable rename — which is the design.

**And the self-test was changing two settings it never named.**
`admin/translation/save` upserts six installation-wide keys from its own
defaults when a field is absent, so section J's eleven presses silently reset
`translation.anthropic.model` and `translation.openai.model` to the handler's
defaults — measured with marker values, after a run reporting "88 passed, 0
failed" with the clean-up check green, because that check counts rows in the
test's own number range and a settings row is not in it. `cleanup()`'s docblock
claimed it put back everything the run changed. **This was round 3's
`libre_base` finding one key over**, where the fix had been to post that one
field: the instance again. `rememberSetting()` now records every key the
handler can write before anything presses it, and all six marker values survive
a run.

**A SIXTH ROUND DEFEATED THE PIN WITH ONE LINE, AND THE CHARACTER WAS INVISIBLE.**
JavaScript ends a `//` comment at FOUR characters — LF, CR, **U+2028 LINE
SEPARATOR** and **U+2029 PARAGRAPH SEPARATOR** — and the blanker ended one at
`\n` only. Python's read folds a lone CR by accident, so that was safe;
U+2028 came through, the blanker ran past it to the end of the physical line,
turned the real code after it into spaces, and `splitlines()` then had nothing
to split, so the line was dropped as blank. **One added line put
`output.innerHTML = …` live with this gate green and every audit check green** —
executed in node, the planted markup ran. That defeated both guards at once: the
whole-file pin, and the `innerHTML` search, which is the one security rule here.

**The likelier case is an accident, and it is worse.** U+2028 is what text
pasted out of a PDF or a word processor carries. A `//` comment whose *text*
contains one, with no code after it at all, makes the whole file fail to parse —
so the Translate control silently does nothing on every page while the gate
says OK. The check folds both characters at both places the script is
read, which is a no-op on the current file.

**And the residue I had written down was understated in the direction that
bites.** "A double space inside a string literal collapses to one" is true but
incomplete: so does a tab, and so does a non-breaking space, and the dangerous
direction is turning one space INTO two. **`'CSRF check failed'` really depends
on its single space** — it is compared with the exact words `ApiAuth` sends — so
any of those three silently shows a member the raw words "CSRF check failed" on
every press, which is the thing the script's own comment says it avoids. Saying
"no string in the pinned file depends on that" was a reassurance the check could
not support. That one comparison is now checked separately and un-normalised,
and all three forms go red.

**A SEVENTH ROUND FOUND THE SAME CLASS TWO MORE WAYS, AND ONE IS AN ORDINARY
ACCIDENT.** The U+2028 fix closed one route to "the file does not parse, so the
control silently does nothing, and the gate says OK" — and left two open. **A
`/*` that is never closed**, after the last statement: Python treats it as a
comment running to the end of the file and blanks it, JavaScript refuses the
whole file, and because no statement follows it the normalised code is
unchanged, so the pin matched. That is a comment begun and not finished, or a
paste truncated at the end of a file. And **U+001F inside a statement**: Python
counts it as whitespace and deletes it, JavaScript rejects it as an illegal
character — it is the one C0 control Python strips *without* splitting, which is
why U+0085, U+001C, U+001D and U+001E all failed the pin by accident and this
one did not.

`js_will_not_parse()` now asks, before anything else, whether JavaScript would
refuse the file at all. Both routes go red with a message naming the character
or the character offset, and the fix is a no-op on the current file.

**Two smaller things from the same round.** `repin()` was the one read of the
script that did not fold U+2028, so the generator and the checker really could
disagree — exactly what one shared function exists to prevent. It failed safe
(the gate stayed red and nothing was blessed), but the failure message says to
run `--repin`, and on that one input `--repin` could never make it green with
nothing saying why. Both read sites fold now, and `--repin` refuses outright to
pin a file JavaScript would not parse. And `\v`/`\f` used as whitespace made the
pin go red over source JavaScript is perfectly happy with — a cry-wolf that
predates this round; both are folded to spaces now, which is what both
languages agree they are.

Guards: `tools/audit-checks/check_translation_text_from_db.py` (a hard gate in
`pr-security.yml`; it pins the allow-list whole, so adding a table fails on
purpose) and `tools/content-translation-selftest.php` (88 checks over real HTTP,
with a stub provider on its own port so nothing reaches the internet). Faults have
been planted into the real files at every round, and **the total is deliberately
not written down here**: three rounds each found plants the round before had let
pass, so any total is true only until the next round. What is recorded, per
round, is which check caught which plant. Exactly one plant is known to be
uncatchable here — the handler's gate refuses before the engine is reached, so no
request can tell the engine's internal order from the handler's. **Neither of these has run on GitHub**, which
is #754 and not this package.

### Granting a coordinator reached the whole installation, and the refusal was invisible (#511)

**Three faults in one statement.** `admin/calendar/coordinators/save` resolved
the person with `WHERE emailAddress = ?` and nothing else:

1. **It reached the whole installation.** One organisation's administrator could
   make a member of **another** organisation a coordinator of their event — and a
   coordinator can see and act on it.
2. **It accepted a closed account.** `tblUsers.isActive` was never asked.
3. **The two replies revealed whether an address has an account anywhere**, which
   is a fact about somebody who may belong to a different customer entirely.

The lookup is now the same join `leadership/assign.php` already uses — an INNER
JOIN on `tblUserSites` for the event's own organisation with `us.isActive = 1`,
plus `u.isActive = 1` on the account. **Both halves matter:** a membership
switched off and an account switched off are different states, and either must
refuse. Every refusal now reads identically, so nothing is revealed.

**This waited on something else, and the order was the whole difficulty.**
Narrowing it was refused while `admin/users/save.php` created an account with no
membership row, because an administrator who had just added somebody could not
then make them a coordinator. That page adds the row now, so the narrowing is
safe — which is exactly the order #511 suggested.

**And the page printed no message at all.** `coordinators.php` had **zero**
mentions of `flash_msg`, so "Coordinator granted.", "Invalid email address." and
the new refusal had never been shown to anybody: an administrator typed an
address, pressed the button, was returned to the page and saw **nothing** — the
same outcome whether it worked or was refused. Nothing in this portal prints a
flash centrally (141 pages print their own), so a handler's message is swallowed
by any page that forgets; that is the shape recorded for `recordings/view.php` in
#276. **A refusal nobody sees is not a refusal that helps anybody**, which is why
this and the narrowing had to land together.

**Nothing exercised this handler at all** before today — measured with
`grep -rln coordinators-save tools/`, which answered nothing. Section N of
`tools/go-live-button-selftest.php` covers it with seven checks, each person
holding exactly one condition (#616's lesson): a member of the other
organisation, an address with no account, a closed account whose membership is
live, a live account whose membership is off, and an ordinary active member as
the control. **Planted:** the old broad lookup fails N1, N4 and N5 on their own
merits while the control still passes, so none of them passes vacuously.

**One trap worth recording.** N3's first version stripped the tags off the whole
page and compared that — and it failed on two identical refusals, because the
page carries #625's asset-fallback script and `App::cspNonce()` is fresh on every
response, so no two renders are ever equal. That is the trap already recorded for
the password-reset comparison. It reads the one flash element now, which is
better than stripping the nonce: there is nothing else in it to drift, so the
comparison cannot be blinded by widening a pattern.

### The installer's six gaps: four were already closed, one is fixed, one is inherent (#594)

Measured each against a real MySQL 8.0.36 rather than read.

**Item 1 — the continue-or-wipe page could not be used: already fixed.**
`db_state.php` is `require_once`d for every request now, with a comment
recording the exact "Undefined constant DB_STATE_FRESH_REQUIRED" fault, and the
step resolution keeps `$isChoiceStep` alive once the database details are held.
`installer-selftest.php` passes 136 of 136 and its L20 covers **all ten**
installer pages including that one.

**Item 2 — every installer pass added three more email templates: already fixed
by migration 222.** The cause was #487's shape: `(siteID, templateKey)` unique
with `siteID = NULL`, and in MySQL a unique key stands aside for any row where
any part is empty, so it refused nothing. Migration 222 added
`siteScope INT AS (COALESCE(siteID, -1)) VIRTUAL` and
`uq_template_key_scope (templateKey, siteScope)`. **Measured:** replaying
migration 051 twice over a fresh install leaves **3** portal-wide rows, not 6 or 9.

**Item 4 — FIXED, and it is the only code change here.** Two links migration 179
adds, `fk_event_venue` and `fk_event_room` on `tblEvents`, were declared by the
migrations and not by the install script — so a database built from the install
script alone lacked both. They cannot be written inline: `tblEvents` is declared
about **seven thousand lines above** `tblVenues` and `tblVenueRooms`, and a
foreign key cannot name a table that does not exist yet. They are added in a
guarded block at the end of `full_schema.sql`, the same way #554's
`fk_att_sess_event` was, each with an `UPDATE` in front that empties a pointer
naming a deleted venue or room — without it the `ALTER` is error 1452 and the
installer stops at the first error in that file, so "carry on with the existing
database" would be stopped by a row nobody can see.

`KNOWN_REPLAY_ONLY_LINKS` in the harness is now **empty**, so a link difference
is a hard failure with nothing in front of it. The other half of item 4, three
apps the install script seeded off while migrations switched them on, was fixed
by migration 225 on 29 October. **So the replay is a complete no-op again** —
and that header has now been wrong in *both* directions, which is recorded
where it says so.

**A check cried wolf over the correct change, and it is worth knowing why.**
`check_install_script_wording()` compared **every** `SET @fk_exists := (…)`
block in each file by concatenating an `awk` range. That worked only while the
install script had exactly one. With two more it reported that the two files
"no longer say the same thing about the link" — when both say exactly the same
thing about the link it is named for. Narrowed to the block whose body names
`tblAttendanceSessions`, it is **stricter**: it now also fails on no such block,
or more than one.

**Item 5 — the header said "000-223" while covering through 247.** It had said
"000-187" while covering 210 when #594 was written, so the number has gone stale
twice. **The number is gone**: the header says it covers every migration file,
gives the two commands to count it, and records the measurement of the day (244
marks for 244 files, none missing).

**Item 3 — INHERENT, recorded rather than fixed.** If `tblEvents` is lost and
**no** session points at an event, the install script makes it again, empty, and
reports success. The guard requires a pointer because **a pointer is the only
evidence in the database that it ever held events** — and a brand-new database
is in the identical state, `tblEvents` absent and no pointers. No extra
condition can separate them: whatever is asked, a fresh install answers the
same. The limit is now stated beside the guard, with why the installer's own
"carry on" choice cannot be used from inside a file that the harness and people
also load by hand.

**Item 6 — split to #759, deliberately not claimed fixed.** It concerns an
*upgraded* database against a fresh install; the harness's clean report is
*install-script versus replay*, a different comparison. It was not re-measured,
and the figure of 25 is from 12 October with three dozen migrations since.

Checks: the migration harness passes **all 42** on MySQL 8.0.36 with both
exception lists empty; `full_schema.sql` loads twice over itself unchanged;
installer self-test 136 of 136; seed parity clean. **Planted:** removing the two
links while leaving the exception list empty fails phase 2, naming exactly those
two — so the change is load-bearing rather than decorative.

### How work is recorded: all three of #678's problems are closed (#678, D-048)

**1. Finished issues were never closed.** `gh issue close` was refused once on
30 October and that single refusal was recorded as a standing block. It is not:
it has worked every time since, and **six issues were closed today** (#475,
#730, #735, #747, #756, and #754's half). Closing is still two actions on
purpose — `gh issue close` **and** the `status: done` label — so a refused close
is still visible.

**2. Three safety settings recorded as "DONE and PROVED" did not exist.** They
exist now: the owner chose to add all three (**D-048**), so
`~/.claude/settings.json` holds a `permissions.deny` block of twelve entries and
an `env` block setting `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS` to `6`.

**And the three passages describing this were stale in the OPPOSITE direction**,
which is the more interesting half. Each said the settings were absent and that
the written rule was therefore what binds. The first clause is now false. All
three are corrected to say both things: the rules are there, **and the written
rule still binds** — because a deny rule cannot catch every form of a command,
does not bind Codex at all, and a file can change under you.

**How that was established, and how it must not be:** by opening the file and
reading it, which is what this rule has always demanded. **Never by running one
of the commands to see whether it is refused** — destructive if the rule does
not hold, and a test you must not repeat is not a test.

**3. Deferrals living only in prose.** The one genuinely open question #678 found
buried in a finished handoff entry — what `tblWorkflowSteps.assigneeValue` may
hold — now has its own issue, **#758**. The handoff is rewritten to current
state: 116 lines, pointers only for decisions, and every unscheduled item has an
issue number beside it.

**The register's own drift gate caught me doing the thing it guards.** Writing
"the owner, 4 November 2026 — they chose 'Add all three'" into `.claude/CLAUDE.md`
with no `D-NNN` nearby failed `check_decisions_recorded.py`, correctly: it was a
decision stated in prose and recorded nowhere. That is what produced D-048.

### The volunteer photo tier is a real gate now, and it takes photos away (#756, D-047)

**A behaviour change the owner decided on 4 November 2026, not a tidy-up.** The
volunteer photo rung checked for the `volunteer` role and returned tier 1 — and
the line immediately below returned 1 as well for every signed-in member, so the
gate decided nothing, and had not since `8625b9e`. The comment beside it claimed
access was granted "ONLY if you've explicitly granted them", which was untrue in
the reassuring direction.

Asked which of the two was intended, the owner chose the comment. The
fall-through returns 0, the rung is real, and a real rung is a capability
(D-017): `Capabilities::PHOTOS_VOLUNTEER`, shipping pointed at `volunteer`.

**What it costs somebody:** a signed-in member holding neither photo tier now
sees what a visitor sees. **Albums shared with everybody are unaffected** — a
public photo is let through before any tier is considered.

Hard-coded role gates are down to two, both taking their key from a row a
customer filled in. `PHOTOS_STAFF`'s "an empty set costs…" sentence is corrected:
it said albums shared with volunteers were unaffected "because every signed-in
member already reaches that tier", which this change makes false.

Pinned by three new checks in `tools/capabilities-selftest.php` (300 checks, 0
failed, real MySQL), each proved by planting. **Nothing drove the ladder before
this** — measured with `grep -rln userTierRank tools/`, which answered only an
audit script that reads it as text, and that is how the no-op survived.

### Six workflows have never run on GitHub, and two of them cannot (#754)

`portal-selftests.yml`, `calendar-selftests.yml`, `mail-selftests.yml`,
`backup-selftest.yml`, `package.yml` and `end-of-life-watch.yml` exist only on
the working branch, so GitHub has never registered them. **"Wired into
`portal-selftests.yml`" is therefore true of the file and false as a claim about
what is being checked today**, and several recent packages said it without the
qualifier. Five such claims across the two instruction files are corrected.

**Two are worse than "never run": they CANNOT run.** `package.yml` — which
builds the customer's installation zip — triggers only on a push to
`main`/`rc`/`beta`/`alpha` or a `v*` tag, and on `workflow_dispatch`, which needs
the file on the DEFAULT branch. So pushing this branch fires nothing and nothing
can dispatch it: GitHub will first execute the release build at the merge.
`end-of-life-watch.yml`'s `schedule` is in the same position, so "runs it
monthly" was untrue; its path-filtered `pull_request` trigger can reach it.

**One real provisioning gap, found by asking what each test NEEDS rather than
whether it passes here.** `calendar-selftests.yml` did not request the `intl`
extension, and `ics-reader-selftest.php` SKIPS checks L5 and L6 without it — the
only guards on the committed Windows-time-zone list (#557) — and no other
workflow runs that test. Its own footer says a skipped check is not a pass.

Three candidates were **false alarms**, named so the next sweep is narrower
rather than wider: `rclone` in `backup-page-selftest.php` is a stored setting
value and not a program; `package-selftest.sh` builds a stand-in when `gitleaks`
is absent and three of its cases need it absent; and `build.sh`'s outright
refusal without `shasum` is satisfied, because the runner image ships Perl 5.38.2
and `shasum` comes with Perl — measured against the image's own README, which is
why `build.sh` was left alone rather than changed on a guess.

No audit check was added: one that failed on any workflow absent from `main`
would go red on every new workflow added on a branch, which is the normal case
here. Both instruction files carry the one-line command to list the gap instead.

### Two checks cried wolf and exited 0; both are now silent and both are gates (#730, #747, D-046)

**The owner's decision, 4 November 2026 — D-046:** once the false complaints
were gone, make both checks stop the work. The order mattered: gating a check
that cries wolf blocks every push (#483), so the wolf-crying was fixed first.

**`check_bind_param_arity.py` (#730).** It reported
`web/_apps/calendar/manage/save.php:981` as "type-string length 11 but **23**
bound argument(s)". The call is correct — eleven columns, eleven placeholders,
eleven letters, eleven values.

The cause is this repository's most-repeated trap: an **apostrophe inside a `//`
comment**. Between two of the call's arguments sits

```php
// 📅 The series' OWN first date, not the one typed on the
```

and from "series'" onwards every later quote was out of step, so the walk ran
past the closing parenthesis and swallowed the rest of the function — 24
"arguments", most of them fragments of prose. The same cause has broken
`check_page_head_tags.py` (an apostrophe in `// don't`),
`check_no_brotli_decode.py` (a `//` inside a URL) and
`check_no_new_role_gates.py` (an apostrophe inside a heredoc).

The remedy is the one the repository already knows: **blank comments and mask
string contents before pairing quotes, never delete them** — same length, with
newlines kept, so reported line numbers stay true (#716: deleting them put line
numbers 370 out). Heredocs and nowdocs are handled, because that branch's
absence was a live hole in another check (#739).

**And the type-string is read from the ORIGINAL, not from the mask.** Masking
replaces a string's contents with `x` of the same length, so the LENGTH is right
either way and only the letters printed to a developer are wrong. That is why a
first attempt to pin it was a **clause that could not fail**: a case shaped like
the others passed with the mask read, because every case compares counts.
Measured: reading from the mask leaves all 24 count cases green while the message
reads `bind_param('xxx', …)`. A dedicated check on the MESSAGE closes it.

Nine new self-test cases, each shape twice — right and wrong — because a fix
that simply stopped reporting would pass the "right" half on its own. Proved by
planting: with the heredoc branch disabled the wrong-direction case is missed;
with a real one-letter-short type string in the very call that was falsely
reported, it is caught and the message now names the real letters and the right
count.

**`check_fk_references_unique_key.py` (#747).** It reported
`tblLiveRateLimits`.`idx_ratelimit_fingerprint` as a key an upgraded database
would not have. False: migration 236 reaches that name by **renaming**
`idx_ratelimit_ip`. A rename is a **third** way a name comes to exist, besides
"created by a migration" and "predates the migrations", and the check knew only
two.

**Teaching it about `RENAME INDEX` then surfaced two TRUE findings**, which is
the check working rather than a new false alarm: two `STARTING_SET` entries for
`tblTrustedDevices` claimed their keys predate the migration history, when
migration 210 section F renames both to the names a fresh install uses. Their
reason text had gone stale **twice over** — it still called the naming drift
unfixed months after migration 210 fixed it, and it cited #553 as "open to fix"
that drift, when #553 is closed and is about event-category names, not this
table. Both entries are gone, the starting-set count is 30 rather than 32, and
five stale passages in the module docstring are corrected.

Proved by planting: with the rename parsing disabled, three findings appear
instead of none; with a key added to `full_schema.sql` that no migration
creates, it is still reported and the script now exits 1.

### The erasure review's two races are exercised now, and one "untestable" claim was wrong (#735)

Two guards in the erasure review were backstops no test reached. Both are
driven by real code now, and **each was proved by planting the fault it exists
to catch** — the plant applied with `diff`, the test confirmed red, the file
restored and checked byte-identical with `shasum -a 256`.

**A line appearing DURING a run (section S).** `GdprEraser` asks
`ErasureReview::whyNotReadyToClose()` twice — once at the top of `execute()`,
and again inside the transaction in `closeRequest()`. The second ask covers the
case the first cannot: a row carrying reviewable free text being written while a
run is already going. Nothing reached it.

**The reason given for that was wrong, and that is the part worth keeping.** The
code's comment said no end-to-end test could reach it "because the test harness
runs one request at a time". True, and it does not follow: **one run is
sequential** — top check, every step, then the close — so a row appearing
anywhere in the middle of that one run reaches the second ask. It needs no
second request, no second connection and no second process. The row is made to
appear by a database trigger on `tblErasureAudit`, which every step writes to —
the same technique `tools/password-writer-selftest.php` section H uses to reach
a state the portal cannot produce on demand.

Measured with that second ask deleted: the request **closes as `completed`**
with the person's own words still in the row, and `execute()` reports
`failed: 0` over 233 steps. S4 and S5 catch it; section I's text pins catch it
too, so four checks go red.

**Two deciders at once (section T).** Section R (#753) already admitted that
R1 to R4 stay green with ` FOR UPDATE` deleted from `record()`, because **R
takes the lock in the test, so it proves the database locks rather than that
`record()` asks it to**. T closes that: this connection holds the row while the
real `record()` runs in **its own process**, so the lock cannot be taken on the
method's behalf. A separate process is required — the decider under test has to
be blocked while the test carries on, and one process cannot wait on itself.

The harm is specific, and was read out of `record()` rather than guessed:
without the lock, the second decider's in-transaction read is a
consistent-snapshot read taken before the other one committed, so it still sees
the words, carries on, and writes `keep` — and because the decision is written
with `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE`, that `keep` lands on top of the other decision.
**The record then says the words are still there over a cell somebody else
emptied**, which the class's own docblock says must never happen. Measured three
runs out of three with ` FOR UPDATE` deleted: R1 to R4 green, T2 and T3 red,
T3 reporting "the cell is empty; the record says 'keep'".

**Keep both kinds of check.** R5 reads the method's text; T reads its
behaviour; neither covers the other's half.

**Measured LOCALLY on both engines `portal-selftests.yml` runs** — MySQL 8.0.36
and 8.4.11, 145 checks, 0 failed, three consecutive runs on 8.0.36 to show it is
not timing-dependent. **Not measured by that workflow, which has never run on
GitHub at all (#754)**; an earlier draft of this entry said "green on both
engines `portal-selftests.yml` runs", which reads as a CI result and would have
broken this project's own rule never to claim the automatic check ran.

Sections S and T need two things the rest does not — the database user must be
allowed to `CREATE TRIGGER`, and `proc_open` must work — and each now fails with
the requirement named. "Now", because an independent check found **S2 could not
fail at all**: this test reports mysqli errors as EXCEPTIONS, so `query()` never
returned the `false` it was testing for, and a user without that privilege got
an unexplained stack trace naming no requirement while the docs claimed a loud
refusal.

**That same check found section T vacuous at the margins — the shape this
package was written to fix, one level up.** T2 matched only the word `REFUSED`,
and `record()` refuses an already-empty line in TWO places: before its
transaction (the line is no longer an item) and inside it under the lock. With
a short sleep the worker returned the FIRST of those, so at a sleep of zero the
whole of section T was green **in both states**, lock or no lock — and nothing
asserted the 1.5-second sleep had been long enough. T2 now requires the
in-transaction wording, and T1b asserts the worker is still blocked when the
line is emptied. Measured with the lock removed and the sleep at zero: T2 red,
where before it was green.

### A check was looking for the wrong text, because PHP interpolated it away (#757)

`tools/expense-rules-selftest.php` asked
`str_contains($approveTight, "$decision='';")` in **double** quotes, so PHP
interpolated `$decision` — undefined there — and the needle became `='';`. The
check looked for *any* `x='';` anywhere in the file, and printed an
undefined-variable warning on every run.

**Why it matters more than a typo.** The comment above it says the check exists
*because a reviewer once changed only the initial value*, and that it was
deliberately written as an assignment rather than plain text so the block's own
opening condition could not satisfy it. The interpolation undid exactly that
care: the guard for a recorded past fault was silently blunted.

**Be exact about how bad it was: latent, not live.** That file holds exactly one
`= '';`, so the weakened needle still happened to catch the fault it was written
for. Planted — the decision initialised to `'approve'` instead of `''` — the
corrected needle goes red.

A warning beside it now says **not to widen the pattern** if it ever goes red,
which is what the original comment was already asking for.

**The sweep for siblings, and why the obvious version of it is useless.**
Looking for any double-quoted string containing `$` across the self-tests gives
**797** hits, nearly all of them deliberate (`"{$pass} passed"` and the like) —
a check that would be switched off within a day (#483). The narrow question —
a needle *inside* `str_contains()` and friends carrying an unescaped `$` —
answers **1**, which was this one, and **0** now. All 78 similar needles
elsewhere are correctly escaped as `\$`.

### Gating a feature is a capability now, almost everywhere (#739)

Phase two of #727. **Hard-coded role gates went from 16 call sites to 3**, and
capability gates from 51 to 64 — counted with `php tools/role-gate-count.php`,
which uses PHP's tokeniser. **Never `grep` for this:** it counts comments, and
converting a gate *leaves a comment naming the gate it replaced*, so the grep
figure went **up** to 73.

Six new capabilities cover thirteen gates, grouped by **the door** rather than
the role: `groups.manage` (six gates — the five small-groups pages and
`SmallGroups::canManage()`), `expenses.approve`, `giving.records`,
`prayer.moderate`, `venues.manage`, `photos.staff`. Two single-reader constants
went with them (`ExpenseRules::EXPORT_ROLE`, `Giving::ROLE_KEY`), because a
shipped role kept beside the capability's own list is two places to read it
from.

**Access changed for nobody**, and that is now *pinned* rather than asserted —
see below. With no stored choice, `App::can(C)` is
`globalAdminPasses(isRootAdmin, true) || Roles::hasAnyOf([shipped key])`, which
is the same three joins, the same `isActive = 1` and the same key normalisation
as `App::hasRole(key)`. Every call site kept its own `App::isAdmin()` ground, so
an organisation's administrator is never shut out and the Roles page itself is
always reachable — **no capability can be emptied unrecoverably.**

`giving.records` is deliberately **not** folded into `expenses.treasury`
although both ship with `treasurer`: folding them would hand the donor list to
whoever a customer later made responsible for paying claims, without telling
them.

**The independent check found eleven real problems. The worst is the one worth
remembering.**

* **The shipped roles were pinned by nothing, so "nobody's access changed"
  passed on broken code.** Changing one word — `giving.records` shipping with
  `['approver']` instead of `['treasurer']` — left **all 60 audit scripts
  green**, reproduced independently. On upgrade that one word would hand
  donors' names and home addresses to whoever decides expense claims;
  `photos.staff => ['volunteer']` would open the staff photo tier to every
  signed-in member. The cause was a list named `$fiveShouldShipWith` while
  eleven capabilities existed, and a second list of holders named
  `$fiveHolders` — **a list named after a number is the shape that goes
  stale.** Both now cover every offered capability and are named for their job;
  the test went 227 → 287 checks, and planted, that one word now fails two of
  them, the telling one reading *"capability says true, the old gate said
  false"*.
* **A heredoc containing an apostrophe made the new hard gate report "Nothing
  wrong" over a real hard-coded gate.** `mask_php()` had no heredoc branch, so
  `<p>Don't change this</p>` opened a bogus string literal that swallowed the
  call that followed — the exact fault its own docstring claimed to have
  closed. Latent rather than live (the repository's one nowdoc happens to hold
  an even number of apostrophes) and it would have fired the first time anybody
  wrote English prose in a heredoc. Fixed in both checks that share that walk.
* **Two more ways to write a role gate were caught by nothing and admitted
  nowhere, and both are live here:** `Roles::hasAnywhere()`
  (`web/_core/Gatekeeper.php`) and `Roles::keysHeldBy()` with `in_array`
  (`web/_core/Workflow.php`). The check now matches all four methods on that
  class, with both call sites named and reasoned — otherwise the whole guard was
  one method name away from decorative, which is the argument the check already
  made for the other two.
* **Six untrue sentences**, every one measured: a docblock naming `canSee()`
  where the method is `canView()`; "22 files name `tblUserRoles`" where its own
  command answers **25** and its breakdown summed to **21**, leaving four files
  uncategorised; "12 remaining gates naming 6 role keys" where it is **14
  fixed-key gates naming 7**, with `Photos.php`'s staff rung — a real
  conversion — in no bullet at all; "six offered capabilities and FIVE declare
  `globalAdminFallsOpen`" where it is **12 and 11**, written one paragraph below
  that docblock's own lesson about stale counts; "the seven added by #739" where
  there are six; and a blind spot claimed that **is not one** — a fully
  qualified `\Portal\Core\App::hasRole()` is caught, because a backslash is a
  word boundary. The stale-count sentence now names no number at all and points
  at the registry.

Two pre-existing faults it found are raised rather than fixed here: **#756**
(the `volunteer` photo tier is a no-op — both branches return the same rank —
while the comment above it claims the role gates it) and **#757** (a check in
`expense-rules-selftest.php` interpolates an undefined variable, so it searches
for `='';` instead of `$decision='';`, blunting the guard for a recorded past
fault).

### The erasure review's row lock is exercised now, and getting there took three attempts (#753)

`ErasureReview::record()` takes a row lock so two Data Controllers cannot both
decide one line. **Nothing exercised it**, and a comment claimed it was "proved
at class level instead" — untrue: that test opened one connection, and
`FOR UPDATE` appeared in neither test.

**The three attempts are the lesson, because the second looked best and was the
worst.**

1. **Racing two real processes** for opposite decisions on one line. It worked —
   and caught the fault **one run in six**, measured. A guard that fires one in
   six reads like proof and is not.
2. **Demonstrating the mechanism from two connections, interleaved
   deliberately** — this repository's established pattern, from
   `tools/expense-payment-race-selftest.php`. Deterministic, and **vacuous for
   the thing it was written for**: it takes the lock *in the test*, so it proves
   the database locks, not that `record()` asks it to. Measured: with
   ` FOR UPDATE` deleted, four runs of four stayed **green**. Worse than flaky,
   because it reads like proof while passing on the broken code.
3. **A pin on the method's own text** — plus one that the transaction still
   opens *before* the lock (#697: "a lock outside a transaction is
   decoration"). Both go red on **every** run.

All of it is kept, with each part labelled for what it does: R1–R4 show the
mechanism and what the lock buys (a second decider arriving after the line was
emptied is refused, and the record can never say "the words are still there"
over an emptied cell), and **R5–R6 are the guard**. The section says in terms
that R1–R4 provably do not catch removal, so nobody reads them as the guard.

Two smaller corrections found while building it. The racing version first asked
that "exactly one was recorded", which is **wrong and flaky with it** — it
failed once with the lock in place, because a "keep it" does not change the cell
and keep-then-empty is a legitimate sequence in which both are recorded. That is
the same mistake #731's own race check made. And a check looked for the method's
internal words ("already empty") where the real refusal is deliberately general
— "already emptied, or the row changed, removed, or in another organisation" —
because `record()` cannot tell those apart and this repository's rule is to say
"the likeliest reason is…" rather than assert one.

Also: `record()` really does reach `Portal\Core\GdprEraser` at run time, which
a static scan with comments stripped said it did not. Ask the run, not the regex.

### A member whose only sign-in is Microsoft, Google or a passkey can give themselves a password (#731, migration 247)

**Until now such an account had no route to a password at all.** The
administrator side refuses it on purpose (#586); "Forgot password" finds nothing,
because it joins `tblLocalAccounts` and `Auth::createUser()` — the first-time
single-sign-on path — creates no row there; and there is no password to change.
So if the identity provider was unreachable, or the Microsoft or Google account
was lost, or the passkey's only device went, the member was out and only a
server-level operation got them back.

`Portal\Core\SelfServicePassword` is the one place that decides whether
somebody may, and the one place the proof that they have **just signed in
again** is recorded, read and spent. They prove themselves by a method they
really hold — not an e-mail link, because their e-mail may *be* the single-sign-on
account. The proof lasts five minutes, is used once, and is refused when it names
somebody else. **Never put a privilege grant behind nothing but an existing
session:** a session can be borrowed, which is the whole reason that gate exists.

Nothing is removed — the identity-provider link and every passkey survive, pinned
by a test rather than merely intended. It is recorded as `PasswordAdded`, never
`PasswordChanged`, and the account's own address is e-mailed, so a stolen session
cannot add a way in quietly. The password is stored only through
`Auth::setPassword()` (#728, which is why that had to land first). An
administrator still cannot do it for somebody else.

**Three things were guarded by nothing, and the independent check found all
three.** Each left the suite at **88 of 88 green**:

* **Deleting the handler's form-token gate.** Every other check fetches a real
  token first, and the one that posts "anyway" does so with a *good* token and no
  proof — the opposite case. So the only thing standing between a member and a
  page that posts this form *for* them, inside the five-minute window, was
  guarded by nothing. That is a second way into the account chosen by somebody
  who is not its owner, which is exactly what #586 refuses on the other side.
* **Making the page renew the proof's moment each time it is drawn.** A sliding
  window turns five minutes into "five minutes after you stop looking", so a
  borrowed session that reloads the page holds the proof open indefinitely.
  **And my own first version of that check could not fail either** — the run
  finishes inside a second, so a renewal writes back the same `time()` and
  compares equal. The proof has to be *aged* first, still inside the window, for
  a renewal to be visible at all.
* **Deleting the second rule check inside the transaction.** Which exposed an
  untrue sentence: the test said two simultaneous adds are protected by "the
  transaction and the lock `Auth::setPassword()` takes". **The lock makes them
  sequential; it does not refuse the second** — `storeHash()` would simply UPDATE
  and report success, so both members would be told their password was set. What
  refuses it is that second ask.

**And the organisation half of the rule cannot be reached through any page,
while three places said it could.** Measured: nothing under `web/` writes
`auth.password.selfAdd` outside the class, and `_apps/settings/save.php` refuses
to add a per-organisation row for a key the installation already holds — the four
`mail.queue.*` numbers are the only exception. That is the shape #668 already
recorded, re-created. The rule in the class is right; the control is now **#755**,
and the test's own fixture says plainly that it inserts a row no administrator can
produce.

Two smaller corrections worth keeping: the new method had been inserted between
`Auth::safeRedirectUrl()`'s docblock and the function, so that docblock — **including
the "do not narrow this back to `string`" warning that is the lesson of the
27 October sign-in bypass** — was documenting the wrong function. (The same
mistake was made in #728 with `RESET_LINK_FORM`, twice in one sitting.) And the
documents claimed a seventh planted fault before one existed; the remedy was to
add the plant, which really does go red, rather than to soften the sentence.

### The reserved-word list had gone stale for the two engines #475 part 1 had just proved (#475 part 2)

**Part 1 took the migration harness to MySQL 9.7 and MariaDB 12.3. The
hard-coded reserved-word list did not follow, and the live test that exists to
catch exactly that was pointed at neither engine.** So the staleness was live.

Measured on real servers, not taken from any summary — the committed list
**fails** on both and passes with the fix:

| Engine | Reserves, and the list lacked |
|---|---|
| MySQL 9.7.4 | `external`, `library` (both fine on MariaDB 12.3) |
| MariaDB 12.3.3 | `conversion`, `current_path`, `to_date`, `vector` (the first and last fine on MySQL 9.7) |

Each refused as a column name with a real parse error. **None of the six is a
column name in this schema**, checked rather than assumed, so nothing was
broken — luck, not coverage. `vector` is the one to notice: both engine
families are adding vector types, so it is a plausible column name in a product
that may later store embeddings.

**The fix is two changes together, because one without the other is no fix.**
The six words went into the list, *and* `calendar-selftests.yml`'s matrix went
from three engines to five — the same five as the harness. Adding a word
without pointing the test at the server that reserves it would leave the next
version just as blind.

Those two engines and no others, deliberately: both are already in the
harness's matrix, so this opens no gap between what these tests run on and what
`DbServer::TESTED_LINES` describes. **That constant is NOT touched and must not
be** — it describes the migration harness alone, and folding these tests into it
would overstate the sentence a customer reads. Verified: its own both-ways
guard still passes.

**A warning from doing the measuring.** A first probe loop reported `phase` and
`recover` as reserved on MariaDB as well. Tried one at a time, both are
**accepted** — the loop's generated table names collided, and a collision looks
exactly like a refusal. Two false alarms would have been worse than none here,
because a check that cries wolf gets switched off (#483). **Probe one word at a
time and read the error, never just the exit code.**

**And a larger thing was found while doing it, now #754: six check workflows —
`portal-selftests`, `calendar-selftests`, `mail-selftests`, `backup-selftest`,
`package` and `end-of-life-watch` — are not on `main` and have never run on
GitHub.** Not once. That is #646 one level up, and it makes "wired into
`portal-selftests.yml`" true of the file but not yet a live gate. `pr-security.yml`
is registered and does run, so its hard gates are real.

**What DreamHost actually offers, for the record.** Shared hosting is MySQL
8.0, moving to 8.4 "on a proactive schedule" with no dates published, and the
customer gets no choice — its own help pages answer "Can I update the MySQL
version?" with "No". **MariaDB is not offered.** Its reserved-word page still
names `MANUAL` and `PARALLEL` as newly reserved in 8.4, which this repository
measured as wrong two months ago and which is still wrong on 9.7.4 — one more
reason the standing rule is to ask the server, never a summary of the server.
Whether the 9 November move happened could not be established from DreamHost's
own documentation or status page.

### One place hashes and stores a password (#728)

**EIGHT places did it, each with its own SQL:** the installer,
`invites/accept.php`, `users/api/create.php`, `auth/reset-password/save.php`,
`auth/account/change-password.php`, **two** sites in `admin/users/save.php`,
and `offboarding/do.php`. Every one of them was correct about the hashing.

**What could not be done was enforce a rule about passwords anywhere** — and
#586 was exactly such a rule: a password cannot be stored for an account with
no sign-in row. Its fix was a read-back inside one page's transaction, which
protected that page and nothing else, and even there asked only whether a hash
was *present*.

`Auth::setPassword()` and `Auth::setUnusablePassword()` now own the storing:
the hashing, whether the row must be created, two honest refusals on the
sign-in name, and a read-back that compares the hash. **They deliberately do
not own who may set a password** — each caller has its own rule, and moving
those would be a behaviour change dressed as a refactor.

**Three live faults the conversion fixes rather than moves:**

* **`users/api/create.php` left every account it created looking as though it
  had a password nobody could use.** It wrote `password_hash()` of random
  bytes — unmatchable, but *unrecognisable*. **FOUR places read it and ONE writes it.** READ: `Auth::loginLocal()` refuses an empty hash before `password_verify()` is reached; `_apps/auth/account/change-password.php` and `_apps/auth/2fa/disable.php` both refuse on `($row['passwordHash'] ?? '') === ''`; and the disaster-recovery runbook reads `passwordHash <> ''` as "this account has a password". WRITES: `_apps/offboarding/do.php`, to take a sign-in away. So the empty
  marker is the one the portal enforces, and a random hash defeated every
  reader. Measured first that the forgot-password flow puts no condition on the
  hash, so the reset route stays open.
* **`invites/accept.php` and the installer could skip the password write
  silently.** Both were `if ($stmt !== false) { … }` with nothing in the else.
  The invite path would then mark the invitation accepted and sign the person
  in — an account they could never sign in to again, with their one-use
  invitation spent. Unreachable under strict mode, but the shape is the fault.
* **`admin/users/save.php` could create a SECOND sign-in row for one account**
  — two names, two passwords, either working — because `userID` carries no
  unique key and the branch chose INSERT from a hidden form field rather than
  from what was there. The flash message now follows what *happened* rather
  than what was asked for.

**`offboarding/do.php` is deliberately NOT converted**, and the reason is in
`Auth::setPassword()`'s own docblock: taking a password away must reach **every**
row, where this method refuses an account with more than one set of sign-in
details rather than choosing between them. Choosing is the dangerous option — a
draft took `MIN(localID)`, which is deterministic but still leaves the other
row's old password working, so a member who resets because they fear their
account is compromised would still be signable-in with the password they just
replaced.

**The guard is `tools/audit-checks/check_one_password_writer.py`**, a hard gate
in `pr-security.yml` (a new script is not a gate here until that file *names*
it). It fails both ways: an unlisted writer, and a named exception that has
stopped being one. Every converted call site was reverted one at a time and
each was caught; count the plants from the commit message, not from here (#671).

**The independent check got three shapes past the first version of that guard**,
each measured: `REPLACE INTO` (a verb it did not know), a joined
`UPDATE tblUsers … SET LA.passwordHash` (the table named is not
`tblLocalAccounts`, and the column is reached through an alias), and an INSERT
whose column list runs past 300 characters — which defeated the **window**, not
the pattern, so the guard's own "cannot see a name built by joining pieces"
admission did not cover it. The distance windows are gone: it now splits a file
at each SQL write verb and flags a span naming both the table and the column, so
a long list, an alias and a join are all inside reach. A read-only file stays
green, which was checked.

**It also caught a stale exception the moment the conversion landed:**
`check_account_writes_guarded.py` went red because `change-password.php` no
longer writes the table it was listed for. That is the both-ways half working.

**`tools/password-writer-selftest.php` proves the writer itself** against a real
MySQL — 53 checks. **Its section H exists because the fault was planted and
sections A–G did not catch it:** weakening the read-back to "does a row exist",
exactly the old `LENGTH(passwordHash)` question, left the test at **49 passed, 0
failed**. Sections A–G all check the database before and after, so they prove
the write *landed*; the read-back only matters in the state they never produce
— the write lands, a row exists, and the value is not the one we made. Section H
makes that state with a database trigger and goes red on it.

**And I claimed a race was impossible when it was not** — the shape the owner's
own standing note calls out. `storeHash()` said "nothing in this portal creates
a second one" in five places. Measured on MySQL 8.0.36 with two connections,
each in its own transaction, both setting a password for the **same** account
with **different** sign-in names: **both reported success and the account ended
with two rows.** Under REPEATABLE READ neither transaction sees the other's
insert, so neither `COUNT(*)` finds a clash. The harm is what follows — that
account can never have a password set through the one writer again, while
**both** old passwords go on working, so a member who changes their password
because they fear their account is compromised cannot. The unique key is on
`username`, so it catches only the case where the two names *match*, which is
the harmless one.

It now locks the account's own row before counting. That lock is real only
inside a caller's transaction (#697: a lock outside one is decoration), and
every caller that can create a row is inside one — the one that is not passes
no sign-in name and so can only update. New **section I** runs two real
processes, because two connections driven one after another from a single
process just deadlock; planted, removing the lock turns all three of its checks
red with `2 row(s)` and `created, created` on the failure lines.

Two faults in my own test came out of building that: its brace walk read a `//`
comment as code, so the apostrophe in "a caller's transaction" opened a quote
that never closed and the walk ran three methods past its target — **the exact
fault this repository names, found the only way it can be, by a comment gaining
an apostrophe**. And check I2 first demanded that one of the two requests be
*refused*, which is the pessimistic answer: with the lock in place the loser
waits and then correctly *updates*, so the check now asserts that at most one of
them **created** a row.

### A cancelled date came back if it fell in the hour that happens twice (#654)

**Fixed.** A date cancelled with `EXDATE` was not removed when it fell in the
repeated hour on the night the clocks go back — in the form Google, Apple and
Outlook all write. `RECURRENCE-ID` (a "this one date is different" block) had
the same fault and worse: the date appeared at **both** its old time and its
new one, so a congregation could see one service twice.

**The cause.** A date's identity is its start turned into UTC. In the repeated
hour one wall-clock reading names TWO moments, so one date has two possible
identities. The repeat pattern carried the previous day's offset forward and
keyed the date as the earlier moment; a cancellation went through a different
route and took PHP's own pick. Nothing compared the two.

`keysForDate()` is now the one place that says which identities a date can be
known by. **Only the date being identified is widened, never the `EXDATE`
set** — widening the set would remove a service the line never named, and that
reasoning was measured rather than argued.

**Nothing stored is renamed.** `keysForDate()[0]` is always the exact identity,
so `externalRecurrenceKey` does not move — verified by reading all 64 fixtures
through both the old and the new reader in three organisation zones: **2,363
stored keys, byte-identical.** A renamed key would make the importer delete and
re-add every date of this shape.

**The independent check found three real problems, and the first is the one
worth knowing about: the fix was incomplete, and a comment said it was not.**

* **The cancelled service still went ahead at its moved time in 3 of the 9 ways
  the two lines can be written** — measured independently, 1 of 9 right on the
  committed reader, 6 of 9 with the fix as first written, 9 of 9 now. The cause:
  a value ending in `Z` states an instant, so its own zone is UTC, and UTC has
  no repeated hour — the block got ONE identity where the series date had two.
  The changed-date block is now also named in the series' own zone. **The
  comment claimed the cancellation wins "whichever way round they were
  written", which was false**, and the suite was green because the fixture used
  only the one form.
* **The written-zone rule was pinned by nothing.** Swapping the zone a reading
  was written in for the *organisation's* zone — one token — left all 396
  checks green while a real date vanished from a diary with no warning. That is
  the mistake `.claude/CLAUDE.md` names in capitals and which #653 shipped as a
  no-op three times. New check **I35n** closes it.
* **"Reachable only by an `RDATE` written in UTC" was false**, in the
  reassuring direction, in four places. An `RDATE` in the series' own zone —
  the form Google and Outlook write — reaches the same state, so the documented
  cost of this fix is ordinary rather than exotic. Measured and corrected
  everywhere it was claimed.

Two new checks, **I35m** and **I35n**, each catching exactly the plant written
for it and nothing else; the test is 398 checks, up from 375. Twelve planted
faults in all, and the "which check catches what" table now names the two that
passed all 396.

**Cost:** a 2,000-date calendar goes from about 9.0 ms to 12.1 ms — roughly
1.5 microseconds a date, recorded rather than called free.

### The two erasure-review pages are asked as real requests now (#732)

`/admin/erasure-requests/review` and `/admin/erasure-requests/review-save` are
where a Data Controller reads a member's own free text in full and decides
whether it is emptied. **No request was made of either page anywhere** — their
guards were pinned as TEXT by `tools/erasure-review-selftest.php`, with whole
conditions and comments stripped by `token_get_all()`.

**The independent check of #724 measured what a text pin is worth.** In one
edit it removed `AND siteID = ?` from the request look-up on *both* pages and
`Auth::verifyCsrf()` from the handler. All 52 audit scripts exited 0, the
class-level test passed 91 of 91, and `php -l` was clean. Nothing noticed. A
text pin is a claim about the source, not about what a request does.

Section J of `tools/erasure-pages-selftest.php` is the request: fourteen checks
over real HTTP, taking the test from 66 to 80. Two failure lines prove the harm
rather than reporting a mismatch — `the other organisation's words on the page:
YES — THEY LEAKED`, and `B line now: NULL; decisions against B: 1`, which is
organisation A's Data Controller really destroying organisation B's member's
own words.

**The fixtures are where the work went.** Five people hold one ground each and
nothing else (#616: one account carrying two grounds means a gate can be
deleted green). Organisation B holds a real line of free text, and J6 proves
B's own Data Controller can read it — without that, J4 and J5 would pass on an
empty organisation and prove nothing (#645).

**The independent check then found three untrue sentences and a missing press,
and the missing press is the one worth knowing about.** J9 proves that naming
*another* organisation's request is refused — but that is refused by the
handler's own `AND siteID = ?`, before `ErasureReview::record()` is reached. It
says nothing about the next gate. **Changing `record()`'s own per-row narrowing
to `$siteColumn = ''` left section J passing 79 of 79 while a Data Controller
of A really emptied organisation B's card**, by posting his *own* request
number with B's row key. New check J9b makes that press; planted, the test now
fails 78 of 80. The product was never exposed — the class test goes red on the
two checks written for it — but a gap in the HTTP test is still a gap, and that
is a request only a real POST can make.

The three untrue sentences, each corrected at the point it was written:

* **"The row lock in `ErasureReview::record()` is proved at class level
  instead" — it is proved by nothing.** Measured: that test opens ONE
  connection, and `FOR UPDATE` appears in neither test. The ` FOR UPDATE` could
  be deleted and nothing would go red. Now stated plainly and tracked as #753.
  **It survived because the other two items in the same list are honestly
  covered** — an untruth in good company is the hardest kind to see.
* **`tblCapabilityRoleMap` is not a table here.** The real ones are
  `tblCapabilityMap` and `tblCapabilityMapRole`, and they mean different
  things: a row in the first with none in the second means "nobody,
  deliberately", which is not the same state as "never chosen". Sent to a table
  that does not exist, a reader cannot tell which state the fixture is in.
* **"Organisation B holds a real line of this same person's own words" — they
  are somebody else's.** The only account column on `tblSalvationCards` is
  `assignedToID`, which IS in `GdprEraser::ACTOR_COLUMNS`, so the card is
  reached through the worker it was *given to*. The file contradicted itself:
  J5 nine lines below requires the page to print "only says this person ACTED
  on the row". What it changes is the section's reach — the one "Empty it"
  performed is on a third party's words, and the line genuinely in this
  person's own words is the booking note, whose "Keep it" alone is covered.

Two clauses that **cannot fail** by any single edit are now labelled as the
belt-and-braces they are rather than left reading as guards, and the
"four people, one ground each" count is three (it was counting the person the
requests are *about*).

### The documents said the deploy did something it stopped doing in October (#637)

**Fourteen statements across four files described the deploy arrangement as it
was planned, not as it is.** `README.md`, `DEV_NOTES.md`,
`docs/offsite-backup-setup.md` and both instruction files all still described
**one shared base folder** with `public_html/`, `public_html_beta/` and
`public_html_dev/` as siblings — the arrangement `c61211e` replaced on
27 October 2026 with a complete, separate installation per channel.

**The two worst were standing warnings telling somebody not to deploy.**
`DEV_NOTES.md` section 3c said "do not deploy until the #493 work has landed.
The deployment does not yet know about `admin_html/`". It does, and had for a
week: `STAFF_WEB_DIR_DEFAULT='admin_html'` at
`tools/deploy/resolve-settings.sh:129`, overridable per run with
`DEPLOY_STAFF_WEB_DIR`. And six setting names the documents told a reader to
configure are retired and read by nothing — they sit in `RETIRED_SETTINGS` at
`tools/deploy/resolve-settings.sh:207`, which warns and carries on.

**Sections 3b and 3c are deleted, not annotated** — 365 lines of superseded
instruction replaced by 43 saying what was wrong and where the truth is. That
is this repository's own rule: where something no longer applies, delete it
rather than explaining that it no longer applies. **A superseded instruction
behind a warning is still an instruction**, and somebody setting up a server
reads the table, not the warning above it.

**Two stale counts went with it**, both of the shape `.claude/CLAUDE.md`'s own
"counts are not kept in this file" rule exists to stop. It said the version was
1.4.0 (it is 1.4.1 on `main`, and since D-024 the number is set at release
time, so the file now says how to read it rather than what it is), and that
**fourteen** pages were outstanding on `check_install_wide_prefill.pending.txt`
when the check itself prints **twelve**. Both files now point at the command.

**The transferable part:** every one of the fourteen was a document describing
correct machinery inaccurately, and each had been read as true for weeks. Read
the workflow and `tools/deploy/resolve-settings.sh` — which is the one place
that decides where files go, and refuses when it is unsure — never a document's
copy of them.

### The version number is set at release time, and `alpha` and `beta` are guarded at last (#474, #476, #748 — D-024)

**`alpha` had been reporting version 1.4.0 while `beta` and `main` reported
1.4.1, for four months.** The cause (#476): `version-bump.yml` and
`changelog.yml` ran on push, and `auto-merge-alpha.yml` merges pull requests
with GitHub's built-in token — which GitHub deliberately does not let start
another job. Measured: **three runs in `version-bump.yml`'s whole history, the
last on `alpha` on 7 July 2026.**

```bash
gh api --paginate '.../actions/workflows/version-bump.yml/runs?per_page=100' \
  -q '.workflow_runs[] | [.created_at[0:10], .conclusion, .event, .head_branch] | @tsv'
```

**And those two jobs were the one thing standing between `alpha`/`beta` and the
branch rules #474 asks for**, because a ruleset that requires tests refuses any
direct push. `changelog.yml`'s own header had already recorded that shape for
`main` ("gets rejected with GH013"). The obvious fix — have them open a pull
request — **does not work**: GitHub starts no checks on anything the built-in
token creates, so such a request could never merge.

So, the owner's decision (D-024): **the number is set at release time.** Both
jobs now run on `workflow_dispatch` only, and **refuse to run against `alpha`,
`beta`, `main` or `release-candidate`** — a confusing push failure is worse than
an honest refusal, and the refusal says where to run them instead. The number
travels through the merge, and `package.yml` still refuses to build a release
whose number was not raised above the last tag, which is what makes the
hand-run step impossible to forget. `web/_core/version.php` is raised to 1.4.1
here, so the merge brings `alpha` in line rather than anybody pushing to a
release branch.

**Two faults this would otherwise have introduced, caught before committing.**
Both jobs read `github.event.head_commit.message`, and **there is no
`head_commit` on a `workflow_dispatch` event**. So `beta` would have taken a
**patch** bump for ever — no message means no "BREAKING CHANGE" and no
"feat(" — and a release that should have been 2.0.0 would quietly have been
1.4.2, with nothing saying so. The bump is now worked out from every commit
since `web/_core/version.php` last changed, which is the right basis for a
number set at release time rather than on one push. And both carried
`if: !contains(github.event.head_commit.message, '[skip ci]')`, which on a
dispatch can never fire: a condition that cannot fail, removed rather than left
to mislead the next reader.

**With that settled, #474 is complete.** `PHP -l lint` and `Static security
checks` are now required on `alpha`, `beta`, `release-candidate` and `main`.
Administrators keep their bypass on the core ruleset — D-022 removed it for the
live branch only, deliberately. `tools/audit-required-checks.py` reports both
names matching a real workflow job, no orphans.

## [Unreleased] (alpha)
<!-- #744 -->

### The in-app help is read by something now (#744)

**The first version of this entry said "nothing in this repository loaded any
help page", and that was untrue** — caught by the independent check, and it
broke this repository's own rule that such a claim must carry the command that
established it.

**Thirteen of the twenty help pages were loaded by nothing.** The other seven
were already fetched over HTTP, for their *words*, by `feed-admin-selftest.php`
(`/help`, `/help/calendar`, `/help/approvals`, `/help/calendar-imports`),
`mail-pages-selftest.php` (`/help/admin`, `/help/admin-first-steps`, both
asserting HTTP 200), `mail-queue-pages-selftest.php` (`/help/admin`),
`channel-selftest.php` and `page-head-selftest.php` (`/help`), and
`portal-address-selftest.php` (`/help/support`, `/help/admin`). **None of the
seven was checked for whether the page finished**, which is the gap that
remains.

```bash
git grep -nE "(req|pw_req|[$]get)[(].*'/help" 55b0f78^ -- tools
```

The help is what an end user actually reads —
this project's own plain-English rule says it matters MORE than the developer
notes, not less — and it is PHP, so a page can throw and nobody would know
until a member opened it. The worst case is `help/disaster-recovery.php`, which
somebody opens when something has **already** gone wrong, and which #583 found
telling customers to do two things that would have destroyed their data.

Two things were built, and the owner decided the shape of both on 4 November
2026.

**1. `tools/audit-checks/check_help_page_references.py` — a hard gate.** Every
runbook section number a help page shows a reader must be a numbered heading in
`docs/disaster-recovery-runbook.md`. That one check would have caught the
"runbook section 4.4" that #488's reorganisation left stale — found by hand,
weeks later. The owner chose to make it binding rather than advisory, knowing it
binds everyone.

**It cannot judge whether any advice is correct. No check can**, and its header
says so rather than implying the help is verified.

Getting it to not cry wolf took measuring, and **my own planting found three
false alarms in the first version.** It replaced each `<?php … ?>` block with a
single space, which pulled text hundreds of lines apart into the same
60-character window — so "Version 4.4 of the portal", "About 4.4 million
records" and the date "4.4.2026" were each reported as a stale runbook
reference, governed by a "runbook" nowhere near them. Each block is now a fence
the window cannot read across. Twelve plants: five that must fail (including
`section&nbsp;7.99` and a bare `runbook 12.3`) and seven that must stay quiet.

Two findings worth recording from building it. **Every one of the seven live
references is correct today**, so the check is a tripwire for the future rather
than a repair. And `help/disaster-recovery.php` really does still contain
"section 4.4" twice — **inside a PHP comment** recording the #583 correction, so
a check that read the whole file would fail on the very comment documenting the
repair. Only the text outside `<?php … ?>` is read.

**2. `tools/help-pages-selftest.php` — all twenty help pages, over HTTP.** 50
checks. As an administrator every help address must answer a whole page; as an
ordinary member, a whole page or a clean refusal; no answer may carry PHP's own
error text; every page on disk must have a registered address and every address
a file.

**"Whole" is the point.** A page that throws part-way still answers HTTP 200,
because its header has already gone — what arrives is the top of a page with
nothing wrong *in* it. Only the closing `</html>` shows it finished. #669 and
#715 are both on record as that shape.

**And part B would have been vacuous without one more check.** "A whole page or
a clean refusal" is satisfied completely by twenty refusals, so if every help
page turned an ordinary member away, all twenty checks would pass while proving
nothing about a page opening for the person most likely to read it. B99 counts
how many the member really read — **20 of 20** — and fails if it is none. The
I7d lesson (#645): when a check exists to prove something ordinary still works,
check that the fixture is actually ordinary.

Three planted faults prove the test can see a broken page: one that throws
part-way (still HTTP 200), one that prints PHP's own error text, and the page
put back so that a later failure cannot be a plant's leftovers.

**One fault of mine, caught by running it.** The first version read
`tblRoutes.routePath`. The column is **`routeKey`**, and the test died on its
first run with "Unknown column 'routePath'" — CLAUDE.md's "name things by the
right identifier" trap, which says to check a name against the thing that uses
it rather than against what looks similar. The comment at that line now records
it.
