### Two checks that proved less than they claimed (#742, #743)

**#743 — a `.php` address hidden inside a PHP string was invisible to all three
checks written to catch it.** Measured by planting the house style's own form
into a real page:

```php
<a href="<?php echo htmlspecialchars('/admin/users.php', ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8'); ?>">
```

| Check | Verdict |
|---|---|
| `check_no_php_in_urls.py` | **green** |
| `check_site_aware_addresses.py` | **green** |
| `check_registered_addresses.py` | **green** |

The **same address** written as a plain `href="/admin/users.php"` is caught by
two of the three. **It is the form they could not see, not the address** — and
the form they could not see is the one the codebase mostly uses, because
`htmlspecialchars()` round an address is the house style for anything built in
PHP. The harm is a dead link: `.htaccess` answers "page not found" for every
address ending in `.php` bar three, so the page looks finished and only the
person who clicks finds out. That is not hypothetical — this rule found three
live Expenses forms in September 2026 whose Save button went to a 404.

`check_no_php_in_urls.py` now looks inside PHP strings, and decides by what
else is on the line rather than by the string alone, because a bare `.php`
string is usually innocent — `require`, a route's target file, a comment, a
fixture — and a check that cries wolf gets switched off (#483). Nine plants,
both directions: four shapes that must be caught (the `htmlspecialchars` form,
`Site::url()`, a `header('Location: ')`, and a `Router::url()` with a query
string) and five that must stay quiet (`require __DIR__`, a leading comment, a
relative route target, an `is_file(PORTAL_APPS . …)`, and a correct
`Site::url('admin/users')`).

**And the silencing list was matched by SUBSTRING, which an independent check
measured the cost of.** Of 3,740 lines under `web/` carrying an address
marker, **13 were silenced and not one of them for a file reason**: `require`
matched `?err=required`, `dbs_required_for_coordinators` and the ordinary prose
"are required."; `include` matched help-page prose; and `unlink` matched the
real **address** `Site::url('account/unlink')` — five lines in
`web/_apps/auth/account/unlink.php` alone, so the check went quiet on exactly
the kind of line it exists to read. The markers are whole words now, and calls
where they are functions. Three more plants prove it: an address followed by
`?err=required`, a `/account/unlink.php` address, and one on a line ending
"fields are required." — all three were silenced before and all three are
caught now, while `require __DIR__`, `is_file(PORTAL_APPS . …)` and
`basename('/admin/users.php')` on a line containing the word `href` stay
quiet. Its header lists what it still cannot see — read it
rather than trusting a count here, because the first version of this sentence
said "four things" and there were five. One of them it shares with the patterns
that were already there: **a trailing comment quoting such an address IS
reported**, measured and left alone on purpose, because stripping a trailing
`//` would cut a line at the `//` inside any `https://` string — a fault this
repository has already paid for (#716).

**#742 — two checks proved a refusal by a pattern that could find the NEXT
refusal in the same file.** `tools/capabilities-selftest.php` asked whether a
gate really stops with `\{.{0,900}?exit\(\);\s*\}` and the `s` modifier, so
`.` crossed newlines. `web/_apps/admin/roles/save.php` holds **twenty-two**
`exit(` calls and **twenty-one of them are followed by `}`**, so there is
almost always another one to find.

**Be exact about what was and was not broken, because the issue overstated it
and measuring disproved the stronger claim.** Deleting the `exit();` from
either of the two blocks made the old pattern go **red** — correctly — because
the nearest other refusal happened to be more than 900 characters away (2,011
and 1,181). **They were sound by accident of spacing, not by design.** One
ordinary edit changes that, and this is the plant that shows it: delete the
`exit();` **and** add a new, perfectly normal refusal just after that block —
which is what a developer adding a guard does —

```
    old idiom (bounded dot, /s) : says the refusal is THERE  <-- WRONG
    new brace walk              : goes RED  <-- correct
```

and the real self-test goes red with it. `cap_blockFrom()` is now the one way a
block is cut in that file: it walks the braces and **steps over string
literals** (#647 records a walk that did not, where one `{` in a log message
swallowed the rest of a function and the check passed on a removed gate). It
also replaced a second, newer helper that cut at "the closing brace at N
spaces" — which worked, but trusted the read file's indentation and made the
caller supply N, and **both** blocks #742 was raised about contain braces of
their own. All five refusal checks in that file use the one walk now, and each
was proved by planting its `exit()` away: five plants, five reds, each restored
byte-identically.

**Two checks that look like the same shape and are NOT**, so they were left
alone: the two in `tools/expense-rules-selftest.php` pinned on
`ExpenseRules::isOwnClaim(...)`. They are **anchored** at the start of a slice
cut from the gate itself and spell out the whole block, so a deleted `exit()`
cannot be satisfied by a later one — proved by planting, which the first
version of this entry had only argued by reading.

**AND THE SWEEP WAS NOT AS COMPLETE AS THIS ENTRY FIRST CLAIMED.** It said "the
other 54 apparent matches across the tests are the harness's own
built-in-server router, not refusal pins". The independent check could not
reproduce 54 from any search — the natural figure is **53**, `exit('403')` 27
times plus `exit('404')` 26, which really are the router shims — and, more to
the point, **the rest are not all router shims.** There are at least **seven**
other genuine refusal pins across `tools/`:

| Pin | How it cuts its block | Sound? |
|---|---|---|
| `capabilities-selftest.php`, the "could not read the role key" branch | was indentation, **now the walk** | yes, planted |
| `expense-payment-race-selftest.php` | brace walk | yes |
| `expense-rules-selftest.php` (a third pin) | brace walk to the matching close | yes |
| `expense-withdraw-selftest.php` | exact squeezed text | yes |
| `setting-limit-selftest.php` | indentation | yes |
| `retention-caps-selftest.php` | indentation | yes |
| `gdpr-coverage-selftest.php` | **was a 1,100-character window** | **changed** |

Two needed action. The **sixth pin in `capabilities-selftest.php` itself** still
cut by indentation, which made "`cap_blockFrom()` is the one way a block is cut
in that file" untrue while four documents said it; converted, and it was sound
before (planted). And **`gdpr-coverage-selftest.php` asked for an `exit();`
within 1,100 characters of its question** — #742's own shape, on the guard that
stops an erasure request being cancelled after it has already changed
somebody's records. Measured: the question sits at byte 1,500 and the
`UPDATE … "cancelled"` at 2,391, so the window reached **209 characters past
the write**, with exactly one `exit();` in between. It now asks the question
actually meant — **is the refusal before the write?** — which needs no window
and no brace walk, and which a refusal added after the write cannot satisfy.
**Honest limit: no plant was found that fooled the old window form, so this
rests on the arithmetic and on the better property, not on a demonstrated
failure.** Deleting the gate's own `exit();` turns the new form red (planted).

The remaining four are sound and left alone; a shared block-cutting helper
across the self-tests is its own piece of work.

**Found, not built — raised as its own issue.** The in-string blindness is
wider than #743: a **bare** address with no `.php` in it is invisible to
`check_site_aware_addresses.py` in exactly the same way, and that is #536's
rule, where the harm is quieter — a bare `/page` drops the organisation's part
of the address. A probe over every page found **nothing with that fault today**
(its two candidates were a plain literal and a regular expression's own `/i`
delimiter, which is itself the cry-wolf trap to avoid), so the gate could be
tightened with no pending list. Left for its own package because that check is
a hard gate with `--strict` and an empty pending list, and changing what blocks
other people's work deserves its own independent check.

## [Unreleased] (alpha)
<!-- #475 part 1 -->

### The two newest database versions are proved, three customer-facing sentences were untrue, and something now watches for end of life (#475 part 1)

**MySQL 9.7.4 and MariaDB 12.3.3 both pass all seven phases of the migration
harness and all 42 of its checks** — the same 42 that pass on MySQL 8.0.36,
8.4.11 and MariaDB 11.4.13, counted rather than assumed. **Nothing in this
repository had ever been run on MySQL 9.x or MariaDB 12.x before**, so
`DbServer::MYSQL_SUPPORTED_SERIES` and `MARIADB_SUPPORTED_SERIES` had been
naming them as supported on the strength of nobody having tried. Both are now
in `e2e-migrations.yml`'s matrix, which runs five jobs side by side.

**MySQL 8.0 stays accepted, with a warning — the owner's decision, 3 November
2026.** Offered the choice between refusing a database that no longer gets
security fixes and carrying on with a warning, the owner chose the warning. So
`DbServer::MIN_MYSQL` stays `8.0.0` and `MIN_MARIADB` stays `10.6.0`, although
MySQL 8.0's support ended on 30 April 2026 and MariaDB 10.6's on 6 July 2026.
**That is a decision, not an oversight: do not "tidy" those two constants
upwards.** It also makes the warning the only protection there is, which is why
the next part matters.

**Two sentences the portal shows a customer were untrue, and both were found by
reading the real output rather than the code.**

* Every MariaDB answer said this project's automated tests "only ever run
  against MySQL" — **eight days after the migration harness began replaying
  every database change on MariaDB 11.4** (#487).
* Every supported-MySQL answer said the tests "run against the MySQL 8.0 line,
  so if you are on something newer you are ahead of what is routinely tested
  here" — which told somebody on MySQL 9.7 that nobody had tested their
  version, when 9.7 is tested.

Both were stale in the modest direction, which is the safer one, and a
customer-facing sentence that is untrue is a fault whichever way it points —
the next one to go stale could as easily say a version is tested when nothing
runs on it. Two more copies of the same claim were in the class's own docblock
and in the MySQL 8.0 message ("this is the version everything here is tested
against"), and one in `db-server-selftest.php`'s comments. All five corrected.

**The cure is that the sentence is now DERIVED, and the list is CHECKED.**
`DbServer::TESTED_LINES` names the release lines the harness really runs on,
`testedLinesCaveat()` is the one place the sentence is built, and it now
differs **by line** — because that is what is true: the harness runs on MariaDB
11.4 and 12.3 and on none of 10.6, 10.11 or 11.8, which the portal still
accepts. The new hard gate `tools/audit-checks/check_tested_db_lines.py`
compares the constant with the workflow's own matrix and **fails both ways**,
with no exception list, because there is no honest reason for the two to
differ. For a tested line the wording is "replays every one of its database
changes on it and checks the result", never "supported", and it still says out
loud that nobody runs this portal on MariaDB in production.

**PHP 8.5 is now linted.** `php-static-analysis.yml` ran `php -l` on 8.4 only,
so the version the portal *recommends* (`PhpRuntime::PREFERRED_SERIES`) was
never checked by the gate that exists to stop a syntax error reaching a
customer. Both versions now run **as two steps in one job**, deliberately not
as a matrix: a matrix would rename the check to "PHP -l lint (8.4)" and orphan
the branch rule that requires "PHP -l lint", leaving every pull request into
`main` waiting for a check that never arrives. All 906 PHP files under `web/`
are clean on 8.5.11 locally.

**And something watches for end of life now**, which #475 asked for:
`tools/check-end-of-life.py` reads the supported-version lists **out of**
`DbServer` and `PhpRuntime` — never a second copy — and compares them with
endoflife.date. It is not in `tools/audit-checks/` because it needs the
internet, and everything in that folder must run offline so the pre-push hook
can run all of them in about nine seconds. `end-of-life-watch.yml` runs it
monthly, keeps exactly **one** issue, rewrites that issue's body every run so it
is always current, and comments **only when the findings change** — because a
real finding here stays true for months, and a monthly comment about the same
fact is how an issue stops being read. A run that cannot reach endoflife.date
**fails the monthly run**, and says that run proves nothing — but it
deliberately does **not** fail a pull request, because somebody else's website
being down is not a fault in the change under review, and a check that goes red
for reasons outside the change gets ignored. The workflow's own comment says
so; an earlier draft of this entry asserted the "fails" half unqualified.

It earned its place on the first run: **PHP 8.4 loses active support on
31 December 2026**, and `PhpRuntime::MIN_PHP` is 8.4.0. (This entry said
"58 days away" and the commit message said 57. The house rule is not to quote
a count in prose at all: run the check.) Two other
things it found, neither urgent: MySQL now has year-based release lines (26.7,
26.10) above the 9.7 we record as newest known, and MariaDB has 13.0.

Planting found a real fault in the watcher itself, and it is the repeat this
repository keeps recording: with the site unreachable it printed "Nothing we
support is within the warning window" **directly underneath** "COULD NOT ASK".
The exit code was right and the words asserted the comforting half of a thing
it had just said it could not establish. It now says so, for every product, and
never reassures.

**THE INDEPENDENT CHECK FOUND NINE MORE, AND THE FIRST TWO ARE THE ONES TO
REMEMBER.**

**1. The new hard gate ran in NO WORKFLOW AT ALL** — the #646 shape re-created
in the very package that cites #646, and of all 56 audit scripts it was the
only one. **The cause is a standing fact about this repository that I got
wrong: `pr-security.yml` names every audit script INDIVIDUALLY, and there is no
folder glob in any workflow here.** `.githooks/pre-push` *does* glob the
folder, which is what misled me — but that hook is turned on per clone and
`git push --no-verify` skips it. So four documents called it "a hard gate"
while the only thing running it was a local hook. It is now a step in
`pr-security.yml`. **A new script under `tools/audit-checks/` is not wired up
until it is named in that file.**

**2. The gate could be switched off by an ordinary COMMENT.** It matched its
pattern over the whole file and took the first match, so a comment recording
the constant's previous value — which the house style actively asks for
("record what was tried and rejected") — was read instead of the real
constant. A line the portal claimed and nothing tested then passed with `OK`
and exit 0: precisely the direction the check's own header calls "the
dangerous direction and the reason this is a hard gate". Comments are blanked
now, in both readers, keeping every line and column so reported line numbers
stay right (#716's remedy). Three plants: a `//` block showing the old value, a
`/* */` block, and a commented-out matrix entry in the YAML. **And blanking
them introduced a second fault immediately:** the blanked lines became pure
whitespace and `^(\s*)include:` matched across them, so the "indentation" came
out as 1,918 characters. `[ \t]` now, never `\s`, which matches a newline.

**3. The sentence this package exists to fix was pinned by NOTHING.** Planting
`return '';` at the top of `testedLinesCaveat()` removed the caveat from every
answer, and `db-server-selftest.php` still passed 36 of 36 — because the one
clause that claimed to guard it **could not fail**: it tested
`$got['untested'] !== true`, and `'untested' => true` is set for every MariaDB
answer, so the condition was unfalsifiable, and it was never about the sentence
anyway. The test now reads the sentence itself and asks the only question that
matters — does what the customer is told match `TESTED_LINES`? Proved by
planting: that same `return '';` now fails it.

**4. "`testedLinesCaveat()` is the one place the sentence is built" was untrue,
and the exception was the one line the gate cannot protect.** The MySQL 8.0
branch hand-wrote "this is one of the versions tested here". That matters
beyond tidiness: #475's direction is to stop accepting MySQL 8.0, and **the day
8.0 leaves the matrix the gate forces `'8.0'` out of `TESTED_LINES` and goes
green**, while a hand-written sentence would go on telling every 8.0 customer
their version is tested. Derived now.

**5. "An honest caveat goes on every answer" was untrue in both halves.** Of
six MySQL branches exactly one carried it. It goes on **three** kinds of answer
— every MariaDB answer, every supported-MySQL answer, and the MySQL 8.0 answer
— and each absence now has a stated reason: a version too old to install, or a
preview build nobody should put real data on, is not improved by a sentence
about what is tested, because it invites somebody to stay.

**6. `db-server-selftest.php` still carried the untrue sentence this entry said
had been corrected** ("every MariaDB answer must admit that nothing here is
tested against MariaDB"), five lines from the claim "all five corrected". The
shape `.claude/CLAUDE.md` names: a document asserting a fix while stating the
thing it fixed is worse than one that says nothing.

**7. The watcher would have closed its issue, with an all-clear, on the day the
thing it warned about happened.** Measured by moving the date: PHP 8.4 answers
`soon` on 30 December 2026 and `fine` on the 31st, because its security fixes
run to 2028 — so the run would exit 0, the close step would fire, and the only
durable record of the finding would go, under the words "Nothing this portal
says it supports is now within the warning window", while `MIN_PHP` was still
8.4.0. `security-only` is its own state now and is reportable, as is `unknown`
— whose exclusion had made the header's "silence is not success" a promise the
code did not keep.

**8. One commit held two contradictory statements about MySQL 26.x.**
`DbServer`'s comment said the year-based numbering "has NOT been confirmed
here" while this package's own documents and its new tool reported it. The
comment is corrected, and says plainly that `MYSQL_NEWEST_KNOWN` stays at 9.7
on purpose — 9.7 is the newest *long-term* line, and nothing here has been run
on a 26.x server — with the measurable cost stated: somebody on MySQL 26.7,
whose support ended on 20 October 2026, is told `ok`.

**9. A docblock documented the wrong function.** The new method was inserted
between `series()`'s docblock and `series()`.

Smaller things fixed in the same round: the second lint step now **asserts** PHP
8.5 is really active rather than printing `php -v` and checking nothing; the
watcher's issue lookup no longer turns a GitHub API failure into "no issue
found", which would have opened a duplicate; closing that issue also adds
`status: done`, as the standing rule requires; the job summary stopped pasting
an expression into a shell script two steps below a comment saying not to; the
derived sentence says "its database tests" rather than "its automated tests",
because `TESTED_LINES` describes the migration harness alone; the install
guide's "those four are the ones the portal's own tests really run against" was
wrong (five lines are tested, MySQL 8.0 among them); `feed-importer-selftest.php`
carried the same stale MariaDB claim in a file the sweep never opened; and an
unreachable branch now says it is a deliberate backstop.

## [Unreleased] (alpha)
<!-- #745 -->

### Every security gate stopped running a week ago, and one `${{ }}` was why (#745)

**"PR Security Checks" had failed on every push since 28 October 2026 with no
jobs at all** — so every hard gate in that file (thirty-five steps whose names
say so: the PHP lint, the two-factor gate
order, the account-change guard, the reserved-word check, the personal-data
coverage check and the rest) ran on GitHub for a week without running anything.
It had succeeded 234 times before that, twelve of them on the version of the
script this change replaced. (**An earlier draft of this entry, and commit
`812d992`'s message, said "eleven times"** — that was the number of RUNS in
October 2026, nine of them successful, read as a count of successes. Corrected
after the independent check counted them: `gh api --paginate
'.../actions/workflows/pr-security.yml/runs?per_page=100' -q
'.workflow_runs[].conclusion' | sort | uniq -c`.)

**The cause.** GitHub's Actions service puts a ceiling of 21,000 characters on
any single value that carries a `${{ ... }}` inside it, and a step's script is
one value. The "Heuristic anti-pattern scan" script held two of them, on its
ninth and tenth lines, so the whole script counted. Commit `c61211e`
(27 October) took that script from 14,910 characters to 24,525 — over the
ceiling — and GitHub then refused the entire file before starting any job.

**Nothing here could see it, which is why it lasted a week.** The file is valid
YAML and every parser on this machine accepted it. **actionlint accepted it too,
and still does** — the ceiling belongs to GitHub's service, not to the workflow
schema — so the "Lint Workflows" job was green on every one of those failing
days. The only sign on GitHub is a run with zero jobs, the words "This run
likely failed because of a workflow file issue", and the run named after the
**file path** instead of "PR Security Checks", which is the real giveaway:
GitHub falls back to the path when it cannot read the file.

**The fix** (`812d992`): the two commit names come in through `env:`, so the
script itself holds no `${{ ... }}` and has no ceiling on it. That is also the
safer way round and GitHub's own hardening advice — never paste a `${{ ... }}`
straight into a shell script, because whatever the value holds becomes part of
the script. Proved by pushing: before the fix every push to the branch produced
an error run for the file, and the push carrying the fix produced none.

**TWO THINGS THIS DOES NOT CLAIM, both raised by the independent check.**
First, the file is **readable** again — the gates themselves have **not run**.
`pr-security.yml` triggers on `pull_request` only, there is no open pull
request, and its last completed run was 26 October. Given that this package
exists because checks looked wired and were not (#646), that distinction is the
whole point: nothing here proves the thirty-five gates pass, only that GitHub
will read the file again. Second, **the loss was the GitHub half, not all of
it.** `.githooks/pre-push` arrived on 29 October (`1e4da0e`) and globs
`tools/audit-checks/*.py`, so from the outage's second day every audit-check
script still ran locally before every push. What really went unrun for the week
is what only GitHub does: the PHP lint on a clean runner, gitleaks, the inline
heuristic greps, and the pull-request comment — plus everything, including the
audit scripts, for the first two days.

**The guard**, because a note in a comment is not a check:
`tools/audit-checks/check_workflow_expression_length.py` fails when a script
carrying a `${{ ... }}` goes over the ceiling, when a workflow file goes over
GitHub's 500 KB file limit, and when a script with no expression is over the
ceiling anyway and is not listed in `LONG_SCRIPTS_ON_PURPOSE` with a reason —
that list fails BOTH ways, so it cannot quietly stop describing the code. It
runs in the pre-push hook (which globs `tools/audit-checks/`) and as a hard gate
in `lint.yml`. **It cannot live in `pr-security.yml`: a workflow cannot run from
a file GitHub will not read.** Planted faults, named rather than counted, because
which shapes were tried matters and a number does not: an expression put back
into the long script; a one-line `run:` over the ceiling; a `.yaml` file; a
`${{` inside a shell comment; a `run: >` folded script; a renamed step; a
script shortened below the ceiling with its allow-list entry left behind; a
file over 500 KB; and — found by the independent check, each of which the first
version MISSED while printing OK — a trailing comment on the `run: |` line, a
quoted `"run":` key, and a step whose first key is `run:`. **The first of those
three is the one that matters: adding a comment to the very script the guard
protects switched the guard off, silently.** Each plant was restored
byte-identically. Planting also found a real wording fault in the guard, which
told the reader to delete an allow-list entry that was still correct.

**What this does not do.** It does not measure a long `${{ ... }}` in a `with:`,
`env:` or `if:` value, which would hit the same ceiling — nothing here is near
it, and doing it properly needs a YAML parser this machine has not got. And the
24,500-character script is still a 24,500-character script: splitting it into a
file under `tools/` is better engineering and is its own piece of work.

## [Unreleased] (alpha)
<!-- #492 parts 2, 3 and 4 -->

### Erasure: the borrower, the registration's subject, and the claimant (#492 parts 2, 3 and 4, migration 246)

Three follow-ups from `4349c76`, all three decided by the owner on 3 November 2026.

**Part 2 — the borrower is the person a loan record is about.** `assets/loan.php`
hides only the three counterparty pickers, so the free-text "Contact details"
box is shown for every kind of borrower, and `AssetRegister::createLoanRequest()`
stores it whatever the kind. So a MEMBER's own telephone number sat on a row that
named their account, and an erasure emptied the account number and left the
telephone number beside it. **The classification was the fault, not the guard:**
`tblAssetLoans.counterpartyUserID` has left `GdprEraser::ACTOR_COLUMNS` and
stayed in `LINK_COLUMNS`, and `counterpartyName` and `counterpartyContact` are
now emptied. `approvedByID` and `requestedByID` STAY actor columns — emptying
text on an approver's number is a blanket `= NULL` over the borrower's details
on every loan they ever approved. No migration: both columns were already
nullable (read out of a loaded MySQL 8.0.36). `counterpartyName` is named by the
instruction and CAN NEVER MATCH, because a loan records its counterparty as
EITHER an account OR that typed name and never both; the limit is in the
instruction's reason, the #708/#723 precedent, because the #635 check fails a
column explained in `notEmptiedHere` while an instruction empties it — that
check went red on the first run of this change and is what moved the sentence.

**Part 3 — a registration records who it is FOR as well as who typed it.**
`calendar/event-register-save.php` recorded whoever was signed in, with no test
of their relationship to the person being registered. Because an erasure DELETES
a registration rather than merely unnaming it — the row holds the registered
person's name, date of birth, allergies and medical notes — erasing a volunteer
who had registered somebody else's child **deleted that child's registration**,
and that child's family had asked for nothing. Migration 246 adds
`tblEventRegistrations.registeredForUserID`, which says whose record it is; the
delete goes on that and the submitter is merely detached. The public form now
asks a signed-in person whether the registration is their own, with neither
answer pre-selected. **For rows that already existed the person who typed one in
is treated as the person it is for** (the owner: true of anyone who registered
themselves, which is most of them; where a volunteer typed one the child's name
is still on it). Rejected, with the reason: matching the typed name to an
account, because a wrong match attaches one person's record to another.
`tblEventRegistrations` has accordingly left
`GdprEraser::DELETE_ON_ACTOR_COLUMN` — nothing on that table is deleted because
of what somebody DID any more — and the data download now reads both columns, so
it hands back what the erasure removes.

**Part 4 — the claimant's identity stays, as a decision.**
`tblExpenseClaims.userID` is `INT NOT NULL`, so "we keep the claimant for six
years for HMRC" was an accident of the schema rather than anybody's decision. No
schema change; the reason is written into the catalogue and the in-app help as a
deliberate retention decision. **And the old wording was untrue in the
reassuring direction**: both the catalogue and the help page said the claimant's
name "is removed" / "comes off the claim". It is not — the erasure tries, the
database refuses, and the sealed trail records a step that could do nothing
("nothing could be emptied: the database does not allow userID to be empty…",
measured on MySQL 8.0.36). Both now say the claimant is kept, say why, and say
that the attempt fails.

**Also corrected, found while writing the help page:** that page still listed a
room booking's stated reason and decline note under "not reached, which is a
fault rather than a decision". #723 fixed both on 3 November and the page had not
been brought into line — a document asserting a fault that has been repaired.

<!-- #472 and #581: the restore, and a snapshot taken at one moment -->

### A snapshot says whether it was read at one moment in time (#581)

`DbBackup::snapshot()` already asked the database for one consistent view of
every table. It now asks whether it was really **given** one, and writes the
answer into the manifest as `one_moment` (`yes`, `no` or `cannot tell`). The
snapshot's own result says so at once, the Backup page badges a snapshot that
was not read at one moment, the Inspect page carries the whole sentence, and a
restore repeats it to whoever is putting the snapshot back. Nothing is refused
over it: a snapshot taken while nobody was using the portal is unaffected, and
the fault it warns about already shows up as a row pointing at a row that is not
in the snapshot, which the restore refuses by itself.

### The Backup page says whether anything is really calling the backup job (#581)

`cron/backup-run` records every call it accepts, in a file beside the snapshots.
The Backup page then says, in one sentence from `DbBackup::scheduleWords()`,
whether the hosting company's scheduler is calling the portal — or that nothing
ever has. The setting ships as `daily`, so until now every new installation
showed "Every day" chosen in a box while, on most of them, nothing was calling
the job at all.

### Fixed in passing

`tools/audit-checks/check_event_visibility.py`'s allowlist entry for
`DbBackup.php` is keyed by line number and was moved by the header addition
above.

<!-- #491, #492 and #481 -->

### Fixed

- **One organisation's setting no longer clears out every organisation's
  history (#491).** The activity-log and error clear-outs read one pair of
  settings through `App::settings()` — the current organisation's value — and
  then deleted across the whole installation. An administrator of one
  organisation choosing "keep activity logs for 7 days" shortened every other
  organisation's history, including one that had deliberately chosen a year;
  and run from the scheduled job, which has no current organisation at all,
  whichever value happened to resolve decided for everybody. Both clear-outs
  now loop the organisations and ask `log_retention_days()` for each, the same
  shape the registration, check-in, giving, webhook and transcript sweeps
  already use. Records belonging to **no** organisation — written before the
  organisation was decided, written by a scheduled job, or left behind when an
  organisation was deleted — are cleared by the installation's own figure
  rather than kept for ever. Each organisation's figure is held to what the
  installation allows (#668's three tiers), and the cap is in the reader the
  clear-out uses, because a save-time cap is not a cap. The Retention page now
  shows the visiting administrator's own organisation's figure and the
  installation's beside it.

- **Replaying a migration no longer switches an app back on (#481).**
  `008_calendar_events_schema.sql`, `009_attendance_schema.sql` and
  `017_leadership.sql` forced four settings with plain `UPDATE` statements, and
  the installation wizard replays every numbered migration over an existing
  database — so an administrator who had switched Calendar, Attendance or
  Leadership off found it on again after an upgrade retry, and a customised
  calendar icon was replaced by the default. All four are now the house seed
  idiom (`INSERT … ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE settingKey = settingKey`), which
  leaves an existing row completely alone, exactly as #466 corrected
  migrations 012 and 021. Nothing is lost: the values they forced are what
  `full_schema.sql` seeds and what migration 225 corrected the stored default
  to. **Nothing can be done for a database where a replay has already
  overwritten a chosen value** — the old statement left no record of what was
  there before.

### Changed

- The personal-data catalogue's reason for `tblAssetLoans.counterpartyContact`
  was untrue of the commonest case and is corrected (#492). It said an erasure
  could not reach the column because an outside borrower need not have an
  account; in fact the loan form shows that box whichever kind of counterparty
  is chosen, so it is routinely a member's own telephone number on a row that
  names their account. The reason now says what really stops it being emptied,
  and that the decision is on #492.

<!-- #583: the backup and off-site pages, and the disaster-recovery help -->

### Fixed

- **The disaster-recovery help page told a customer to use tools the portal
  does not have, and one of its instructions would have destroyed every
  integration secret (#583, item (g)).** `/help/disaster-recovery` is the first
  page somebody opens when something has gone wrong, and four of the seven
  items in its "Common failure modes" list were untrue:
  - "Stolen credentials — clear every session, force password reset, rotate
    `enc.key` …". There is **no** button that signs everybody out and **none**
    that makes everybody choose a new password: both are #582, a feature
    request, not built. And replacing `_auth_keys/enc.key` by hand is the one
    thing the runbook spends a whole section (7.9) forbidding — nothing
    re-encrypts what that key protects, so every integration's secret and every
    person's two-factor sign-in becomes unreadable the moment it is swapped.
    The item now says what works today, warns against the key swap in bold, and
    points at the two integration pages that really do let an administrator
    replace a credential.
  - It cited "runbook section 4.4", which has not existed since the runbook was
    reorganised under #488. The link's own anchor had already been corrected to
    `#7-after-a-break-in`; only the words a reader sees were left behind, so the
    link text and the page it opened disagreed.
  - "Disk full — … prune `_uploads/photos/queue/` older than 30 days" told a
    customer to do exactly what the runbook forbids ("Do not delete anything
    under `_uploads/` by hand. The database points at those files."). It is not
    merely stale, it is destructive: a queued photo has a `tblPhoto` row whose
    `filePath` is `queue/<name>` and whose status is `pending_approval`, so
    following that advice throws away members' photos still waiting for a
    moderator and leaves the rows pointing at nothing.
  - "Compromised account — Disable user + revoke sessions, then run the
    offboarding flow." "Revoke sessions" names nothing — there is no session
    revocation anywhere under `web/` — and it is no longer needed, because
    `Auth::ensureSession()` ends the session of an account that has been
    switched off. Offboarding is the route for somebody genuinely leaving;
    pointed at a victim's account it erases their records rather than protecting
    them.
  - "DB connection lost — … check DreamHost status" named one customer's
    hosting company as though it were everybody's (#500).
- **The same page's first recovery step no longer implies the holding page says
  what you tell it to (#583).** `Maintenance::renderHoldingPage()` always prints
  "<portal> is being upgraded" after whatever message is stored, so a portal
  closed because of an intrusion tells its members it is being upgraded unless
  the administrator types something of their own. The card now says so. The
  hard-coded sentence itself is #583 item (f) and is **not** fixed.

---

- **Fixed — the holding page says WHICH of the two reasons the portal is closed for (#583 item f)**
  - `Maintenance::isActive()` answers true for two different reasons — an explicit flag an
    administrator or the installer set, or a database upgrade waiting — and the page said
    **"is being upgraded" in both.** A visitor told the portal is being upgraded when an
    administrator has simply closed it is told something untrue, and the sentence promised an ending
    the portal cannot know.
  - **A waiting upgrade WINS, and my first version had that backwards.** The Upgrade page sets the
    flag *itself* while it works, so during a real upgrade both reasons are true at once — and asking
    about the flag alone would have told visitors an administrator had switched the portal off.
    Found by a test that could then not tell the two sentences apart; measured, not reasoned.
  - **Nothing tested the wording at all before this**, which is why it could be wrong for however
    long it was: the existing checks prove the page *appears* (503 and its heading) and that one
    withdrawn sentence is gone. "It appears" and "it says something true" are different questions,
    and only the first had an answer.
  - **It took three tries to make the fixture real**, and that is the lesson worth keeping. Checking
    both branches at the end of `upgrade-pages-selftest.php` gave **HTTP 302**, because by then every
    migration is recorded and the portal is correctly *open*. Winding the recorded version back was
    not enough either — **being behind is not the same as having something waiting**, which is the
    #499 distinction the portal is built on. The upgrade branch is checked at the one moment the test
    genuinely has a half-failed migration; the flag branch at the end, where nothing is waiting.
<!-- #727: gating a feature is a capability, not a hard-coded role -->

### A feature can be gated on a role an organisation created (#727, migration 243)

`Portal\Core\Capabilities` is the one place a gated "capability" is declared,
the one place an organisation's chosen roles for it are read or written, and
the one place "may this person do this?" is answered. A capability is a door a
person recognises — "decide the free text an erasure cannot" — rather than a
line of PHP, and an organisation can point it at roles of its own from
Admin → Roles without anybody editing code, which a customer on shared hosting
cannot do.

- **Any-of, never all-of.** A capability holds zero or more role keys and
  holding any ONE of them opens the door.
- **An organisation that never opens the page sees no change.** With nothing
  chosen, the roles in force are the ones the capability ships with — the same
  role its hard-coded gate used.
- **The empty set is allowed and must be confirmed in as many words**, with the
  capability's own sentence about what it costs. It is never permanent: the page
  that changes a mapping is gated on `App::isAdmin()` and on no capability, so
  any administrator can put it back. **Both halves of that are now checked** —
  check J of `check_capability_registry.py` refuses a capability being asked
  anywhere under `web/_apps/admin/roles/`, and check P pins the administrator
  gate itself in both files of that page, which nothing did until the
  independent check turned it into `if (false)` with every test green.
- **A capability can declare that it does NOT fall open for a global
  administrator**, which is what makes #724's erasure-review gate expressible
  as a capability at all. Its two files now ask
  `App::can(Capabilities::ERASURE_REVIEW)`, and a global administrator who has
  not been granted the Data Controller role is still refused.
- **The installation can reserve a capability to itself** (`capabilities.locked`,
  installation-wide), because the two administrator levels may be different
  parties.
- Deleting a role that is the LAST one opening a capability is refused, naming
  the door to point elsewhere first.
- `Capabilities::NOT_YET_ASKED` — the list a capability sits in while its gate
  is still hard-coded — is **empty**, because all five of the capabilities that
  were written down there on the morning of 3 November 2026 had their gates
  converted the same day (see the next entry). It is kept, not deleted: it is
  where the next one goes.
- New: `tblCapabilityMap`, `tblCapabilityMapRole`,
  `tools/audit-checks/check_capability_registry.py` (a hard gate),
  `tools/capabilities-selftest.php` and `tools/role-gate-count.php` (which
  counts the remaining hard-coded gates with PHP's tokeniser, because four
  documents had quoted a `grep` figure as a fact). **Count a test's checks from
  its own last line, never from here.**

---


### Added
- **Five more features can be pointed at a role an organisation created
  (#727).** The asset register, the pastoral care register, children's
  check-in, the treasury side of expenses and the livestream chat moderation
  queue are now gated on a *capability* rather than on a role key typed into
  PHP. 49 gates across 48 files were converted, and
  `web/_core/Capabilities.php` is still the ONE place that decides which roles
  open which door. An organisation that never opens Admin → Roles sees **no
  difference**: each capability ships pointing at the role its hard-coded gate
  used.
- All five declare `globalAdminFallsOpen => true`, which is the owner's
  decision of 3 November 2026 — "organisational global admin having automatic
  access to everything, who can then re-assign later". #724's erasure review
  keeps `false` and is the one door a global administrator does not open
  without the role.

### Changed
- The live chat moderation handler's refusal no longer names the
  `stream_moderator` role ("You need to be an administrator, or hold a role
  that may moderate the livestream chat"), because which roles open it is now
  the organisation's own choice. `tools/live-chat-moderation-selftest.php` was
  updated with it.
- `Capabilities` now remembers *which roles open a door here* for the rest of
  one request. A person's answer is never remembered, so granting a role still
  takes effect on the next call.

### Fixed
- `Capabilities::definition()` throws, naming the capability and the field,
  when an entry leaves a field out. There is no default for any field, because
  `globalAdminFallsOpen` is true for five capabilities and false for one.

<!-- #685 and #722: a limit the clear-out really uses -->

### Fixed

- **An organisation already over the attendance retention limit is now held to
  the installation's figure (#685).** #668 part 1 made
  `/admin/settings/attendance` refuse a longer period; it did nothing about the
  organisations that already had one, and the nightly clear-out reads the stored
  value. So attendance personal data could still be kept ten years on an
  installation intending ninety days — in every database that predates the
  check, and in any that got such a row by hand or from a whole-database
  restore. `AnonymousCheckins::readRetentionDays()` now asks
  `SettingLimit::cappedForSite()`, so the reader caps as well as the form. **It
  shortens retention of data already held**, which is the safe direction for
  privacy and is still a change to what happens to existing rows; both pages
  that show the figure now say when a stored figure is being held down.
- **An installation that chose "keep transcripts for ever" really keeps them
  (#722).** `TranscriptRetention::daysForSite()` worked its own three-tier
  arithmetic out against `installationAllows()`, which never answers 0 — it
  hands back the hard maximum, because what a form's `max` needs is a number of
  days. So "for ever" was impossible and every transcript was deleted at ten
  years, under a branch in `run_transcript_sweep()` whose comment said it kept
  them: a guarantee the code had forgotten to implement. The arithmetic now goes
  through `SettingLimit::cappedForSite()`.
- **Admin, Transcription prefilled 3650 where the installation had chosen "for
  ever"**, so the "Kept for ever." sentence could never print and a plain Save
  over an untouched form turned for-ever into ten years. The page asks both of
  #668's questions now.
- **Admin, Maintenance, Retention printed the uncapped figure.** It read the
  merged settings array, so after #685 it would have stated a period the
  clear-out does not use — on the page whose job is to say what the clear-out
  will do. It asks `readRetentionDays()` now.

### Added

- **A per-organisation transcript retention page (#722, migration 244).**
  `/admin/settings/transcription`, for an organisation's own administrator. One
  field: how long this organisation keeps the written-out words of a recording,
  up to — never beyond — what the installation allows. An empty box means
  "follow the installation" and removes the organisation's own row, which is the
  limitation the attendance page states and cannot fix. The save re-reads the
  ceiling live with the installation's own row locked inside the transaction
  that writes (#687, #647), refuses with the reason rather than clamping, and
  records both the refusal and the save.
- **`tools/retention-caps-selftest.php`** (56 checks), wired into
  `tools/run-all-selftests.sh` and `portal-selftests.yml`: the clear-out's own
  readers against rows put in by SQL, and the lock proved from a second process.
- **Section T of `tools/transcription-pages-selftest.php`** (12 checks, 165 in
  all): the new page over real HTTP.

---
<!-- #724: the Data Controller role and the erasure review -->
### Added

- **The free text an erasure cannot decide about on its own now gets a human
  decision, and a request cannot be completed without one (#724).** Seven
  columns hold text where the right answer depends on the request in front of
  you: "Jane's laptop" on a licence seat is somebody's name, and "spare
  projector" on the next row is not. A person holding the new `data_controller`
  role opens **Erasure review**, sees each line, and chooses — empty it, or keep
  it. Until every line is decided, pressing Execute on the request changes
  **nothing at all** and writes a line on the report saying who can deal with it
  and where.
  - `Portal\Core\ErasureReview` is the one place that says which columns need a
    look (read from `_core/personal-data-catalogue.php`, never a second list)
    and the one place a decision is recorded and acted on.
  - New table `tblErasureReviewDecisions` (migration 242). It holds **no text**:
    which row was judged, which of the two answers, who decided and when.
  - New pages `/admin/erasure-requests/review` and its save handler.
  - New hard gate `tools/audit-checks/check_erasure_review_items.py`; new test
    `tools/erasure-review-selftest.php` (91 checks on a real database).

### Changed

- `GdprEraser::execute()` asks before anything changes, and
  `GdprEraser::closeRequest()` asks again inside the transaction that closes a
  request.
- `tools/gdpr-eraser-selftest.php` leaves the seven reviewable columns empty
  when it builds its made-up world, so its 267 checks still exercise the walk
  rather than the review (which has its own test).

### Fixed

- The fold block for migration 241 in `full_schema.sql` claimed
  "`installFinish()` grants it instead". **There is no such function**
  (`grep -rn installFinish web tools` finds nothing), and the installer creates
  the first administrator at step 4, *after* step 3 has loaded the install
  script and replayed every migration — so on a fresh install nobody holds the
  `data_controller` role. The comment now says so. See the issue below.

---

## For CHANGELOG.md

* **The erasure review counts without a limit and shows a page (#724).** `ErasureReview` separated
  counting from showing. `whyNotReadyToClose()` asks the new `countUndecided()`, which counts in the
  database with no limit, so a request refuses while any undecided line remains anywhere; the page
  shows at most `SHOW_AT_MOST` (500) lines per column, undecided first, and SAYS how many there are
  and how many it is showing. `record()` looks one line up directly rather than searching that list,
  so a line past the page-full can still be decided.
* **The review is narrowed to one organisation (#724, the owner, 3 November 2026).** Every
  reviewable table that records a `siteID` is narrowed to the organisation the request was filed in.
  The two that record none are shown and labelled as not tied to one organisation. The cost — a
  request for somebody in two organisations needs each organisation's own Data Controller — is in
  `ErasureReview::organisationScopeNote()`, printed on the page and appended to the refusal.
* **`tblErasureReviewDecisions.decidedByID` is really left empty when the decider is the subject
  (#724).** The audit line had always masked the number; the row stored it. Migration 242 and
  `full_schema.sql` changed with it (the column comment, and the header's wrong claim that this is
  the table that is never erased — `tblErasureAudit` is).
* **The installer's grant of the Data Controller role is really soft (#724).** A statement error is
  logged and the administrator is kept; before, it rolled the whole administrator creation back and
  said "nothing was saved".
* **An organisation created after install grants the role and says when nobody holds it (#724).**
* **`check_erasure_review_items.py` is a hard gate on every pull request (#724, #646's shape).**
* **"Add User" refuses a typed password with no sign-in name (#586 part two).** It used to drop the
  password and say "created successfully".
* **`admin/erasure/process.php` says what actually clears a review refusal (#724).**

<!-- #586: a password reported saved but not stored -->
### Fixed

- **Admin, edit a user: a new password is really stored now (#586).** Typing a new
  password for an account that had never had one reported `User "…" updated
  successfully.` and stored nothing: the handler looked for the account's sign-in row
  (`tblLocalAccounts`) and wrote the password only if it found one. An account made by
  an invitation nobody accepted, or one that signs in with Microsoft, Google or a
  passkey, has no such row — so an administrator setting somebody a password during an
  incident was told it had worked and that person still could not sign in. The handler
  now works out BEFORE anything is written whether the password can be stored: where the
  account has no other way in it creates the sign-in row (its e-mail address becomes the
  sign-in name, which is what the installer and the users API already do), and where it
  cannot it refuses the whole save and says why. Nothing is written and no success
  message is shown unless the database really holds a password afterwards, which is now
  read back inside the same transaction. New test: `tools/admin-password-selftest.php`
  (39 checks over real HTTP), wired into `portal-selftests.yml` and
  `tools/run-all-selftests.sh` with the change rather than later.

---
- **Fixed — a room booking's stated reason is emptied on an erasure request now (#723)**
  - **The classification was the fault, not the guard.** `tblResourceBooking.bookedByID` was in
    **both** `LINK_COLUMNS` and `ACTOR_COLUMNS`, and the coverage test refuses `nullCols` on an actor
    column — emptying a column on an actor-matched instruction is a blanket `= NULL` over every row it
    matches, which is how one person's erasure destroys a third party's details. That guard exists
    because seven tables were once set to delete a whole row on such a column, and it was **not**
    weakened to get this.
  - **A booking is made BY the person it is about**, so the owner decided on 3 November 2026 that the
    booker is the booking's subject. `bookedByID` has left `ACTOR_COLUMNS`; the booker's stated reason
    for wanting the room (`purpose`) and the note refusing them (`declineReason`) are emptied. The
    booking itself is kept, with its times, resource and status, because the room's history belongs to
    the organisation.
  - **Be exact about what that amounts to, because the first version of this entry was not.** It said
    "a room booking's own words", and an independent check showed that overstates it twice.
    **`tblResourceBooking.notes` is ALSO the booker's own words** — `_apps/resources/book.php` is its
    only writer and reads `$_POST['notes']` from the booker's own form, on the same row in the same
    request (`grep -rn "tblResourceBooking" web/ --include='*.php' | grep -iE "INSERT|UPDATE "` finds
    one INSERT there and two UPDATEs that touch only status, approver and approved-at). The catalogue
    said it was "the organisation's own note … rather than anything the booker wrote", which was
    simply false. **The owner was told exactly that on 3 November 2026 and chose to KEEP it**, so the
    catalogue now gives that as the reason rather than a description of the column that is untrue.
    And **`declineReason` is written by NOTHING** — the decline branch sets only status, approver and
    approved-at, and there is no form field for it — so its place in `nullCols` can never match. The
    limit is recorded in the instruction's own reason, which is the #708 precedent, rather than the
    column being dropped: if a decline reason is ever stored, the erasure already reaches it. **So
    what #723 actually empties of the booker's own words is `purpose`.**
  - **`approvedByID` STAYS an actor column, and that pair is the whole point of the two lists.**
    Emptying text on an approver's number would wipe the purpose of every booking they ever approved.
    The eraser self-test now holds a booking somebody **else** made and this person only approved:
    without it the reclassification could have been widened to both columns and every check would
    still have passed. Planted exactly that — it fails one check.
  - Rejected, so nobody re-opens it: a separate "who it is for" column. It models reality better — a
    booking can be made on somebody else's behalf — but it is a schema change plus every writer and
    reader, and nothing writes a booking for anybody but its maker. No migration was needed: both
    columns were already nullable.
- **Fixed — a part-written PDF an interrupted run left behind is reached by an erasure, and swept
  (#721)**
  - **This was a cost of #711's own fix, recorded at the time.** `Pdf::writeOrWhyNot()` writes under a
    temporary name and renames it into place, which is what stops a failed write destroying a good
    file. A process killed in between leaves `statement-7-2026.pdf.part-a1b2c3d4e5f6` behind, and
    `GdprEraser`'s glob was `statement-<donorId>-*.pdf` — which does **not** match it. A giving
    statement holds the donor's name, home address and every gift they have made.
  - **Before #711 the same crash left a truncated `statement-7-2026.pdf`, which DID match and was
    erased**, so this was a narrow regression in erasure reach taken in exchange for not destroying
    good files. One statement wide, needing a process killed inside a window of microseconds —
    unlikely rather than impossible, and exactly the kind of file an erasure exists to remove.
  - **The privacy half took TWO changes, not one, and an independent check is what found that.**
    Widening the glob to `*.pdf*` made the erasure **find** the stray file — and
    `statementFileIsKept()` then **kept it**, two ways round: with the keep set to "every gift" it
    answers "kept" for anything; and with it set to "receipted gifts only", the `-4` chop for `.pdf`
    left the period as `2026-01-01_2026-12-31.pdf.part-…`, which does not parse, so the "a name that
    gives no period is kept" fallback applied — to a file that is not a statement at all. Measured on
    the real method: the genuine statement was *not* kept and the rubble *was*. Worse, the step then
    **counted it and told the administrator it had been kept with the donor's giving records as tax
    evidence.** A file carrying `Pdf::PART_MARK` is a write that never finished, so it is evidence of
    nothing and is now always deleted — tested first, before the scope. **Nothing caught this because
    the test world never wrote a kept-donor row for the erased person**, so that whole branch was
    dead; the proof was inside the test, whose own fixture period does not parse either.
  - `Pdf::sweepPartFiles()` removes stray temporaries older than an hour in the nightly job, so they
    stop accumulating. The glob is the half with a
    privacy consequence; the sweep only wasted disk. **Never describe the sweep as what makes an
    erasure complete** — an erasure between the crash and the next sweep would otherwise still miss
    the file, which is the whole reason the glob was widened too.
  - **One hour** is the owner's choice. A statement PDF is written in well under a second, so the
    margin is some thousands of times over and no write in flight can be caught; the job runs nightly,
    so a shorter age buys nothing. The test gives it a file written **this second** and requires it to
    survive — that is the check that matters, because a sweep that took a live write would be worse
    than the litter it removes.
  - **`Pdf::PART_MARK` is the ONE place the mark is named**, because the writer and the sweep have to
    agree: two literals would be two places to change, and the one that mattered would be the sweep —
    it would simply stop finding anything, with no error, no log line and no symptom. The hard gate
    `check_pdf_write_verified.py` **went red on that change**, which is the gate doing its job; it now
    accepts the constant form and additionally fails when the constant is missing or empty.
  - **THE SWEEP DELETED A MEMBER'S OWN UPLOAD, and that was the worst thing in this package.** The
    first version swept the whole of `_uploads` for any name *containing* the mark, under a docblock
    saying "nothing else uses this mark today" — the reassurance, and false.
    `_apps/documents/upload.php` and `_apps/recordings/upload.php` take the stored file's extension
    **straight from the client filename** with no allow-list, and
    `pathinfo('report.part-x', PATHINFO_EXTENSION)` is `part-x`, so a member who uploaded
    `report.part-x` had it stored as `20261103_082700_aabbccdd.part-x` and **deleted an hour later** —
    while the database row survived, so the portal went on offering a file that was gone, with nothing
    logged. `.part` is what download managers call an unfinished file, so an accident was as likely as
    an attack.
  - **The owner chose both guards (3 November 2026) and neither is enough alone.**
    `Pdf::PART_FOLDERS` is the one list of folders the sweep may touch — the four
    `Pdf::create()` really writes to, read one by one; `documents` and `recordings` are deliberately
    absent. And the name must **end** with the mark plus exactly twelve hexadecimal characters, the
    shape the writer builds, so rubble like `notes.part-x` inside a swept folder survives too. Belt
    and braces on purpose, because this method deletes and a one-condition guard rests on nobody
    editing that condition.
  - Symbolic links are **not** followed, in two ways that are both needed: the iterator is built
    without `FOLLOW_SYMLINKS`, so a symlinked **folder** is not recursed into, and `isLink()` skips a
    symlinked **file**. Either alone leaves a way out of the root. And `CATCH_GET_CHILD` is there
    because without it one unreadable subfolder makes the whole walk throw and the sweep removes
    nothing at all — measured.
  - **FOUR of section H's checks could not fail, and planting found every one.** The "it leaves a real
    PDF alone" fixture was created and never aged, so the age guard was doing the mark test's work —
    removing the mark test left all 31 checks green while a day-old giving statement, an expense PDF,
    a document and a recording were all deleted. The symlink check planted a link to a *file*, which
    `isLink()` skips whatever the iterator flags are, so adding `FOLLOW_SYMLINKS` passed. Nothing
    exercised the folder list, and nothing exercised an unreadable folder. All four are pinned now,
    and each plant fails the check named for it.
  - **And the whole suite caught a stale pin that no test in this package could.**
    `tools/erasure-pages-selftest.php` found the booking on the room page and in the approvals queue
    by searching for **the booker's own words** — the very text #723 now erases, so finding them would
    mean the erasure had failed. The CODE was right: `resources/resource.php` prints
    `$b['purpose'] ?? '(no purpose given)'`, so the slot is still listed and the room does not look
    free, and `approvals.php` simply omits its "Purpose:" line while the row still awaits a decision.
    Both checks now pin what they are NAMED for and fail in both directions: red if the booking
    vanishes, red if the booker's words come back. Nothing in this package renders those pages, which
    is exactly why the suite runs whole (#695).
  - Tests: sections H and I of `tools/pdf-write-selftest.php` (31 checks) and the decisive behavioural
    one in `tools/gdpr-eraser-selftest.php` — a part-written statement belonging to the erased donor
    goes, and the control person's stays. Planting the old glob back fails that one check.
- **Fixed — a base64-uploaded document is recorded only when every byte of it was stored (#720)**
  - `web/_apps/documents/api/create.php` tested `file_put_contents(...) !== false`, which **accepts a
    short count**, so on a full disk or over a hosting quota a part-written document got a
    `tblDocuments` row and was offered for download with nothing reporting a problem. It now compares
    the byte count, removes the part-written file, and refuses **before** the INSERT.
  - **The multipart branch beside it was already right** — `move_uploaded_file()` answers a boolean and
    has no count to compare — and is deliberately unchanged. The two sharing one `$written` variable is
    how the wrong test looked like the right one; they are judged separately now and both feed one
    reason string, so neither can be "tidied" into the other's shape.
  - **It does NOT need the temporary-name-and-rename shape, and that was checked rather than assumed.**
    `$storedFilename` is `bin2hex(random_bytes(16))` plus an allowlisted extension — fresh every
    request, never from the client — and the only other writer of `_uploads/documents/` is the legacy
    `_apps/documents/upload.php`, whose names always contain underscores and so can never equal a
    32-character pure-hex name. A failure therefore has nothing to destroy. **If stored filenames ever
    stop being freshly generated, that reasoning goes with them.**
  - **No behavioural test is possible here and the guard is static for stated reasons:** a genuine short
    write needs a quota or a tiny filesystem, the page refuses anything but an authenticated POST in
    its first statements, and its destination basename is a fixed 36 characters, so the long-name trick
    `pdf-write-selftest.php` uses is unavailable. `check_document_write_verified.py` pins whole
    conditions instead — including that the refusal comes **before** the INSERT, which is the one thing
    every other pin stays green through — and `tools/document-write-check-selftest.py` plants fifteen
    weakenings into the real file, requiring each to be caught by the expected complaint **and by no
    other**. One case must stay green on purpose: a closing brace inside a string in the gate's body,
    because a brace walk that cannot step over string literals cries wolf on correct code.
  - Both are wired into `pr-security.yml` as hard gates, rather than left to the pre-push hook's glob:
    a proof that runs once is not a guard (#646). Raised and not built: **#725** (there is no
    behavioural test of the documents API at all) and **#726** (whether `move_uploaded_file()` can
    report success after a partial write — not established either way, and the comment says so).
- **Changed — a person's own words are emptied on an erasure request, and the fifteen free-text
  columns each have a decision (#715)**
  - **Emptied now, on the owner's decision of 3 November 2026:** a prayer request's `subject` and
    `body` (what somebody asked to be prayed for, in their own words), its `partnerNote` (a prayer
    partner's note **about** them), and a pastoral case's `summary`.
  - **The prayer request's half-measure was the hard part to defend.** The portal already emptied the
    submitter's name, e-mail and network address from the very same row and left what they had said
    about themselves — often the most sensitive thing they ever typed into the portal. The row keeps
    its value without the text: the request still shows that one was made, moderated and answered.
  - **The pastoral case exposed an inconsistency inside one feature.** #709 carefully empties a visit
    note ("Ces says the ward is noisy") while the case **summary** ("Ces is in hospital") was left on
    the parent row — and the catalogue's own explanation said so out loud: *"this summary is not, so
    it can still describe them"*. Both are a third party's words about the erased person's health. The
    case, who opened it, when and its status all stay.
  - **Matched on the subject's column and nothing else.** A prayer request's two other instructions
    (moderator, assignee) empty no text, because emptying there would destroy **somebody else's**
    request because the person who moderated it left — #709's lesson, which is about this exact shape.
  - **Kept, on the owner's decision:** a presenter's name typed by hand (on service plans and on
    recordings), a licence seat's `deviceName` and `seatLabel`, and a small group's `meetingNotes` —
    these relate to the organisation directly. `tblErrors.errorDetail` and `.requestURL` are kept
    because they **expire anyway**: that table is the one on the list with a time limit already, and
    the nightly sweep deletes the whole row.
  - **Two things the decision could not reach, and both are recorded rather than forced.** A salvation
    card's `prayerRequest` **cannot be found**: nothing ties a card's subject to an account, and the
    only account column is the follow-up worker it was given to — emptying on that would destroy a
    card about somebody else because a volunteer left. And a room booking's `purpose` and
    `declineReason` are blocked by a guard I would not weaken: `bookedByID` is classified as "who
    acted", and emptying a column on an actor-matched instruction is a blanket `= NULL` over every
    matched row. **For this table the emptying would in fact be right**, and `ACTOR_COLUMNS`' own
    docblock names `approvedByID` rather than `bookedByID` as its example — but reclassifying a
    load-bearing list is more than #715 asked for. That is **#723**.
  - **Every one of the fifteen now carries a decision rather than a tracking note.** Three still said
    "Tracked as #715", which is the stale shape #678 warns about: a record that says somebody will
    decide later reads, to the next person, exactly like a record that nobody has looked at.
  - **And the owner's own suggestion is raised as #724:** a case-by-case review step, for a global
    administrator or a data-controller role, over the free text an automatic rule deliberately does
    not touch — because whether "Jane's laptop" matters depends on the request in front of you.
  - **The independent check found ten real problems and the two worst were mine. First: a page that
    would really have thrown.** `prayer-requests/index.php` printed `$req['subject']` with **no
    cast**, twice, and the congregation feed is not filtered by submitter — so an erased person's
    congregation-visible request stays in the list and `htmlspecialchars(null)` is a `TypeError`
    under `strict_types`. The page would have thrown mid-render, the error handler would have printed
    the footer, and the answer would have been an **HTTP 200 ending in an ordinary `</html>` with the
    feed missing**. `php -l` cannot see it. Migration 240's own header had claimed "every reader
    prints the column through `htmlspecialchars((string) …)`" — and also said there were three
    writers where there are **five**. Both halves of a paragraph written to reassure the next reader
    about NULL safety.
  - **Second: #715's whole behaviour was pinned by NOTHING.** The checker stopped the portal emptying
    a prayer request's `body` and a pastoral case's `summary`, gave each a plausible catalogue
    excuse, and **every gate stayed green** — 263 eraser checks, 93 coverage checks, both hard gates.
    Nothing read those columns back out of a database. `MUST_BE_EMPTIED` exists for exactly this and
    its own comment says so ("an instruction that quietly promised LESS changed the expectation with
    it and nothing failed"); #715 had added four columns to the instructions and **not** to that
    list. Both reverts now fail one check each, proved by planting.
  - **And the customer-facing help page was stale for four packages, not one.** Its "Not reached,
    which is a fault" list still named the payment-provider bodies (#713 gave them a time limit),
    visitors' network addresses (#712 replaced them with salted fingerprints and a prune), the
    transcript (#714 gave it one) and the expense receipt's filename (#714 renamed it) — and listed
    the prayer request and case summary as unreached in the same change that empties them. It is the
    one sentence a customer reads before accepting a loss, and it understated the fix in three places
    and overstated it in none. It is now four separate lists: emptied on request, cleared on a timer,
    kept on purpose, and the two genuinely not reached.
- **Added — the hard-coded reserved-word list is now checked against a real server, and it was
  already behind on both engines (#719)**
  - **Why a hard-coded list at all.** `check_reserved_words_quoted.py` has to carry MySQL's reserved
    words in code, because an audit script must run with **no database** — that is what lets the
    pre-push hook run every one of them in about nine seconds. The cost is that a hard-coded list **goes
    stale silently**, and the reserved set is not static: 8.4 added `QUALIFY` and `TABLESAMPLE` to
    8.0's. That was your concern when you asked about reading the words dynamically, and it was a
    fair one.
  - **The answer to the dynamic half is still no**, for the reason already recorded: escaping
    identifiers at run time means parsing SQL in PHP, where a parser bug corrupts queries silently —
    worse than the fault being fixed. **The verification half is yes**, and this is it.
  - **It earned its place on the first run.** MySQL 8.0.36 reserves `master_bind` and
    `master_ssl_verify_server_cert`, and the list did not carry either — so a bare reference to one
    would have passed review and then failed to parse. **MariaDB 11.4 reserves seventeen more**:
    `current_role`, `delete_domain_id`, `do_domain_ids`, `ignore_domain_ids`,
    `master_demote_to_replica`, `master_demote_to_slave`, **`offset`**, `page_checksum`,
    `parse_vcol_expr`, `portion`, `ref_system_id`, **`returning`**, `sql_after_gtids`,
    `sql_before_gtids`, `stats_auto_recalc`, `stats_persistent` and `stats_sample_pages`.
  - **`offset` and `returning` are the ones to notice:** both are thoroughly plausible column names,
    and a column called either would have passed review and then broken on a customer running
    MariaDB. **None of this schema's 1,170 distinct column names is any of the nineteen** — checked,
    not assumed — so nothing was broken. That was luck rather than coverage, which is the point.
  - **The list is now the union of both engines**, which is what a product supporting both needs: the
    check runs with no database and cannot know which engine a customer has, so it asks for a
    backtick on a word that may be legal on the one in front of it. That costs nothing — a backtick is
    never wrong.
  - **The two directions are not symmetrical and only one fails.** A word the server reserves that
    the list lacks is a word the check cannot catch: that **fails**. A word the list carries that the
    server does not reserve means the list is conservative, which is safe and happens in both
    directions as versions move — that is **reported**, never failed. Otherwise the test could not run
    on both the MySQL versions this portal supports.
  - **MariaDB cannot be asked, so it is measured.** Its `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.KEYWORDS` has a `WORD`
    column only, with no `RESERVED` flag, and membership does not mean reserved — `FULLTEXT`,
    `STATUS` and `WINDOW` are all listed, yet only `FULLTEXT` fails bare. So there the test **tries**
    each candidate as a column name, which is the only thing that answers the question.
  - Wired into **both** places that give it value: `portal-selftests.yml`, whose matrix is MySQL
    8.0.36 **and** 8.4.11, and `calendar-selftests.yml`, the one matrix in the repository that runs
    self-tests on all three engines including MariaDB 11.4. Test:
    `tools/reserved-words-live-selftest.php`, which reads the list **out of the audit script** rather
    than keeping a second copy — two copies would agree with each other and with nothing else.
- **Added — an erasure request whose only remaining work is work done by hand can be finished
  (#710)**
  - **What was wrong.** #709 gave the routine a step that can refuse **permanently and correctly**:
    once an earlier run has cut the link a parent-matched step looks through, no number of further
    runs will reach those rows, and saying so beats writing "nothing held for this person" over a
    safeguarding note that is still there. But `execute()` closes a request only when **nothing**
    failed, so such a request could never be closed — and never cancelled either, because
    `runHasChangedAnything()` is correctly true. An administrator who had done exactly the right
    thing was left with a request reading as unfinished for ever and no action that resolved it.
  - **It runs the request one final time, and that is the design.** The obvious shape — ask whether a
    step *would* refuse, then close — answers the wrong question: it says nothing about whether some
    **other** step still has work left, so it would close a request with real work outstanding.
    `GdprEraser::finishByHand()` calls `execute()` and judges what actually happened, so **you cannot
    close a request by hand without the portal having just tried everything it can.** There is no
    force-close.
  - **The record is the feature, not a side effect.** The risk was this becoming a button that closes
    any request nobody has acted on, so the design makes that impossible rather than discouraged:
    `closeRequest()` stays private and this is the only other way to reach it, with the audit line and
    the close in one method. **There is no free-text box**, deliberately — asking an administrator what
    they did by hand invites them to describe what they did to a safeguarding note, which would put
    that note's content into `tblErasureAudit`, a table deliberately absent from the personal-data
    catalogue (#510 rule 7d) and never erased. The line is composed from facts: who, when, which steps
    cannot run, and why.
  - **How a permanent refusal is told from any other failure, without matching on words.** The one
    branch that produces it records the step in a run-scoped list, the way `$dueAtErasure` is
    collected, and `execute()` reports it. Reading the audit trail for the refusal's wording would
    have found a line from an **older** run too, and then offered to close a request whose latest run
    failed for a quite different reason — a real hole.
  - **`closeRequest()`'s own line had to stop claiming "none failed"**, which a close after hand work
    would have made a plain untruth in the sealed trail — the one record nobody can correct
    afterwards.
  - The in-app help and the failed-run message both said there was **no such button**; both are
    corrected in the same change, and #709's own changelog entry carries a forward pointer rather than
    being rewritten, because it records what was true when it shipped.
  - Test: section 21 of `tools/gdpr-eraser-selftest.php`. Its decisive case is the third:
    a request that **also** failed for a recoverable reason must not be closed, and nothing may be
    recorded as done by hand, because closing would bury the failure that a later run could clear.
    Its fourth case exists because the independent check found that the guard leaving an
    administrator's number out of the sealed trail — when the request is their **own** — was pinned by
    nothing: removing it left every check green, because cases A to C all use an administrator who is
    never the person being erased. **A fixture in which a guard's condition can never be true cannot
    test the guard.** Count the planted faults from this commit message, never from here (#671).
  - **A fixture lesson worth keeping:** my first version of that third case named `startedByID` where
    the column is `triggeredByID`, so the row belonged to nobody, the step matched nothing, the extra
    failure never happened — and the check went **green reporting "closed-by-hand"**, which is the
    very thing it exists to forbid. The catalogue entry names the column; read it rather than guessing.
  - **Two guards here were pinned by nothing, and the second is the lesson.** The guard that leaves an
    administrator's account number OUT of the sealed trail when the request is **their own** — the
    trail is never erased, so writing it would undo the erasure — could be deleted with every check
    green, because cases A, B and C all use an administrator who is never the person being erased.
    **A fixture in which a guard's condition can never be true cannot test the guard.** Case D gives
    it one. And section 22 counted `/\$onlyHandWorkLeft\s*\[/`, which is **one spelling of the
    write**: the same fault written `$x = $x + [$child => …]` has no `[` after the name, so adding it
    to the could-not-read branch left the count at one, the original write still in the permanent
    branch for the position check, and both checks green. **That branch needs no second mistake** —
    one failed read of `tblErasureAudit` would close the request and write into the sealed trail that
    no further run could help. The whole surface is pinned now: exactly four mentions, each in one
    form, with comments removed by **`token_get_all()`** rather than a regular expression, because
    every hand-rolled stripper in this repository has been broken at least once by a `//` inside a
    string (#716, #675).
