  - **The button's confirm text promised a record that the refused path does not write.** "Either way
    your account number and the time go into the report" — false on the `other-failures` path, which
    is the likeliest one and the reason the button exists: the only writes there are the claim's
    status and the put-back's, and `report.php` never selects `processedByID`. The only record is the
    activity log, and that **is** erasable (#626). It was false in the self-erasure case too. Both the
    button and the help page now promise the record only where it is really written.
- **Fixed — three places that held personal data an erasure could not reach (#714, migrations 238
  and 239)**
  - **An expense receipt kept the uploader's own filename, twice.** The database held
    "Jane Smith receipt.pdf" exactly as given and showed it back on the claim — and the **stored name
    was built from it too**, so the same name was the name of the file *on disk*, where it appears in
    any directory listing, backup or off-site copy. The personal-data catalogue said the stored name
    was "made up by the portal"; it was derived from the claimant's. An erasure could reach neither:
    a claim is kept six years for HMRC and only has the account number detached, so the row is never
    deleted, the cascade never fires, and #709's parent matching cannot help because the parent is
    retained on purpose.
  - **Both names are generated at submission now** — your decision, 3 November 2026, and the better
    one: name the file generically when it arrives and there is nothing to clear later and no link to
    break. `Claim_412_Receipt_1_2026-11-03.pdf` says which claim, which attachment and when, which is
    all a treasurer needs to tell receipts apart and all HMRC needs beside the figures.
    `ExpensePdf::generate()` already wrote a generated name into that column, so the column was
    half untrue already; it is `fileLabel` now rather than `originalFilename`.
  - **A transcript is the verbatim words of a recording and nothing ever removed one.** The only
    route was the cascade from the recording, and an erasure never deletes a recording — it detaches
    the uploader and presenter and leaves the row. So a transcript, and its byte-for-byte search
    copy, were kept for ever.
  - **An erasure could not reach them and an instruction would have been worse than nothing:** no
    column says whose words they are (somebody who merely *spoke* is nowhere on the row), and a
    transcript is a record of a meeting involving other people, so deleting it on one participant's
    request would destroy what everybody else said. One keyed on the presenter would have **looked**
    like coverage while reaching only the transcripts where the erased person was presenting. Your
    decision was a recorded limit plus a time limit, and `Portal\Core\TranscriptRetention` is the one
    place the period is decided — 365 days, capped by the installation per #668, zero meaning "for
    ever" and therefore the largest value. The rows are **deleted** rather than emptied, because a
    transcript with no words is not a record of anything, and the search copy goes with it by
    cascade. **The recording is untouched.**
  - A transcript still in the queue has no date and no words and is left alone, so a recording
    waiting to be transcribed is never quietly dropped from the queue.
  - The third part of #714 — the workflow subject label — **was already named by #706**; what it
    lacked was a decision rather than a tracking note. All three entries now record one, including
    the limit to watch: `tableName` is documented as "Source table", so a second kind of approval
    could put a person's name in that label directly.
  - **Two mistakes of mine here, both worth more than the fix.** I renamed the wrong table's column:
    `tblPhoto` also has an `originalFilename` and **that one keeps its meaning**, because the photo
    download hands it back as the filename. The two declarations were in fact distinguishable — one
    carries a `COLLATE` clause and the other does not — but my search matched on the column **name**,
    where they are identical, so the difference never came into it. (A first write-up of this said
    they "differ only in whitespace"; an independent check measured that false, and it matters
    because the stated difference was the evidence for the mistake.) The
    coverage self-test caught the half that broke; nothing would have caught the half that silently
    broke three photo pages. That is the same conflation migration 236 was written to prevent one
    package earlier — and knowing about it was not enough.
  - And I wrote a **bare `fullText`** in a transcript fixture — the reserved word `FULLTEXT`, the very
    identifier whose bare reference shipped a statement that could not save a transcript (#276), in
    the same session as the guard for it. `check_reserved_words_quoted.py` could not see it, because
    it read only `web/`. **It reads `tools/` too now**, and planted at the exact line it missed, it
    names it. Self-tests write SQL by hand against the real schema; the rule applies there too.
  - Test: section F of `tools/webhook-retention-selftest.php` (9 of the file's 33 checks), which proves
    the transcript goes, its search copy goes with it, the recent one stays, a queued one is left
    alone, and every recording survives.
  - **The check round found four real problems, and two were checks of mine that could not fail.**
    The per-organisation `siteID` predicate was pinned by **nothing** — the fixture had one
    organisation, so replacing `r.siteID = ?` with `(r.siteID = ? OR 1 = 1)` left all 32 checks green.
    There are two organisations in it now, with different periods, and that plant goes red. And the
    "a queued transcript is left alone" check could not fail either, because its row's `queuedAt` was
    left at today: the sweep's basis column could be changed from `generatedAt` to `queuedAt` and the
    check stayed green. It is backdated now.
  - **One clause turned out to be redundant, and saying so is the fix.**
    `AND t.generatedAt IS NOT NULL` guards nothing: `NULL < <date>` is NULL in SQL, so the comparison
    already excludes a row with no date — deleting the clause leaves every check green, measured. It
    is kept as documentation and both the code and the test now say plainly that it is not
    load-bearing, because a clause that looks protective and is not is worse than no clause.
  - **`totalDeleted` and the breakdown an administrator reads had come apart.** Transcripts are
    really deleted, so they belong in the total — but the sweep's message itemised only three
    figures, so "deleted N rows" had no breakdown reaching N. The message names transcripts now, and
    the assertion in `gdpr-eraser-selftest.php` that pinned the old three-term formula **both
    described the wrong formula and could never fail**, because that test's transcript rows are
    orphans the sweep's `INNER JOIN` cannot reach.
  - **And three public methods existed for a page that does not exist.**
    `daysForThisOrganisation()`, `installationAllowsForEver()` and `whyNotAllowed()` were called by no
    file under `web/`, under a docblock saying "an organisation may tighten it" that nothing could
    achieve. #687's shape exactly. They are removed, the period is now settable where the other
    transcription settings live (installation-wide, global administrator only, refused rather than
    clamped), and **#722** records what removing them gave up.
- **Fixed — the change history about an erased person now covers every kind of membership (#717)**
  - `GdprEraser::eraseAuditTrailAboutPerson()` (#707) reached an entry about somebody's account and
    about which **organisations** they belonged to. Three more membership tables are audited and were
    not reached: `tblUserDepts`, `tblUserGroups` and `tblUserRoles`. All four are covered now.
  - **Stated fairly: there was no identifying residue.** Those payloads carry account numbers and no
    names — a deliberate choice recorded under #518 — and the account itself is emptied by the main
    walk, so after an erasure they already read "account 4211 was added to department 7" where 4211
    identifies nobody. What this closes is **the day somebody adds a name to one of those payloads**:
    #707's fault would be back in a table nothing covered, and nothing would have noticed.
  - **The check is the point, not the three tables.** Nothing anywhere compared the set of membership
    tables that are audited against the set the step reaches — a guard only ever measured against
    itself, which is the #706 shape. Section 21 of `tools/gdpr-coverage-selftest.php` reads **both
    sides out of the code** and goes red if they differ, so a fifth membership table cannot be added
    silently. Planted by dropping `tblUserRoles` from the step: caught, naming the missing table.
  - **The ordering got more load-bearing, not less.** The step runs before the catalogue walk because
    it finds rows by looking the person's membership rows up and the walk **deletes** them. That was
    true of one table; it is now true of four, each with `'action' => 'delete'` on `userID`, so there
    are four ways a reordering could make this step quietly find nothing. Recorded at the call site.
  - The in-app help and the catalogue comment both named the two covered memberships and the three
    that were not; both are corrected in the same change, because a document that states the
    limitation a fix has just removed is worse than one that says nothing.
- **Security — a rate-limit row no longer holds a network address, and both tables are cleared out
  (#712, migration 236)**
  - **What was wrong.** A network address is personal data. `tblLiveRateLimits` recorded the viewer's
    address **unchanged**, and **nothing ever removed a row**: no clear-out anywhere under `web/`, no
    foreign key that could cascade in, no scheduled job, no admin page — all four measured, not
    assumed. So every installation kept a growing record of which addresses had used the live chat,
    for ever, outside every retention rule the portal has. The table even carries an index named
    `idx_ratelimit_prune`, for a prune that did not exist.
  - **And the code said otherwise.** `LiveChat::recordSend()`'s docblock read "pruning is done
    incidentally (next call rolls forward via the time window)". The window only narrows the *count*
    the throttle reads; it has never deleted anything. That is the shape this project keeps being
    bitten by — a comment stating the guarantee the code forgot to implement.
  - **`tblApiRateLimits` was worse in one respect**, because the bucket is a single piece of text and
    two kinds of bucket built it from the raw address: the two-factor code check and the
    push-notification sign-up. **The two-factor one paired an account number with an address**, so
    the row was a record of which person signed in from where. And for exactly those two, the
    opportunistic tidy-up only ever matched the same bucket again — so a bucket never used a second
    time, which is the normal case for a one-off code check or a single sign-up, was **never tidied
    at all**. Four other buckets did hash — but with a plain unsalted SHA-256, which is not the
    same as being safe (see below).
  - **The fix.** `Portal\Core\AddressFingerprint::of()` is the one place that decides what the
    portal stores in place of an address, and `LiveChat::senderFingerprint()` is the chat's own name
    for it, asked by the writer *and* the reader so they cannot drift. The column is renamed
    `senderFingerprint CHAR(64)`; the three API call sites hash the address and each passes a family
    prefix so a later hit tidies every stale bucket of that kind; and `recordSend()` now tidies the
    throttle log as it writes, keeping twice the window, read from the same setting the throttle
    reads so the two cannot disagree about which rows still matter.
  - **The column is renamed, not just widened, and the second reason is the useful one:**
    `tblLiveChatMessages` has a column of its own called `senderIP`, and **that one stays raw on
    purpose** — the moderation screen shows it to an administrator deciding whether to block
    somebody. Two columns of the same name in one feature, one to be hashed and one not, is how the
    wrong one gets changed.
  - **The first version used a plain SHA-256, and an independent check measured that away.** IPv4 is
    32 bits; this machine computes 4.87 million SHA-256 a second, so the **whole address space takes
    about fifteen minutes** — the checker recovered a stored value back to `192.0.2.44` in under a
    second by walking one `/8`. The reasoning borrowed from `Logger::sessionFingerprint()` (#622) did
    not carry across: a session identifier has around 128 bits, and #622's stated reason — that a
    clean-out must recompute the value in SQL — is **false here**, because this clean-out is purely
    time-based and every comparison happens in PHP. So there was no constraint to honour and the
    weaker form bought nothing.
  - **It is salted with the installation's own key now**, which is not in the database and so is not
    in a database backup either. `AssetRegister::saltedHash()` had done exactly this since #410, for
    exactly this purpose, and the first version neither used it nor mentioned it. Asset Register
    keeps its own copy on purpose — its stored hashes are already on disk and its comment promises
    they are bit-identical to the pre-#410 values.
  - **Six buckets were built from an address, not two.** Two used it raw; four hashed it plainly,
    which was not the same as being safe. All six now go through the one helper — found because the
    strengthened audit check reported the four, which is the gate doing its job.
  - **Called a fingerprint, not anonymisation.** Whoever holds the installation's key *and* a list of
    addresses can still test that list. What it stops is anybody who has only the database — a
    backup, a copy, a stolen dump — learning which addresses the portal has seen.
  - **Every one of the eleven places that records a hit now passes a family prefix; eight did not.**
    Including the per-user second tier of the two-factor limit, which `totp_verify:%` cannot match —
    so every failed code check left a row holding an account number that nothing deleted, and the
    catalogue entry this package rewrote claimed otherwise. **A fix applied to one tier of a
    two-tier limit is half a fix.**
  - **No new setting.** A rate-limit row has no value once its window has passed, so the clear-out
    needs no retention figure and no installation cap (#668) — unlike the webhook payloads in #713,
    where how long to keep the evidence is a real choice.
  - **Two guards, because they fail differently.** `tools/audit-checks/check_no_raw_address_stored.py`
    is a new hard gate reading the code; `tools/rate-limit-privacy-selftest.php` (15 checks, real
    MySQL) proves the throttle **still works** once the value is hashed — the half that would break
    quietly, since nothing would log it and no page would change, somebody could simply flood the
    chat. Eight faults planted across the two, each caught by the one that should catch it.
  - **Two traps worth recording from building the guard.** Matching `hash('sha256', $ip)` against
    source with string contents masked can never work — the mask turns it into `'xxxxxx'` — and
    reading the raw file instead lets a commented-out copy satisfy the check (#569). Comments are
    stripped and strings kept for that one pin. The same mistake hid a second plant: a check for
    `senderIP` beside `tblLiveRateLimits` read the masked source, where both names live *inside* a
    SQL string and so had vanished — planted, it missed an `INSERT` naming the old column.
  - The two personal-data catalogue entries, written by #706 and each citing #712, are rewritten:
    they asserted "nothing removes it" and "no time limit", which this change makes false.
  - **The whole suite then caught two regressions neither package's own tests could.**
    `tools/sign-in-limits-selftest.php` kept its **own copy** of how the password-reset buckets are
    built (`hash('sha256', $ip)`), so salting the handlers made eight of its checks fail — every one
    about throttling, none about anything broken. That is this repository's own recorded remedy, in
    the file the lesson came from: ask the portal's function, never keep a second copy of the rule in
    a test. Its clean-up also had to stop matching buckets by exact name, which with a new random key
    each run could never have matched an earlier run's rows anyway. And
    `tools/gdpr-eraser-selftest.php` requires the retention sweep by hand with no autoloader, so it
    had to be given the sweep's new dependency — and then that class's dependency. **Requiring a file
    by hand means owning its whole dependency chain, in order.**
  - **Three more findings from the check round, each a real fault rather than polish.** The new hard
    gate **passed the real pre-fix file**: it required the text `clientIp()` inside the bucket
    assignment, and the live code assigned `$clientIp` on one line and built the bucket from it on
    the next — proved by restoring the file from `HEAD` and watching the check exit 0. It follows one
    hop through a local now. The self-test's prune check **could not fail**: every row in its fixture
    was seconds old, so no positive horizon could remove one, and a prune set to wipe the entire
    throttle log passed 15 of 15 three runs running. Its fixture now plants rows either side of the
    horizon — one that must go, one that must survive. And a pre-#712 snapshot **blocked a whole
    database restore**, because `tblLiveRateLimits.senderIP` was not added to
    `DbBackup::REMOVED_COLUMNS`; the rule was applied two entries above in the same session and
    forgotten here.
  - **One more untrue comment, and it had a real consequence.** The prune was wrapped in
    `if ($prune === false) { return; }` under a comment claiming it failed open. Under
    `MYSQLI_REPORT_STRICT | MYSQLI_REPORT_ERROR` both `prepare()` and `execute()` **throw**, and `@`
    suppresses a diagnostic rather than an exception — both measured. `recordSend()` runs after the
    message row is inserted and before the success answer, so a lock-wait timeout on the new
    500-row `DELETE` would have handed the viewer a bare 500 with the message already saved. It is a
    real `try`/`catch` now.
- **Fixed — a PDF that was not written in full is no longer handed back as a finished one (#711)**
  - `Pdf::create()` discarded `file_put_contents()`'s answer and decided success with
    `is_file($filePath)`. **`is_file()` is true for a file that is empty or half written**, which is
    exactly what a failed write leaves behind: on a full disk or over a hosting quota the write
    returns a short count or `false`, and `is_file()` then said "yes". So the path came back and the
    caller treated a truncated file as a finished PDF. This class makes giving statements, expense
    paperwork, asset labels and venue invoices — a donor's annual giving statement that is half a
    page, served as though it were correct, is worse than one that failed outright, because nothing
    anywhere recorded a problem. Same reasoning as #705, where `fclose()`'s answer was thrown away.
  - **Every caller was already written correctly**, which is what makes this worth saying: four of
    the five test `!== false` on the spot and **three** of those four fall back to rendering the same
    HTML as a print-CSS page; the fifth hands the answer up to two callers that both test it. The
    fault was that `create()` never returned `false` for a short write, so none of that could be
    reached. (Each is now named with its line in `Pdf.php`'s header, because two drafts of that
    sentence miscounted and invented a method name.)
  - `mkdir()`'s answer was discarded too, so a folder that could not be made carried on to the write
    and failed there instead — reported as a write problem, which sends whoever is diagnosing it to
    the wrong place. It is reported where it happens now. The question asked is still "is the folder
    there?" and never "did my own `mkdir()` win?", because two requests can make the same folder at
    once and the loser gets `false` for a folder that is perfectly usable.
  - **The first version of this fix was worse than the fault, and an independent check measured it.**
    It wrote straight to the real path and deleted whatever was there when the write failed — but
    `file_put_contents()` can fail at **open** (the target read-only, a read-only mount, the name
    taken by a directory), leaving the existing contents untouched, and it deleted them anyway.
    These paths use stable names recorded in the database (`_uploads/pdfs/claim_<id>.pdf`, named in
    `tblExpenseClaims.fileName` and in the HMRC-retained `tblExpenseClaimFiles`; and each donor's
    statement). So a working, if stale, PDF was removed while the row went on naming it: **a broken
    download link where a moment earlier there was a working one.** Measured on an existing 28-byte
    PDF at mode 0444.
  - **So the PDF is written under a temporary name in the same folder and renamed into place** — the
    pattern `DbBackup::snapshot()` already uses for its manifest, for the same reason. The real file
    is replaced only once a complete one is ready, in one step, and a failure anywhere leaves what
    was there exactly as it was. It also made the message honest: the old code said "the part-written
    file was removed" whenever there was nothing to remove, so an administrator diagnosing a full
    disk was told a stub had been cleaned up that never existed.
  - The write path answers a **reason** instead of logging, so that it can be tested: logging needs a
    database and a request, and dompdf is not in this repository at all (`_libraries/` is never
    committed), so a test that had to render could not run anywhere.
  - **Two guards, because neither catches the other's half (#646).**
    `tools/pdf-write-selftest.php` (23 checks, no database, no dompdf, no network) is wired into
    `portal-selftests.yml` and `tools/run-all-selftests.sh` in the same change — a test in no
    workflow is #646's exact failure. Its section F is the one that matters: a valid PDF already in
    place must survive a failed write, byte for byte.
    `tools/audit-checks/check_pdf_write_verified.py` is a new hard gate for the half no test on this
    machine can reach — a genuine short write cannot be forced without a quota or a tiny
    filesystem, and **replacing the byte comparison with "did anything get written" was measured to
    leave every check in that test green.** It pins the whole condition, because a check that looks
    for the text of a guard stays green when `&& false` is added to it.
  - **A second review round found the regression test did not reproduce the fault it was written for,
    and that is the lesson worth keeping.** Its fixture made the *folder* read-only with the existing
    file inside it — but writing to a file that already exists needs permission on the **file**, so
    the write succeeded and the one check that named the harm could never go red. Measured
    consequence: adding one line, `@unlink($filePath);`, to the failure branch put the whole original
    fault back **with every check green**. The fixture now forces the failure in a *writable* folder
    by giving the file a name long enough that the temporary suffix crosses the limit on a name — the
    same class of failure as a full disk, needing no quota and no root. **A regression test must
    reproduce the measured fault, not a cousin of it.**
  - That round also found the fix could be **switched off at the call site** with both guards green:
    `if (false && $whyNot !== '')` in `create()`, or deleting the call while leaving the method
    intact, each left all 23 self-test checks and the whole audit check green while `create()` handed
    back the path of a PDF that was never written. The gate now pins the call and the condition that
    acts on its answer — #709's lesson in a new file: when you pin a call, pin the gate that decides
    whether it is entered at all. It also found a **commented-out** copy of the pinned line satisfied
    one of the gate's five checks, because that one read the raw file instead of the stripped source.
  - Two checks that **could not fail** were deleted rather than kept for the look of the thing, and
    the costs of the new design are now written beside it: a killed process can leave a `.part-…`
    file that nothing sweeps and an erasure would not match (**#721**), a rename replaces the inode
    so a hand-tightened file mode returns to the default, and the gate refuses three correct
    refactors by design.
  - Faults planted across the two rounds, each caught by the guard that should catch it and the
    source restored byte-identically: the original `is_file()` test; the clean-up switched off;
    writing straight to the real path; accepting any non-false write; the comparison with `&& false`
    appended; the call's gate switched off; the call deleted; the pinned line commented out; and the
    one-line `@unlink()` that restored the original harm.
  - **The same fault is still live elsewhere and is raised, not fixed here: #720**, the base64 branch
    of the documents API. Widening the audit check to catch it would make it cry wolf, which is how a
    check gets switched off (#483).
- **Removed — two stocktake note columns nothing ever wrote (#708, migration 235)**
  - `tblAssetStocktakes.notes` and `tblAssetStocktakeItems.notes` arrived with the stocktake tables
    in `4764c06` ("Asset Tracker — Phase 3") and **no version of the portal has ever written to
    either**. Two commands establish it, both quoted in the migration's header: one returns every
    statement ever written against either table — **five**, across every commit, not one of them
    naming `notes` — and a second closes that one's blind spot, because this codebase builds SQL by
    concatenating strings, so a `SET` or `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` clause on a later line never
    appears in the first command's output at all. So in a database the portal filled, both columns
    are `NULL` in every row.
  - **Two obvious searches look like proof and are not**, which is worth more than the columns.
    `git log -S"notes" -- web/_apps/assets/` returns the Phase 1 and Phase 2 commits, which predate
    these tables and are about `tblAssets.notes` — a different column. And
    `git log -S"tblAssetStocktake" -- web/` is **blind to the very edit being ruled out**: adding a
    column to an existing `INSERT` does not change how many times the table name appears, so the
    count `-S` watches never moves.
  - **Nor was "the word is not in a SELECT list" enough**, and an independent check caught that in a
    draft of this entry. Three of the four stocktake queries select `st.*` or `i.*`, and a wildcard
    is a `SELECT` list that names no column — so both values really were read back on every call.
    What makes the drop safe is that nothing **consumed** them: only two files ever receive such a
    row, neither contains any occurrence of "note", neither walks a row's keys generically, and the
    scan handler, which writes rather than reads, builds its reply field by field.
  - **A second check round found five more faults in the prose above, two of them inside the very
    paragraph that corrected the first round.** The worst claimed MySQL's
    `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` "can only name a column the INSERT list already holds" — which would
    have made the first command's blind spot harmless by construction. **Measured false on a real
    MySQL 8.0.36:** the clause assigns to any column of the table, and a `notes = 'x'` in it really
    does write one absent from the INSERT list. The true statement is a fact about this code, not a
    rule of MySQL — *in that upsert as written* the clause names only the four columns the INSERT
    list holds — and the second command is what establishes it for every version of it.
  - **Why drop rather than leave.** The same reason migration 201 gave for the check-in browser
    description: a column that exists reads as a column meant to be used, so the next person to
    touch these screens would reasonably start filling one in — and an untyped free-text box on an
    audit record is where personal information lands without anybody deciding that it should.
  - **The honest write-up was the tell.** Both columns had an entry in
    `web/_core/personal-data-catalogue.php` from the day that file was created (`7a0f203`), and
    **#635** (`17dce1b`) then required each to carry a written reason — a paragraph explaining why a
    note that nobody can type is nevertheless kept rather than emptied on an erasure request.
    (Earlier drafts of this entry, the migration header and the developer notes all credited #706.
    Measured wrong: `git show e9934e7 -- web/_core/personal-data-catalogue.php` does not mention
    either table. A wrong issue number is worse than none, which is the whole reason the rule is to
    cite numbers and commit hashes.) Two such paragraphs in the
    file a data subject's request is answered from made the erasure coverage read **wider than it
    is**. Dropping the columns deletes the question instead of answering it. Both entries now name
    the columns an erasure really acts on, and **both** entries needed it: `tblAssetStocktakes`
    gained `closedByID` beside `startedByID`, because a run records two people and the erasure
    detaches both; and `tblAssetStocktakeItems` gained `scannedByID`, which is the larger of the
    two — before this edit the only column that entry named was the dead one, so an entry saying
    "unlink" named nothing an erasure could unlink.
  - **No data the portal wrote can be lost**, because there is none — a claim about this
    repository's history and **not** about any particular database. No customer's data is at risk,
    because there is no live installation yet; a note typed by hand into a developer's or a test
    database would be lost, a drop cannot be undone, and whether such a note exists has not been
    checked, because it cannot be from the repository. Both columns are on
    `DbBackup::REMOVED_COLUMNS`, so a snapshot taken before migration 235 can still be restored into
    a database that has run it — without that entry such a restore is refused with "Unknown
    column", which is the deliberate behaviour for a column nobody has thought about.
  - The migration is idempotent through the `information_schema` + `PREPARE`/`EXECUTE` guard
    migrations 194 and 201 already use; MySQL 8.0 has no `DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS`.
- **Added — a reserved word used as a database identifier must be backticked or qualified (#718,
  #276), before the reference host moves to MySQL 8.4 on 9 November 2026**
  - **The fault this guards already happened.** MySQL ignores case in keywords, so `fullText` **is**
    the reserved word `FULLTEXT`. A bare `fullText = ?` cannot parse — and it was in the statement
    that saves a finished transcript, so it threw *after* the outside transcription company had been
    called and charged. `php -l` cannot see it, and until now no check here could either; the
    developer notes said so in as many words.
  - **Why now.** DreamHost upgrades the reference host's MySQL from 8.0 to 8.4 on 9 November 2026,
    and 8.4 adds reserved words. The question "is this column name a keyword?" is live again.
  - **Exactly one identifier in 229 tables needs the exemption** — `tblTranscript.fullText` — and
    every reference to it today is already backticked or qualified. The check passes as it stands
    and would have failed on the original fault.
  - **The host's documentation is wrong about half its list — in two places — and the check does
    not inherit that.** DreamHost's upgrade notice *and* its help page "Using reserved words in
    MySQL 8" both name four new reserved words: `MANUAL`, `PARALLEL`, `QUALIFY`, `TABLESAMPLE`.
    **Only two are reserved.** Settled three ways: the server's own
    `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.KEYWORDS` on a real 8.4.13 (`MANUAL` 0, `PARALLEL` 0, `QUALIFY` 1,
    `TABLESAMPLE` 1), a parse test, and MySQL's published keyword list. A guard built from the
    host's wording would have refused a perfectly legal column named `manual`. **When a hosting
    company and the database disagree about the database, ask the database** — the check now
    records the query that regenerates its list. None of the four appears in the schema, the
    migrations or the PHP, so the upgrade needs nothing from us.
  - **An alias rule was written and deleted**, which is the right answer rather than an oversight.
    `... AS rank` is the same parse error by another route, but `AS <word>` cannot be told from
    English — "as long as", "as not", "as if", "as is" — and `CAST(x AS BINARY)` is valid SQL. It
    produced fifteen reports and not one was real. A check that cries wolf gets switched off.
  - **"Does this string look like SQL" had to be strict for the same reason.** Asking whether the
    text contained select/set/where/from matched ordinary prose throughout the help pages; it now
    requires a `tbl…` table name or a leading SQL verb.
  - **Nothing else was needed for the upgrade.** The MySQL 8.0 end-of-life warning already exists
    and is shown in four places — `DbServer` classifies 8.0 as *"works, but no longer getting
    security fixes"* and 8.4 as supported. The migration harness already runs against 8.4.11.
  - Checks: `tools/audit-checks/check_reserved_words_quoted.py`, a new hard gate. Five planted
    cases, each behaving correctly — the original `fullText` fault, a new reserved column, `qualify`
    itself, a stale exemption, and a control proving a column named `manual` is **not** reported.
- **Security — correction: the Brotli fix of `8dc848a` did not work, and the real one is to ask for
  no compression at all (#716, CVE-2026-111497 "HTTP2Shell")**
  - **What was wrong.** `8dc848a` changed `SafeFetch` from `CURLOPT_ENCODING => ''` to
    `'gzip, deflate'`, and six documents said that removed the decode path. **It did not.** Setting
    that option to *any* non-null value switches libcurl's content decoding **on**, and libcurl then
    chooses the decoder by name from the **reply's** `Content-Encoding` header — from everything it
    was built with, Brotli included. What we advertise is irrelevant.
  - **Measured against a server that declares `br` without being asked** (libcurl 8.22.0,
    brotli/1.2.0): option unset → 33 raw bytes, not decoded; `''` → decoded; **`'gzip, deflate'` →
    still decoded**. An independent check found this and it was reproduced before acting.
  - **Why it mattered so much here.** The threat this guards against is a hostile or compromised
    calendar feed — **the server is the attacker**. "We did not ask for it" is worth nothing against
    somebody who simply sends it.
  - **The fix is to set nothing.** `CURLOPT_ENCODING` is now absent, which is what every other curl
    call site in the portal already did — and why every one of them was already immune. With the
    option unset, libcurl sends no `Accept-Encoding` **and ignores a `Content-Encoding` the server
    declares anyway**.
  - **What that costs, plainly:** compression on the wire. A large calendar now downloads
    uncompressed. Accepted deliberately rather than reaching for a cleverer option straight after
    getting this wrong once. If the bandwidth ever matters more, the right answer is to switch
    libcurl's decoding off and decode gzip in PHP — which would also make the size limit count
    *compressed* bytes, closing a decompression-bomb gap that exists today.
  - **The guard was wrong in the same way and is rebuilt.** It now fails on the option being set at
    all, not merely on an empty value or one naming `br`. Two parsing faults found with it: a `//`
    inside a string (a URL) deleted the rest of that line including the offence, and a `/*` inside a
    string swallowed everything to the next `*/` — the same fault recorded twice for
    `check_page_head_tags.py`. Masking strings instead **broke both detectors**, because the value
    being read *is* a string; it now walks the source and steps over literals. Block comments are
    replaced by their own newlines, so reported line numbers are right — they were 370 lines out.
  - **The behavioural test now asks the real question.** It used to assert only that we do not
    *offer* Brotli, with a label claiming that meant nothing reaches the decoder — the comforting
    half of the sentence, and false. It now serves a reply that **declares** `Content-Encoding: br`
    unasked and proves the bytes come back exactly as sent. Planted: the withdrawn `'gzip, deflate'`
    fails it, which the old test passed.
- **Security — the portal no longer asks for a reply it would decode with Brotli (#716,
  CVE-2026-111497 "HTTP2Shell")**
  - **The flaw.** An out-of-bounds write in Google's Brotli decoder, in Brotli 1.0.3 to 1.2.0
    (fixed in 1.0.10, 1.1.1 and 1.2.1). Remote, unauthenticated, no user interaction: it is enough
    that something decodes a crafted Brotli stream. CVSS 9.8, and on CISA's actively-exploited list
    since 27 October 2026.
  - **The portal contains no Brotli code**, so the flaw cannot be in ours. What our code controlled
    was whether we ever asked anything to decode Brotli *for* us — and exactly one place did.
    `SafeFetch` set `CURLOPT_ENCODING` to an empty string, which reads as "no compression
    preference" and means the **opposite**: libcurl advertises every coding it was built with,
    Brotli included, and then decodes the reply itself, in the web server's own process, with
    whatever Brotli library it is linked against. So a calendar feed at an address somebody typed
    could hand a crafted stream to the system decoder.
  - **It now names gzip and deflate and not Brotli.** One line. The bandwidth saving that matters
    for a large calendar is kept, and the decode path is gone.
  - **Why fixed here rather than waiting for a host to patch.** The portal is a product installed on
    hosting we do not control, so we cannot know which Brotli a customer's PHP links — and a version
    number could not prove a vendor-patched build either way, the rule #640 already records for PHP.
    Not asking for it removes the path on every installation at once.
  - **Measured, not assumed.** On the development machine on 2 November 2026, PHP's libcurl reported
    `brotli/1.2.0` — inside the affected range — with the Brotli feature bit set. So this really
    would have accepted and decoded it.
  - **The size cap was not a guard against this**, and reading it as one was the mistake to avoid:
    its own comment says it counts the bytes *after* decompression, so the decode has already
    happened by the time it applies.
  - **Nothing else was exposed**, checked rather than assumed: every other curl call site in the
    repository leaves the encoding unset, so libcurl sends no `Accept-Encoding` and decodes nothing.
    The `.woff2` fonts are decoded by the visitor's browser, not by us. Apache's `mod_brotli`
    compresses what we send, which is the other direction and not this bug.
  - Checks: `tools/audit-checks/check_no_brotli_decode.py`, a new hard gate, and two behavioural
    checks in `tools/safefetch-selftest.php` (252 → 254) that read the `Accept-Encoding` the server
    actually received — because `CURLOPT_ENCODING => ''` looks harmless in the source and still
    offers Brotli. Five planted faults, each caught, each reverted byte-identically; the original
    fault turns both the guard and the self-test red.
  - **Still outstanding, and not the product:** this workstation's own Node is v26.11.1 against a
    fixed 26.12.1, and its libcurl links the affected Brotli 1.2.0 — both want updating, and neither
    ships to a customer. No workflow pins a Node version, so CI uses whatever its runner image
    carries. Recorded on #716.
- **Fixed — the change history about an erased person is emptied, and the easy way of doing it would
  have destroyed other people's records (#707, #708)**
  - **What could not be reached.** The change history records *who* made a change in one column and
    *what was changed* as a pair — a table's name and a row's number. There is no column saying who
    a row is **about**. So an entry reading "somebody edited this person's account" matched nothing
    any erasure instruction could look at, and was reachable by nothing. That mattered because the
    history keeps the values: a creation records the whole new row and a deletion the whole old one,
    so a change to somebody's own account wrote their name and e-mail address into it, where it
    stayed after an erasure. (Measured. An earlier draft of this entry said "telephone number and
    home address" as well; the two places that audit that table pass a name, an e-mail address and
    three yes/no flags, and nothing audits a deletion of it, so neither has ever been written
    there.)
  - **Anonymised, not deleted** (the owner, 2 November 2026). The before-and-after values are
    emptied; who acted, when, which table and which record all remain. A change history is worth
    having because it shows who changed what and when, and that survives in full. Deleting the
    entry would destroy the evidence that the account was changed at all, which is often exactly
    what somebody asks a change history.
  - **The obvious shortcut would have emptied other people's records.** Adding those columns to the
    table's ordinary instruction looks right and is wrong: that instruction matches on *who made the
    change*, so it would have emptied the before-and-after of every change this person had made to
    **somebody else's** record — third-party data — while still missing every entry about the person
    themselves. One check exists purely to fail if anybody ever takes that shortcut, and it does
    fail: planted, it reports exactly that.
  - **The order is load-bearing, and it is the same trap as #709.** Entries about the person's
    *memberships* are found by looking their membership rows up — and the main walk deletes those
    rows. So the step runs before the walk. Run it after and that half silently matches nothing
    while the audit line still says the step ran.
  - **What it still cannot reach, said plainly.** An entry about some other record whose values
    happen to quote the person — an announcement whose text names them. Nothing on such a row says
    they are in it, so only searching the values themselves would find it, and that would also match
    a namesake. **And it covers their account and their organisation membership, not every kind of
    membership:** department, group and role membership entries are audited too and are not reached.
    They record account numbers only, with no names, and the account itself is emptied by the walk,
    so nothing identifying is left — but "every entry about this person" would not have been true,
    and an independent check measured that rather than taking the word for it. Raised as its own
    issue so that the day one of those payloads gains a name, it is not forgotten.
    **That limit is gone: #717, later in this same release, covers all four membership tables and
    adds a check comparing the set that is audited against the set the step reaches.** This
    paragraph is left as it was written because it records what was true when #707 shipped.
  - **Also recorded (#708).** A pastoral visit's follow-up owner has a correct erasure instruction
    that can never match a row, because nothing writes the column. The limit is now written beside
    it rather than the instruction being deleted or the page changed: whether a visit should have an
    assignable follow-up owner is a question about how pastoral care is run. The third item of that
    issue — matching the name of whoever collected a child — was already decided and recorded on
    1 November 2026 and needed nothing.
  - Checks: `tools/gdpr-eraser-selftest.php` 251 → 258, including the third-party check above.
    Three planted faults — the step never called, the shortcut taken, and the step moved after the
    walk — each caught and each reverted byte-identically. Whole suite 66 of 66 green.
- **Fixed — every table now has a decision about the personal information in it, and the check that
  was meant to notice a gap no longer depends on somebody's memory (#706)**
  - **What was wrong, and it was worse than the issue said.** `personal-data-catalogue.php` records,
    table by table, what personal information the portal holds and what happens to it when somebody
    asks for a copy or asks to be forgotten. **Sixty-six tables were in it nowhere at all**, and
    **thirty-seven columns holding a person's details were named in no entry.** The issue listed
    eleven columns found by reading; the real figures came from reading the database structure.
    **Be exact about what that cost, because a first draft of this entry was not.** For about a
    dozen of the thirty-seven the erasure was already clearing them and only the written record was
    missing — `tblUsers.phoneNumber` and `displayPhone` were already emptied, and
    `tblPrayerRequests`' submitter name, address and network address too. For the rest — a walk-in's
    name on a register, a small group's street address, the adults authorised to collect a child —
    nothing reached them and still does not. Both are faults, but they are different faults: the
    first misdescribed the portal to anybody answering a request, the second left personal data in
    place. And naming a column does **not** add it to the copy somebody can ask for: that copy
    reports each table's name, row count, action and reason, never a column's value.
  - **The root cause was one level up from the issue's description.** There is already an automatic
    check that reads the database structure and refuses a table holding personal data with no
    decision recorded — and it was passing over all thirty-seven. Its list of what counts as a
    personal column is **written out by hand, name by name**, so it only ever found a column
    somebody had already thought of: it knows `phone` but not `phoneNumber`, `address` but not
    `addressLine1`, `visitorIP` but not `createdIP`. Its own notes record eleven separate occasions
    on which somebody had to remember to extend it. A guard that looks as though it reads the
    database was in fact reading somebody's memory.
  - **It now asks about the SHAPE of a column's name as well.** The words of the name are examined
    one by one: a contact word (e-mail, telephone, address, postcode, network address) or a `name`
    whose qualifier says *whose* — a reporter, a submitter, a walk-in, a counterparty. The
    hand-written list stays beside it, because a shape cannot recognise an account-number column.
    **The judgement about each column stays in the catalogue, where a person reads it**; the check
    only insists that somebody has written one.
  - **It is deliberately a narrow rule.** A first attempt flagged 283 columns across 150 tables,
    nearly all of them harmless classifications — `categoryName`, `deptName`, `tuneName`. A check
    that cries wolf gets switched off, and then it catches nothing. As written it finds 37 and
    every one is real.
  - **Four of the new entries record a fault rather than a position, and each has its own issue.**
    Writing an honest reason for every table is what exposed them: **#712** two tables holding a
    visitor's network address in full that nothing ever clears (one of them carries an index named
    for a tidy-up that does not exist); **#713** payment messages from Stripe or PayPal kept whole
    and for ever — including messages stored *before* the check on who sent them is acted on, and
    carrying the payer's name, e-mail address and billing address; **#714** three places an erasure
    cannot reach, namely a recording's transcript and its second searchable copy, an expense
    receipt's original filename (the claim above it is kept for six years for HMRC, so the usual
    cascade never happens), and a workflow's subject label.
  - **Among the thirty-seven, the ones worth naming**: a member's own telephone number and second
    telephone number; the network address kept against a password reset, a trusted device and a
    Gift Aid declaration; a prayer request's submitter name, address and network address; the
    adults authorised to collect a child; a walk-in's name on an attendance register; and — the one
    nobody would guess — a small group's street address, because a small group usually meets in
    somebody's **home**.
  - **A free-text column is listed, not refused.** 216 `text` and long `varchar` columns (as at 2 November
    2026) are printed as an inventory with a count. Most hold nothing personal and a few certainly do; a
    written reason for each would be mostly boilerplate, and filler nobody reads is a cost rather
    than cover. They are worked down later, with an issue each. **So a green run means every
    contact-shaped column is named — not that every personal column is**, and the check says so
    itself.
  - Checks: `tools/gdpr-coverage-selftest.php` 90/90, `check_personal_data_coverage.py` extended
    and still a hard gate, whole suite 66 of 66 green. Four planted faults, each caught by the
    check that should catch it and each reverted byte-identically.
- **Added — PHP 8.6 is supported, and two fixes that are right on every version (#705, #627)**
  - **Measured against a real PHP 8.6.0RC4, not read about.** All 1,069 PHP files in the
    repository parse on it, and the self-tests that need no database pass on it unchanged. 8.4
    stays the minimum and 8.5 stays the recommended version, both the owner's decisions.
  - **A session id the portal never issued is now refused.** Up to and including PHP 8.5, PHP
    *adopts* any well-formed session id a request sends — even one that names no session — and
    starts a session under it. PHP 8.6 refuses such an id by default; the portal now sets
    `session.use_strict_mode` itself, in `Auth::prepareSessionStart()` and in the installer, so the
    behaviour is the same on 8.4, 8.5 and 8.6 rather than changing under a customer whose host
    moves on. Proved by planting: with the setting removed, a session file really was written under
    the id the request chose.
    **What this does not fix, stated because the first draft of this entry got it wrong.** It is
    not the familiar "plant an id, wait for them to sign in, then use it" attack — that never
    worked here, because every place that signs somebody in already gives the session a new number
    first. So this change does **not** make those renumberings unnecessary. What it closes is
    session state that nothing renumbers: above all the asset kiosk, where a shared terminal puts a
    real member's account into the session and never renumbers it, so an id somebody else chose
    could be the one that member is identified under.
  - **A file that could not be closed is no longer treated as written.** `BackupArchive` discarded
    the result of `fclose()` when closing an archive it had just written, and when closing each
    file written out of one during a restore. A close fails on a full disk or over quota, and the
    old code carried on — so a truncated backup was left on disk, named and dated like a good one,
    and a truncated restored file was counted as one that had been written. Both now refuse: the
    archive is deleted rather than kept, and the restore stops with a message saying which file.
    `DbBackup` already did this correctly and was the pattern followed.
  - **What #705 asked for that would have done harm, and is therefore NOT done.** The issue says
    `PhpRuntime::PHP2SHELL_FIXED_IN['8.6']` must move from `8.6.0RC4` to `8.6.0` when 8.6.0 ships
    on 19 November, and calls it a dated action with a security consequence. Measured: the finished
    8.6.0 **already** counts as supported and patched with the pin untouched, because
    `version_compare()` ranks a finished release above its own candidates — and making the move
    would tell everybody running 8.6.0RC4 that they are unpatched, when RC4 is the first build that
    genuinely carries the October 2026 fix. Planted: that one edit turns RC4's verdict from `ok` to
    `warn`. The constant means "the first **build** carrying the fix", so `8.6.0RC4` is the right
    answer permanently. **Nothing falls due on 19 November.**
  - **The 8.6 change that could have bitten, and why it cannot.** On 8.6 seven filesystem *test*
    functions — `is_file`, `is_dir`, `file_exists`, `is_readable`, `is_writable`, `filesize`,
    `filemtime` — throw an error on a NUL byte in the path, where 8.4 and 8.5 answered "no". A
    visitor can send a NUL, so a page that built a path from a request and expected a tidy "not
    found" would answer a bare 500 instead. Every such path was traced: each is either a whole
    number, or narrowed by a strict allow-list before any file is touched, or filtered out by a
    database look-up that no such value can match.
  - **Also measured and needing no change:** no 8.6 deprecation is reached by any portal code.
    The only two warnings anywhere in the tree are test fixtures holding a backtick on purpose, to
    be caught by an audit check, and neither is ever run — and that deprecation is **8.5's, not
    8.6's**: measured on all three, PHP 8.4.27 is clean while 8.5.11 and 8.6.0RC4 both warn, so it
    was already printing on the version customers are pointed at. Argument values still cannot
    reach a logged error trace. And `scandir()` and `pathinfo()`, the two functions 8.6 made
    stricter about their second argument, are passed the proper constants at all five places that
    call them — one `scandir(…, SCANDIR_SORT_DESCENDING)` and four `pathinfo(…, PATHINFO_*)`.
  - Checks: `tools/php-runtime-selftest.php` 82 → 96, `tools/sign-in-limits-selftest.php`
    114 → 117, whole suite 66 of 66 green.
- **Fixed — an erasure can now reach a row through its PARENT table, so a pastoral visit's note is
  emptied for the person it is about (#709)**
  - **What could not be reached.** A pastoral visit's note describes the person being **cared
    for**, but the only account numbers on the row are the two workers who dealt with it:
    `visitedByID` and `followUpAssignedToID`. Every instruction in the erasure said "this table,
    this column, this person's number", so that note could not be reached at all, and
    `personal-data-catalogue.php` recorded it as owed with its issue number. An instruction may now
    find its rows by looking the subject up one table higher. `tblCareVisit.notes` is emptied
    through `tblCareCase.personUserID`, and it is the only instruction that works this way.
  - **A visit on somebody else's case keeps its note.** The obvious shortcut — hanging the note off
    the worker who made the visit — would have emptied the safeguarding notes of every visit that
    worker ever made, about people who never asked for anything, and would still have reached none
    of the erased person's own. The same mistake is available one table up: a case the erased
    person **opened**, about somebody else, must keep its notes too.
    `GdprEraser::whyParentMatchUnusable()` is the one test of whether an instruction may match this
    way, and it refuses a parent column that says who **acted** rather than who the row is
    **about**.
  - **The visit keeps its date, its kind, its follow-up and its case.** Only the note goes, plus
    whichever worker's number named the person being erased. The link to the case is never emptied:
    a visit detached from its case is not an anonymised record, it is rubble with every word of the
    note still in it.
  - **The order is guarded twice, because getting it wrong is silent.** The parent's own step
    empties the column this look-up uses, so running the child's step afterwards finds nothing,
    leaves every note where it was, and writes "nothing held for this person" into the sealed audit
    trail. In the list as it stood the parent came first, so an instruction added in the obvious
    place would have done exactly nothing. One check pins the position in the list; another refuses
    at run time.
  - **The run-time guard was wrong twice, in opposite directions, and the independent check found
    the second one.** Reading the request's whole history refused the step on every later run, so a
    request with one failed step could never be completed. Reading only the current run's lines
    then reopened the original fault one step further on: on a second run the parent's change is
    not "from this run", so the step was allowed, the link was already gone, and the step wrote
    "nothing held for this person" while the request closed as **completed** with the safeguarding
    note still in it. **No mistake by anybody was needed** — one transient error on that single
    step in the first run is enough, because the walk carries on and the parent's step still cuts
    the link. It now tells "changed earlier in this run" (an ordering mistake) from "changed by an
    earlier run" (the link is gone for good), and in the second case allows the step only where it
    had already answered while the link was intact. Where it had not, the step **fails and says the
    rows must be checked by hand**, because running the request again will not reach them. A
    request that needs a human look is far better than one that reports success it has not earned.
  - **"What we hold about you" counts these rows too**, through the same clause the erasure itself
    uses, so the count and the change cannot disagree about which rows are the person's.
  - **`personUserID` is now on the one list of columns that tie a record to a person.** It was on
    neither list, although the database links it to the account table and a hand-written
    instruction had always matched on it — so nothing could judge whether it named a row's subject
    or somebody who acted on one.
  - **Eight things were covered by nothing, across two rounds of independent checking, and every
    one was found by planting rather than by reading.** Round 1: replacing the run-time guard's
    whole call with `if (false)` left both self-tests and all 46 audit scripts green; reverting the
    "what we hold about you" half was equally invisible; swapping two of the four names in the
    clause builder could not be seen, because the one real instruction uses `caseID` for both; and
    deleting a case from the list of ways a parent match can be wrong stopped testing it instead of
    failing. Round 2, after those were closed: `if (false && isset(...))` on the line ABOVE switched
    **both** guards off in one word, with every check still green — the inner pins were satisfied by
    text that never ran; the rule's own call was pinned by nothing at all; putting the
    250-character cut back around the refusal's audit line was invisible, because the check whose
    label claimed to guard it measured the guard's returned sentence rather than the line as
    stored; and adding `failed` to the list of actions counting as "this step already answered" put
    the whole fault back, because a probe failure writes the same "matched through" sentence the
    look-up matches on. All eight are now pinned, the outer condition included.
  - **One step can now refuse for ever, and that is deliberate — but it means such a request cannot
    be closed.** Raised as **#710 — and fixed later in this same release: there is a "Dealt with by
    hand" action now, so the paragraph below records what was true when #709 shipped.** Every other
    step still runs, so the rest of the erasure is
    done, and both the help page and the failed-run message say plainly that running it again will
    not help and that the request will go on showing as not complete. Before this change those
    notes were never erased at all, so nothing erased got worse; what is missing is a way to record
    that they were dealt with by hand.
  - **A parent-matched step names two tables, and only one of them going missing is safe.** Error
    1146 against the CHILD is still a skip, because nothing can be held in a table that is not
    there. Against the PARENT it is now a FAILED step: the child's rows may be sitting there with
    every word of the note in them, unmatchable because the table that says whose they are is
    absent — and the old branch called that "table-missing" against the child's name and skipped it,
    so the request would have closed as completed having never looked.
  - **What nothing covers**, said plainly: the live path through the step with a real refusal — the
    audit line it writes and what an administrator sees afterwards. Reaching the ordering half needs
    a list the other check refuses outright, and reaching the earlier-run half needs an audit trail
    a correct run never produces, so the guard's logic is asked directly over a hand-made trail.
  - Tests: sections 8c and 8d of `tools/gdpr-coverage-selftest.php` (90 checks, no database) and
    section 19 of `tools/gdpr-eraser-selftest.php` (251 checks, on a real database). Count the
    planted faults from this commit's own message, not from here. No database change, so no
    migration.

- **Fixed — switching "Event reminders" off now stops the reminder e-mails, and the morning summary no
  longer crosses organisations (#666, #616, #683)**
  - **The consent failure.** A member could switch "Event reminders" off, the portal saved the
    choice, and the reminder e-mails kept arriving. `cron/event-reminders.php` read **no**
    preference for the e-mails at all: its recipient query asked only who had answered "going". The
    only mention of `notifyPrefs` in the whole job was a comment about the companion **push**, which
    did honour its own switch. The preferences page carried a standing warning admitting it. It was honest about the e-mails,
    which is what it existed to admit, but its other half was **wrong**: it implied the push obeyed
    this key, and the push has always had its own. Both the notice and the fault are now gone.
  - **The test is `WebPush::notifyPrefAllows()`, deliberately not a new copy.** That idiom already
    had **four** implementations — `WebPush::notifyPrefAllows()` (public), `Workflow`'s own private
    copy, `cron/user-reminders.php`'s plain function, and `Giving::isOptedOutOfStatements()` (the same
    rule inverted). All four agree — checked — and a fifth here would have made the drift worse.
    `ImportNotifier` holds no copy: it already **asks** `WebPush`, which is the precedent this change
    follows. (`auth/account/save.php` only writes the column and holds no test; an earlier draft of
    this entry counted both of those as copies and said six, which was wrong.) A missing key, empty text or unreadable JSON all still mean **yes**, so somebody
    who has never opened the page is reminded exactly as before.
  - **One mailbox, two accounts.** The recipient list is keyed by e-mail address, and a couple may
    share one. A refused row is dropped **before** the full-detail merge, so an address is written
    off only when every account reading it has said no, and an account that said no can never widen
    what an account that said yes is told. The run's log line now carries `off=N` as well as `n=N`,
    because "nobody was reminded" and "nobody wanted to be reminded" are different facts.
  - **The morning summary went to every organisation (#616).** Its recipient query tested
    "coordinates this event" OR `u.isAdmin = 1` — the older portal-wide flag — with no organisation
    anywhere in it, so every holder received a summary for every event on the installation. A
    hosting provider's administrator was reading each customer's diary, across the boundary between
    two separate parties. Everybody named must now be an **active member of the event's own
    organisation**.
  - **The per-organisation admin flags were added as part of that fix, not as an extra.** Scoping
    alone would have made the ordinary case worse: an organisation's own administrator holds
    `tblUserSites.isSiteAdmin`, not the legacy flag, so they were already being missed and the join
    would not have given them anything. The legacy flag is kept as a third test, because it is still
    how a single-organisation install marks its administrator — it now only reaches the
    organisations that person actually belongs to.
  - **#683 was real, and not where the issue said.** The issue blamed the reminder job. It could
    not have been: all three reminder bodies are built as HTML, and `Mailer::send()` only wraps a
    body in the branded base when it does **not** look like HTML — so no reminder e-mail has ever
    carried a footer at all. The live instance is the **giving statement**. `Mailer::sendTemplated()`
    always goes through `renderBase()`, which read `global $SETTINGS` — merged once, before the job
    began walking organisations. **`Site::forceContext()` does not help and that is the trap:** it
    updates the site id and reloads the site row, so the footer's *link* was always right, while the
    name and the support mailbox stayed with whichever organisation the job's own request resolved
    to. Every donor in every organisation received a statement of their giving history footed with
    one organisation's name and support address.
  - **The fix is an optional organisation on the footer.** `renderBase()` takes a `?int $siteId`,
    and `send()` and `sendTemplated()` read it from `options['siteId']`. **Left out, nothing
    changes** — the merged settings answer, which is correct for a web request. `Giving` now names
    the statement's own organisation. The two values are read with `App::settingForSite()`, which
    already answers "this organisation's value, else the installation's" — the fallback #677
    describes, and the reason migration 231 deliberately did not copy the support address down. A
    first draft of this wrote its own two-layer query, which was a second copy of one rule for no
    gain. Where a message names its organisation the support address is checked with
    `FILTER_VALIDATE_EMAIL`, and a value that is not an address is left out. With no organisation named
    — every ordinary web request — the merged value is printed as it stands, exactly as before, so
    this is not a promise about every message.
  - **Proved by three new checks in `tools/time-zones-selftest.php`** (134 in all), which is the
    harness that runs this job at many clock moments against a real database. They read `tblEmailLog.toRecipients`,
    so each one says **who** was written to. The switch covers the day-before and one-hour reminders —
    not the day-of summary, which goes to coordinators and administrators and is a different
    notification. The member who switched it off is not written to, the member who left it on and the
    member who never touched it are, and the second organisation's summary reaches that
    organisation's coordinator, its own `isSiteAdmin` holder, its own `isSiteRootAdmin` holder, and a
    portal-wide administrator who IS one of its members — but not the installation's global
    administrator, who is a member of organisation 1 only and who, in the same check, **is** told about their own organisation's event the next
    morning, so the absence means something. `tblEventReminderLog.recipientCount` is deliberately not
    used: it counts only messages a mail service really took, and this test points the portal at an
    empty SMTP mailbox on purpose, so a clause requiring it to be 0 could never fail.
  - **The independent check found that the first version of the #616 check proved nothing**, and this
    is the part worth keeping. The administrator in that made-up world holds all three ADMINISTRATOR
    grounds at once, so **each of those three `OR` clauses could be deleted on its own with every check
    still green** — measured, one at a time. (Three, not four: the coordinator clause was never
    deletable-green, because that administrator coordinates nothing. An earlier draft of this entry said
    four, which overstated its own measurement.) The three refusing conditions were worse: `AND
    us.isActive = 1`, `WHERE u.isActive = 1` and `AND revokedAt IS NULL` could EACH be deleted with all
    134 checks green, because nothing in the made-up world could trip any of them — so a person removed
    from an organisation, a closed account and a coordinator who had been stood down all went on
    receiving the organisation's morning diary. Seven people now stand in that world: one per ground
    that admits, one per condition that refuses. All six plants go red, each caught by the #616 check.
    The three refusal plants name the person who leaked in; the three admitting plants show a person
    dropping out of the expected list. `tools/mail-queue-selftest.php` also calls this job over real HTTP and
    asserts on the day-of summary's recipients, but its own check is satisfied by the portal-wide flag
    alone — so it would not have noticed a per-organisation flag being dropped either.
- **Fixed — thirty-five tables named a personal column that nothing emptied; every one now has a decision
  and a written reason (#635)**
  - **What was wrong.** `web/_core/personal-data-catalogue.php` is the written list of where personal
    information lives, and it names the columns that make each table personal. The erasure routine built its
    instructions from that list but only ever acted on the names holding an **account number** — so a column
    holding an address, a hand-typed name or a note was named as personal and emptied by nothing. That was
    #626 on the activity log. It was true of thirty-five other tables.
  - **Five columns are now emptied, across three tables.** `tblErrors` loses the visitor's address, the
    browser name and the copied request headers; `tblAuditTrail` loses the address a change came from;
    `tblEventAttendance` loses a note on the row that says this person was present. A sixth named column,
    `tblCareVisit`'s pastoral note, is **not** emptied yet: reaching it needs matching through a parent
    table, which is **#709**.
  - **`tblErrors` and `tblAuditTrail` are hand-written instructions on purpose, and this is the trap worth
    knowing.** For a column that is not an account number the routine emits a plain `= NULL` on **every row
    the instruction matched** — only account columns get the per-person `IF()` scoping. So such a column is
    safe only where the matched column says who the row is **about**. `tblErrors` has two account columns, and
    the three diagnostic columns belong to the subject one alone: on the "who resolved it" instruction they
    would have blanked an unrelated visitor's address from every fault the erased administrator ever ticked
    off. A hand-written entry also **wins over the derived one for the whole table**, so both of that table's
    instructions are written out; dropping the second would silently stop the other link being detached.
  - **Several tables keep a personal column because the only available match is the WRONG PERSON.** In
    `tblLiveChatMessages`, `tblEventRSVPInvites`, `tblVenues` (the caretaker's name and telephone),
    `tblKidCheckins` (who collected a child) and `tblSmallGroups` (a meeting place that may be a member's
    home), the only account column is the moderator who approved or hid the message — a chat sender has no
    account at all, being identified by an anonymous token — or the coordinator who sent the invitation,
    whoever added the venue, or the helper who did the checking. Nothing records whose home a group meets in. Emptying would have deleted a
    **third party's** details from rows that have nothing to do with the person who asked, while reaching none
    of their own — and would have lost the only record of who to ring for a building's keys, and the only
    record of who collected a child. An earlier draft of this work called these "the same fault as #626" and
    would have emptied all four; the owner's decision of 1 November 2026 keeps them with the limit written down.
  - **Twenty-two were only a free-text note; twenty-one of them keep it, and the owner's rule decides by
    what the ROW is** (the twenty-second is the attendance note, now emptied): empty it
    where the row is the person's own record, keep it where the row is the organisation's record of a thing or
    a transaction. So a note on a pastoral visit goes and a note on a venue invoice stays. Whoever typed the
    note is still detached, by cutting the account link; the text is not theirs to erase.
  - **Six columns were never personal at all** and have come off the list: an `AUTO_INCREMENT` primary key,
    a venue's postcode and map position (a building in a directory), and a stored filename that is
    `bin2hex(random_bytes(16))` and never derived from anything a visitor sends.
  - **`notEmptiedHere` replaces a list of 35 table names that lived in a test file.** Each named column that
    an instruction does not empty now carries its reason **beside the column, in the file a request for
    somebody's information is answered from** — so a person asking why a column is still there can read the
    answer. Three new checks stop it becoming an excuse list: a reason must be long enough to be a reason, an
    explanation for a column the entry no longer names fails as stale, and an explanation for a column that
    **is** now emptied fails — so the list shrinks as the work is done. `$leftBehindOnPurpose` is empty and
    must stay empty.
  - **Also corrected:** a comment in the erasure routine claimed thirteen columns could never be emptied and
    named `createdByID` on the venue register as an example. Migration 192 made exactly those nullable and the
    schema now says `createdByID INT DEFAULT NULL`. The guard is still right — a customer's database is what
    refuses, and it can be out of step with the schema file — but the example was false.
  - **Found and raised, not fixed here:** #706, the catalogue is **incomplete** — `tblAuditTrail`'s
    `oldValue`/`newValue`/`changeSet` hold a JSON copy of a whole row, `tblErrors.errorDetail` holds a full
    backtrace, and ten more personal columns appear in **no entry at all**, so they are invisible to this
    issue and to its checks. #707, an audit row *about* the erased person is reachable by nothing. #708, two
    dead columns and two loose ends.
  - Proved by `tools/gdpr-coverage-selftest.php` (73 checks), with planted faults at build time and more
    against the three checks the independent rounds added — each caught by the check that should catch it,
    and each reverted byte-identically.
- **Added — an optional ceiling on how long giving records keep a donor's name (#687, migration 234)**
  - **The decision, in the owner's words (31 October 2026):** "An installation Global Admin, or
    Organisation global admin can have the option to enforce such a limit - but can also choose not
    to. so customisable." So it ships with **no ceiling** and nothing changes for anybody until an
    administrator deliberately sets one.
  - **Why this one limit is opt-in where #668 makes every other one compulsory.** Everywhere else the
    installation allowing less means less personal data is held and nothing breaks. Here the figure is
    a **statutory retention period** — the portal's suggestions come from per-country research and an
    administrator confirms the figure with their own adviser — so forcing it DOWN could make a
    customer destroy records their own law requires them to keep. That is why #687 was raised as a
    question rather than fixed as a cap.
  - **How the two levels combine.** `GivingRetention::capInForce()` is the ONE place that answers it
    and it asks `Portal\Core\SettingLimit`, the ONE general place that decides a three-tier limit
    (#668). An organisation may hold itself to a lower ceiling and may never raise its own above the
    installation's. **A stored 0 means "no ceiling", which makes 0 the LARGEST value rather than the
    smallest** — #668's zero trap — so `$zeroIsLargest` is passed rather than the conversion done by
    hand at either end, which is what broke both ends before.
  - **What keeps it a real ceiling rather than a save-time courtesy.** #668's rule is that a cap
    applied only at Save is not a cap, because the clear-out job reads the stored figure. There are
    **two** save-time gates here, and between them `years <= ceiling` holds by construction: a figure
    above the ceiling is refused with the reason, and **a ceiling below a figure an organisation has
    already chosen is also refused, naming the organisations that block it.** So the job never meets a
    figure it would have to shorten, and deliberately does not apply the ceiling itself.
  - **The two gates are SERIALISED, and the first version was not.** They both re-read the ceiling
    LIVE and both lock the installation's own row, inside the transaction that writes — the rule the
    four money writers follow (#647). The first version compared against the request's settings
    snapshot, taken at start-up, and the independent check measured two ordinary web requests storing
    **50 years under a ceiling of 7** with both saves reported successful, reproduced in **60 of 60**
    simultaneous pairs. Five places in this package had said the only way into that state was
    hand-written SQL or a restored backup, which was the stated reason the clear-out job need not
    apply the ceiling at all. It could happen, and that sentence is what would have stopped the next
    reader looking.
  - **The gate is on the figure the save really STORES, not on `$years`.** `$years` is the typed
    number OR the country suggestion where none was typed, and gating it refused saves that store no
    figure at all: on a fresh installation with a ceiling of 7, **switching the HOLD on was refused**
    — the one control that stops records being cleared — as was setting the financial year end, and
    pressing Save on the form exactly as drawn, with a message about "that number" when the box was
    empty and the page's own help said to leave it so. An organisation only stores a figure by typing
    one or by ticking "confirmed", which adopts the suggestion; both are gated, and an unadopted
    suggestion above the ceiling is genuinely harmless because nothing is cleared while it is
    unconfirmed.
  - **The one hole left, stated rather than left to be found:** a figure written by hand in SQL, or
    arriving in a restored backup. The job then obeys the **stored** figure and keeps the records
    longer, and the page says so. That is the safe direction here — keeping too long is a privacy
    fault to be fixed, while destroying too early can be unlawful and cannot be undone.
  - **Three more the independent check found, each measured:** the activity log said "Nothing was
    different." for a save that really changed the ceiling, because the old value was read AFTER the
    transaction committed and `settingsAt()` has no cache — `save.php`'s own header promises a record
