    of who changed it "and from what", so that promise was dead. The organisation's own ceiling box was
    prefilled above its own `max`, which is the fault #668 names in so many words ("the browser then
    refuses to submit the whole form"), reproduced five lines below the comment citing it; `max` is
    now the hard maximum, the handler does the refusing, and the page explains an own ceiling that the
    installation's supersedes. And a comment justified the "did the field arrive" design with a
    protection that does not exist — the box is drawn for every administrator — which is worse than no
    comment, because the next person removes the design when they find the protection missing.
  - **The race fix was then PROVED by a second check**, which is worth recording because the first
    version of it was not: 116 genuinely simultaneous pairs (20 at the same instant, 70 with head
    starts from 0.05s to 0.5s, 26 on a database where migration 234 has not run and there is no row
    to lock) ended **0 of 116** with a figure above the ceiling; both orders were then forced with an
    external session holding the lock, and each path blocked for about five seconds, woke, saw the
    committed value and refused. Removing just ` FOR UPDATE` brought the original fault straight back,
    so the LOCK is what closes it and not merely the live read. At `innodb_lock_wait_timeout` both
    paths roll back, log and refuse — no bare 500, no transaction left open.
  - **Three FALSE REFUSALS the same check found, and the gate was never too weak — only too eager.**
    The figure was gated before the un-tick branch had been decided, so an administrator clearing the
    years box with the tick left on (how the page draws it) was refused while the identical end state
    saved if they also unticked by hand; the gate now runs after rules 1 and 2, on `$yearsOwn`, which
    by then is exactly what will be stored. An organisation's own ceiling was judged even when the
    save did not change it, so an own ceiling the installation had later been lowered past blocked the
    hold, the year end, confirming and a plain Save — a number the organisation never raised and the
    page itself had prefilled; it is now judged only when it CHANGES, which is the #667/#677 rule
    ("ask whether the field changed"). And **the years box was itself prefilled above its own `max`**
    when a stored figure exceeded the ceiling — #668's named fault, in the same edit that fixed it for
    the ceiling box five lines below, under a comment citing the rule; measured in headless Edge, the
    form would not submit at all, so the only way to use the page was to shorten a statutory
    retention period.
  - **A pre-existing deadlock, raised as #700 rather than fixed here:** two organisations saving this
    page for the FIRST time in the same instant can deadlock on the gap locks of their seven inserts.
    Established as pre-existing by running it against `git show HEAD:` of the class (6 of 6 without
    #687's lock), and it cannot recur once each organisation's rows exist.
  - **"The seven settings" was left in ten places**, five of them in the file being edited, one line
    from a comment this package wrote about counts going stale. All now say what they mean without a
    number; the historical changelog entries are left as the record of what shipped then.
  - **An organisation that has chosen nothing is untouched.** It follows the country suggestion, which
    can be above the ceiling, and that is harmless: nothing is ever cleared until somebody ticks
    "confirmed", and confirming WRITES the figure through the same refusal.
  - **It is set on the giving-records page, not the general settings editor.**
    `GivingRetention::lockedInGeneralEditor()` still refuses every `giving.retention.*` key there
    except the hold. The issue suggested that method "has to change"; it does not, and the reason is
    worth keeping — that editor asks this class about the LOCK and nothing else (checked, at
    `_apps/settings/save.php`), so a ceiling written there would skip the refusal that makes a ceiling
    mean anything.
  - **The refusal an organisation reads never says WHO set the ceiling**, matching
    `SettingLimit::refusalWords()` and for its reason: the two levels may be different parties.
    Naming organisations to the **installation's** administrator is the other direction and is their
    own business, so that refusal does name them — while the activity log carries only a count.
  - **The tripwire now requires it.** `GivingRetention.php`'s exemption in
    `tools/audit-checks/check_limit_settings_capped.py` is deleted, so that hard gate — which fails
    both ways — now demands the cap. It reported the stale entry itself.
  - Tests: section 6 of `tools/giving-retention-selftest.php` (9 new checks, 63 in all), covering every
    sentence the feature can print, including that none of them reads as if the portal knows the law.
    **The two save paths are covered by no automatic test and that is #699**, raised in the same
    action: this file has no database, and the gates that keep the invariant are exactly what is
    untested.
- **Fixed — putting a backup back no longer throws away the rows an earlier restore kept for you (#697)**
  - **What went wrong.** #694 gave the portal a holding table, `tblRestoreHeldRows`, for rows a
    restore could not put back, so an administrator can put them back or discard them deliberately.
    But that table was an ordinary one, so the next whole-database restore emptied it and filled it
    again from the snapshot — and a snapshot taken BEFORE some rows were kept holds none of them. The
    waiting rows simply went, and a waiting row is the only copy of itself anywhere outside the
    snapshot being restored from. That is the silent loss #694 exists to stop, one door along.
  - **What was there before.** A warning, before and after, saying the rows had been replaced and to
    deal with them first. It asks somebody mid-recovery to read a warning and act on it, which is
    exactly what #694 says not to rely on.
  - **What happens now.** The restore reads the waiting rows before it empties anything and writes
    them again after every table is back — the same read-early, write-late order #694 already uses,
    and for the same reason: the holding table is itself in the snapshot, so anything written earlier
    would be emptied again when that table's turn came. The result says how many were carried
    through. The Backup page's card and the disaster-recovery help page both say so. The HELP PAGE
    used to say the opposite; the card said nothing on the subject at all, and this adds the
    paragraph — a first draft of this entry claimed both had said the opposite, which
    `git show HEAD:web/_apps/admin/maintenance/backup.php` disproves.
  - **A row already put back is deliberately NOT carried.** It is history — a record that a row was
    kept and returned, with its copy of the data emptied when it went home — and putting a database
    back to an earlier moment is supposed to put its history back with it. Written down beside the
    code and pinned by a check, so it cannot change by accident.
  - **A one-table restore of the holding table is now refused by name.** `tblRestoreHeldRows` joined
    `DbBackup::WHOLE_DATABASE_ONLY`: the button for it is gone and a posted request is turned away
    with the reason, because putting that one table back on its own would throw away every waiting
    row and there is no carry to save them.
  - **What that addition does NOT do, because a first draft of this entry said it did.** It was
    written up as also making an OLD-FORM snapshot leave the table alone, "so it cannot write over
    kept rows at all". That is a no-op for every snapshot a customer can have: a snapshot with no
    "covers the whole database" flag was written before that flag existed (27 October 2026,
    `b7496b7`) and the holding table arrived with migration 233 (31 October 2026, `ac1b19e`), so such
    a snapshot cannot contain the table and there was never anything to hold back. The only
    whole-restore case the addition changes is a MODERN snapshot somebody has edited the flag out of,
    which is what the flag exists to catch. **An old-form snapshot is safe for the simpler reason
    that the table is not in it** — and so is any snapshot that does not contain it. Found by the
    independent check, which restored a genuine old-form snapshot and read the answer: three tables
    held back, not four. The in-app help page had been changed from a true sentence ("leaves three
    tables alone") to a false one in the process, in the one place a customer reads before deciding
    whether to accept a loss.
  - **How a carried row is recognised, since it cannot simply be inserted again.** A snapshot taken
    AFTER a row was kept holds that same row, under the same number, so each carried row is looked up
    by its own number first: nothing there and it goes back under its own number; the same row there
    and it is left alone; a DIFFERENT row there and it goes back under a new number. "The same row"
    compares which table it came from, whose it was and when it was kept, and deliberately not the
    copy of the data — a row already put back has had that copy emptied, and a JSON column is
    rewritten on storage by MySQL and not by MariaDB, so comparing it would mean two different things
    on the two engines.
  - **A failure stops the whole restore** rather than reporting success with the rows gone, the same
    direction `holdRescuedRows()` already takes. The table has no foreign keys and nothing but its
    own number to clash on, so the only reachable causes are infrastructural.
  - **More than 20,000 rows waiting no longer loses them.** The carry holds the rows in memory, so
    it has a ceiling; past it the first version carried NOTHING and let the snapshot's older copy of
    the list replace them — measured at 20,001 rows in and ZERO out, with the Backup page and the
    help page both promising that could not happen. The decision now happens BEFORE the restore
    starts, and past the ceiling that one table is simply not put back: the rows stay exactly where
    they are, everything else in the snapshot goes back as usual, and the answer says so. It is the
    same mechanism `WHOLE_DATABASE_ONLY` already uses, and the ceiling is decided in one place so two
    readers cannot disagree about it.
  - **An ARRAY SUBSCRIPT is the same comparison, and fixing only the `in_array()` calls turned a
    silent loss into a BLOCKED RECOVERY.** `$facts['tblRestoreHeldRows']` kept matching exactly, and
    `columnFacts()` keys its answer by `information_schema`'s own `TABLE_NAME` — lower case on such a
    server — so the carry threw "the shape could not be read" and **every whole-database restore,
    the rehearsal included, was refused while any row was waiting**, naming the wrong cause. The only
    route to it was #694's rescue succeeding. `DbBackup::forTable()` is the helper for fetching an
    entry out of an array keyed by table name, and `self::REMOVED_COLUMNS[$table]` used it too.
    Four documents had said "all five sites use it"; they were wrong, and that sentence is what
    invited the next reader to stop looking.
  - **And a draft of the line above called `forTable()` "the ONE way", which it is not — the same
    mistake one round later.** `DbBackup.php` holds about eighteen other table-keyed subscripts, and
    the next review round found a THIRD live fault among them: `columnFacts()[$table]` in
    `putHeldRowsBack()`, where `$table` carries the SOURCE's spelling because `keepsRowsFor()` has
    just demanded it match `CASCADE_RESCUE` exactly. On a lower-case server the Backup page then
    offered a kept row and drew both buttons, and **only the one that throws the data away worked** —
    "put it back" always failed, naming the wrong cause. **The rule for it took a further round to state correctly:**
    a table-keyed lookup is safe when BOTH SIDES COME FROM THE SAME PLACE, and unsafe when one side is
    folded by the server and the other is not. The first attempt — "safe only where both sides came
    from the server" — was wrong both ways: it cleared `REMOVED_COLUMNS[$table]`, which was one of
    the very faults being generalised (its index comes from the manifest, its keys from the source),
    and it condemned the three correct `CASCADE_RESCUE[$table]` sites, where capitals matter by
    design. **Three rounds were spent fixing instances of this one class rather than the class**, which is why the audit script now
    flags `columnFacts()` subscripts by shape and pins `forTable()`'s body as well as
    `namedIn()`'s — a one-token change inside `forTable()` had passed every check in the repository.
  - **Two PRE-EXISTING faults of the same shape, found on the way:** `$restored` is a fourth
    server-reported list, so on such a server restored mail was NOT held and a restored held text was
    NOT recorded as not sent. Their own docblocks say the cost — "three waiting messages came out as
    six copies when this was run", and a text sent "a SECOND time, to somebody's phone and at the
    customer's cost".
  - **The one case where a waiting row deliberately stops waiting is now SAID OUT LOUD.** A row the
    snapshot records as already put back is not carried, because the restore honours that snapshot's
    history — and that happened in complete silence, measured at zero warnings, while the Backup page
    claimed "the result always tells you what happened" and the help page listed it among the things
    the portal will not do silently. `DbBackup::stoppedWaitingWarning()` reports it, which makes both
    sentences true rather than merely softened.
  - **Verified on a real server with the setting on**, by driving the class directly: the restore
    succeeds, the waiting row survives, restored mail is held, and the held text is recorded. Each of
    the three fixes was then planted away in turn and reproduced its exact fault — the refusal, the
    silently lost row, and the unheld mail. **The repository's own harness cannot do this**: it
    compares table names exactly in its OWN checks, so running it against such a server fails on the
    test rather than the portal. That is why the guard is an audit script and not a self-test.
  - **Two safety nets were inert on a server with `lower_case_table_names = 1`, and one of them was
    #694's.** Table names from `SHOW TABLES` come back in lower case on such a server, and both this
    carry and #694's cascade rescue compared them with `in_array(..., true)` against a name typed in
    the source — so neither ran, and a waiting row was lost with the restore reporting success and
    printing no warning at all. Measured on `mysql:8.0.36 --lower-case-table-names=1`. All five such
    comparisons now ignore capitals, which is what `isWholeDatabaseOnly()` has always done, and for
    the reason its comment gives. The two halves had disagreed about what a table is: the tables
    were held back while neither protection fired.
  - **Still not covered, said plainly:** the over-20,000 path is reached by no automatic test (the
    independent check reached it by hand), and neither is the branch where the holding table cannot
    be read at all.
  - **The wording faults the independent check found, because they are the kind no check can see.**
    `carriedWarning()` said "All %d rows kept for you ... were carried through", where the number
    counts only the rows actually written again — so an administrator with four waiting rows and two
    of them in the snapshot was told "All 2 rows kept for you", a number that is not the count of
    anything they can see. The same sentence ASSERTED that the snapshot "does not include them",
    which is untrue of exactly those rows. And `tooManyToCarryWarning()` asserted that the rows
    "are no longer offered on the Backup page" when, in that branch, no rows are read at all and
    nothing knows whether the snapshot holds copies of them. All three are now stated as what is
    known: how many were written again, and nothing more. A first attempt at that fix ended each
    sentence "Every row that was waiting is still waiting", which swapped an undercount for an
    ABSOLUTE promise that ONE branch breaks — a row the snapshot already records as put back stops
    waiting, deliberately, because the restore honours that snapshot's own history. (A draft of this
    entry said "two branches" and named the ceiling as the second; the ceiling leaves every row
    waiting, so it is not one.) That case used to happen in SILENCE, which made "the result always
    tells you what happened" false on the Backup page; it is reported now.
  - **A read of the kept rows that fails now says so.** Two `=== false` returns answered "nothing
    was waiting", which is indistinguishable from an empty table, so the restore would have written
    over the waiting rows with no warning — the exact failure this fixes. Unreachable while
    `MYSQLI_REPORT_STRICT | MYSQLI_REPORT_ERROR` makes a statement error throw; it is there so it
    cannot fail silently if that stops being true.
  - **A new hard gate, because no test here can catch the case-sensitivity fault returning.** Every
    self-test in this repository runs one database server with `lower_case_table_names = 0`, where the
    names match exactly, so the fault is invisible to all of them — the #646 situation exactly.
    `tools/audit-checks/check_table_name_comparisons.py` fails on a case-sensitive `in_array()`
    against a list of server-reported table names, and also fails if `DbBackup::namedIn()` stops
    existing or stops CALLING `strcasecmp()`, because without that second half the first is satisfied
    by deleting the comparison. Wired into `pr-security.yml` as a hard gate (`if: always()`, no
    `|| true`), with the step name quoted so a `#` cannot truncate it, and the YAML parsed before
    pushing.
  - **That gate's first version passed on two planted faults, and the fixes are the general lesson.**
    It required the `in_array()` call to be followed by a comparison, so assigning the result to a
    variable escaped it entirely — and it listed the three haystack variables it knew about, where
    `$restored` was a fourth holding two live faults. It now anchors on the NEEDLE (a `'tbl...'`
    literal) and matches the call's own parentheses, so neither the haystack's name nor what follows
    the call matters. Its second half asked whether the WORD `strcasecmp` appeared in the helper's
    body, which `$how = 'strcasecmp';` satisfied while the comparison used `===` — the
    `check_no_outside_qr_service.py` lesson word for word. It now requires a CALL, with comments and
    string literals masked first. It also matched haystack names by substring, so an ordinary
    `in_array($column, $orderedColumns, true)` turned it red; anchoring on the needle fixed that too,
    and #668's rule is that a check which cries wolf gets switched off. Five plants now: the assigned
    call, the literal `strcasecmp`, the array subscript, the mail comparison, and a correct unrelated
    helper that must NOT trip it.
  - Tests: proof 28 of `tools/backup-restore-selftest.php` (61 checks against a real database — the
    rehearsal, the singular and plural sentences, the no-duplication case, ONE SUB-CASE PER IDENTITY
    COLUMN, the one branch where a waiting row deliberately stops waiting, and a hand-edited
    manifest), proof 26 for the one-table refusal, and section P of `tools/backup-page-selftest.php`
    for the card. Thirty-one planted faults across five rounds, each caught by the check that should
    catch it — and the count matters less than the fact that five of them were bypasses of the new
    audit script itself, each measured reaching the code and reproducing a fault the script exists
    to stop. Two are worth naming. **Narrowing the row identity to `tableName` alone left all thirty
    of the original checks green while a real waiting row was silently lost** — and the later fix for
    that was itself incomplete: three sub-cases for four columns, so dropping `tableName` stayed
    invisible until a fourth was added. And **a plant that cannot change behaviour proves nothing**:
    adding `putBackAtUtc` to the identity looked inert because the lookup does not select that
    column, so reversing the decision properly takes two edits, and only then does the new section
    E2 fail.
- **Fixed — putting back a backup taken before 27 October 2026 no longer loses every organisation's
  address and everybody's sign-in codes in silence (#694, migration 233)**
  - **What went wrong.** A snapshot in the older form does not say that it covers the whole database,
    so a full restore deliberately leaves `tblMigrations`, `tblSettings` and `tblTotpBackupCodes`
    alone — each records what has already happened, and putting one back without the rest loses data.
    That part is right. But the restore *does* replace `tblSites` and `tblUsers`, and two of those
    three tables are their children with `ON DELETE CASCADE`. So the database's own rules deleted
    every per-organisation settings row and every two-factor backup code, spent ones included, and
    nothing put them back. Measured on MySQL 8.0.36: one per-organisation settings row before, none after, and the
    restore reported success.
  - **What it cost a customer.** Since migration 231 (#677) each organisation keeps its own postal
    address, map position, what3words address and support e-mail in rows of its own. All of them went,
    and the support address then silently fell back to the installation's. For the codes: every
    person's remaining single-use sign-in codes.
  - **What happens now.** The restore reads those rows *before* anything is emptied and writes them to
    a new holding table, `tblRestoreHeldRows`, *after* every table is back. The Backup page lists what
    is being kept, with one button to put it back and one to discard it. **Nothing removes them on a
    timer** (the owner's decision, 31 October 2026): they exist while somebody is mid-recovery, and a
    clock that deleted them part way through would be this same silent loss one step further on. What
    stops them being forgotten is the page naming them.
  - **The warning now says what went, not which table.** It used to say "1 table(s) that are NOT in
    this snapshot were changed as well", which tells an administrator nothing about what they have
    lost — and they are reading it at the worst possible moment. It now names the rows, the link that
    took them, and where they are being kept. **That sentence is an ADDITION, not a replacement:** the
    older, wider one still runs and still covers every table outside the snapshot, the ones that
    cannot be rescued included. A draft of the code comment claimed it had replaced it; both appear,
    and proof 6 now pins both, because pinning one would pass with the other deleted.
  - **The codes are kept too, so the erasure half was the condition, not a nicety.** A kept row from
    `tblTotpBackupCodes` is a second copy of authentication material outside the table erasure
    protects. `GdprEraser::catalogue()` deletes this table by `userID` — whole rows, not blanked
    ones, because a kept row with its person taken out could not be put back anywhere — and it may
    never be added to the pinned "left behind on purpose" list in `tools/gdpr-coverage-selftest.php`.
  - **Only two tables are ever kept**, by an allow-list (`DbBackup::CASCADE_RESCUE`) rather than by
    working it out from the schema. Without that, a table joining `WHOLE_DATABASE_ONLY` later would
    start depositing rows of unreviewed content into a table whose privacy handling was thought
    through for two known shapes. It is also what makes the table name safe to put into a statement.
  - **Over twenty thousand rows and NONE is kept**, deliberately, with the count said out loud:
    keeping some would read as keeping all of them. That ceiling's code path is **not** exercised by
    any test, and proof 27 says so in its header rather than leaving it to be assumed.
  - **Two faults of my own here, both caught by a test and neither by reading.** The mark saying a row
    had gone back was written `if ($put > 0)`, which marked *every* row as put back the moment *one*
    succeeded — so a row that could not go back would have stopped being offered, which is the single
    thing this feature exists to prevent. And the INSERT skipped any column whose `EXTRA` contains the
    word `GENERATED`, which is how MySQL describes **any** column declared `DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`
    — so `updatedAt` was dropped and re-stamped with the moment of the put-back. The row was back,
    with the right key and the right value, and the wrong "last changed" date. The class already had
    `columnFacts()`, which reads `GENERATION_EXPRESSION` and whose comment warns against exactly that
    test; I wrote a worse copy beside it. Only the check that compares *every value of every table*
    caught it — every row-exists check passed.
  - **A database whose upgrade has not been run degrades honestly.** The holding table is not there
    until migration 233 has run, and files reach a server before anybody presses "Run migrations". So
    every reader asks first (`SHOW TABLES LIKE`, the house pattern); the restore then goes ahead, the
    rows are named and lost as before, and the warning says why they could not be kept. Refusing the
    restore instead would block a recovery at the one moment somebody is recovering.
  - **Five things the independent check found, and two of them were untrue sentences an administrator
    would read.** First, the words naming the lost settings rows said "its postal address, map
    position, what3words address and support e-mail" — but the rescue takes EVERY row with a
    `siteID`, whatever its key — `attend.detailRetentionDays`, `giving.retention.years` and the four
    `mail.queue.*` numbers are per-organisation too, and **seven** files under `web/` can write such
    a row. Naming four address fields to somebody whose retention periods had just gone would be worse
    than saying nothing. The sentence is now general, and the page names the actual **keys**, lifted
    out of each kept row — a key says what a setting is without being a value. Second, two comments
    claimed a kept sign-in-code row carried its owner's e-mail address; `tblTotpBackupCodes` has no
    such column, so two clauses of the privacy check **could never fail**. They are replaced with
    clauses that can.
  - **A row put back kept its whole copy for ever, and four documents said otherwise.** Nothing
    anywhere deletes a marked row — Discard takes only waiting rows and the page lists only waiting
    rows — so a hash of somebody's sign-in code, or a stored setting value, would have sat in the
    holding table indefinitely and travelled into every later snapshot and off-site copy. That is the
    unbounded second copy of authentication material the owner was warned about when they chose to
    keep the codes. `rowJson` is now **emptied in the same statement that marks the row**: once the
    row is back, the copy has no purpose, and what is worth keeping is the record that it was held and
    returned. The column is nullable for that reason.
  - **The rescue asked the wrong question, and no existing check could catch it.** It asked whether a
    table was on the held-back list — which is built only from names the manifest itself holds. So a
    snapshot that simply did not CONTAIN `tblSettings` (an imported one, or a hand-edited manifest)
    restored `tblSites`, let the cascade wipe every per-organisation row, rescued nothing and printed
    no #694 warning at all. It now asks whether the table is being **put back**, which covers both.
    Section F of proof 27 is the check, and it is decisive because its snapshot still says it covers
    the whole database, so nothing is held back and the old reading would rescue nothing.
  - **Smaller things from the same round:** the waiting-rows read takes `FOR UPDATE`, because without
    it two administrators pressing at once could be told "1 could not be put back and is still being
    kept" about a row that is back (the house rule the four money writers follow, #647);
    `discardHeldRows()` answers **-1** rather than 0 for a table it keeps no rows for, because
    answering 0 for both made the page say "0 kept row(s) for <anything posted> discarded" and write
    that name into the activity log; the row-count ceiling's recount loop was missing the identifier
    check its sibling applies; and the long docblock explaining `WHOLE_DATABASE_ONLY` had been
    orphaned onto the new constant, taking its `@var` with it.
  - **A second round found five more, and two of my own numbers were wrong.** I wrote "32 files under
    `web/` write such rows". **Seven** can. 32 was not even the count of the thing I cited: the grep I
    put in the notes (`grep -rln "INSERT INTO tblSettings" web/_apps web/_core | wc -l`) gives **30**,
    and it counts files that write *any* settings row — nearly all of which bind `siteID` as the
    literal `NULL`. `.claude/CLAUDE.md` **already said "seven per-organisation writers"** from #668
    and I contradicted my own instruction file. Establish this by reading each INSERT's column list
    against its VALUES, never by counting files that mention the table. This is the same shape as the
    fault the first round existed to repair, two rounds running.
  - **The `FOR UPDATE` took no lock at all.** It was added to a SELECT that ran *before*
    `begin_transaction()`. Nothing in `web/_core/` touches autocommit, so the implicit transaction
    around that SELECT committed the moment it finished and every row lock went with it — while an
    eleven-line comment, the changelog and both instruction files all claimed it stopped two
    administrators reading the same rows. The transaction now starts first. **A lock outside a
    transaction is decoration, and the comment was the only thing asserting otherwise.**
  - **"Because this snapshot does not cover tblSettings" is false in the commonest case**, and the
    restore contradicted itself in one answer. An old-form snapshot *does* contain `tblSettings` —
    the held-back list is built from the manifest's own list, so a table has to be in the snapshot to
    be held back at all. The same answer already said "tblSettings … were left exactly as they are".
    So an administrator mid-recovery was told their settings were not in their backup when they were.
    Both the warning and the card now say the **restore** could not put the table back, which covers
    held-back and simply-absent alike. Nothing held that wording until the independent check; two new
    checks do now, including one that the contradicting sentence is still there.
  - **`put_held_back` still wrote a posted table name into the activity log**, under an event type
    saying a put-back had been attempted and failed. The discard branch had just been fixed for
    exactly that; the put-back branch had not. Both route an unknown name to `BackupActionRefused`
    with no name now.
  - **Section 18 of the eraser test gave an untrue reason, 25 lines below its own correction.** It
    said a marked row "still holds their sign-in codes"; after the fix above a marked row has
    `rowJson` emptied, and it never held an e-mail address. The real reason it must go is that it
    still **names the person** in the column the instruction matches on. Its fixture now nulls
    `rowJson` as the portal does, because a fixture in a state production can never reach is testing
    nothing.
  - **Also corrected: "unused" two-factor backup codes**, in five places. The cascade takes every row
    with a `userID`; `auth/2fa/verify.php` marks a spent code `isUsed = 1` and keeps the row, so the
    record of which codes have been spent goes too — and that record is exactly what
    `WHOLE_DATABASE_ONLY` exists to protect.
  - **A third round found three more, and two were failures to APPLY a correction already written
    down.** Round 2 recorded that "unused" two-factor codes was wrong in five places, and that
    "address rows" understated what the cascade takes. Round 3 found both wordings still live in the
    in-app help page, migration 233's own header, section 18 of the eraser test, this changelog,
    `.claude/HANDOFF.md`, and — on the very line recording the correction — `.claude/CLAUDE.md` and
    its `.OpenAI` mirror. **A document that asserts a fix while stating the thing it fixed is worse
    than one that says nothing**, because the next reader stops looking. The help page mattered most:
    its own comment says it is said there because it is the page somebody opens when they are about
    to put a backup back — so it was the one sentence a customer reads *before* deciding whether to
    accept the loss, and it understated it.
  - **Making the lock real made a new path reachable that the broken version never could.**
    `prepare`, `bind_param`, `execute` and `get_result` sat outside the `try`, and under
    `mysqli_report(MYSQLI_REPORT_STRICT | MYSQLI_REPORT_ERROR)` all of them throw — it takes BOTH
    flags on the statement path, which I had wrong in four documents after correcting it in the two
    code comments — and then got wrong a second way, see below. With the lock genuinely held a second
    administrator now BLOCKS; the page has already called `TimeLimit::atLeast(900)`, so PHP will not
    cut it off first, and at `innodb_lock_wait_timeout` (50 seconds by default) `execute()` throws
    ERROR 1205 — escaping with the transaction **open**. That gave a bare 500 instead of the honest
    message the method exists to give, and because `Logger::db()` hands back the *same* connection
    the `tblErrors` row was written inside the open transaction and rolled back on disconnect: **the
    fault left no record anywhere.** The read is inside the `try` now, with a `finally` that frees and
    closes on every path, and the message tells the second administrator to wait and try again.
  - **A check made only of absences passes when the thing stops happening at all.** Section P
    asserted that the posted table name was *not* in the activity log and the event type was *not* a
    failed put-back — so deleting the `$record()` call entirely left it green, under a name claiming
    "the refusal is recorded WITHOUT the posted name". The positive clause comes first now. Same
    family as #668's section D.
  - **A fifth round found three more, and one of them I had corrected in the code and left wrong in
    four documents.** I wrote that `MYSQLI_REPORT_ERROR` is what makes mysqli throw. It is not:
    **it takes BOTH flags**, and my first
    "correction" was wrong too. Measured on the statement path (`prepare()` on a missing table):
    `ERROR` alone returns false and warns; `STRICT` alone returns false **silently**; only
    `STRICT | ERROR` throws. My original measurement was of a *connect* error, which is reported
    whatever `ERROR` says — so `STRICT` alone does throw there, and I generalised that to statements.
    **Measuring the wrong code path and then writing "measured, not reasoned" against the conclusion
    is worse than reasoning**, because the next reader has no cause to doubt it. The two code comments had been corrected a round
    earlier; `.claude/CLAUDE.md`, `.OpenAI/CONTEXT.md`, `CHANGELOG.md` and `DEV_NOTES.md` were left
    telling the next reader that the wrong flag is load-bearing — the fifth time in this package that
    a correction was recorded and applied in one place.
  - **Also: a pronoun with no antecedent, and a log line that said the opposite of what happened.**
    The over-the-ceiling sentence read "as they stood when **it** was taken", where "it" was first
    defined later in the same sentence. And a discard REFUSED by the database was recorded as
    `BackupHeldRowsDiscarded` — the same event type as a successful one — so a log search by type
    counted a run in which nothing was discarded. The put-back branch separates its success from its
    failure and its comment names that exact harm, so this was the same half-applied fix a fourth
    time. It has its own type now, `BackupHeldRowsDiscardFailed`, added to the page test's allow-list.
  - **Then the design changed, because the same thing kept failing.** The warning sentence had grown
    to ninety lines and nine nested ternaries over five rounds, and **four of the six wording faults
    those rounds found were inside it** — every one a ternary in the middle of a clause, and not one
    findable by any check, because nothing judges how an assembled sentence reads. It is now
    `DbBackup::cascadeWarning()`, holding **eight complete sentences** named by the three facts that
    choose between them (ahead/done, kept/lost, one/many). A missing combination is obvious and a
    wording fault is visible without evaluating anything in your head. All sixteen outputs were
    printed by calling the real method, so nothing was transcribed. This is the project's own rule
    being followed: when the same item fails two rounds running, simplify before refining again.
  - **A sixth round found four more, and the worst was that my own correction was wrong the same way.**
    I had written that `MYSQLI_REPORT_STRICT` is what makes mysqli throw, with "measured, not reasoned"
    beside it. I had measured a **connect** error. On the STATEMENT path — the four calls the sentence
    is about — `ERROR` alone returns false and warns, `STRICT` alone returns false **silently**, and
    only both together throw. A connect error is reported whatever `ERROR` says, which is why `STRICT`
    alone throws there and why the measurement looked conclusive. **Measuring the wrong code path and
    then writing "measured" against the conclusion is worse than reasoning**, because the next reader
    has no cause to doubt it. `web/_core/bootstrap.php`'s own comment carried the same untruth, in the
    authoritative place, and is corrected too — one comment line outside this package's file list.
  - **A sentence that was wrong both ways round.** It first hedged on whether the snapshot CONTAINS the
    table and said nothing about row currency; the round-4 fix hedged on currency and ASSERTED
    presence — false for the case round 2 had just added coverage for, a snapshot that does not contain
    the table at all. Wrong in the reassuring direction: it told somebody mid-recovery that rows they
    had just lost for good were readable from their backup. All three places now state both
    conditions, the Discard button's confirmation included. The CAUSE is no longer asserted either
    ("most likely this database has not had its upgrade run"): all the code knows is that the table is
    absent, and a hand-dropped table looks the same.
  - **A fourth clause that cannot fail**, and the same shape deleted forty lines below it in the same
    edit with the reason attached: `discardHeldRows('tblSettings') >= 0`, when the method ends
    `return max(0, $gone)`. Gone, with what it failed to test said plainly instead.
  - **Half the eight sentences were exercised by nothing.** The `canKeep === false` branch — what an
    un-upgraded database sees — was reached by no check in either test, and proof 27's own "what this
    cannot show" list had not mentioned it. **Section G reaches all four now**, and it caught two
    faults of its own in two runs, both mine: it first restored a snapshot taken while the holding
    table still existed (so the restore failed outright, correctly, on a table the database no longer
    had — an un-upgraded database's snapshots have no such table either), and then ran the rehearsal
    AFTER the real restore, by which point there was nothing left to lose and nothing to warn about.
    `brs_tidy()` also puts the table back if that section is killed between its two renames, so a
    killed run cannot poison the next.
  - **What this did not do at first was #697, and that is now fixed** (see the entry above this one):
    `tblRestoreHeldRows` was an ordinary table, so restoring a snapshot taken before some rows were
    kept replaced them, and those waiting rows are the only copy outside the snapshot being restored
    from. The restore warned, before and after, which is not a fix. It now carries them through.
  - Tests: proof 27 of `tools/backup-restore-selftest.php` (the class, against a real database),
    section P of `tools/backup-page-selftest.php` (the page, over real HTTP), section 18 of
    `tools/gdpr-eraser-selftest.php` (the erasure really runs and touches nobody else's row).
- **Changed — a date a series pattern change ADDS now arrives as a draft (#692, the owner's decision of 31 October 2026)**
  - It used to inherit the template date's status, so on a published series the new dates appeared on
    the public calendar the moment somebody pressed the button. They now arrive unpublished and
    somebody has to publish them from Manage Events.
  - **Why:** an added date is a copy of the series and nothing more. It has no registration window of
    its own — the template's `registrationClosesAt` is a moment just before the TEMPLATE's own date,
    so a date added weeks later would arrive with registration already closed — and nothing beyond
    the series' description. A draft is one click from being right; a wrongly published service is
    not, and **there is no way in this repository to bring back a date that has been hidden** (#691).
  - **Saying so is half of it.** The preview says it before anything is written, and the message
    afterwards says "N date(s) added as drafts" rather than "added" — without that, the first thing
    anybody does is go looking for the dates on the public calendar, where they are not. Both
    wordings are pinned by checks of their own (S15b, S15c), because they live in two places and
    either could be dropped alone.
  - **Publishing them all at once already works**, and the independent check found that out after I
    had written the opposite in three places. The handler redirects to the series' **bulk edit** page,
    which lists every date including drafts with a tick-box each and a bulk Status control. The
    preview, a code comment and `FEATURES.md` all said "one at a time" and pointed at the wrong page;
    all three are corrected, and **#696 is closed as not planned** — I raised it from an assumption
    without reading the page the handler redirects to.
  - **And the message told subscribers the opposite of the truth, which the independent check also
    caught.** It said "Anybody subscribing to this calendar now sees one repeating entry" whenever the
    repeat rule was written — but `calendar/export.php` reads a series' run with
    `AND e.status = 'published'` and collapses it only when the *published* dates match the rule. With
    the added dates in draft they never can, so a subscriber sees each date on its own: the sentence
    claimed the opposite of what the feed does, for exactly the change just made. Before #692 the
    added dates were published, the two agreed, and it was true. The message now has **three**
    answers, not two, and says how many drafts are holding it up. The rule row is still decided on
    the dates alone, which is right — the pattern either describes the series or it does not.
  - Eight planted faults, all caught, including the one that matters most (the added date quietly
    going back to inheriting the template's status) and both directions of the subscriber sentence.
    Covering the second direction needed a new check on a change that only RE-TIMES dates: that
    branch of the message had never been exercised, which planting proved by making the page claim
    drafts remained when none did — and nothing failed.
  - **A correction worth recording, because I reported it wrongly on the way.** I claimed
    `calendar/manage/series-edit.php` had never printed the flash message it was given, and changed
    it. That was **false**: `git show HEAD` shows one read and one print block, and it had always
    worked. The real cause of the failing check was my own test — it first read the message from the
    wrong page, then built its address by joining two already-built addresses (#536, "never join two
    built addresses"), which doubled the organisation's part. My "fix" then added a second read of
    the session, which consumed the message before the page's own block could print it — so for a
    while I had broken a working page while believing I was fixing it. That page is untouched;
    **#692 changes two files.** The lesson is the one already in memory: check the thing that would
    disprove it, which here was two seconds of `git show`.

- **Fixed — three more self-tests that were red at HEAD, found by running the WHOLE set for the first time (#695)**
  - The lesson from #690 was to run every self-test at the end of each package, not only the ones
    that touch what changed. Doing that found **three red tests, none of them broken by the work in
    hand**: `gdpr-coverage-selftest.php`, `mail-pages-selftest.php` and `sign-in-limits-selftest.php`.
    All 66 tests now pass, together with the 45 audit checks.
  - **The erasure coverage test** pins exactly which pages may file a data-erasure request as ALREADY
    CONFIRMED — no e-mail link needed. It named two; the #569 offboarding work added a third,
    `_apps/offboarding/do.php`. That caller is legitimate: it needs a signed-in administrator of the
    open organisation, a POST with a valid form token, and `AccountGuard::check()`. So the check now
    names all three AND pins those gates, because what makes the third one safe is its gates, not its
    name. It matters more than most: in `after_undo_window` mode the daily sweep carries out a
    confirmed request with nobody looking at it.
  - **And the first attempt at pinning those gates passed on broken code, three ways** — found by the
    independent check, by planting, the same day. It matched each gate's `if (...)` line, so deleting
    the REFUSAL inside the braces passed; and it named callers by `basename()`, so moving the call
    into a new, completely ungated `zzplant/do.php` was indistinguishable from the gated
    `offboarding/do.php`. Now: callers are named by their path under `web/`, every gate must refuse
    (an `exit` before the closing brace), the three must appear in order, and the source is masked so
    a `}` or the word `exit` inside a message cannot answer that question falsely. Seven planted
    faults, all caught.
  - **The two password-reset tests** compare the page a person lands on across four cases — address
    with an account, address with none, mail server refusing, certificate expired — to prove a
    stranger cannot tell which addresses have accounts. Both were failing, and the pages were
    measured rather than reasoned about: the ONLY difference was `nonce="…"` on the inline script
    `Asset.php` writes, which arrived with #625. The portal was right and the tests were comparing
    noise. The nonce is stripped **by name**, not by widening the hex pattern to 32 characters, which
    would blind the comparison to any real difference of that length — proved by planting a 32-hex
    value that is not a nonce and watching it still be caught.
  - **A clause in the sign-in limits test could never fail.** "The ELEVENTH try is refused … and the
    link is not used up" looked a reset link up by `hash('sha256', $link)`, while the portal stores
    `hash('sha256', 'reset-link-utc:' . $token)`. The row was never found, `null['usedAt']` is null,
    so it passed on a row that did not exist while raising a PHP warning nobody read. It now calls
    the portal's own `Auth::resetLinkFingerprint()` and requires the row to exist.
- **Added — one command that runs every self-test (#695, `tools/run-all-selftests.sh`)**
  - Starts the three throwaway MySQL servers, loads `full_schema.sql` into a database per test, runs
    every self-test with exactly the environment its own workflow step gives it, prints one line per
    test, removes the containers and exits non-zero if anything failed. `--list`, `--only <substring>`
    and `--keep`. Deliberately **not** in the pre-push hook: that hook is nine seconds and this is
    about fifteen minutes, and a push gate that slow gets bypassed with `--no-verify`.
  - **It found a bug in itself on the first run, which is the argument for having built it:**
    `docker exec -i` reads standard input, and the loop was being fed the test list on standard
    input, so the first schema load swallowed the rest of the list. One database was built and 37
    tests reported "Unknown database". Both loops now read the table on file descriptor 3.
  - **Five more faults found by the independent check**, each of which would have made it report
    green or near-green while something was wrong:
    - `php -S` with `PHP_CLI_SERVER_WORKERS=6` forks six workers, and killing the master **orphaned
      them, still bound to the port**. A later run then failed to bind (into a log nothing reads),
      its readiness probe got an answer from the *old* server and said "ready", and the importer test
      ran against a previous run's calendar fixtures and reported green. Measured: six such workers
      were still serving two hours later. The children are now killed by this run's own scratch path,
      and the port pre-flight covers **every** port the table names, not just the three database ones.
    - `tools/maillib/tests/run.php` was missing from the table, so "every self-test" was untrue and a
      full local run missed the one thing #592 exists to protect.
    - The header promised it "refuses rather than running a reduced set that looks complete". Untrue
      for five programs, which warn and carry on; it now says so, and says what each costs.
    - A mistyped `--only` printed "0 tests ran; 0 not green" and exited **0** — a typo read exactly
      like a clean run. It now refuses.
    - `--help` printed a fixed line range that stopped just before the two sections a reader most
      needs.
  - Also: `--only` no longer builds all 38 databases for one test; an interrupt now stops rather than
    tearing the servers down and running the rest against nothing; the QR test gets
    `--with-qrencode` when qrencode is present, as the workflow does; and the API description's check
    runs with `-I`, as `pr-security.yml` does.
- **Fixed — two self-tests that ran in no workflow at all (#646's shape again, #671, #668)**
  - `tools/setting-limit-selftest.php` and `tools/offsite-settings-selftest.php` were invoked by
    nothing. Both now run in `portal-selftests.yml`, on every pull request with no path filter —
    `backup-selftest.yml` would have been the natural home for the off-site one, but it is
    path-filtered and does not even list the off-site files, so a change to them would have run
    nothing. The off-site test REFUSES without `rclone`, which GitHub's image does not carry, so the
    job installs it from Ubuntu's own archive; the three rclone commands used (`copyto`, `deletefile`,
    `lsf --files-only`) all predate that version, and the step prints `rclone version` so the one
    actually used is on record.
  - Three counts came out of that workflow's header, which had gone stale in silence: it said
    "twenty-three throwaway databases" while the loop built twenty-six.

- **Fixed — two self-tests that had been failing at HEAD, and nothing had run them since 27 October (#690)**
  - `tools/gdpr-eraser-selftest.php` (now 230/230) and `tools/backup-restore-selftest.php` (now 364/364,
    25 proofs) both failed on the committed tree. Every later package inherited a red baseline, and
    because they run on any pull request touching `web/_sql/**`, the next pull request would have been
    red whatever it contained.
  - **One root cause behind most of it, and it was my own work.** Migration 231 (#677) copied each
    organisation's address into its own `tblSettings` row — **the first row that table had ever held
    with a non-empty `siteID`**. Several long-standing expectations had been true only because no such
    row existed, and the behaviour they tripped over is older than they are.
  - **The erasure test** compared `tblEventAttendance.attendeeRef`, the VIRTUAL generated column added
    by migration 224. A generated column is a function of the stored ones, so it necessarily moves when
    an erasure empties one of its inputs — from `u:920001` to `w:…` here. The comparison now steps over
    columns the database works out, as the test's own row-builder already did. **Checked rather than
    assumed that this is not an erasure gap:** both real writers in
    `calendar/event-attendance-mark.php` set either `userID` or `walkinName` and never both, so on a
    real row `attendeeRef` becomes EMPTY after erasure — exactly what #487 requires, since two erased
    people must not be tellable apart.
  - **A second, separate fault in the same test:** the retention-race proof spawns a child process, and
    an EMPTY value in the environment array handed to `proc_open()` does not reach the child as an
    empty string — the variable is simply absent, so `getenv()` answers `false`, which PHP 8.5 refuses
    for `new mysqli()`'s `?string $password`. The child died before connecting. An empty password is the
    ordinary local setup (the file's own header starts a container with `MYSQL_ALLOW_EMPTY_PASSWORD=1`)
    and CI sets one, so this could only ever fail off CI.
  - **The backup test** was failing because an OLD-FORM snapshot deliberately holds `tblMigrations`,
    `tblSettings` and `tblTotpBackupCodes` back, while still restoring `tblSites` — and
    `tblSettings.siteID` carries `ON DELETE CASCADE`, so replacing the sites takes the per-organisation
    row with it and nothing puts it back. The restore warns about both halves, and **those two warnings
    are now pinned by checks of their own**, so the comparisons that had to be narrowed are more than
    paid for. The proofs that break the world now mend it where they break it, bounded to rows a
    cascade could really have taken — a row with every link empty is left missing for the comparison to
    catch, which was proved by planting.
  - **A timing flake in the same test, which would have failed on a fast CI runner too:** proof 19
    pre-creates the folder names for "this second" and the next to prove a snapshot will not reuse a
    taken name — but a snapshot taken a few lines earlier can land in that very second, in which case
    the check demanded that a folder holding 229 files be empty. It now checks only the folders it
    really created.
  - **And one guard removed for being unexercised.** A catch-all mend in the between-proof reset turned
    out to catch nothing once the two per-proof mends existed: deleting it failed not one of the 364
    checks. An unexercised guard is worse than none, because it is believed.
  - Raised and not fixed: **#694** — restoring a pre-27-October backup silently loses every
    organisation's address and support e-mail, by the mechanism above. The restore says a linked table
    was changed, but names the table rather than what was lost, and nothing offers to put it back.

- **Added — the pattern of a repeating series can be changed after it exists (#669, migration 232)**
  - Repeating events have shipped since #569 but **on creation only**, deliberately rather than
    half-offered. The new page `/calendar/manage/series-repattern`, reached from the series list, does
    the four things that were missing: shift every future date (the service moves from 10:00 to 10:30),
    go weekly to fortnightly, extend a run that stopped at the ceiling, and cut the rest of a run short.
    All four fall out of one rule — an existing date is paired with a new one **by the day**, never by
    the time.
  - **Nothing is written without a preview.** `Portal\Core\SeriesRepattern` is the ONE place that
    decides what a change would do; it takes facts and returns a plan of four named lists (re-timed,
    added, removed, left alone with the reason), so the page that shows the preview and the handler
    that applies it cannot disagree about what is about to happen. The confirmation carries a
    fingerprint of the previewed plan: if the series has moved in between, the change is refused and
    the new preview is shown. An EMPTY fingerprint is refused too, because `hash_equals('', '')` is
    true — the shape of the OAuth `state` hole of 27 October 2026.
  - **A future date with anything attached is never moved and never removed.** The owner chose this on
    31 October 2026 over a tick-box per attached date: the worst case here is a date that needs a
    manual fix, the worst case there is a lost attendance register, and that tick-box can only be as
    safe as the list of what-would-be-lost written beside it. `SeriesRepattern::ATTACHMENTS` names all
    **32** tables with an `eventID` foreign key, and
    `tools/audit-checks/check_series_attachments_complete.py` compares it against `full_schema.sql`
    and fails BOTH ways — a table missing from it, and an entry naming a table that no longer points
    at an event.
  - **"Edited by hand" is worked out, not remembered.** Migration 232 adds `tblEvents.patternStart`:
    the moment the pattern produced that date. Equal to its start means nobody moved it. `updatedAt`
    could not do this job — it carries `ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`, so the existing bulk-edit page
    already moves it on rows nobody edited. The column is deliberately **not backfilled** (claiming
    every existing date is untouched would move exactly the dates it exists to protect); instead an
    unrecorded date is judged against the series' own stored rule, which is what makes the feature
    work on an installation that already has series in it rather than only on a fresh one.
  - **A date that stays is updated in place** — only its start and end — which is what keeps a
    hand-changed title, venue or description safe without having to detect those changes at all. **A
    date that goes is soft-deleted**, so nothing cascades and it can be put back. The whole change
    runs in one transaction: a half-applied pattern is the worst outcome, because the diary would then
    hold some dates on the old pattern and some on the new with no way to tell which.
  - Afterwards the old rule row is always removed, and a new one written only when the series holds
    exactly the dates the new pattern makes. Otherwise subscribers see each date on its own, which is
    the #670 decision and the usual outcome for a series that has already started.
  - **A real bug the HTTP test caught that nothing else could.** The "which week" dropdown looped over
    `['1' => 'First', …]`; PHP turns a numeric array key into an **integer**, and with
    `declare(strict_types=1)` handing an int to `htmlspecialchars()` is a TypeError. The page rendered
    its heading, its explanation and most of its form, threw there, and the error handler printed the
    footer — so the answer was HTTP 200 ending in an ordinary `</html>` with the preview silently
    missing. `php -l` cannot see it and no audit script here can either.
  - **The independent check found six real problems, and the worst was in the safety list itself.**
    `ATTACHMENTS` was built from the schema's FOREIGN KEY declarations, and **two tables name an event
    with no foreign key at all** — `tblEventRSVPs`, whose `eventID` is `NOT NULL` and which holds
    every member's going/maybe/no answer, and `tblZoomMeeting`. So the list that exists to protect
    records silently missed the table holding the very thing the owner's decision names out loud, and
    the page offered to remove such a date with no reason beside it. And be precise about what that costs,
    because an earlier wording here was not: this page SOFT-deletes, no ON DELETE rule fires on an
    UPDATE, so all three values behave identically here — every attached row survives, pointing at a
    date nobody can see. `'no rule'` is the worst of the three only if something later really DELETEs
    the event row. Measured on MySQL 8.0.36. The check now looks for the
    `eventID` COLUMN, excluding a table whose own auto-increment key is called that
    (`tblWebhookEvent`), and the constant now matches what MySQL itself reports — 34 and 34, verified
    against a loaded database rather than against the SQL. **Its docstring had asserted "Nothing in
    this schema does that today (checked)", which was written without checking and was false.**
  - The other five: a day removed and then re-added collided on `eventSlug`, because
    `uq_event_site_slug` covers soft-deleted rows — the whole change rolled back with "Something went
    wrong … please try again", which retrying could never cure, and **intermittently**, because the
    address was built from the date's position in the add list. The address is now asked of the
    database. A date the pattern ADDS copied every column of its template but four, so extending a run
    whose next date had been cancelled by hand created new dates that were **already cancelled**,
    carrying that date's reason — and copied `submitterName`/`submitterEmail`, a private individual's
    name and e-mail, onto rows they had nothing to do with, which `GdprEraser` clears on neither
    column. `followsPattern()` compared the START only while promising it caught "a changed TIME", so
    a service lengthened by hand was silently shortened again (`patternEnd` now records the finish and
    both are compared). The one remedy the page offers for a date it refuses to touch was a link built
    as `?eventID=`, which `calendar/manage/index.php` reads nowhere — the repository's own "name
    things by the right identifier" trap. And 31 of the 32 attachment tables were never exercised by
    any test, so a one-line edit making thirty kinds of record invisible passed all 202 checks.
  - Also fixed from the lesser findings: the attachment list is **re-asked inside the transaction**
    before anything is hidden, so a register created while somebody was confirming cannot be orphaned
    (and that refusal has its own honest message, not "something went wrong"); two dates on one day
    get their own reason rather than being called "moved by hand"; a stored `custom` frequency no
    longer prefills a form the page then refuses; and the fingerprint's comment now says what it is
    for — guarding against a mistake, not against intent.
  - Tests: `tools/series-repattern-selftest.php` (72 checks, no database — the class has no
    dependencies and that is checked too) and sections R and S of
    `tools/event-repeat-pages-selftest.php` (230 in all over real HTTP, reading the rows back out of
    the database). Both are wired into the workflows, and the audit check is a hard gate. Twenty-two
    faults were planted, each proved applied, caught and reversed byte-identically — **and four of
    them were not caught at first, which is the most useful thing in this package.** Dropping the "did
    they press the confirm button" requirement failed nothing, because the only request carrying a
    fingerprint was one that also confirmed; the hidden fingerprint sits in the same form, so a real
    browser's second press of the preview button would have applied the change. Two checks passed on
    the rule row written when the series was *created*. One pinned the recorded finish on a pattern
    change that re-timed nothing. And the slug check removed dates the *save handler* had named, whose
    addresses cannot collide with the page's. **A check satisfied by state the change never touched is
    not a check, and a guard never exercised alone is not covered.**
  - **A second, narrow check of the fix round found four more**, which is why it was run. The safety
    list's own documentation still said "every table with an `eventID` **foreign key** — 32 of them" in
    three places, restating the exact false premise the round had just corrected. The claim that
    section S covered the list's **last** entry was wrong — `tblEventRSVPs` is the 33rd of 34, and a
    loop stopping one table short passed all 230 checks (the real last entry, `tblZoomMeeting`, is
    covered now, and the wording says plainly that a loop skipping a MIDDLE table still is not). A date
    the pattern adds was inheriting its template's **registration window**, whose closing moment is
    just before the template's own date — so a date added weeks later arrived with registration already
    closed, which both register pages treat as a hard gate. And three places promised "an administrator
    can put it back" about a hidden date when **no restore path exists anywhere in this repository**
    (#691); the only code that ever clears `isDeleted` is inside `FeedImporter`.
  - Two silent false negatives in the audit check were measured and fixed: an `eventID` column declared
    `INTEGER` was not matched at all (`INT` listed first consumed its leading three letters), and the
    word `AUTO_INCREMENT` inside the column's **own comment** excluded the whole table, because SQL
    string literals were not blanked. Both made a table vanish from the comparison while the check
    still passed.
  - **`registrationEnabled` is given its default rather than NULL**, and that was found by the test
    rather than by reading: it is `TINYINT(1) NOT NULL`, so binding null to it failed every add. The
    first round's note that "every one of these columns is nullable" was true of the original eleven
    only.
  - **Three more vacuous checks, found by planting — six in all across the package.** The zone check
    could not fail while every event in the made-up world shared one zone (it now builds a series whose
    template and earliest date hold different zones). The Zoom check attached a record to a date an
    earlier check in the same section had already removed. And nothing read the sentence a person
    actually sees for two dates on one day, because `plan()` held its own copy of the wording while the
    class test exercised an unreachable second copy.
  - **Not done, and it needs the owner:** nothing covers two administrators changing one series at the
    same moment. `access-pages-selftest.php`-style harnesses run the built-in server with one worker,
    so two requests never overlap and such a test would pass on broken code.

- **Fixed — the off-site backup's six settings now really decide what a run does, and a run is recorded at last (#671)**
  - **The settings were decorative, on every installation.** `/admin/maintenance/offsite-backup`
    saved six `backup.offsite.*` rows and **nothing in the repository read any of them** — the sync
    script used the variables written into its own copy on the server, and said so in its own header
    and in the setup guide. So an administrator could choose a destination, type an rclone remote,
    set how many copies to keep and an alert address, press Save, be told "Off-site backup settings
    saved." and have none of it affect anything, with or without a command line. The owner decided on
    30 October 2026 to make them real rather than delete the feature.
  - **A new bridge, `tools/offsite-backup/read-offsite-settings.php`**, copied to `_backups/` beside
    the script. It reads the INSTALLATION's rows, validates each value and prints them for the script.
    **It refuses rather than escapes:** a value that does not match its pattern is not printed at all,
    the script keeps the value in its own file, and a `WARNING` says which setting and why. An escaped
    destination is still a destination nobody chose, and a copy of the whole database is what is at
    stake.
  - **The script (now 1.2.0) reads that output without `source` or `eval`**, accepts only six keys and
    re-checks every value in bash as well — two guards, because the bash one is what would have to
    hold if the bridge were edited on the server. Switched off on the page now means a run sends
    nothing, records itself `skipped` and exits 0.
  - **A second, separate fault, and it was known: no run was ever recorded on a real installation.**
    `log-offsite-result.php` required `'../../web/_core/bootstrap.php'`, which resolves only when the
    portal's folder is literally named `web` — true in a checkout of this repository, where it was
    tested on 12 October 2026, and false on a customer's server, where that folder is named by the
    customer. So the recorder could not load the portal, `tblOffsiteSyncLog` stayed empty, and the
    page showed "No runs logged yet" however many copies had really been sent — a FAILED run
    included. **The setup guide had written this down as a limitation rather than treating it as a
    bug.** Both files now find the portal instead of assuming its name.
  - **The page stops implying things that are not true.** A standing notice says it needs a command
    line on the server and a sending program, and does nothing on shared hosting without one. The
    page also reads the script actually sitting on the server and says whether the settings are **in
    force**, **ignored by the script** (a copy from before 30 October ignores them) or have no script
    to obey them. The `Weekly` / `Monthly` boxes no longer imply a rotation the script does not do —
    it adds the two numbers — and the total is shown. The destination list now says that the S3 and
    SFTP addresses are set in the script file, not there (#688).
  - **Also fixed, the #674 shape:** the page prefilled from the merged `App::settings()` while saving
    installation-wide, so a global administrator inside an organisation with its own row could press
    Save on an untouched form and make that organisation's value everyone's. It reads
    `InstallationSettings::layer()` now — the same layer the bridge reads, so the page and the script
    can no longer disagree about where a copy is going. Removed from
    `check_install_wide_prefill.pending.txt` (13 → 12).
  - **Tests.** New `tools/offsite-settings-selftest.php`: 112 checks against a real MySQL database,
    real bash, real `openssl` and real rclone sending to a folder on the test machine — including
    section D, which removes the override and proves the end-to-end check then fails. New section O of
    `tools/backup-page-selftest.php`: 25 checks over real HTTP (181 → 206), including a script whose
    call to the bridge is **commented out** while every mention of it remains, which is why the page's
    check strips comments before looking. Existing tests re-run green: site-modes 136, access-pages
    334, live-chat-moderation 64, page-head 19, static-calls 150.
  - **The independent review found 14 real problems and they are fixed.** The worst was that
    `log-offsite-result.php` **threw away every run's log**: its flag pattern
    `/^--([a-z\-]+)(=(.*))?$/` has no `s` modifier, so `.` cannot cross a newline and the WHOLE
    match failed for any multi-line value — and a run's log is never one line. So
    `tblOffsiteSyncLog.output` was NULL for every run ever recorded. That mattered far more than it
    sounds: the bridge **refuses** a value it will not put on a command line, and a `WARN` line was
    the only record of which setting and why — so a mistyped destination left no trace anywhere an
    administrator could reach, while the page badged the settings "in force". Two comments written
    in this package claimed the opposite. Fixed by splitting at the first `=`; the page now reads
    `output` and shows each run's warnings, prominently for the newest run.
  - **`Portal\Core\OffsiteSettings` is now the ONE place that decides whether a stored off-site
    value can be used.** The rules lived only inside the bridge, so the page could not ask them: it
    accepted an rclone remote with a space or a capital (an ordinary typo), stored it, said
    "saved", showed it back and badged the settings in force, while every run used the remote inside
    the script file — and where the customer had set that fallback to a real remote, as the guide
    tells them to, **the copy went somewhere the administrator had not chosen**. The page now warns
    at the moment of saving, and under the box itself for an already-stored value. Writing the
    pattern a second time on the page was rejected: two guards that can drift apart are worse than
    one.
  - **"Run now" no longer reports green success for a run that sent nothing.** Exit 0 stopped
    meaning "a copy went" the moment the skip path was added, and the one reader of it was not
    changed — so on **every fresh installation** (the setting is seeded off) the first thing an
    administrator did after setting it up said "Off-site sync completed in 1s." It reads the status
    of the row the run just wrote, and says plainly when it cannot confirm either way.
  - **Three sentences this package had added were measured false and are reworded.** The banner's
    "nothing here is sending a copy unless Recent runs shows one" — recording is allowed to fail
    without failing the run, so an empty list means "nothing recorded", not "nothing sent". The
    "switched off, so nothing is being sent" notice — the script's documented fallback is to SEND
    when it cannot reach the database, so that notice was false in exactly the cases that matter.
    And "each of those three cases prints a WARNING" in both the script header and the setup guide —
    a setting with no row stored prints nothing, deliberately.
  - **Three smaller faults, all real:** a very large stored value broke the pipe the script read the
    bridge's first line through and, under `set -o pipefail`, **aborted every backup** while blaming
    the wrong line (now bounded at 256 characters by the class, and the script no longer uses a pipe
    there); a value the bash guard rejected was skipped in total silence, which its own comment
    denied (it now names the setting); and an out-of-range stored keep figure was prefilled into an
    input carrying `min`/`max`, which makes the browser refuse to submit **the whole form** — the
    #668 trap, written down and then walked into.
  - **Also fixed:** the script-reads-settings detection required `"${READ_PHP}"` and so reported a
    script written `$READ_PHP` — the same call — as disobedient, in a red alert; it now accepts
    both. The page's "what it cannot see" list now admits the two shapes it genuinely cannot: a call
    disabled by its own condition (`false && php ...`), and the recorder, which is asked separately.
  - **A second review round found four more, including a fault in the first fix.** "Run now" read
    `ORDER BY logID DESC LIMIT 1` with nothing tying it to the run just made, so "recorded no run"
    really meant "the log table has never held a row". **Measured: with one older `success` row on
    file and a script that recorded nothing, the page answered "Off-site sync completed in 0s." in
    green** — the exact wording the check was added to stop. So the fix worked only on a fresh
    installation, the one case where the fault is invisible; and last week's `skipped` row would have
    decided this week's message. The handler now reads `MAX(logID)` before the run and asks only
    about rows after it. The same misreading disabled the fallback insert: `$mostRecent === null`
    meant "no row has ever existed", so on any installation with history a failed run that never
    reached its own logger **recorded nothing at all**. Pinned by O11b, the one check in that section
    an empty table cannot satisfy — which is exactly why the fault survived the first version of it.
  - **The keep range was decided in four places** (the save handler's literals, the display clamp,
    the boxes' own `min`/`max`, and the bridge). All four now come from
    `Portal\Core\OffsiteSettings`, so changing a constant cannot leave one behind.
  - **A third overstated guarantee of mine, caught by measurement.** Both the bridge and the class
    said the length ceiling was "the second of two guards" alongside the script's pipe fix. Measured
    by raising the ceiling: the run then gets past the settings step and **rclone** refuses the
    200,000-character remote instead, so the backup still does not happen. The two stop different
    things and the ceiling is the only one that keeps a copy going out. Also noted beside the code:
    an over-long alert address is held back twice over, because `filter_var` refuses a local part
    beyond about 64 characters anyway — so that branch is belt and braces, not the only thing.
  - **Final counts.** `tools/offsite-settings-selftest.php` 112 → **195** checks; section O of
    `tools/backup-page-selftest.php` 24 → **77**, taking that file to **259**. Twenty-nine planted
    faults across the two, each proved to have applied, each caught, each reversed and checked
    byte-identical. Two checks in section O were found **already red** when the page moved under
    them, and one check of its own passed on a planted fault until it was narrowed to read a single
    block — both written up where they happened.
  - **Not done, with issues raised:** #688 (no box for the S3 bucket or SFTP host, so two of the three
    destinations are only half-controlled by the page) and #689 (`access-pages-selftest.php` counts
    through `mysql.general_log`, which is server-wide, so it fails spuriously beside anything else on
    the same MySQL server — it cost two false failures in this run).
- **Decided and closed — a repeating series' feed falls back rather than publishing exceptions (#670)**
  - **The issue's premise was stale.** It said the feed "sends the pattern only", so cancelling, moving
    or editing one date was invisible to subscribers. Measured over real HTTP: all three were already
    handled. `calendar/export.php` expands the stored pattern, compares it against the dates the viewer
    may actually see **and** every detail the published entry carries, and publishes the series one date
    at a time when they differ. That guard arrived with #569's independent check — the same check that
    found the two faults #670 credits it with — and it covers all three symptoms, not two.
  - **The owner's decision, 30 October 2026: the fallback IS the answer.** `EXDATE` and
    `RECURRENCE-ID` overrides are not wanted. So FEATURES.md no longer says the feed "cannot yet"
    show a changed date; it says the behaviour is deliberate, and states what it costs — a year-long
    weekly service with one cancelled date becomes about fifty entries in a subscriber's calendar
    rather than one.
  - **Four checks added**, because two of the three symptoms had none: N20–N23 of
    `event-repeat-pages-selftest.php` now cover **cancelling** and **renaming** one date alongside the
    existing move and delete, each starting from a series the feed really does collapse so none can
    pass vacuously (126 → 130 checks).
  - **What N21 proves, precisely.** Two things stop the collapse when a date is cancelled and **they
    mask each other**: `status` is one of the compared columns, and the feed's status filter drops a
    cancelled event before the comparison sees it. Planting proved it — with `status` removed from the
    compared list N21 still passes, because the cancelled row is simply absent and the date lists
    differ instead. So N21 proves the behaviour, not which half carries it. `export.php`'s own note
    says the same of the pair, and the first version of my comment claimed the wrong one.
