- **Fixed — the mail queue's four numbers were the live half of the limits rule, and a tripwire now guards the lot (#668, part 2)**
  - **Every one of #668's 32 candidate settings is judged**, and the answer is narrower than the list
    suggests. All 32 are seeded installation-wide, and `_apps/settings/save.php` **refuses to add a
    per-organisation row for a key the installation already has** — so for almost all of them an
    organisation cannot override at all, whatever the name suggests. The complete exposure was
    `attend.detailRetentionDays` (its own page; fixed in part 1) and the **four `mail.queue.*`
    numbers** in `MailQueue::NUMBERS`, which are the one deliberate exception to that refusal. (An
    earlier draft of this entry said five, contradicting its own heading two lines above.)
  - **The mail-queue numbers, fixed.** `MailQueue::ownNumberCheck()` tested only `sensible()` — the hard
    range **in code** — and merely *mentioned* the installation's value in its words. The Settings page
    needs `App::isAdmin()`, not `isRootAdmin()`, so **an administrator of a single organisation** could
    set `keepFailedDays` to 365 where the installation chose 7, keeping a failed message's body
    (encrypted, but on the installation's disk) for a year, or `maxAgeHours` to 720 where it chose 48,
    sending a reset link a month old. It now refuses with the ceiling named. **The CAP had no test** —
    be precise, because an earlier draft said the method had none, which would have meant a
    regression in it went unnoticed: section F8 already drove `ownNumberCheck()` through the real
    page with four checks. What nothing covered was the comparison with the installation's value.
    F8 now drives all four numbers against their ceilings over real HTTP (155 → 159 checks).
  - **The cap is not save-time only.** `MailQueue::numbers()`, which is what the JOB uses, also takes
    the smaller of the organisation's value and the installation's — so a row stored before this
    check existed, written by direct SQL, or brought back by a whole-database restore of an older
    backup is brought down rather than obeyed. The independent check measured the first version
    using 365 days where the installation said 7, which also made the comment beside
    `ownNumberCheck()` untrue: it justifies reading the installation's row there precisely so that
    the save test and what the job does cannot disagree.
  - **It reads the installation's own row rather than asking `SettingLimit`, deliberately:** the queue
    reads these numbers with one `LIKE 'mail.queue.%'` query because a scheduled job serves many
    organisations and cannot use the request's merged settings. Two readers could then disagree about
    what the job will actually do, which is worse than a little duplication. The rule is the same.
  - **The noticeboard, which the owner asked about specifically:** `noticeboard.upload.maxBytes` is
    seeded installation-wide, read with `App::settings()` by `noticeboard/api/upload.php`, and written
    by **no page at all**. Not exposed today, and the tripwire will catch it if a settings page appears.
  - **The tripwire — `check_limit_settings_capped.py`, a hard gate.** It asks the narrow question
    instead of grepping for `max`: *which files can create a per-organisation settings row, and do any
    write a limit-shaped key without asking what the installation allows?* Two such files today, both
    asking; `NOT_A_LIMIT` is empty and fails both ways. **It resolves constants, and that is the only
    reason it works** — the live breach is written as `AnonymousCheckins::RETENTION_KEY` and appears
    nowhere as a literal in the page that writes it.
  - **Three faults in the tripwire, each found by planting.** It asked whether a VALUES list
    *contained* a placeholder — true of every such INSERT — and so **accused two global-administrator-only
    pages that write `siteID NULL` only**: two false alarms out of four findings, on a check whose issue
    says in so many words that crying wolf gets it switched off. It did not recognise
    `EventRecurrence::installationAllows()`, so it reported **the worked example the issue points at**.
    And it found **nothing at all** until it joined adjacent string literals, because the house style
    builds `'INSERT … ' . 'VALUES …'` in pieces and the one file it exists for is written that way.
  - **A SEVENTH route, found by the independent check and NOT fixed on purpose (#687).**
    `/admin/settings/giving-records` is gated on `App::isAdmin()` and writes `giving.retention.years`
    **per organisation**, 1 to 50 years — how long a donor's **name and home address** are kept — with
    **no installation layer at all**, and `lockedInGeneralEditor()` means the installation's
    administrator cannot even express a ceiling. Identical in shape to the attendance breach and more
    sensitive in content. It is **not capped**, because for this one setting capping is the
    **dangerous** direction: the figure is a statutory retention period, the owner chose a country per
    organisation deliberately, and an installation forcing it DOWN could make a customer destroy
    records their own law requires them to keep. That is the owner's decision, so it is **#687**, and
    the tripwire names the file in `NOT_A_LIMIT` with the reasoning so the judgement is on record
    rather than looking like an oversight.
  - **The tripwire cried wolf twice more, and missed five keys, before it was right.** Widening the
    word list to catch `keepFailedDays` made it match `min` inside `venues.reminder_roles` and `count`
    inside `org.address.countryCode`; testing every segment made the NAMESPACE decide, so six
    `giving.retention.*` settings that are not limits were reported beside the one that is. The rule
    that is precise on all twelve keys judged: **the LAST segment, split into words, matched whole.**
    It also read `web/_apps` only, so it could not see `GivingRetention` at all — two of the seven
    per-organisation writers in this application are in `web/_core`.
  - **A correction to my own record:** I reported four settings as seeded-but-unread. **Two of them are
    read** — `expenses.followUpDays` via `$SETTINGS['expenses']['followUpDays']`, and
    `photos.maxUploadMb` via a differently-scoped `$settings['maxUploadMb']` that no longer carries the
    dotted path. That is a **fifth** shape hiding a key from a search. The two genuinely dead ones are
    **#686**; `forms.responseRetentionDays` matters more than cosmetically, because its name promises
    that form responses stop being kept and nothing deletes them.
- **Added — the installation caps the organisation, and the first live breach fixed (#668, part 1)**
  - **The rule** (owner, 29 October 2026, application-wide): for a setting that is a **limit**, an
    organisation may hold itself to a **lower** one but may **never** raise its own above what the
    installation allows. One installation serves many organisations and the two levels of administrator
    may be **different people**, so this is a boundary between parties. `$SETTINGS` has already merged
    the two layers by the time a page runs, so the merged array cannot express it.
  - **`Portal\Core\SettingLimit` is the general resolver** — three tiers, each able to tighten the one
    above it and none able to loosen it: a hard maximum in code, then the installation, then the
    organisation. `EventRecurrence::limitsFrom()` stays as it is; it resolves two limits at once from
    arrays it is handed, which suits its callers.
  - **The rule is one line, and that is the useful finding.** `min(merged, installation)`, with no query
    to discover whether an organisation has a row of its own — because the merged value already **is**
    the organisation's own where it has one and the installation's where it has not. The independent
    check tried to break that and could not. It makes the remaining sweep far more tractable than the
    issue's 31-setting list suggests.
  - **The live breach:** `/admin/settings/attendance` accepted 0–3650 days **per organisation with no
    installation cap**, so an organisation could keep attendance personal data for ten years on an
    installation whose administrator intended ninety days. It now refuses with the reason, **records the
    refusal** (a request to exceed another party's limit crosses a line), and the form offers only what
    the installation allows.
  - **ZERO IS THE TRAP, and it was wrong in both directions until the independent check broke it.** For
    this setting `0` means "keep for ever" — the **largest** value there is, not the smallest — so
    compared as a number it sails through any limit, because 0 is less than everything. The first
    version converted only the **posted** number, in the handler, which was worse than not converting:
    an installation that chose "for ever" (offered by its own form) got a ceiling of 0 and **refused
    every organisation save, including a tighter one** — 30 days refused on an installation allowing for
    ever, with the organisation's two visibility settings blocked too, because the refusal exits before
    all three writes. And an installation that chose 3650 let an organisation store 0 and keep the data
    **for ever**, which is strictly longer, because `3650 > 3650` is false. The rule now lives in the
    class, read at **both** levels, and is stated once: **"for ever" is allowed only when the
    installation itself allows for ever.**
  - **The issue's own list was a starting point, not the answer — exactly as it warned.** Four shapes no
    key-name search can see: nested-array reads, a `LIKE 'mail.queue.%'` query, keys referenced through
    **constants** (which is how `attend.detailRetentionDays` hid from every grep), and four settings
    seeded but read nowhere by name. Measured, only **one** dedicated page names a limit key directly, so
    a tripwire has to resolve constants — which answers the issue's open question with evidence rather
    than a guess, and is part 2.
  - **Four self-test faults of my own, every one a check that passed on broken code.** Three were `strpos`
    offsets measuring the wrong region — a bare function name found its own **definition**, and one slice
    swept in the very code it was meant to exclude. The fourth was worse: section D asked only whether
    certain *text* was present, so it passed on **four different disabled gates** — `if (false)`,
    `&& false` added to the condition, a refusal that logs "nothing was saved" and then writes anyway, and
    a refusal that silently clamps. `.claude/CLAUDE.md` names the `&& false` shape twice and this file
    walked into it regardless. It now pins the whole condition, requires the refusal block to end the
    request, and requires it not to assign to the number on the way past.
  - **And a planted fault that never applied**, giving a false pass: the plant's replacement string had a
    trailing newline the sliced block did not. Checking that a plant produced the state you meant is a
    rule in this repository and this is the third time this month it earned its place.
  - **Tests:** `tools/setting-limit-selftest.php`, 47 checks — the rule's whole table by hand, zero in
    both directions at both levels, refusing versus clamping, and the handler read as text. Deliberately
    **not** the tripwire or the other 30 settings; that is part 2. **#685** carries the half part 1 does
    not fix: an organisation that *already* stored more than the installation allows keeps it, because
    the clear-out job reads the uncapped value.
- **Fixed — the sign-in page had no icon, so every visitor's first request 404ed (#680)**
  - **What was wrong.** With no `<link rel="icon">` a browser falls back to `/favicon.ico` by
    convention. There is no such file in the web root and nothing answers that address. The three icon
    links were written by `header.php`, and **`auth/login/index.php` draws its own `<head>`**, so it
    reached none of them — on the page every visitor sees first, because `/` redirects to `/login`.
    Found by the browser audit (`tools/visual-audit.php`) on its first real run, as a console error
    nobody had been looking for.
  - **Fixed for the whole class, not one page.** The icon links moved into **`head-meta.php`**, which
    every own-`<head>` page already requires and which `check_page_head_tags.py` already fails a non-exempt page
    for not requiring. One require that is already in place, already guarded, closes the class —
    rather than a new partial for the next own-head page to forget. `header.php` keeps working out
    `$siteFavicon` and `$brandIconPath`; `head-meta.php` takes them with `??=` so there is still
    exactly one copy of the resolution chain.
  - **The pages on that check's exempt list deliberately still have no icon** (no count written down: the
    first version of this entry said 13 when there were 12) — printouts, e-mail
    previews, wall displays and kiosk screens, none of them a browser tab anybody looks at. `admin/maintenance/backup.php` is the careful one, and my
    first comment got both halves of it wrong: that file requires `header.php` on both ordinary paths,
    so it reaches `head-meta.php` every normal request — it is its CLOSED-DATABASE RECOVERY BRANCH that
    must not. And the reason is not the icon code: `Site::branding()` reads the row already in memory
    from bootstrap. The reason is the pre-existing `PortalAddress` query in that file.
  - **Guarded, because nothing else would notice those three lines going.** Every page would still
    require the partial and still pass while every visitor fell back to a 404. `check_page_head_tags.py`
    now fails when `head-meta.php` stops printing a `rel="icon"` link — **read through
    `printed_markup()`**, which is load-bearing: the first version read the raw file and **passed on the
    link commented out inside `<?php /* … */ ?>`**, every character still present and nothing printed.
    That is the #623 QR-guard mistake for a third time. Two shapes still get past it — the links wrapped
    in `if (false)`, and an early `return` before them — both measured, both now written into that
    check's "WHAT THIS CHECK CANNOT SEE" list, and the first of them caught by section F over HTTP. Also
    recorded there: **nothing guards the two `apple-touch-icon` links at all** (#682).
  - **Tests.** Section **F** of `tools/page-head-selftest.php`, over real HTTP (15 → 19 checks): the
    sign-in page links an icon; **following that link really returns 200**; `/favicon.ico` still 404s,
    so the link is genuinely needed; and **an ordinary page has not lost its icon** in the move, which
    is one require away from being a regression for every page in the portal rather than a fix for a
    few. Putting the links back in `header.php` alone turns F01 and F02 red while F04 stays green.
    The browser audit that found the fault now reports no problems and exits 0.
- **Fixed — one organisation's postal address was every organisation's (#677, migration 231)**
  - **What was wrong.** `admin/settings/organisation/save.php` wrote all nine `org.*` keys — address
    lines, town, region, postcode, country, latitude, longitude, what3words — plus
    `portal.support.email` through one helper whose INSERT put **NULL in `siteID`**: the row every
    organisation on the installation uses. The page is called Organisation settings and sits under
    Admin → Settings → Organisation, so nothing about it suggested that is what Saving did.
  - **Be precise about what it cost, because the issue overstated it and measuring corrected that.**
    #677 said a second organisation's pages "would display the first organisation's address". They
    would not have: searched on 30 October 2026, **nothing outside that admin page reads any of the
    nine `org.*` keys** — not a member page, not a public page, not an e-mail. `GivingRetention` only
    *mentions* `org.address.countryCode`, in a comment explaining why it deliberately does not read
    it. The support e-mail **was** read, by `Mailer`, and did appear in every organisation's e-mail
    footer. So the real cost was an address stored at the wrong level, a Save button that lied, and a
    fault that would have become a leak the moment anything read it.
  - **Each organisation now holds its own**, and `$upsert()` takes the level as an argument **with no
    default** — a default here would be the same mistake waiting for the next caller. Migration 231
    copies each non-empty installation-wide value down to every organisation, so a single-organisation
    installation (almost all of them) keeps exactly the address it had. An empty value is not copied.
  - **`portal.support.email` is per-organisation with a FALLBACK to the installation's** (owner,
    30 October 2026), which is why migration 231 deliberately leaves that row alone: copying it down
    would mean changing the installation's support address later reached nobody. **An empty box
    therefore REMOVES the organisation's row** rather than storing an empty string: the merge falls
    back only where there is no row at all, so a stored `''` wins and would have masked the
    installation's address for ever with no way back from the page.
  - **`Mailer` needed no change for anything sent from a web request**, and the limit of that is worth
    stating rather than discovering: `renderBase()` runs **before** `MailQueue::add()`, so a message's
    footer is built by the sending request and a queued copy keeps it. **A scheduled job is the
    exception** — `cron/event-reminders.php` and `cron/giving-statements.php` select across every
    organisation while `$SETTINGS` was merged once, so one organisation's support address reaches
    another's members. Harmless while the setting was installation-wide; a wrong address now. Raised
    as **#683**, with the measurement.
  - **No page sets the INSTALLATION's support address any more** — only the installer and the generic
    dot-notation editor. Raised as **#684**, because migration 231's justification depends on that
    value being changeable.
  - **The global-administrator gate narrows to the one setting that really is shared.** An ordinary
    administrator may now set their own organisation's address and support e-mail; `site.url`, which
    decides where every e-mailed link points (#500), stays with a global administrator, and a request
    that sends it anyway is **refused with the reason**, never quietly ignored.
  - **The fault my own first attempt introduced, found by the new test and not by reading.** I guarded
    *who may send* the portal-address field but then wrote the result regardless. The page disables
    that box for an ordinary administrator, **a disabled control is not submitted**, so `?? ''` gave
    an empty string, `PortalAddress::check()` reads empty as "no address", and an ordinary
    administrator saving their **support address** therefore **cleared `site.url` for every
    organisation** — after which every e-mailed link would have been built from whatever host the next
    request arrived at, which a visitor can choose. The handler now asks whether each field *arrived*,
    never what it contains. That is the #667 shape for the second time in a month.
  - **The check went blind to its own fix, which was the worst part.** Passing the level as a
    parameter stopped `check_install_wide_prefill.py` matching the literal `NULL` it looks for, so the
    saver stopped being a saver and **the whole folder stopped being examined** — proved by planting an
    installation-wide write back and watching nothing notice. That matters because passing the level in
    is exactly the pattern the fourteen pages still on its pending list should adopt: each one fixed
    that way would have left the check's view and the list would have emptied while the coverage
    emptied with it. Such savers are now named in `LEVEL_CHOSEN_AT_RUN_TIME` with the reason the fault
    cannot arise, failing **both** ways. Measured first: exactly two files have that shape, so the list
    is two lines, not fifty.
  - **I did not run the one existing test of this page, and it was failing.** `portal-address-selftest.php`
    runs on every pull request and covers this exact card; five of its 93 checks went red, and the
    package's own new test passed throughout. Four were **stale assertions** reading `siteID IS NULL`
    for a key that is now the organisation's, and one was the card's contract, which this package
    changed on purpose. It now has `storedForSite()` / `rowsOfForSite()` helpers, and each rewritten
    assertion says what it used to require and why that changed. **The fifth was behaviour**, not
    staleness: it is what traced the stored-empty-string masking above.
  - **Three more of my own faults, each caught by a test rather than by reading.** The support box
    prefilled from the merged array while Save wrote the organisation's row — so one press of Save on
    an untouched form would have pinned the installation's value as the organisation's own, which is
    exactly the outcome migration 231 refuses to cause. It now reads the organisation's own row and
    shows the inherited address beside it. That inherited address was read from
    `$SETTINGS_INSTALLATION`, which **a page does not inherit** (`.claude/rules/app-pages.md`: only
    `$mysqli` and `$SETTINGS`), so the help text silently took its "nothing to fall back to" branch
    and told administrators the opposite of the truth; it reads `InstallationSettings::layer()` now.
    And section O deleted the four installation-wide rows it borrowed instead of restoring them,
    leaving the fixture poorer than it found it while the suite's own clean-up check could not see it.
  - **Tests.** Section **O** of `tools/access-pages-selftest.php`, 14 checks over real HTTP (320 → 334),
    including the two things most likely to be got wrong again: an ordinary administrator's save must
    not touch `site.url`, and an organisation that has set no support address must still be shown the
    installation's. Both planted faults turn it red. Migration 231 was proved on a two-organisation
    database — copied down, did not overwrite an organisation's own value, byte-identical on a second
    run — and the **end-to-end migration harness passes all 42 checks and all seven phases** with it.
- **Fixed — a visible Export button on a money page that refused most of the people it was shown to (#675)**
  - **What #675 said, and why all three of its claims were wrong.** The issue reported `expenses/export` as
    a handler that had "never answered a request", that "nothing links to it", and that four
    `api.expenses.*` switches were seeded with no handler behind them. Measured over real HTTP and against
    a real MySQL 8.0.36 loaded from the install script: it answers **200 with a real CSV**; a **live Export
    button on the approvals page** links to it; and **none of those four switches exists on any
    installation** — migration 186 deletes them and `full_schema.sql` folds that DELETE in after every one
    of their INSERTs. A fresh database holds exactly three `api.expenses.*` rows. The issue's own grep
    missed the button because it searched for `expenses/export` while the address is `expenses/api/export`.
  - **One qualifier, because the issue was not wrong about everything.** Its narrower wording — that
    `api.expenses.export.enabled` is not seeded, so **that address** has never answered — is **true**, and
    deliberately still is. What was wrong was the conclusion: the handler is not dead, because it is reached
    at a different address altogether.
  - **What was actually wrong was worse.** The Export button was drawn **unconditionally**, and
    `/expenses/approve` has no gate beyond being signed in — it just shows an empty list to somebody with
    nothing to decide. So every member saw the button, and the handler then refused most of them with a
    bare, unstyled **`Forbidden`**: no portal page, no message, no way back. Measured on six kinds of
    account, **four were refused that way**, and they included the department leads and department
    approvers that page exists to serve.
  - **One rule now, asked by both.** `ExpenseRules::mayExportClaims()` is the ONE place that decides who
    may download the spreadsheet — an administrator, a global administrator, or a holder of the `approver`
    role. The button asks it and so does the handler. **Who may download has not changed**; the button is
    simply no longer offered to people it refuses, and there is one rule where there were two copies.
  - **`isApprover` and the `approver` role are different things with confusingly similar names.**
    `tblUserDepts.isApprover` means "may decide **one department's** claims"; the `approver` role (seeded
    as "Expense Approver") means trusted with the organisation's claims as a whole. The file is every
    department's figures, so it is the second. Widening it to department approvers, scoped to their own
    departments, is **#681** and is a deliberate decision rather than an oversight here.
  - **`api.expenses.export.enabled` is deliberately NOT seeded** (owner, 30 October 2026). The same file
    also sits at `api/expenses/export`, which ApiRouter would serve; seeding it would publish a second
    address for the same CSV that a bearer token still could not use, because the handler needs a session
    and reads its token from the query string. The working address is documented in `api-spec.json`
    instead, said plainly to be a browser download and not a REST endpoint.
- **Fixed — the API check read a seed and a deletion as the same thing, and called a page route dead (#675)**
  - **The blind spot, and its dangerous direction.** `check_api_spec_matches_code.py` found seeded switches
    with one regex over `full_schema.sql`, which both seeds and deletes settings. A key written inside a
    `DELETE` matched exactly as one inside an `INSERT`. Reporting four switches that do not exist was the
    harmless half. **The dangerous half is check G:** a handler whose switch is seeded and then deleted is
    403 to everybody, and the old reading called it seeded and passed. Proved by planting — with a
    `DELETE` of `api.events.create.enabled` appended to the install script, the old reading still answered
    "seeded: True". The two statement kinds are now applied **in file order**, and the function says
    plainly what it still cannot see (a `DELETE` by `LIKE`, by subquery, or from application code).
  - **A file in an `api` folder is not necessarily an API endpoint.** The check assumed any
    `_apps/{app}/api/{action}.php` could only be reached by ApiRouter. `Router::dispatch()` resolves a
    `tblRoutes` target under `PORTAL_APPS` first, so `expenses/api/export` reaches that same file with
    **neither** the `api.{app}.{action}.enabled` row **nor** the app's own API-folder switch in front of
    it — two fewer gates than the folder name implies. New **check I** names every such file and why, and
    fails both ways, so a new one is a decision rather than a discovery. There is exactly one today.
  - **The first version of that fix was ALSO wrong, in the same silent direction, and the independent
    check caught it.** It ended a `DELETE` at the next `;` **character**, so a semicolon inside the
    statement's own `--` comment ended the span early, the key fell outside it and was read as a seed —
    and its docstring had claimed that case was merely over-reporting. These two differ by one character,
    and the first passed while the second correctly failed:

    ```sql
    -- these are gone; nothing reads them any more
    -- these are gone and nothing reads them any more
    ```

    `read_install_script()` now scans the file once, blanking comments and tracking quoted literals, so a
    semicolon in a comment or a literal cannot end a statement and **a key quoted inside a comment is not
    read as live at all**. That last part fixed a second finding: a route target left behind in a comment
    was being read as a live route, which made check G stop guarding a handler that had really become
    unreachable. The `'#0f766e'` colours the install script seeds are why the scanner has to know that `#`
    does not start a comment inside a literal.
  - **Its own test grew from 26 planted faults to 33**, each still required to be caught by the expected
    check and **by nothing else**. Three of the new ones are the scanner faults above.
  - **Two more from the same check, both fixed.** An organisation with **no claims** downloaded a file of
    three bytes — the byte-order mark alone — because `CsvExporter::download()` derives its headings from
    the first row and there was no first row, while the API description promised a heading row and a column
    order; the handler now passes the headings explicitly, which also makes the documented order
    load-bearing rather than a side effect of the query's alias order. And the file name's date used PHP's
    default zone rather than the organisation's, so late on a Sunday evening in Sydney it was named for
    Saturday; it now comes from `Site::timezone()` (#604).
- **Added — the browser half of the look-and-feel audit, which was never blocked (#569)**
  - **What this is.** `tools/visual-audit.php` stands a real portal up over HTTP — copies `web/`, writes a
    throwaway `auth_creds.php` and key, starts PHP's own server behind a router imitating `.htaccess` —
    and drives `tools/layout-audit.mjs`, which looks at every page at **320, 390, 768, 1024 and 1440**
    pixels wide and writes a screenshot of each. One command, because a check somebody has to assemble by
    hand is a check that does not get run.
  - **Nothing is installed.** Microsoft Edge is driven over the DevTools protocol using **node's own
    built-in `WebSocket`** — no Playwright, no Puppeteer, no `npm install`. This was reported as blocked
    for want of a headless browser; that was simply wrong, and Edge was already on the machine.
  - **It found a real fault on its first run:** `/login` draws its own `<head>` and links **no icon**, so
    every visitor's browser falls back to `/favicon.ico`, which 404s — on the first page anyone sees
    (**#680**). It also reports 10 tap targets under 44px across the signed-out pages.
  - **The trap that makes the obvious overflow test useless, measured before anything was written.** With
    `mobile: true`, Chromium **widens the layout viewport to fit the content**: a 900px page asked to
    render at 390 reports `innerWidth` of 900. So `scrollWidth > window.innerWidth` is **permanently
    false**. Everything is compared against the width the driver asked for.
  - **Four ways it passed on a broken page, every one found by planting.** The test router served every
    static file as `text/html`, so the logo rendered broken and controls measured 4px short while the
    audit said "no problems" — **it nearly shipped a false defect report about the sign-in page's logo**.
    A guard for that asked for *zero* stylesheets when the real failure was partial. That guard then
    counted raw `<link>` elements, so a page legitimately linking one file twice was hard-failed. And an
    independent check found a fourth: **a page whose JavaScript dies still renders, still has a title, and
    passed** — the #625 shape exactly. It now reports the browser's own errors and failed requests.
  - **Five more from that check, all fixed:** a page regressing to a 500 was skipped while the run exited
    0; the navigation result was never read, so pointing at a dead port **measured Chromium's own error
    page and reported it as the page**; Edge was left running on every failure path, and with a fixed port
    the *next* run silently attached to the leftover browser; `Ctrl-C` left a 22 MB copy of `web/` on disk
    **including the database password**; and `php-errors.log` cannot see a fatal at all, because the
    portal sends uncaught exceptions to `tblErrors` and swallows them — so it now reads both.
  - **Honest about its reach.** It audits **four distinct pages** of roughly thirty signed-out ones, covers
    **no page behind a sign-in**, and checks neither favicon, Open Graph, canonical nor social preview.
    All of that is written in its header rather than left to be discovered.
- **Fixed — three places let you set an event status the database has never had (#676, migration 230)**
  - **What was wrong.** `tblEvents.status` is `ENUM('draft','published','cancelled','postponed')`. Three
    writers allowed **`archived`**, which the column has never had, and left out **`postponed`**, which it
    has: the API's create and update endpoints, and the CSV importer. Nothing compared the two.
  - **What it cost depended on the server, and both halves were measured on MySQL 8.0.36.** Since #593
    (12 October 2026) every connection is strict, so the write failed with `ERROR 1265 Data truncated for
    column 'status'` — a **500** to the caller. **Before #593 it was worse:** MySQL stored the **empty
    string**, which an ENUM keeps in its "invalid" slot, so **no status filter can find it**.
    *(An earlier draft of this entry said such an event was "unfindable, uneditable and undeletable
    through the interface". That was wrong and the independent check caught it:
    `calendar/manage/index.php` adds a status condition only when one is chosen, and its badge is a
    `match` with a `default` arm, so the event **is** listed, counted and editable there — with a blank
    status badge. Measured: 86 of the 130 places that read `tblEvents` never mention status.)*
  - **And `postponed` could not be set through the API or the importer**, while the API happily returned
    it in `Event.status`. *(It has always been settable from the ordinary admin event form and the series
    bulk editor — an earlier draft said "through any route", which was wrong.)*
  - **It was FIVE writers, not three.** The independent check found two the premise had missed:
    `calendar/manage/save.php` — **the main admin event form** — took `$_POST['status']` and bound it
    straight into the INSERT and the UPDATE **with no allow-list at all**, and
    `calendar/submit-save.php` supplies `status` as a literal `"draft"` inside its INSERT's `VALUES`
    list, a shape the new check could not see until it was taught to. The CSV page's **on-screen help**
    also still told the user to send `archived`.
  - **Fixed by making the code match the column** (the owner's choice on 30 October 2026 over adding
    `archived` to the database). All five lists are now the column's four words. `postponed` becomes
    settable for the first time, and **an event cannot be archived** — said plainly rather than left to be
    discovered.
  - **Migration 230 gives the vanished events back as drafts.** `draft` was chosen because it never
    publishes anything and never asserts an event was cancelled: it hands the event to an administrator,
    visible to them and not to members. What was originally intended **cannot** be recovered — MySQL
    stored the empty string, not the word it rejected. Proved on a real database: an event with no status
    came back as `draft`, `published` and `postponed` rows were untouched, and a second run changed nothing.
  - **An untrue comment, fixed.** `admin/calendar/moderate.php`'s header said "Reject = status='archived'"
    for weeks. The code has always written `draft`; had it done what the comment said, **every rejection
    would have been a 500.**
  - **A tripwire, and it took three goes to make it honest.** `check_event_status_matches_column.py` reads
    the column out of the install script and compares it with every allow-list, every status written
    straight into an events statement, and the API description. **Version 1 cried wolf 14 times** — all
    false: `confirmed` is an RSVP's status, `pending_review` an erasure request's, and service plans' own
    column really is `draft/published/archived`. **Measured on the shipped check, removing the file
    scoping alone brings back one of those, not fourteen** — the narrower search window does most of that
    work, so crediting the scoping with all of it would be the #641 "28 versus 19" mistake again.
    **Version 2 read only lists written inline**, so
    `events/api/update.php` — one of the three files this issue is about — was never examined, and putting
    `archived` back into it left the check **green while it reported three lists checked.** Both were found
    by planting the fault. It now reads both shapes, is scoped to files that write `tblEvents`, and its
    17-case `--selftest` pins the cry-wolf direction as well as the fault.
- **Fixed — 37 calls that PHP 8.5 deprecated, each one writing to the error log (#673)**
  - **What was wrong.** `curl_close()` has done nothing since PHP 8.0, when the cURL handle became
    an object that is freed when it goes out of scope. PHP 8.5 deprecates it. The portal called it
    **37 times across 15 files**, and each call wrote a `Deprecated` line to the error log every
    time it ran — payments, text messages, Zoom, geocoding, transcription, translation, the
    webhook sender, the asset register and the hymnal among them. **Not every outside call the
    portal makes:** `SafeFetch`, `WebPush`, `MailerGoogle` and `Auth` had already removed theirs,
    so fetching an address a person typed, sending a push and sending mail were never affected.
  - **Why it mattered more than tidiness.** The error log is where a real fault is found. A portal
    that writes a deprecation line every time it talks to a payment provider buries the one line
    that matters under hundreds that do not.
  - **Fixed.** Every call removed; the handle is freed when it goes out of scope, which is what four
    files (`SafeFetch`, `WebPush`, `MailerGoogle` and `Auth`) had already worked out and documented.
    Each of the fifteen now carries the same short note in place of its first call.
  - **The issue's own figures were wrong, and are corrected here.** It said 43 calls across 19 files.
    Six of those lines were **comments mentioning `curl_close`** in the four files that had already
    removed it. Counted with PHP's tokeniser rather than by searching text: **37 calls, 15 files.**
  - **A tripwire, and `curl_multi_close` is deliberately not covered.**
    `check_no_curl_close.py` refuses `curl_close()` and `curl_share_close()`. Measured on PHP 8.5.11
    rather than assumed: **`curl_multi_close()` raises no notice**, so flagging it would make the
    check cry wolf, and a check that cries wolf gets switched off. It has **no exemption list** —
    there is never a reason to call these — and it reads the code through PHP's own tokeniser,
    because a text search would report all six of those explanatory comments as faults.
  - **It covers both spellings, and the first version did not.** PHP tokenises a bare
    `curl_close` and a fully-qualified `\curl_close` as *different* token types. The check looked
    only at the first, so it reported **clean on a real, live deprecation** — found by the
    independent check, which planted `\curl_close($ch);` into a namespaced file. That spelling is
    not exotic: a leading backslash is ordinary style in namespaced code, and **fourteen of the
    fifteen files this package changed are `namespace Portal\Core;`**. A name still holding a `\`
    after the leading one, such as `\Vendor\curl_close`, is somebody else's function and passes.
    *(Two claims in an earlier draft of this entry were wrong and were corrected by the second
    review round: "every file under `web/_core/`" — it holds 190 PHP files, of which 105 are
    `namespace Portal\Core;`, 15 are `MWBM\Mail` and **70 declare no namespace at all**; and that
    php-cs-fixer's `native_function_invocation` rule writes `\curl_close(` by itself — its default
    `include` is `@compiler_optimized`, which does not list `curl_close`, and there is no
    php-cs-fixer here to settle it. Neither claim was needed.)*
  - **It fails rather than passes when it cannot run** (the #646 lesson): a missing `php`, a
    tokeniser that answers nothing, or a scan that reads zero files is a failure. Its `--selftest`
    runs **17 cases** — thirteen on the scan and **four on the verdict itself**, because changing
    `len(hits) == 0` to `>= 0` once left all thirteen green while the check reported clean on a
    tree holding a real call. Both plants were confirmed caught at the right file and line, then
    the files restored from saved bytes.
- **Fixed — a form could push one organisation's setting to every organisation on the installation (#674, #668)**
  - **What was wrong, and it needed no mistake by anybody.** `$SETTINGS` has already merged the
    installation-wide settings with the open organisation's own by the time any page runs. Admin,
    Transcription filled its boxes from that merged array while its Save writes **installation-wide**.
    So a global administrator who opened the page while in an organisation holding its own value saw
    that value in the box, and **pressing Save without touching anything made it the installation's,
    for every organisation on it.**
  - **Why that direction matters.** The installation's administrator may be a hosting provider and
    the organisations its customers, so this is a boundary between two parties rather than one person
    wearing two hats. One customer's choice quietly becoming everyone's default is the wrong way
    across it.
  - **Fixed, and the page now says when the two differ.** Every box reads the installation's own
    layer. Where the organisation you are in holds a row of its own, the page names the settings that
    differ — because everything that actually runs a transcription reads the merged value, so the
    difference is real, and because nothing in the portal creates such a row, so one being there is
    worth knowing. Only the key names are shown: a value could be an API key.
  - **The harm is now demonstrated rather than argued.** Section S of the transcription page test
    puts the old read back and records the installation's provider changing from `openai` to
    `assemblyai` on a Save that touched nothing. Six checks, and S06 proves the new notice is not
    simply always shown.
  - **It is fifteen pages, not one.** A new check, `check_install_wide_prefill.py`, found the same
    shape on fifteen admin forms — captcha keys, Zoom's client secret, the Cloudflare Stream token,
    the what3words and geocoding keys, the SMS credentials and daily cap, the AI-assist monthly
    budget (a money limit, so a #668 instance in its own right), translation keys, monitoring,
    push, hymns and the Microsoft 365 mailbox fields. **Fourteen are named on a pending list so the
    check can gate from today and no new page can join them**; `--strict` fails while any remain.
    They are not all fixed at once because the fix is not mechanical — each page needs reading field
    by field, and a page may legitimately show a merged value beside an installation one.
  - **The independent check came back NOT CLEAN with eight real problems, all fixed.** Four are worth
    recording. **The test pinned one field out of nine** — putting the merged read back on `language`
    and `batchSize` left all 149 checks passing and the gate green, so section S now pins every box
    the form submits, each with a different installation and organisation value so a wrong box names
    which layer it read. **Judging readiness on the installation layer broke the page's agreement
    with the queue runner**, which reads the merged value: with no installation key but an
    organisation row holding one, the page said "no transcription company is set up" and disabled
    the button while a posted run would have worked. The boxes now show the installation's settings
    and the statements about what a run will do read the merged value, which is the distinction that
    was missing. **The check's own write pattern was wrong twice** — it believed there was one
    spelling when three savers insert straight into the column, and it treated a `SELECT … siteID IS
    NULL` as a write, which produced a false accusation against a page whose paired "saver" only
    reads. And **two blind spots were missing from its list of limits**, one of them hiding a live
    instance: a read through the inherited `$SETTINGS` variable, and a page that is its own saver —
    which `maintenance/backup.php` is, and really does have the fault.
  - **I deleted two documentation headings with a replace that should have been an insert**, for the
    third time in this run. Both restored. The rule is in the handoff: find the exact text first, and
    never chain a commit to an unverified patch.
  - **The check cried wolf on its own fix, which is why it has one more term than you would expect.**
    A page that has reckoned with the two layers often reads both deliberately. So it reports only a
    form that reads the merged array and **never reads the installation layer at all**. The cost is
    stated in its header: a page fixed for one field and not another passes.
- **Fixed — the API description's last untrue statements, including five replies that left out the envelope (#641 part 3)**
  - **Five operations declared their payload where the envelope belongs.** `events/list`,
    `events/detail`, `noticeboard/list` and both Event Team Hub operations described the inside of
    `data` as though it were the whole reply. So a developer reading the description would look for
    `eventID` at the top level when it is at `data.eventID`, and for the event itself at `data` when
    it is at `data.event`. All five now describe what the handler really sends, and each says what it
    used to claim, so somebody who built against the old text can see what changed.
  - **`PaginatedListResponse` is removed.** It described flat paging and an array called `items`;
    its one user nests paging under `data.pagination` and calls its array `events`, and also sends
    `hasNext` and `hasPrev`, which the schema never declared. Rather than keep a shape nothing
    returns, that operation now describes its real reply and the schema is gone. **A schema that
    documents a reply nobody sends is worse than none, because it looks authoritative.**
  - **All 48 `Allow` examples said `GET, POST`.** The real header is built by the router from the
    handler files that exist on disk, so it differs by resource — and now each example is computed
    the same way rather than written by hand. **Worth recording because the first attempt made it
    worse:** it ADDED the computed example beside the stale one instead of replacing it, so every
    one of the 48 briefly carried two contradicting values, and the entry describing the fix was
    untrue while it did. An edit that adds where it meant to replace leaves the original fault in
    place AND a claim that it is gone. They range from `GET, POST` for the noticeboard to
    `GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE` for events; prayer requests have no DELETE, and expenses and
    leadership have no PUT or PATCH.
  - **Thirty-two operations a bearer key can reach did not document being refused for too many
    requests**, although every such request is rate-limited and answered with a `Retry-After`.
    They do now. A sign-in session is not rate-limited this way, which the new wording says.
  - **`GET /api/v1/events/{id}` called itself "the only v1 resource with a detail route".** Assets
    has one too.
  - **A measurement trap worth recording.** The list of endpoints a bearer key can reach was first
    taken by searching the handlers for `ApiAuth::requireWrite`. That matched a COMMENT this very
    package had added to `livechat/api/prompt-publish.php` — a comment explaining that a bearer key
    **cannot** reach it — giving 46 where the answer is 45. Reading it with PHP's tokenizer, so
    comments are stripped, is the only honest way; it is the same trap as a check that searches for
    the text of a guard.
- **Added — the API description now has a schema that is executed, and every property explains itself (#641 part 2)**
  - **What was wrong.** This project's rule is that where it produces JSON, a JSON Schema lives
    beside it with a `description` on every property, wired into a check "so it actually runs; a
    schema nothing executes is a document, not a check". `web/_core/api-spec.json` **had no schema
    at all**, and 286 of its properties and 42 of its query parameters said nothing about
    themselves. A developer reading it had to guess what a field meant, which units it was in, and
    whether a limit refused a value or quietly changed it.
  - **There is now `web/_core/api-spec.schema.json`**, and `check_api_spec_schema.py` executes it as
    a hard gate. The validator is **dependency-free on purpose**: there is no JSON Schema library on
    the development machine and every other check here uses the standard library only, so bringing
    one in would mean the check could not be run before pushing — the #646 failure over again. The
    cost is stated in its own header: it implements the keywords the schema uses and would ignore
    any other, so it **fails when the schema uses a keyword it cannot see**, rather than letting
    that part of the schema become decorative.
  - **All 286 properties and 42 parameters now say what they mean**, written from the code rather
    than from the field names. What that turned up is the useful part: money fields that are in
    **pence** and ones that are in **pounds**, limits that **quietly shorten or clamp a value rather
    than refusing it**, fields that are **write-only** (a licence key can be set and never read
    back, and never cleared), a breakdown list that **replaces rather than adds to** what is stored,
    a poster list that is **the whole board** so an empty one hides everything, and an identifier
    that is the **assignment** rather than the role it fills.
  - **Three more things in the description were untrue, and are corrected.** `format: date-time`
    promised RFC 3339 on fields that return a plain database timestamp with no offset.
    `PaginatedListResponse` describes a shape **no handler returns** — its one user nests its paging
    differently and names its array differently — which is now said in the schema rather than left
    to be discovered. And the `Asset` shape, which the prose sent readers to while **nothing pointed
    at it**, is now used by the four endpoints that return it, with the two caveats measured: `list`
    returns a subset of it, and `detail` returns four fields it never declared.
  - **The test of the checks now covers both**, with 26 planted faults. Eight are new and aim at the
    schema check: a removed description, a removed parameter description, a missing tag or summary,
    a `$ref` that resolves to nothing, a tag nothing declares, an unreadable file, and a schema
    keyword the validator cannot see. Every one is caught, and every file is restored
    byte-for-byte. Sabotage was measured rather than assumed: `and False` on any of eight separate
    conditions across the two checks leaves the check itself green, and the selftest goes red on all
    eight.
  - **The independent check came back NOT CLEAN with nine real problems, all fixed.** Every one was
    a statement that was untrue rather than anything broken, which is what a description package
    fails at. The four worth recording: the `AssetCreate` summary still said `currency` refuses a
    bad value while the field's own new text said that had been corrected — **so the file documented
    a fix that never happened**; the shared `limit` text told callers to read a page total that four
    of the eleven endpoints never send; `DocumentCreate.isPublished` picked `False` as its example of
    a value meaning true, and that is the one value that means false, because the handler lower-cases
    first; and both asset `detail` operations declared the asset at `data` when the handler nests it
    at `data.asset`. Also found: `oneOf` was implemented as `allOf` in the new validator, so it
    meant "every branch" — nothing used it, but the file claimed to implement what it listed, and
    **a keyword enforced WRONGLY does not trip the guard that catches a keyword that is missing**.
  - **Two improvements that came out of that round.** The selftest now runs 35 cases against the
    validator directly, in both directions, because an end-to-end plant cannot reach a keyword the
    description does not happen to use — measured: neutering the validator's `enum` test left both
    the check and the selftest green. And a `$ref` with a sibling `description` is **ignored by
    OpenAPI 3.0 tooling**, so the carefully written caveats would never have reached a reader of
    `/api-docs/`; they are now wrapped in `allOf`, which does render.
  - **Found and raised: #676.** The events API's status allow-list does not match the database.
    `archived` is allowed by both writers and then refused by the column, so it gives a **500**;
    `postponed` is a real stored value this API returns but **cannot be set** through it. Not fixed
    here because correcting either list changes behaviour.
- **Added — the API description is now checked against the code, and 17 endpoints that were missing from it are described (#641)**
  - **What was wrong.** `web/_core/api-spec.json` is what a customer's developer reads before writing
    anything against this portal, and the browsable page at `/api-docs/` serves it. **Nothing in the
    repository had ever compared it with the code**, so the two had drifted for as long as the file
    existed. 17 endpoints that answer real requests appeared nowhere in it — the whole of live chat,
    the service-plan display and its controls, guided tours, livestream pings, venue availability,
    push notification sign-up, noticeboard uploads, hymn search and stocktake scanning. A developer
    reading the description simply never learned they existed. Two more — creating and changing
    a member account — had their handler described under its REST address while the description
    explicitly denied that their legacy address existed, so 19 addresses were documented in all.
  - **Three operations stated the opposite of the truth.** `POST /api/v1/users` and both update verbs
    said "**Legacy alias:** none — this endpoint is new in v1, exposed only at this path". Both
    handlers are on disk with their switches seeded, and the method gate is only *relaxed* under the
    REST facade, never tightened, so the legacy addresses reach them perfectly well. Corrected to
    name the real address.
  - **There is now a check, and it reads the router's own rules rather than a list.** It decides what
    is reachable from the same `^[a-z0-9-]+$` pattern `ApiRouter` uses, which is why the shared helper
    `_coerce.php` needs no exemption — the leading underscore that already makes it unreachable is the
    same thing that excludes it. It resolves the `api/v1/` facade through the four tables in
    `ApiRouter`, read out of the file, so a handler documented only under its REST address is not
    cried wolf over. Proved by planting 12 faults, every one caught.
  - **The description now says where an endpoint does NOT behave like the others.** Five of them
    answer with their own flat JSON rather than the portal's usual envelope, and two of those
    return the replacement form token as a top-level field instead of in `meta` — so a console drawn
    once and used repeatedly has to carry it forward or every control works exactly once. That is
    now written down for each, because describing them with the standard envelope would have been
    one more untrue statement.
  - **Three code comments that promised something the code did not do.** Live chat's prompt publisher
    said an API key would work, and no key can reach it. The guided-tour endpoint said it only offered
    tours at or below the running version, and nothing in it reads the version at all. Both
    noticeboard upload handlers said their organisation-administrator check "fails closed for bearer
    keys too", when the condition in fact skips it entirely for a key. All three corrected to say
    what happens; no behaviour was changed.
  - **Found and left for the owner (#675).** `expenses/export` is a complete, working CSV export whose
    switch was never seeded, so it has answered 403 to everybody since it was written, and nothing
    links to it. Four more switches are seeded for handlers that do not exist. Both need a decision
    rather than a quiet fix, so they are named in the check — which **fails if either state stops
    being true**, so neither can be resolved silently.
  - **Still open on #641:** the JSON Schema beside the description, and a `description` on every
    property. Also worth knowing: the issue counted 181 properties without one, an earlier pass here
    counted 274, and the traversal used here counts 286. They recurse differently; none of the three
    has been written down as fact.
- **Added — transcription you can actually reach, and that cannot charge you twice (#276, migration 229)**
  - **What was wrong.** Transcription looked finished. There was an app switch, a choice of three
    transcription companies, somewhere to enter an account key, a page that shows a transcript, and a
    search across every transcript. **No page anywhere had a button to transcribe a recording.** So
    nothing was ever put in the queue, no transcript was ever made, and the search looked through an
    empty list for ever. The transcript page even told members "an administrator can queue one from
    the recording's page" — and that page had no such button.
  - **There is now a Transcribe button**, on the recording's own page, for administrators. It says
    before you press it that the audio is **sent to the transcription company your administrator has
    chosen, which charges for it** — because a recording of a service or a members' meeting leaving
    the server is something to know beforehand, not afterwards.
  - **A second fault, found while testing the first.** The statement that saves a finished transcript
    could never run: `fullText` is a reserved word in MySQL unless it is quoted. So even if a
    recording had reached a transcription company, the words it sent back could not have been
    written down — after the work had been paid for. Fixed, and the test now walks the whole way
    through with a stand-in company so the saving is proved and not assumed.
  - **The same recording cannot be sent twice.** Pressing Transcribe while the audio is already with
    the company used to put it back in the queue, so it was sent again and charged for again. It is
    now refused, and the page says waiting costs nothing. **A run the server cuts short no longer
    wedges the recording either** — after two hours it reads as abandoned and can be sent again,
    which the page explains rather than leaving it looking busy for ever.
  - **A monthly budget, with the installation deciding the ceiling.** One account key pays for every
    organisation on an installation, so the installation's figure is the **most** any organisation
    may spend. An organisation can hold itself to less and can never give itself more (#668). Going
    past it refuses the recording and says why, rather than quietly doing nothing. £50 a month to
    begin with — roughly a hundred hours of audio.
  - **Fixed — "Process next" saved the settings instead of transcribing anything.** On the
    Transcription page that button sat inside the Save form. HTML does not allow a form inside a
    form, so the button belonged to the Save form: pressing it saved the configuration, said
    "settings saved", and transcribed nothing. It was the only control that could work the queue.
  - **Fixed — one organisation could see and spend another's.** The queue counts, the month's spend
    and the list of recent transcripts were read with no organisation filter, and that list carries
    recording titles. Worse, pressing "Process next" sent **another organisation's** audio to the
    company on the installation's account. All of it is now one organisation at a time.
  - **Fixed — an administrator of one organisation was offered settings they may not change.** Those
    settings belong to the whole installation and the handler has refused anybody but a global
    administrator since September. The page now shows them what is set and who to ask.
  - **Fixed — members were shown the transcription company's own error text**, which can quote what
    was sent to it. They now see the state in plain words; the detail is for administrators.
  - **Fixed — the search inside transcripts could not be found.** Nothing linked to it. The
    recordings library now does, when the organisation uses transcription.
  - **Fixed — the recording page showed no messages at all.** It had no flash block, and nothing in
    this portal prints one centrally, so every answer from the new button would have been swallowed
    and the button would have looked dead whether it worked or was refused.
  - **Nothing happens on its own**, and the page says so: the queue moves only when an administrator
    presses "Process next". There is no scheduled job, deliberately for now — nobody should be
    billed by a timer they did not know about (#672).
  - **Fixed after an independent review — "Process next" could lose a whole queue.** The only thing
    stopping a run when no transcription company was set up was that the button looked disabled. A
    button is not a boundary: a posted request claimed every waiting recording, got "not configured"
    back, and marked the lot as failed. Queue a few recordings while one company is configured, then
    switch company without entering its key, and that was reachable. The run now refuses and says
    plainly that everything waiting is still waiting.
  - **Fixed — one recording the server could not write no longer ends the whole run.** A fault part
    way through a batch gave a blank error page, and the recordings already done went unreported.
    Each recording is now handled on its own, so a run reports what it managed.
  - **Fixed — a budget of nothing is no longer described as a budget that ran out.** Setting the
    monthly figure to zero said "this month's budget has been used up", sending an administrator
    looking for spending that never happened. It now says no budget has been set.
  - **Fixed — the page could blame an organisation for the installation's own figure.** Where the
    installation asked for more than the product allows at all, the page told a global administrator
    their organisation had asked for more. It now names the organisation only when the organisation
    really did.
  - **Also made honest rather than reassuring:** where a transcription is cut short by the server,
    the page said the attempt "was charged for either way". That cannot be known — the request may
    have died before the company was reached, while it was working, or after it finished. It now
    says so.
- **Added — backups you can keep: taken automatically, downloaded, and brought back (#569, migration 228)**
  - **What was missing, and why it mattered more than it looked.** The portal could already take a
    snapshot, rehearse a restore and put one back, and it e-mailed an administrator when the newest
    backup got too old. But **nothing ever took one unless somebody pressed the button**, and there
    was no way to get a copy off the server. So the staleness alert existed to report a problem
    nothing was preventing, and a customer who lost their hosting account would have lost every
    snapshot with it.
  - **Backups can now be taken on a schedule.** Choose every day, every week or every four weeks on
    the Backup page, and how many to keep. Point your hosting company's scheduler at
    `/cron/backup-run` **once a day** whatever you choose — how often a backup is actually taken is
    decided in the portal, not by how often the scheduler calls, so changing your mind does not mean
    editing a scheduler entry you may not be able to reach. The page says all of this.
  - **Whether a backup is due is worked out from the snapshots themselves**, not from a remembered
    "last run". So a backup taken by hand an hour ago counts, a failed run cannot push the next one a
    whole week away, and restoring the database cannot confuse it. A snapshot **imported** from a file
    deliberately does not count: it is a copy brought back from elsewhere, not evidence that the
    current database has been saved.
  - **A snapshot can be downloaded as one file** and kept somewhere else. **It is always encrypted,
    with a key you choose, and the key is not stored anywhere** — if you lose it, nobody can open the
    file, including us. The page says so before you start. There is no unencrypted option, because
    that file holds every name, address, telephone number, giving record and care note in the
    database, and the download is the one moment all of it leaves the server in one piece.
  - **You can also require the installation's own key file**, so the file is useless to anybody who
    does not have that too. The page warns that this also makes it useless to **you** if the server
    is gone — which is the very situation a backup is for — so it is offered rather than
    recommended.
  - **And brought back in.** Put the file in `_backups/incoming` with your hosting company's file
    manager and press Import, or upload it through the page. The page **reads this server's own
    upload limits and tells you what it will take**, rather than letting you discover it by watching
    an upload fail — a real database backup is usually larger than a shared host allows, which is
    exactly why the folder route exists.
  - **Importing does not restore anything**, on purpose. It unpacks the file so it appears in the
    list, where you can rehearse a restore to check it reads properly before putting it back. One
    press would have meant a second path writing over a live database, and that path would have to
    agree with the first about every guard for ever.
  - **Only a global administrator can download or import.** A backup holds the data of every
    organisation on the installation, not just the one somebody administers, and both refusals are
    recorded.
  - **An imported snapshot is never tidied away** by the scheduled job, and is named for the moment
    it was imported rather than overwriting the snapshot it came from.
  - **Built on libsodium's `secretstream`** rather than anything hand-rolled, because that is the
    primitive for exactly this job: a long file encrypted in pieces where every piece is
    authenticated and tied to its place, so a file cannot be truncated, reordered or spliced without
    the read failing. Nothing is ever held in memory: a 6 MB table packs and unpacks with no
    measurable growth, which is checked rather than claimed.
  - **Found by testing and by an independent review, not by reading** — eight faults in this work,
    none of them visible on the page. Four from building it: the scheduled job read three field names
    that do not exist (so it would have taken a backup every single run and reported nothing); it
    treated a snapshot that merely *failed* as one that succeeded; an imported file suppressed the
    next scheduled backup; and two of the "an administrator of one organisation cannot do this"
    checks were passing because the request was refused by the **form token** rather than by the gate
    being tested.
  - Four more from the review, two of them serious. **Unpacking a file that asked for more data than
    it carried looped for ever** at full CPU, burning a web worker until the host killed it.
    **The `_backups/incoming` folder appeared on the Backup page as a failed snapshot with a Delete
    button**, and pressing it destroyed the files in there — which may be the only copy somebody has
    just brought back after losing their server. Also: the amount of key work a file could demand was
    unbounded, and a file claiming a terabyte of it never returned at all; and a **cancelled**
    download left a full encrypted copy of the database on the server, where nothing would ever have
    removed it.

- **Added — repeating events, which the portal could not create at all (#569, #668, migration 227)**
  - **What was missing.** FEATURES.md listed "Recurring rules: weekly / fortnightly / monthly /
    quarterly / yearly / custom" as shipped. There was no repeat option anywhere on the event form,
    and **nothing in the whole codebase had ever written `tblRecurrenceRules`** — so a weekly
    service had to be typed in one date at a time, for ever. "Series" was only a grouping label.
  - **What you can do now.** Choose how often on the event form, then stop after a number of dates
    or after a date. Weekly and fortnightly take any set of weekdays. Monthly, quarterly and yearly
    go either by the same date each time or by the same weekday — the second Tuesday, the last
    Sunday. Each date becomes its own ordinary event, so **inside the portal** you can move or
    cancel one of them later without disturbing the rest.
  - **The calendar feed now sends the series as one repeating entry.** `calendar/export.php` has
    always known how to collapse a series that has a rule that way. Nothing had ever written a rule,
    so that code had never run. It does now — **and only while that one entry still describes the
    series truthfully**, which the feed works out for itself every time. See below for what that
    means in practice and what it still cannot do.
  - **The time on the clock is what repeats, not a number of hours.** "Every Sunday at 10:00" reads
    10:00 on both sides of both clock changes. This is the opposite rule from the one the portal
    uses when READING somebody else's calendar, where each occurrence has to keep the same exact
    length — so the existing reader was deliberately not reused, and the reason is written beside
    both. Proved in three time zones, including one whose clocks change on a different date.
  - **The repeat you choose wins over the date you typed, and you are told.** Tick "Thursday" above
    a Wednesday and you get Thursdays — including the first one, which moves to the Thursday. The
    message says so. The alternative, keeping the Wednesday and then repeating on Thursdays, cannot
    be described by a calendar feed at all, so the two halves could never have agreed.
  - **A month without that date is skipped, never moved.** "The 31st" makes no date in February
    rather than quietly landing on 1 March. A yearly 29 February series therefore makes dates only
    in leap years, and under the default three-year horizon that is a single date — reported to the
    person rather than hidden.
  - **How big a series may be is now yours to set, not ours** (`/admin/settings/repeats`): a number
    of dates, and how far ahead. These began life as fixed numbers in the code — 200 dates and three
    years — which are sensible for a church with one Sunday service and wrong for a school with a
    daily registration period. Whichever limit is reached first stops the series, and the person
    creating it is told it was cut short so they can extend it later.
  - **The installation's limit caps an organisation's (#668).** One installation can serve many
    organisations, and whoever runs the installation may be a different person from the
    administrators of the organisations on it. So for a limit the installation has the last word: an
    organisation may hold itself to fewer dates or a shorter horizon, and can never give itself
    more. A number above the installation's limit is refused with the reason, and recorded — never
    quietly reduced, because a silently shrunk number is how somebody comes to believe a limit is in
    force when it is not. Raising the installation's limit raises what every organisation may then
    have.
  - **Lowering a limit never deletes anything.** It changes what a NEW series may produce. Dates
    already in the diary are ordinary events and are left exactly alone. The page says so.
  - **What the feed publishes can never exceed what the installation allows.** The repeating entry
    sent to subscribers carries the exact number of dates in the diary, so a limit is a limit in
    what the installation publishes as well as in what it stores. An independent check found both
    halves of this wrong before release: leaving both stop fields empty published a
    **forever-repeating** event while the diary held five dates, and a count typed past the form
    published four hundred where the installation allowed five.
  - **Not included, on purpose:** changing the pattern of a series that already exists — shifting
    every future date, or extending a run. That means adding and removing rows in bulk and is its
    own piece of work; the form offers repeats on creation only rather than half-offering them.
  - **Two tests, and they check different things.** `tools/event-recurrence-selftest.php` proves the
    date rules with no database at all (60 checks). `tools/event-repeat-pages-selftest.php` drives
    the real form and save handler over HTTP and reads the rows back out of the database (126
    checks), because the date rules can be perfect while the form posts a field name the handler
    never reads. That second test earned its place immediately: it caught the form printing a
    constant that had just been renamed, which made every create form raise a fatal error — and
    `php -l` cannot see an undefined constant.
  - **Two rounds of independent review found nine real faults between them, all fixed here.** The
    second round found the two that mattered most, and both lived in the join between the dates
    created and the pattern published: the first date of a series was thrown away whenever the typed
    start did not satisfy the pattern (so the diary held a day the pattern never makes, and the feed
    advertised one the diary had not got); and the portal counts "every other week" from Sunday
    while a calendar feed assumes Monday, so "Sunday and Wednesday, every fortnight" sent three of
    its six dates wrong to every subscriber. The feed now states the week start explicitly.
  - **One rule holds the two halves together, and it is checked where it is used.** A repeating
    series is published as a single pattern only while that one entry still describes the series
    truthfully. The calendar feed works that out for itself every time: it expands the stored pattern
    and compares it against the dates it has, their finishing times, and every detail the entry
    actually carries — the title, description, location, status, time zone and all-day flag. So
    attaching another event to the series, moving a date, deleting one, lengthening one or renaming
    one all make the feed go quietly back to listing every date on its own. Less tidy, always true.
    (A detail the calendar file does not carry at all, such as the hero image, can differ between
    dates without affecting this.)
  - **A third round of review was what forced that design**, and it is worth saying why. The first
    two rounds had the save handler removing the pattern whenever it knew the pattern had stopped
    being true. Round three showed that was unfixable from there: attaching a one-off event to a
    repeating series — two clicks on the ordinary event form, nowhere near the repeat code — left a
    **public event that appeared in nobody's subscribed calendar at all**, and moving a single date
    made the feed advertise a date that had never existed. No amount of care in the save handler
    covers every later edit. Asking the question at the one place the pattern is used does.
  - **And the check compares against the dates the reader is allowed to see**, not every date in the
    series. A series can hold an event a particular viewer may not see; comparing against all of
    them would have found the pattern "true" and published a count covering a date that viewer was
    never meant to know about.
  - **Five rounds of independent review in all. The fifth found no wrong behaviour** — only three
    claims in comments and notes that said more than the code did. One of those mattered: a comment
    gave the map position as an example of something "the calendar file does not render", so the
    coordinates were left out of the comparison and a pin moved on one date was published for every
    date. The file does render them, and they are compared now. Chasing the third claim also removed
    a weekly churn nobody had noticed: the published entry was identified by one occurrence and dated
    at another, so its identifier changed every time a date passed and a subscriber's calendar saw a
    delete-and-re-add each week. The entry is now the series' first occurrence throughout.
  - **A series that has already started is published as one entry too** (the owner's decision of
    29 October 2026). The download itself only carries events from today on, and the first version
    of the check compared against just those — so an ongoing weekly service could never match its
    own pattern and went out one date at a time, which is precisely the series somebody most wants
    as a single entry. The pattern is now read against the whole run and the entry begins where the
    series begins, so a subscriber sees the past dates as well. That is ordinary for a subscribed
    calendar. The two filters had to be told apart to do it: "from today on" decides what the
    download carries and must not stop a pattern being used, while "what this reader may see" must.
  - **The first round found seven real faults, all fixed here too**, and they are
    worth listing because every one was invisible to reading: a posted series number was read
    straight past the check that refuses another organisation's (so copies landed in it); a series
    number that did not exist gave an error page after the first event had already been saved; the
    feed published an endless series, and one of four hundred dates where five were allowed; a date
    pushed out of the hour that does not exist lost its length, and sometimes ended before it
    started; the message told people their series had been cut short when they had simply asked for
    that many dates — and **two checks had been pinning that wrong message**; the settings page
    credited the installation's limit to the organisation; and the stored pattern described dates
    that were never created.

- **Fixed — offboarding offered to erase somebody's details and erased nothing (#569, migration 226)**
  - **What was wrong.** When somebody left, the offboarding form offered three choices for their
    personal details: keep them, anonymise them, or delete them. The choice was written into the
    audit record and **nothing else happened at all.** No erasure, ever. The administrator was told
    the offboarding had succeeded, and the person's name, address and telephone number stayed
    exactly where they were. A note in the code explained that the erasure engine would arrive
    later; it had arrived long before, and is what the Erasure requests page has been using.
  - **What changed.** Choosing to erase now files a real erasure request, through the same audited
    route an administrator uses by hand, so there is one erasure path rather than two that would
    have to agree about every table for ever.
